190.question_text: A 20-year-old female with a history of penicillin allergy unknown to her treating doctor, was given a single injection of penicillin for the treatment of syphilis. Within minutes, she developed diffuse urticaria, tachycardia, and hypo-tension. This patient has experienced:
190.explanation:
• This patient displays the hallmarks of a classical anaphylactic reaction to penicillin.
  • Anergy is the impairment of effector immune responsiveness.
  • Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity is most often localized to tissues bearing epitopes to which the antibody binds.
  • Contact sensitivity results from the epicutaneous application of a reactive antigen/hapten; in the present question, the antigen (penicillin) was administered intramuscularly.

190.question_text: A 30-year-old male presents with headache, fatigue, light-headedness, dyspnea, and tachycardia. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased hemoglobin and a positive direct Coomb's test. The patient is presently on an antibiotic for symptoms of upper respiratory infection. These findings suggest which of the following?
190.option_a: Type I, mediated by IgG antibodies
190.option_b: Type II, mediated by IgG antibodies
190.option_c: Type III, mediated by IgG antibodies
190.option_d: Type III, mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies
190.explanation:
• Type II reactions involve antibodies directed against self-cells (erythrocytes) or membranes. Certain drugs react with erythrocytes to form neoantigens.
  • Type I responses are against foreign antigens (e.g., allergens), cause IgE responses, and do not invoke a Coomb's reaction.
  • Type III reactions involve soluble antigen-antibody complexes, and type IV reactions do not involve antibody.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

190.question_text: True regarding Histamine release from mast cell granules:

190.question_text:
Mr. X is a 68 year-old male who was admitted to the hospital from his long-term care facility after 1 week of dyspnea and cough. He was seen by a staff physician at the long-term care facility and was diagnosed with a COPD exacerbation. He routinely takes fluticasone/salmeterol, and has recently had a heavier reliance on his rescue albuterol inhaler. Review of systems reveals fever, chills, cough (sometimes productive) and dyspnea (worse than baseline).
His vitals are:
Temp 101.2° F
Heart Rate 89 bpm
Respiratory Rate 18 bpm
Blood Pressure 140/86
Oxygen Saturation
84% on room air,
98% on 4L nasal cannula
On culture examination following findings were seen on blood agar and chocolate agar. Identify the causative organism for the patient's symptoms.
190.option_d: The symptoms are due to COPD only
190.explanation:
The above clinical scenario indicates that the patient has pneumonia along with exacerbation of COPD.

S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of lobar (alveolar) pneumonia. Though it starts as a non-invasive illness due to contiguous spread from the nasopharynx, it soon becomes bacteremic and invasive. Patients present with productive purulent cough, fever and chest pain. Important signs are dullness on percussion due to consolidation and crackles on auscultation.

Colonies of pneumococcus:

Alpha-hemolytic draughtsman shaped colonies on blood agar.

Bleaching effect is seen on chocolate agar.

Treatment:

Penicillin G remains the drug of choice, with daily doses ranging from 50,000 U/kg for minor infections upto 300,000 U/kg for meningitis. Cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone can be given alternatively. Oral amoxicillin is recommended for children with acute otitis media.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 609

190.question_text: What constitutes the synergohymenotropic toxin in Staphylococcus aureus?
190.option_d: Gamma, alpha hemolysin and PV toxin
190.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Synergohymenotropic toxins: γ-hemolysin and PV toxin are called synergohymenotropic toxins. Because they are not active individually, but in combination, they are capable of producing hemolytic and leucocidal activity.
  • aureus produces four distinct hemolysins-α, β, γ and δ hemolysins. They are membrane damaging toxins, act on red blood cells (RBCs) leading to hemolysis. They exhibit various actions such as dermonecrotic, cytotoxic, neurotoxic and leukocidal activities.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Alpha hemolysin (Option B & D):
    • Alpha hemolysin is a pore-forming toxin but acts as a single component (monomer that oligomerizes into a heptamer) on the target membrane. It is not a bi-component synergohymenotropic toxin.
  • Leucocidin toxin (Option B & C):
    • The term "leucocidin" typically refers to PVL itself or similar toxins (like LukE/LukD). Grouping it generally with "PV toxin" (which is PVL) in Option C creates a redundant or chemically distinct category that does not fit the specific "synergohymenotropic" classification definition as a pair with Gamma hemolysin.

190.question_text: A 5-year healthy girl presented as shown in the picture. She also had reduced appetite, seemed irritable, and complained of having a sore throat. On examination, the outermost layer of the skin sloughed off (positive Nikolsky's sign). Signs of early bilateral conjunctivitis were also present. At this stage, she did not have a fever. The mother consulted the emergency department. Identify the organism and its respective toxin causing such a clinical picture in this patient.
190.explanation:
The clinical picture described in the patient, including the presence of a positive Nikolsky's sign, early bilateral conjunctivitis, reduced appetite, and sore throat, suggests a condition known as Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS), which is caused by S. Aureus producing Epidermolytic Toxin (Exfoliatin).

Correct Answer: C) S. Aureus: Epidermolytic toxin

  • Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is a serious skin condition typically caused by the exfoliatin (also called epidermolytic toxin) produced by Staphylococcus aureus.
  • The key clinical features of SSSS include skin sloughing (positive Nikolsky's sign), conjunctivitis, irritability, reduced appetite, and often a sore throat.
  • The causative toxin, exfoliatin, is an exotoxin produced by certain strains of S. aureus. This toxin targets desmoglein, a protein that helps bind skin cells together, leading to the separation of the epidermis from the dermis.
  • A) S. Aureus: Enterotoxin B is not the correct answer. Enterotoxin B is associated with food poisoning caused by Staphylococcus aureus but does not cause SSSS.
  • B) S. Epidermidis: Epidermolytic toxin is not the correct answer. Staphylococcus epidermidis is not a typical causative agent of SSSS.
  • D) S. Aureus: TSST (Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin) is not the correct answer. TSST is associated with toxic shock syndrome (TSS) and is not responsible for the clinical features described in this case.

In summary, the organism responsible for the clinical picture in this patient is Staphylococcus aureus producing Epidermolytic toxin, which leads to Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 512

190.question_text: Identify 'B' in the given figure and its correct example.
190.explanation:
Toxic Shock Syndrome toxin (TSST):

  • This toxin is responsible for toxic shock syndrome (TSS).
  • It has two subtypes-TSST-1 and TSST-2; both act as super-antigens.
  • TSST-1 is actually a staphylococcal enterotoxin. Enterotoxin F (formerly called pyrogenic exotoxin C) is the most common type of TSST-1; rarely enterotoxin-B or C may also be associated
  • Risk factors: Initially, toxic shock syndrome was reported from women using highly absorbent vaginal tampons during menstruation. Subsequently, TSS has been reported from both men and non-menstruating women as a complication of staphylococcal abscesses, osteomyelitis and post-surgical, traumatic or burn wound infections.
  • Pathogenesis: TSST-1 gets absorbed into circulation from the tampons; then being a superantigen it stimulates the T-cells non-specifically (by binding to Vβ region of T-cell receptor) causing excessive production of cytokines (cytokine storm), which leads to a potentially fatal multisystem disease.
  • Clinical features: Patients present with fever, hypotension, mucosal (conjunctival) hyperemia, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, myalgia, abdominal pain and erythematous rashes which desquamate later. Subsequently, there is rapid involvement of the other organs such as liver, kidneys, lungs, gastrointestinal tract (GIT) and/or central nervous system (CNS)
  • Case definition of TSS includes:
    • Clinical criteria: (i) fever, (ii) rash, (iii) desquamation, (iv) hypotension, (v) multiorgan (≥3) involvement plus.
    • Laboratory criteria: Negative blood culture for other pathogens and lack of evidence of other causes of infections.
  • Treatment:
    • As toxin causes capillary leak; aggressive parenteral fluid replacement and vasopressor to reverse hypotension should be initiated at the earliest.
    • Examine for and remove any colonized foreign body, e.g. vaginal tampon.
    • Clindamycin is the preferred drug for TSS (as it reduces the toxin synthesis). It is given along with anti -Staphylococcal penicillin (e.g. cloxacillin) for MSSA or vancomycin for MRSA.
    • For clindamycin resistant cases: Linezolid can be used for toxin suppression. In such cases, addition of vancomycin is not required.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 512

190.question_text: Beta lactam antibiotics resistance in staphylococcus is transferred by:
190.explanation:
β-lactamase or penicillinase enzymes cleave the β-lactam rings, and thereby organisms producing these enzymes develop resistance to β-lactam antibiotics. This resistance is plasmid coded, and can be transferred between S. aureus strains by transduction.





Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 517

190.question_text: All of the following are true for MRSA except:
190.option_a: Vancomycin is the drug of choice for MRSA
190.option_b: The resistance is because of the kagA gene
190.option_d: MRSA are detected by using a cefoxitin disk
190.explanation:
• Methicillin resistance in S. aureus is mediated by a chromosomally encoded gene called mecA gene, which alters penicillin-binding protein (PBP) present on S. aureus cell membrane to PBP2a.
  • MRSA are either community or hospital associated.

  • Antimicrobial susceptibility test using cefoxitin disk or oxacillin (MIC based method): These antibiotics are used as a surrogate marker for the identification of MRSA
  • PCR detecting mecA gene
  • Latex agglutination test detecting PBP2a.
  • Vancomycin is the drug of choice for MRSA.
  • Alternative drugs include-teicoplanin, linezolid, daptomycin, telavancin and quinupristin/dalfopristin.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 517

190.question_text: What is the typical incubation period for symptoms of botulism after exposure?
190.explanation:
• 18-36 hours: This is the typical incubation period for botulism symptoms, encompassing the time it takes for the toxin to disrupt neuromuscular transmission, leading to clinical manifestations such as muscle weakness and paralysis. Symptoms can vary based on the amount of toxin ingested and individual susceptibility.

Why Not Others:

  • 6-12 hours and 12-18 hours are both too early for the onset of significant symptoms; symptoms like blurred vision and weakness may begin after 18 hours but not earlier.
  • 36-48 hours is outside the typical range, as symptoms of botulism appear much earlier, typically requiring medical intervention sooner. 36-48 hours: Symptoms generally appear within the 18-36 hour window; waiting longer usually indicates a different condition, as botulism presents early signs in the specified timeframe.

Key Takeaway: Symptoms of botulism typically develop within 18-36 hours after exposure, making early recognition crucial for effective treatment.

Tags: good to know

Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-40 Food poisoning pp-397.

190.question_text: What is the most common source of food-borne botulism?
190.option_b: Homemade improperly canned or fermented foods
190.explanation:
• Homemade improperly canned or fermented foods: This is the most common source of food-borne botulism, as improper canning techniques can create anaerobic conditions that allow C. botulinum spores to germinate and produce toxin. Homemade foods often lack the same safety measures as commercial products, increasing risk.

Why Not Others:

  • Canned commercial foods: This option is less likely to cause botulism due to stringent safety regulations and controlled canning processes, which effectively prevent the growth of C. botulinum.
  • Fresh vegetables: While they can harbor C. botulinum spores, fresh vegetables are not typically associated with botulism outbreaks, as the spores need specific conditions to produce toxin.
  • Pasteurized dairy products: Pasteurization effectively eliminates C. botulinum spores, making these products safe from botulism risk when handled properly.

Key Takeaway: Homemade improperly canned or fermented foods are the primary source of food-borne botulism, emphasizing the importance of safe canning practices.

Tags: fmge 2021

Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-40 Food poisoning pp-397.

The patient is afebrile at the moment but complains of low grade fever at night. Upon urinalysis,pus cells were found but no bacterial agent was isolated. Imaging revealed a thimble bladder. Which specimen should be collected next for establishing a diagnosis?

  • It is seen when tubercular bacilli are disseminated hematogenously.

190.question_text:
A 22 year old presented with headache, low grade fever, night sweats, anorexia, irritability and a positive Brudzinski sign. A Lumbar puncture revealed the following findings in the CSF.

Imaging reveals basal exudation. Given the patient's clinical presentation, the physician orders an acid fast staining of the CSF as well as cell counts. If the normal counts in the CSF are as follows, which of the following observations is incorrect about the CSF Findings in this case?
NORMAL CSF
Appearance - clear
CSF Pressure- 50-150 mm of water
Total WBC- 0-5 per mm3
Predominant cells- Lymphocytes
Glucose - 40-70mg%
Total proteins- 15-45 %
190.explanation:
• The clinical vignette above Tubercular meningitis.
  • TBM results from the hematogenous spread of primary or post-primary pulmonary TB.
  • Typically, the disease evolves over 1-2 weeks or longer, which differentiates it from bacterial meningitis.
  • TBM often presents subtly as headache, slight mental changes, low-grade fever, malaise, night sweat, anorexia, and irritability. Subsequently, it may evolve acutely with severe headache, confusion, lethargy, altered sensorium, and neck rigidity - -Cranial nerves paresis (ocular nerves in particular) is a frequent finding.
  • Stroke may occur due to involvement of cerebral arteritis
  • Cobweb coagulum: When CSF is kept in a tube for 12 hours, a coagulum forms in the form of a cobweb due to higher fibrin content in the fluid .
  • Acid-fast staining of CSF: Direct smear of CSF sediment may reveal long slender beaded acid-fast bacilli.
  • Acid-fast staining of cobweb may give better yield asTB bacilli may be trapped in the cobweb.
  • However, fibrin strands in the cobweb may be mistaken as fungi.

Imaging studies (CT and MRI) may show hydrocephalus and abnormal enhancement of basal cisterns. In more than half of cases, evidence of old pulmonary lesions or a miliary pattern is found on chest X-ray

190.question_text: What is the primary purpose of using an autoclave in sterilization processes?
190.option_a: To use chemical agents to destroy microorganisms
190.option_b: To expose items to high-temperature steam under pressure
190.option_c: To use ultraviolet light for disinfection
190.option_d: To cool items rapidly to prevent microbial growth
190.explanation:
• Option A: Incorrect
    • Autoclaves utilize steam and pressure, not chemical agents, for sterilization.
  • Option B: Correct
    • Autoclaves expose items to high-temperature steam under pressure, effectively killing microorganisms.
  • Option C: Incorrect
    • Autoclaves do not use ultraviolet light; they rely on steam for sterilization.
  • Option D: Incorrect
    • Autoclaves use heat for sterilization, not cooling.

AUTOCLAVE:

Definition:

An autoclave is a device designed for sterilizing equipment and materials by exposing them to high-temperature steam under pressure. It's commonly used in medical, laboratory, and industrial settings to ensure items are free from microorganisms, including highly resistant bacterial spores.

Operation:

  • Temperature and Pressure:
    • Standard sterilization conditions are 121°C (250°F) and 15 psi (pounds per square inch) of pressure, maintained for 15 to 30 minutes depending on the items being sterilized.
  • Mechanism:
    • Steam is generated in the autoclave chamber and pressurized to reach the required temperature, penetrating items and killing microorganisms by denaturing their proteins.

Uses:

  • Medical Sterilization:
    • Sterilizing surgical instruments, glassware, and other medical tools.
  • Laboratory Sterilization:
    • Preparing culture media and sterilizing lab equipment.
  • Industrial Applications:
    • Sterilizing materials used in manufacturing processes.

Advantages:

  • Effective Sterilization:
    • Ensures thorough destruction of microorganisms, including resistant bacterial spores.
  • Reliability:
    • Provides consistent and repeatable results with proper operation and maintenance.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Autoclaves sterilize items by exposing them to high-temperature steam under pressure, effectively killing all microorganisms.

Tags: good to know | inicet 2020

Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). (2020). Sterilization and Disinfection. Retrieved from CDC - Sterilization and Disinfection

190.question_text: What is the standard temperature and pressure used in an autoclave for effective sterilization?
190.explanation:
• Option A: Correct
    • Effective sterilization in an autoclave typically occurs at 121°C and 15 psi pressure.
  • Option B: Incorrect

  • Option C: Incorrect

  • Option D: Incorrect
    • 130°C at 25 psi is also above the standard sterilization conditions.

AUTOCLAVE:

Definition:

An autoclave is a device used for sterilizing equipment and materials by exposing them to high-temperature steam under pressure. It is widely used in medical, laboratory, and industrial settings to ensure that items are free from microorganisms, including bacterial spores, which are highly resistant to heat.

Operation:

  • Temperature and Pressure:
    • The standard sterilization conditions are 121°C (250°F) and 15 psi (pounds per square inch) of pressure, maintained for 15 to 30 minutes, depending on the type and quantity of items being sterilized.
  • Mechanism:
    • Steam is generated inside the autoclave chamber and pressurized to reach the required temperature, penetrating items and killing microorganisms by denaturing their proteins.

Uses:

  • Medical Sterilization:
    • Sterilizing surgical instruments, glassware, and other medical tools.
  • Laboratory Sterilization:
    • Preparing culture media and sterilizing lab equipment.
  • Industrial Applications:
    • Sterilizing materials used in manufacturing processes.

Advantages:

  • Effective Sterilization:
    • Ensures thorough destruction of microorganisms, including resistant bacterial spores.
  • Reliability:
    • Provides consistent and repeatable results with proper operation and maintenance.

Key Points:

  • Autoclaving is a reliable and widely accepted method for achieving high levels of sterilization.
  • Proper training and maintenance are essential to ensure effective sterilization and safety.

KEY TAKE AWAY: The standard autoclave settings for effective sterilization are 121°C at 15 psi pressure.

190.question_text: In the life cycle of Cryptosporidium, what is the role of the oocyst when it is released into the environment?
190.option_a: It directly infects the host's liver
190.option_b: It undergoes asexual reproduction in the host's intestines
190.option_c: It undergoes sporulation and becomes infective
190.option_d: It transforms into a trophozoite in the environment
190.explanation:
• Cryptosporidium oocysts are shed into the environment via feces.
  • Upon release, they undergo sporulation to become infective.
  • Sporulated oocysts are resistant to harsh environmental conditions, surviving in water and soil for long periods.
  • After ingestion by a new host, they excyst in the small intestine, releasing sporozoites that invade intestinal epithelial cells.
  • These sporozoites initiate the asexual replication cycle within the host.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A) Infect the liver: Oocysts do not directly infect the liver; they release sporozoites that target intestinal cells.
  • B) Asexual reproduction in intestines: Asexual reproduction (schizogony) occurs inside the host, but the oocyst itself does not perform this function.
  • D) Transform into trophozoites: Trophozoites form inside the host after ingestion, not in the environment.

Key Takeaways:

  • Oocysts undergo sporulation in the environment to become infective.
  • Sporulated oocysts are resistant and play a key role in the transmission of Cryptosporidium via contaminated water or surfaces.

Tags: neet 2021

Reference: CDC life cycle description of Cryptosporidium.

190.question_text: Where do Cryptosporidium oocysts typically transform into trophozoites in the host?
190.explanation:
• Cryptosporidium oocysts are ingested through contaminated food or water.
  • Upon reaching the small intestine, the oocysts release sporozoites through a process called excystation.
  • These sporozoites invade the intestinal epithelial cells, where they develop into trophozoites.
  • Trophozoites then undergo asexual reproduction (schizogony), forming merozoites that further infect other cells.
  • The infection results in damage to the intestinal lining, leading to symptoms like watery diarrhea, cramping, and malabsorption.
  • Cryptosporidium is an intracellular parasite, but it remains extracytoplasmic, residing in a parasitophorous vacuole within the epithelial cells.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A) Liver cells: Incorrect. Cryptosporidium infects intestinal epithelial cells, not liver cells.
  • B) Muscle cells: Incorrect. The parasite does not invade or develop in muscle cells, but rather in intestinal cells.
  • D) Red blood cells: Incorrect. Cryptosporidium differs from malaria parasites like Plasmodium, which infect red blood cells.

Key Takeaways:

  • Cryptosporidium oocysts transform into trophozoites in the intestinal epithelial cells, where they initiate the infection by damaging the intestinal lining, leading to diarrhea.

Tags: fmge 2021

Reference: CDC information on Cryptosporidium life cycle.

190.question_text: In the life cycle of Cryptosporidium, which stage is responsible for causing infection in the host?
190.explanation:
Oocyst of cryptosporidium species

  • Oocysts are the infective stage of Cryptosporidium, typically found in contaminated water or food.
  • Once ingested, oocysts undergo excystation in the intestines, releasing sporozoites.
  • Sporozoites invade the intestinal epithelial cells, developing into trophozoites, which then replicate asexually.
  • The oocyst stage is highly resistant to environmental conditions and can survive for long periods in water or soil.
  • Oocysts can cause infection through fecal-oral transmission, commonly in contaminated environments like water sources.

Why Not Other Options:

  • B) Trophozoite: Incorrect. Trophozoites are formed after infection begins but are not the infective stage.
  • C) Sporozoite: Incorrect. Sporozoites are released from the oocyst to initiate infection, but the oocyst is the stage that causes infection.
  • D) Merozoite: Incorrect. Merozoites result from the asexual reproduction of trophozoites but are not involved in the initial infection.

Key Takeaway:

  • The oocyst is the infective stage in the Cryptosporidium life cycle, responsible for initiating infection in the host after ingestion.

Tags: fmge 2020

Reference: CDC details on Cryptosporidium infection stages.

190.question_text: In which of the following regions is Onchocerca volvulus, the causative agent of river blindness, primarily endemic?
190.option_b: Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent
190.explanation:
• Onchocerca volvulus, which causes river blindness (onchocerciasis), is primarily endemic in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A) Incorrect. Onchocerca volvulus is not primarily endemic to Central and South America; its prevalence is significantly higher in Africa.
  • B) Incorrect. Although Onchocerca volvulus is found in some parts of Southeast Asia, it is not predominant in that region compared to Sub-Saharan Africa The endemicity in Southeast Asia is less compared to Sub-Saharan Africa.
  • D) Incorrect. This filarial worm is not endemic to North America or Europe.

Key Takeaway: Onchocerciasis is endemic to much of Sub-Saharan Africa, with additional small foci in the Arabian Peninsula (Yemen) and parts of the Americas (Brazil and Venezuela). The disease is transmitted by infected blackflies (Simulium spp.) near rapidly flowing water, emphasizing the importance of vector control in reducing transmission.It causes River blindness

190.question_text: According to the WHO 'Five Moments for Hand Hygiene,' when should hand hygiene be performed?
190.explanation:
• After touching patient surroundings: Correct, as one of the WHO's 'Five Moments,' this helps prevent the transmission of pathogens from contaminated surfaces.

Why Not Others:

  • B. Only before patient contact: Covers only one moment, neglecting the rest.
  • C. Only after body fluid exposure: Addresses just one of five moments, ignoring comprehensive hygiene.
  • D. Only before clean/aseptic procedures: Misses other critical hand hygiene moments.

Key Takeaways: The WHO's Five Moments for Hand Hygiene cover a wide range of actions: before patient contact, before aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact, and after touching patient surroundings. These ensure optimal infection control.

Tags: fmge 2023

Reference: WHO 'My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene.'

190.question_text: What is one example of a situation where routine environmental microbiological sampling is indicated?

• Monthly water surveillance in hemodialysis units: Correct, routine monitoring is critical to ensure safe water quality for dialysis patients.

Why Not Others:

  • A. Outbreak investigation: Focuses on targeted sampling, not routine checks.
  • B. Equipment sterilization: Involves evaluative sampling after changes, not regular monitoring.
  • D. New hospital construction: Involves specific sampling rather than ongoing routine checks.

190.question_text: The following clinical finding is observed at rest. Which nerve is most likely involved?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

The ulnar nerve is responsible for the ulnar claw hand. The ulnar nerve innervates the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including the hypothenar muscles, and the medial two lumbricals.

Injury to the ulnar nerve, such as at the elbow or wrist, can result in ulnar claw hand, where there is hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and flexion of the interphalangeal joints (IP) of the 4th and 5th fingers. This happens because of the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors due to the loss of ulnar nerve function.

Explanation of other option:

Median (Option B): Median nerve involvement typically leads to "ape hand" deformity or "benediction" hand, not ulnar claw hand. The median nerve controls the flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Damage to the median nerve causes weakness and loss of opposition of the thumb, which is not seen in ulnar claw hand.

Musculocutaneous (Option C): The musculocutaneous nerve primarily innervates the muscles in the anterior compartment of the arm (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis). It does not contribute significantly to the intrinsic muscles of the hand and would not be involved in ulnar claw hand.

None (Option D): Since the ulnar nerve is responsible for the ulnar claw hand, the answer is not "None."

Key Takeaways:

The ulnar nerve is involved in ulnar claw hand, and this condition is typically seen in cases of ulnar nerve injury.

References: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulnar_claw

190.question_text: A newborn presents with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, and a scaphoid abdomen, with lung auscultation revealing bowel sounds in the chest. A posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has Bochdalek Hernia which is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). It occurs due to a defect in the posterolateral portion of the diaphragm, caused by a failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close during fetal development.

Explanation of Other Options:

Morgagni hernia (Option B)

Morgagni hernia is a retrosternal or parasternal type of diaphragmatic hernia, due to a defect in the anteromedial portion of the diaphragm, located near the sternum. It is less common than Bochdalek hernia.

Hiatal hernia (Option C)

Hiatal hernia involves the herniation of the stomach through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax and is usually an acquired condition seen in adults, not a congenital diaphragmatic defect.

Inguinal hernia (Option D)

Inguinal hernia occurs in the groin region due to weakness in the abdominal wall and is unrelated to the diaphragm.

Key takeaway:

Posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernias are typically Bochdalek hernias, the most common type causing respiratory distress in neonates, while Morgagni hernias are anterior and hiatal hernias involve the esophageal hiatus.

190.question_text: Which microorganism is most commonly associated with causing bilateral lung infiltrates in an HIV-positive patient?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

In HIV-positive patients, especially those with low CD4 counts, Pneumocystis jirovecii is a frequent cause of bilateral lung infiltrates, resulting in Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). This fungal infection commonly presents with symptoms such as shortness of breath, cough, and fever, and usually affects both lungs.

Explanation for other options:

Cryptococcus (Option A): This fungal infection often leads to meningitis or lung problems in immunocompromised patients, but it usually causes localized infections rather than bilateral lung infiltrates.

Histoplasmosis (Option B): Although common in HIV patients, this fungal infection generally results in granulomas or localized lung infiltrates, not typically bilateral infiltrates.

Aspergillus (Option D): This fungus can cause lung infections, but invasive aspergillosis usually presents with a single, localized lesion rather than widespread bilateral infiltrates.

190.question_text: The given slide is stained using Gomori methenamine silver and shows septate hyphae with acute angle branching. Which organism is most likely responsible?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of septate hyphae with acute angle branching on a Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stained slide is characteristic of Aspergillus species. Aspergillus is a genus of fungi commonly implicated in infections among immunocompromised patients, particularly causing pulmonary conditions like aspergillosis. Its hyphae are segmented (septate) and typically branch at acute angles, around 45 degrees.

Explanation for other options:

Blastomycosis (Option A): Caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis, this organism does not exhibit acute angle branching. Instead, it typically appears in tissue as large, broad-based budding yeast, not as septate hyphae.

190.question_text: A 25-year-old patient presents to the hospital with symptoms of hydrophobia, which is often associated with rabies infection. The clinician decides to perform further diagnostic tests on the patient's corneal scraping to confirm the diagnosis. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate and accurate for confirming the diagnosis in this patient?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is regarded as the most reliable and accurate diagnostic method for rabies, as it directly detects viral RNA. It provides both high sensitivity and specificity, making it superior to other diagnostic approaches. Samples such as corneal scrapings, saliva, or brain tissue can be tested.

Laboratory diagnosis of rabies may include:

  • Antigen detection: Direct immunofluorescence (DIF), usually performed on nape of neck skin biopsy (≥10 hair follicles). In later stages, corneal impression smears can also be used.
  • RNA detection: RT-PCR, which is considered the most sensitive and specific.
  • Viral isolation: Traditionally done by inoculating suckling mice brains, followed by identification of Negri bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusions).
  • Antibody detection: Serum antibodies appear late and are also present in vaccinated individuals. CSF antibodies are more diagnostic since they are not found in vaccinated persons.
  • Autopsy findings: Negri bodies in brain tissue (demonstrated with Seller’s stain or immunoperoxidase techniques).

Explanation of Other Options:

Viral culture (Option B):

  • Relies on animal inoculation (e.g., suckling mice brains).
  • Time-intensive, technically demanding, and not widely practiced.
  • Considerably less sensitive than modern molecular assays.

Antibody detection by ELISA (Option C):

  • Serum antibody detection is not reliable for acute diagnosis since antibodies appear only late in infection or after vaccination.
  • Antibodies in CSF are more specific but still inferior to RT-PCR in sensitivity.

Direct fluorescent antibody test (Option D):

  • Used to detect rabies antigen in skin biopsy or corneal impressions.
  • Provides rapid results but lacks the same sensitivity and specificity as RT-PCR.
  • More useful as a screening tool than as a confirmatory test.

190.question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis for a farmer who has a wart-like skin growth on his foot and histopathology of the growth is shown in the below image?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

The finding of sclerotic bodies (also called muriform bodies or copper pennies) on histopathology is diagnostic for chromoblastomycosis. This is a chronic fungal infection caused by dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi like Fonsecaea pedrosoi, often occurring in tropical regions and affecting individuals with outdoor exposure (e.g., farmers) via traumatic inoculation.

Microscopy: The lesions contain fungal structures that appear as round to irregular, dark brown, yeast-like forms. These structures are characterized by their septate appearance and are referred to as sclerotic bodies, also known as muriform bodies, copper pennies, or Medlar bodies.

Explanation of other options:

Sporotrichosis (Option A): Diagnosed by visualizing cigar-shaped yeast cells or asteroid bodies in tissue, not sclerotic bodies.

Mycetoma (Option B): Diagnosed by finding grains or granules in discharge, not sclerotic bodies in tissue.

Phaeohyphomycosis (Option D): Refers to a heterogeneous group of infections caused by dematiaceous fungi that appear in tissue as dark-walled, septate hyphae or yeast-like cells, not the characteristic spherical, thick-walled, septate sclerotic bodies of chromoblastomycosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous (wart-like) lesions.
  • Sclerotic bodies on histology are pathognomonic.

190.question_text: A chronic asthmatic patient who is on inhaled steroids presents with a history of burning sensation on eating hot or spicy food, and the following findings are seen. What is the most possible diagnosis?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

In the given clinical scenario, the chronic asthmatic patient using inhaled corticosteroids is suffering from oral candidiasis (thrush). The burning sensation with hot/spicy foods is characteristic of mucosal irritation from candidal overgrowth. Inhaled corticosteroids cause local immunosuppression in the oropharynx, disrupting normal flora and promoting Candida albicans proliferation.

Explanation of other options:

Burning mouth syndrome (Option B): Characterized by chronic oral burning without visible mucosal changes or identifiable causes, not associated with steroid use.

Geographical tongue (option C): Presents with migratory, map-like erythematous areas with white borders on the dorsum of tongue, typically asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic.
Oral lichen planus (Option D): An autoimmune condition presenting with white, lacy Wickham's striae or erosive lesions, not typically associated with steroid use and less likely to cause food-triggered burning.

Key Takeaways:

  • Inhaled corticosteroids are a major risk factor for oral candidiasis
  • Characteristic white plaques that scrape off leaving erythematous base
  • Burning sensation exacerbated by hot/spicy foods

190.question_text:
A 5 year old boy presents with sore throat for the last two days.
On examination he has a grayish white pseudomembrane around his tonsils (image shown). Diphtheria is suspected. What prophylactic step should be taken for the 3 years old younger sibling who has received immunization as per the immunization schedule?
190.option_b: Prophylaxis with erythromycin and diptheria antitoxin
190.option_d: Immunize with booster of diphtheria toxoid
190.explanation:
The case is of Diphtheria. Secondary prophylaxis of 3 year old sibling is required. He has receive immunization as per schedule. As per guidelines no any other thing is required.

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option A) Prophylaxis with oral erythromycin → Not required
    • Erythromycin prophylaxis is given to close contacts who are unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated.
    • Since the sibling is fully vaccinated, antibiotic prophylaxis is not needed.
  • (Option B) Prophylaxis with erythromycin and diphtheria antitoxin → Not required
    • Diphtheria antitoxin is used only in symptomatic cases.
    • Erythromycin is used for exposed individuals who are at risk (unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated).
    • The sibling is protected by vaccination, so neither erythromycin nor antitoxin is needed.
  • (OPtion D) Immunize with booster of diphtheria toxoid → Not required at this age
    • The routine immunization schedule includes DTaP (Diphtheria, Tetanus, and Pertussis) at 6, 10, and 14 weeks, with a booster at 18 months.
    • A booster is required at 5 years of age, but at 3 years, no additional dose is needed.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fully vaccinated children do not require prophylaxis if exposed to diphtheria.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis (erythromycin) is for unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated close contacts.
  • Diphtheria antitoxin is only used for symptomatic cases.
  • A booster of diphtheria toxoid is given at 5 years, not at 3 years.

190.question_text:
Disposable pipette tips are sterilized by which of the following methods?
i. Autoclave
ii. Hot air oven
iii. Microwave
iv. 70% ethanol
190.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Disposable pipette tips are typically sterilized using autoclaving.
  • The autoclave uses steam under pressure to kill microorganisms, ensuring that the pipette tips are completely sterilized.
  • Autoclaving is the most common and effective method for sterilizing laboratory tools and equipment that are heat-resistant.

Autoclave

  • An Autoclave is a sterilisation technique that uses moist heat at a temperature > 100°C.
  • The autoclave (steam steriliser) works on the principle of steam production under pressure.
  • When this steam meets a cooler surface, it condenses, transferring its heat to that surface. The process continues until the surface temperature matches that of the steam.
  • The resulting condensed water provides moist heat, effectively killing microbes on the materials by protein denaturation.
  • Its temperature settings are 121oC for 15 minutes at 15 psi pressure.
  • Materials that can be sterilised include linen, surgical instruments(non-sharps only), laboratory ware, pharmaceuticals, autoclavable plasticware, pipette tips, centrifuge tubes, suture material except catgut(cold sterilisation) and culture media except egg and serum containing media(inspissation).
  • Sterilisation control indicator - Geobacillus stearothermophilus

Types of Autoclaves in Healthcare:

  • Laboratory autoclaves
  • Hospital dressing sterilisers
  • Instrument sterilisers
  • Rapid cooling sterilisers

Disinfection and Sterilization by Risk Category (Spaulding Classification)

Explanation of other options:

Hot air oven (Statement ii): While a hot air oven can be used for sterilization, it is not typically used for disposable pipette tips, as they may not be able to withstand the prolonged heating without being deformed or degraded. Autoclaving is more commonly used for these items.

Microwave (Statement iii): A microwave is not an appropriate method for sterilizing pipette tips. It does not provide the consistent and controlled heat required for effective sterilization.

70% ethanol (Statement iv): Although 70% ethanol is commonly used as a disinfectant for surface cleaning, it does not sterilize by killing all microorganisms (including spores), making it unsuitable for sterilizing pipette tips.

190.question_text: An HIV-positive patient presents with watery diarrhoea. Stool examination shows oval-shaped oocysts measuring 20-30 μm (as seen in the provided image). Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

Intestinal Coccidian Parasites

  • Cryptosporidium species
    • C. parvum: Infects mammals
    • C. hominis: Primarily infects humans)
  • Cyclospora cayetanensis
  • Cystoisospora belli

Clinical Features:

  • In Immunocompetent Hosts
    • Causes mild, self-limiting illness with watery, non-bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, nausea, and fever.
  • In Immunocompromised Hosts
    • Leads to severe, persistent diarrhoea (up to 25 L/day)
    • Marked weight loss

  • Severity of disease increases with decreasing CD4+ T-cell counts.

Explanation of other options:

Microsporidia (Option D): These parasites can also cause diarrhoea in immunocompromised patients, but they appear as small spores under the microscope and are smaller in size compared to Cystoisospora belli oocysts.

190.question_text: Most common ocular manifestations in COVID -19
190.explanation:
COVID was respiratory disease. It was causing bilateral pneumonia. Patient were having difficulty in breathing. Spo2 was going down. Pt was experiencing shortness of breath, difficulty breathing. Fatigue. Loss of taste or smell. Muscle ache, chills, sore throat, chest pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.rash

Cytokine storm was occurring in patients.

Apart from lung other organs were involved are eyes. Pt were having red eye that is conjunctivitis. Most common ocular manifestation of COVID 19 was Follicular conjunctivitis.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

Choice A (Pseudomembrane conjunctivitis): Pseudomembrane conjunctivitis is a severe form of conjunctivitis where exudates form a pseudomembrane over the conjunctiva. While it has been reported in COVID-19, it is less common than follicular conjunctivitis.

Choice C (Retinal vein occlusion): Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) is associated with hypercoagulability and vascular damage seen in severe COVID-19 cases. However, it is a rare ocular complication rather than the most common manifestation.

Choice D (Keratoconjunctivitis): Keratoconjunctivitis, characterized by inflammation of both the cornea and conjunctiva, has been observed in some COVID-19 cases but is not as frequent as follicular conjunctivitis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Follicular conjunctivitis is the most common ocular manifestation of COVID-19, presenting with red eyes, tearing, and mild irritation.
  • COVID-19 can involve multiple organs, including the eyes, due to cytokine stormand direct viral entry via the ocular surface.
  • Other ocular complications (e.g., pseudomembrane conjunctivitis, RVO, and keratoconjunctivitis) have been reported but are less common.

190.question_text: The correct order of donning of a PPE kit is:

190.option_b: Gloves first → Face shield or goggles → Gown → Mask or respirator

190.explanation:
In order to minimize the risk of transmission of infection, donning (wearing) and doffing (removing) of PPE must be performed in a particular sequence.

  • Donning (wearing): Gown first → Mask or respirator → Goggles or face shield → Gloves.
  • Doffing (removing): Gloves first → Face shield or goggles → Gown → Mask or respirator.
  • Doffing is extremely important as even a minor breach in the doffing procedure would subject the HCW (health care worker) to a huge risk of acquiring the infection. This could be a potential reason why many HCWs got infected during COVID-19 pandemic. All PPE should be removed just before exiting the patient room except a respirator, which should be removed after leaving the patient room and closing the door.
  • Discard into appropriate BMW bins: Yellow bag: Gown/coverall, mask/respirator, shoe cover and cap Red bag: Plastic apron, goggles/face shield, gloves.

190.question_text: During manufacturing, the prefilled syringes are sterilized using:
190.explanation:
• Sterilization of prefilled syringes today is predominantly accomplished using steam, EO, or gamma radiation.
  • At present, steam sterilization is the primary method employed for sterilization of glass prefilled syringes containing heat-stable products, such as saline. However, because it involves both very high temperature, typically 121°C, and pressure, it is not well suited to sensitive biologics and drugs.
  • EO sterilization presents an alternative to steam sterilization for the external surfaces of prefilled syringes. However, EO also presents its own challenges. Although EO does not use the high temperatures of steam sterilization, it still requires temperatures in the range of 40°C to 60°C, and a relatively deep vacuum in order to achieve sterility. This can have an adverse effect on temperature-labile products, and the vacuum can cause unacceptable stopper movement due to pressure changes. Concerns over the carcinogenic nature of residuals from the EO sterilization process is also there.
  • Another sterilization option is gamma radiation. Gamma does not require long aeration times and has relatively good materials and drug compatibility if a minimal radiation dose can be employed. Additionally, gamma radiation is not ideal for aqueous drug products because it can produce toxic free radicals in the solution that can result in decreased drug activity. It can also break down preservatives used in many drug solutions that are essential to maintaining stability and shelf-life of the product. Gamma radiation has also been proven to interact with lubricants found in plastic syringes. Lastly, the facility cost and mitigating the risk of exposing the operators to radiation must also be considered.

190.question_text: Which of the following is INCORRECT about Spaulding classification?
190.option_a: Guidance about noncritical items is included in classification
190.option_b: Semi critical items are in contact with mucus membrane
190.option_c: Semi critical items need low-level disinfectant
190.option_d: Cardiac catheter is a critical item
190.explanation:
C) Semi critical items need low-level disinfectant is INCORRECT about the Spaulding classification.

The Spaulding classification system categorizes medical and dental devices into three groups based on their potential risk of transmitting infections:

A) Critical items: These items come into direct contact with sterile tissues or the bloodstream, and they must be sterilized to prevent infection transmission. Examples include surgical instruments.

B) Semi-critical items: These items come into contact with mucous membranes or non-intact skin. They do not need to be sterilized but require high-level disinfection to ensure that they are safe for use. Examples include endoscopes and dental instruments.

C) Non-critical items: These items come into contact with intact skin and do not require sterilization or high-level disinfection. Low-level disinfection is typically sufficient. Examples include stethoscopes and blood pressure cuffs.

So, the incorrect statement is that semi-critical items need a low-level disinfectant. They actually require high-level disinfection, not low-level disinfection.

190.question_text: All of the following are required in Polymerase Chain Reaction EXCEPT:
190.explanation:
• Requirement of Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR):
    • Taq polymerase: It is a thermostable DNA polymerase-I named after the thermophilic eubacterial microorganism Thermus aquaticus
    • Primers: They are short oligonucleotides complementary to a small sequence of the target DNA
    • Deoxynucleotide: Deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) are the nucleoside triphosphates containing deoxyribose. They are the building blocks of DNA, and they lose two of the phosphate groups when incorporated into DNA during replication.
    • Mg++ ion
    • Target DNA present in the sample
  • dNTPs vs ddNTPs:
    • The Deoxyribonucleotide/deoxynucleotide (dNTPs) structurally have one hydroxyl group at the 3 position of the sugar of nucleotide.
    • Contrary, the Dideoxyribonucleotides/ Dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) don't have OH or hydroxyl groups on the 3 end. The dNTPs have a hydrogen group at the second position of the sugar while the ddNTPs have a hydrogen group at 3 and 2 position of the sugar.
    • The 3 OH end of the deoxynucleotides facilitate DNA synthesis by Taq DNA polymerase while due to the lack of the 3 end, the Taq DNA polymerase can’t elongate the DNA chain when it encounters the ddNTPs.
    • The dNTPs are used in DNA sequencing and Polymerase chain reaction whilst the ddNTPs are only used in the Sanger sequencing technique to sequence DNA.
    • The dideoxynucleotides or the ddNTPs are the artificially synthesized special type of nucleotides used in the Sanger sequencing technique.
    • The ddNTPs are different from the normal dNTPs as they don’t have the hydroxyl group at the 3 position of the nucleotide.
    • The dideoxynucleotides are known as the chain terminator nucleotides that abort the nucleotide chain due to lack of 3 OH group.
    • During the synthesis of DNA, the Taq DNA polymerase incorporates nucleotides to the growing DNA strand. First, it recognizes the 3 end of the primer and then starts the synthesis reaction. The reason is that it can’t get the free 3 end to elongate the chain, the ddNTPs have two hydrogen groups but not hydroxyl! Hence the polynucleotide chain progression stops.
    • The end of the ddNTP-dideoxynucleotides are labeled with the color dye, the color signal is recorded by the computer.
    • The entire technique of sanger sequencing relies on the use of ddNTPs. ddATP, ddGTP, ddCTP and ddGTP when incorporated into the amplification reaction, the chain got terminated.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 7, Pg 66-69

190.question_text: Which technique is used in molecular biology research to study gene expression by detection of RNA in a sample?
190.explanation:
• The northern blot, or RNA blot,is a technique used in molecular biology research to study gene expression by detection of RNA (or isolated mRNA) in a sample.
  • A Southern blot is a method used in molecular biology for detection of a specific DNA sequence in DNA samples. Southern blotting combines transfer of electrophoresis-separated DNA fragments to a filter membrane and subsequent fragment detection by probe hybridization
  • The far-western blot, or far-western blotting, is a molecular biological method based on the technique of western blot to detect protein-protein interaction in vitro. Whereas western blot uses an antibody probe to detect a protein of interest, far-western blot uses a non-antibody probe which can bind the protein of interest. Thus, whereas western blotting is used for the detection of certain proteins, far-western blotting is employed to detect protein/protein interactions.
  • The northwestern blot, also known as the northwestern assay, is a hybrid analytical technique of the western blot and the northern blot, and is used in molecular biology to detect interactions between RNA and proteins.
  • The eastern blot, or eastern blotting, is a biochemical technique used to analyze protein post-translational modifications including the addition of lipids, phosphates, and glycoconjugates. It is most often used to detect carbohydrate epitopes. Thus, eastern blot can be considered an extension of the biochemical technique of western blot.
  • The far-eastern blot, or far-eastern blotting, is a technique for the analysis of lipids separated by high-performance thin layer chromatography (HPTLC).

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 7, Pg 66-69

190.question_text: Chromosomal mutation can be identified by all of the following techniques EXCEPT:
190.explanation:
• Single-strand conformation polymorphism (SSCP), or single-strand chain polymorphism, is defined as a conformational difference of single-stranded nucleotide sequences of identical length as induced by differences in the sequences under certain experimental conditions. This property allows sequences to be distinguished by means of gel electrophoresis, which separates fragments according to their different conformations. SSCP used to be a way to discover new DNA polymorphisms (variations/mutations) but is now being supplanted by sequencing techniques on account of efficiency and accuracy.
  • Denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) is a method by which fragments of partial 16S rDNA-amplified fragments of identical length but different sequence can be resolved electrophoretically because of their different melting behaviour in a gel system containing a gradient of denaturants. It can detect mutations.
  • Dideoxynucleotide trail DNA (Sanger) sequencing/ Chain-termination DNA sequencing, also called the dideoxynucleotide procedure, is based on the principle that during DNA synthesis, addition of a nucleotide triphosphate requires a free hydroxyl group on the 3′ carbon of the sugar of the last nucleotide of the growing DNA strand. IT can detect mutations.
  • Agarose Gel electrophoresis is used to separate the DNA by charge or by size.
    • It is usually performed to visualize the amplified DNA after PCR, but may be used as a preparative technique prior to use of other methods such as mass spectrometry, RFLP, PCR, cloning, DNA sequencing, or Southern blotting for further characterization.
    • It is only a method of visualizing the DNA after separating it by size. So, it is always used as a part of any molecular method to visualize the DNA. But alone it cannot be used to detect any mutations.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 7, Pg 66-69

190.question_text: Culture media are mostly sterilized by:

  • Inspissation (Fractional sterilization):
    • It is a process of heating an article on 3 successive days at 80–85ºC for 30 min.
    • Used for sterilization of egg based (LJ and Dorset’s egg medium) and serum based media (Loeffler’s serum slope).
  • Tyndallization or intermittent sterilization:
    • It involves steaming at 100°C for 20 min for 3 consecutive days.
    • It is used for sterilization of gelatin and egg, serum or sugar containing media.
    • It kills most of the vegetative forms including spores
  • Water bath: Used for disinfection of serum, body fluids, and vaccines (60°C for one hour)
  • Filtration can remove the microbial population in solutions of heat-labile materials like vaccine, antibiotics, toxin, serum and sugar solution as well as for purification of air in laminar air flow systems.

190.question_text: Antibiotic sensitivity testing is usually done on:
190.explanation:
• Mueller-Hinton agar was co-developed by a microbiologist John Howard Mueller and a veterinary scientist Jane Hinton at Harvard university as a culture for gonococcus and meningococcus.
  • Mueller-Hinton agar is a microbiological growth medium that is commonly used for antibiotic susceptibility testing, specifically disk diffusion tests.
  • It has a few properties that make it excellent for antibiotic use.
    • It is a non-selective, non-differential medium. This means that almost all organisms plated on it will grow.
    • It contains starch. Starch is known to absorb toxins released from bacteria, so that they cannot interfere with the antibiotics.
    • It is a loose agar. This allows for better diffusion of the antibiotics than most other plates. A better diffusion leads to a truer zone of inhibition.

It supports the growth of both spore-forming and non-spore-forming obligate anaerobes and also differentiates between putrefactive and saccharolytic species.

190.question_text: Iso-antigens are:
190.option_a: Found in all individuals of all species
190.option_b: Found in some but not all members of species
190.option_c: Found in different biological species, class and kingdoms
190.option_d: Found in all individuals in a particular species
190.explanation:
• Human antibodies are Y-shaped, tetrapeptide glycoproteins made by two heavy chains and two light chains that are bound together by disulfide bonds.
  • Like any other proteins, antibodies can act as an antigen, if injected into different species or hosts. For example, if antibodies from humans are injected into mice, mice will recognize these antibodies are foreign proteins (antigens) and will form antibodies against human antibodies (i.e. anti-human antibodies).
  • It is observed that the entire immunoglobulin is not immunogenic but it contains antigenic determinants at specific sites.
  • Based on the location of those antigenic determinants, immunoglobulins are divided into, isotypes, allotypes, and idiotypes.
  • Isotype
    • Different among species but same in all members of one species
    • Variations in the constant region of the heavy chain of immunoglobulin
  • Allotype
    • Found in some members of a species
    • Multiple alleles for genes leading to subtle amino acid differences à variations in the constant region of the heavy chain of immunoglobulin
  • Idiotype
    • Different in every individual member of a species
    • Same in genetically identical twins
    • Determinants that arise from heavy and light chain variable region
  • Antigenic determinants on Ig
    • Isotypes : interspecies
    • Allotypes : intraspecies
    • Idiotypes : genetically identical individuals

Reference: Kuby Immunology, 12ed.

190.question_text: What are the possible ABO blood types of children of father  with blood type AB and a mother with blood type O?

  • In this example, children will inherit either the A or B allele from the father and the O allele from their mother and will have either blood type A or blood type B.

190.question_text: DiGeorge syndrome is characterized by all EXCEPT:
190.option_b: Abnormal developmental of third and fourth pouches
190.explanation:
DiGeorge syndrome (Thymic hypoplasia)

  • It results from a congenital defect in thymic development leading to defect in T-cell maturation.
  • Infants are extremely vulnerable to viral, fungal, intracellular bacterial and protozoan infections.
  • Pathogenesis: In 90% of cases, there occurs a deletion affecting chromosome 22q11 → leads to malformation of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches in embryonic life
  • As a result, all the structures that develop from third and fourth pharyngeal pouches such as thymus, parathyroid glands, and portions of the face and aortic arch become defective.
  • Thus, in addition to the thymic defects, there may be associated:
    • Parathyroid gland hypoplasia resulting in neonatal tetany and hypocalcemia
    • Anomalies of the heart and the great vessels (Fallot’sTetralogy).
    • Characteristic facial appearance
  • B-cells and serum immunoglobulin levels are generally unaffected.
  • Treatment: Thymus transplantation

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19 , Pg 187-190
