190.question_text: While reading a case report of infections caused by Burkholderia mallei you come across terms like GLANDER'S DISEASE  and FARCY caused by it in horses. These terms refer to which of the following, respectively?
190.option_a: Glanders - nasal discharge and ulcers in the nasal septum; farcy - skin lesions and lymph node involvement
190.option_b: Glanders - skin lesions and lymph node involvement; Farcy - nasal discharge and ulcers in the nasal septum
190.option_c: Glanders - skin lesions only; Farcy - ulceration in nasal septum
190.option_d: Both Glanders and Farcy are synonymous
190.explanation:
1. Mallei is a pathogen of horses; where it causes glanders (nasal discharge and ulcers in the nasal septum) and farcy (skin lesions and lymph node involvement).

Human infection is characterized by:

  • Local skin nodules and lymphadenitis (if transmitted by inoculation).
  • Pneumonia, ulceration of the trachea and sepsis (if transmitted by inhalation).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 645

190.question_text: Organism most likely responsible for ventilation associated pneumonia is:
190.explanation:
Baumannii causes widespread hospital infections such as:

  • Ventilator associated pneumonia
  • Central line associated bloodstream infection
  • Post-neurosurgical meningitis
  • Catheter- associated UTI
  • Wound and soft tissue infections
  • Infections in burn patients
  • Acinetobacter can be grouped into several genomospecies. A. baumannii is the most pathogenic species. Most other species such as A.calcoaceticus and A. lwoffii are rarely pathogenic to man.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 646

190.question_text: Which of the following are not antipseudomonal cephalosporins?
190.explanation: Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 644

190.question_text: Which of the following amino acids is required for isolation of F.tularensis?
190.explanation:
Isolation of F.tularensis is very difficult as it is highly fastidious.

It needs Special media, such as:

BCG agar (blood cysteine blood agar)

CHAB agar (cysteine heart agar supplemented with 9% heated sheep blood).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 808

190.question_text: Drug of choice for rabbit fever is:
190.explanation:
Tularemia, also known as “rabbit fever,” is a disease caused by the bacterium Francisella tularensis. Tularemia is typically found in animals, especially rodents, rabbits, and hares.

Gentamicin is considered as the drug of choice,given 5mg/kg for 7-10 days.

Doxycycline or ciprofloxacin can be given as alternatives.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 810

190.question_text: Which of the following subspecies of Francisella tularensis is most virulent for humans?
190.explanation:
1. Tularensis has four subspecies: tularensis, holarctica, novicida, and mediasiatica.
  • The first three subspecies are found in North America, whereas subspecies mediasiatica is found in central Asia.
  • Subspecies tularensis is the most common and the most virulent among all.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 808

190.question_text: A 29-year-old truck driver, Paramjit, presented to Dermatology OPD with an itch rash growing on his torso, which is shown in photo below. On examination, his temperature was 100.4°F and BP was 120/80 along with generalized lymphadenopathy. On rapid test, it was suggestive for HIV positive. What is the causative organism for this?
190.explanation:
• Above image is highly suggestive for Kaposi Sarcoma, caused by HHV8.
  • Kaposi Sarcoma is an AIDS-defining illness, in which a tumor grows in skin, lymph nodes, internal organs or mucous membranes as red/purple/brown patches.
  • HHV8 belongs to subfamily of Herpesvirus and infects B-cells.
  • It commonly infects immunocompromised individuals, causing
  1. Kaposi Sarcoma
  2. Primary Effusion Lymphoma
  3. Castleman Disease

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 54-year-old male, Rajendra, presents with a rash on his torso. He was taking immunosuppressants for managing his kidney transplant. What is the most common cause of death in patients associated with this organism?
190.explanation:
• The unilateral, segmental and dermatomal spread of vesicles in this patient is due to Shingle/Zoster, due to reactivation of VZV from neurons following development of immunocompromised state.
  • Most common nerve involved is Ophthalmic branch of Trigeminal Nerve.
  • Most common complication is Post-Herpetic Neuralgia (pain at the site of rash, lasting for months).
  • Most common cause of death is Pneumonia in Shingle patients.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 2-year-old girl, Aarti, presented with diarrhea, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and weakness. She suffered from chickenpox before 1 week, for which her mother gave her a tablet of Aspirin for fever. What is the girl suffering from?
190.explanation:
• Reye’s syndrome commonly occurs in children undergoing recovery phase of viral infections especially Chickenpox and Influenza, and are taking Aspirin.
  • Symptoms in Reye’s syndrome occurs typically due to fatty degeneration of liver.
  • There is no specific treatment, only supportive management is indicated.
  • Hence, Aspirin is avoided as much as possible in infants and children.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 36-year-old male, Rahul, presented with severe fever, impaired awareness, headache and seizures. Neck rigidity was not seen. CSF PCR was conducted which was positive for HSV1. Which lobe is commonly affected in this condition?
190.explanation:
• Fever, impaired awareness, headache and seizures without nuchal rigidity and PCR positive for HSV is suggestive of Herpes Encephalitis.
  • Herpes is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis, and it commonly affects Temporal lobe in adults.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a growth on his penis that has been gradually increasing in size over the past year. He was diagnosed with HIV 10 years ago. He has been divorced for 25 years and has had 'at least 30 sexual partners' since. Physical examination shows a nontender 2.5-cm ulcerated lesion with an erythematous base on the dorsum of the glans. There is firm left inguinal lymphadenopathy. A biopsy of the lesion shows atypical squamous cells with varying degrees of mitotic activity. This patient's condition is most likely associated with which of the following pathogens?
190.explanation:
• This man might be suffering from Carcinoma of penis, after an HPV infection.
  • Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly with types 16 and 18, is a known risk factor for carcinoma of the penis.
  • Other risk factors for carcinoma of the penis include phimosis and HIV infection.
  • Although HIV may directly contribute to carcinogenesis, this association may also be due to the frequent HPV co-infection in this patient group.
  • Apart from the immunosuppression enabling the persistence of HPV infection, HIV also seems to directly promote HPV-associated carcinogenesis.
  • High-risk types of HPV (i.e., 16, 18, 31, 33) are also associated with cervical cancer (almost all cases), as well as anal, oral, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 15-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of the sudden appearance of a rash on her trunk that started 6 hours ago and subsequently spread to her extremities. Four days ago, she was taken to the emergency department because of a high fever and vomiting. She was treated with acetaminophen and discharged the next day. The fever persisted for several days and abated just prior to appearance of the rash. Physical examination shows a rose-colored, blanching, maculopapular rash, and postauricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
• Roseola infantum is a self-limited viral exanthem (usually due to HHV-6 and less commonly, HHV-7) that primarily affects infants and young children and is characterized by a high fever for 3–5 days that is immediately followed by a blanching, maculopapular, non-pruritic rash.
  • The rash initially appears on the trunk but may spread to the face and extremities.
  • It is commonly associated with cervical, postauricular, and/or occipital lymphadenopathy and may also cause febrile seizures.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 36-year-old woman comes for annual pelvic examination and Pap smear. A photomicrograph of cervical cells from the Pap smear specimen is shown. Cells similar to the one indicated by the arrow are most likely to be seen in which of the following conditions?
190.explanation:
• The cell indicated by the arrow is a dysplastic squamous epithelial cell with an enlarged, irregular nucleus and hyperchromasia.

These are features of koilocytes.

  • Koilocytes are pathognomonic of an infection with HPV.
  • Condylomata acuminata, like cervical dysplasia, are caused by an infection with HPV and can therefore present with koilocytes on histopathology.
  • Condylomata acuminata are typically associated with HPV strains 6 and 11.
  • Other manifestations of HPV infection include vulvar and vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia, as well as skin warts (verruca vulgaris) and plantar warts.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain with defecation, anal itching, and blood in the stool. Over the past month, she has also had a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. She has a history of irritable bowel syndrome, HIV infection, and human papillomavirus infection. Digital rectal examination shows a tender mass and bright red blood in the anal canal. Anoscopy shows an exophytic, ulcerated, 2.5-cm mass that is located just above the anocutaneous line and below the dentate line. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
• A history of hematochezia, anal pruritus, painful defecation, and weight loss in a patient with an exophytic, friable, ulcerated mass above the anal verge is suggestive of anal canal cancer.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histological type of anal canal cancer and typically arises below the dentate line.
  • Patients must undergo a biopsy of the tumor to confirm the diagnosis.
  • Women diagnosed with anal canal squamous cell carcinoma should also undergo a gynecological examination for cervical cancer screening.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of diarrhea and wasting. He reports occasional bright red blood in his stools for the past 3 weeks. He admits to using IV drugs for the past 5 years. His ophthalmic exam is notable for the findings as shown in image. Rectal exam is significant for bloody stool in the rectal vault. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
• This patient with a history of IV drug use is presenting with chronic bloody diarrhea, low grade fever, weight loss, and retinitis.
  • These findings are most consistent with cytomegalovirus infection in an immunocompromised state (most likely HIV given IV drug use, lack of healthcare, and temporal wasting).
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis most often presents in immunocompromised patients with a CD4+ count < 50 cells/mL.
  • Additional severe manifestations of CMV infection in immunocompromised patients include CMV pneumonia, CMV esophagitis (linear ulcers), CMV encephalitis (impaired cognitive function and neurological deficits), and CMV retinitis (floaters, photopsia and visual field defects).
  • Treatment for severe CMV colitis and retinitis includes ganciclovir or foscarnet.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with ear pain. The patient states that this morning he had trouble moving one side of his face. Physical exam is notable for right-sided paralysis of the upper and lower portion of the patient's face. Following finding is noted in patient's ear canal. Identify this syndrome.
190.explanation:
Ramsay Hunt syndrome is caused by a Herpes Zoster infection which can affect CN VII (causing facial paralysis) and CN VIII (causing hearing changes).

Other symptoms include ear pain, a vesicular rash that extends into the ear canal, and altered face sensation.

Patients with classic symptoms and no other neurological sequelae can be treated with acyclovir.

The diagnosis can be further confirmed with a Tzanck prep and a viral culture which should not delay treatment.

Other Options:

  1. Moebius syndrome shows palsy of 6th and 7th cranial nerve
  2. Frey syndrome has gustatory sweating and flushing, following head and neck surgery
  3. Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome shows facial palsy + fissured tongue + cheilitis + facial edema

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 40-year-old man comes clinic complaining of anal lesions that have been present for a few months. He says that they occasionally itch but are otherwise asymptomatic. Identify the HPV strain responsible for this condition.
190.explanation:
• HPV has selective tropism for epithelium of skin & mucous membrane. Different strains produce different features:
    • Plantar warts: Type 1
    • Common skin warts: Type 2, 4, 27, 57
    • Verruca: Type 5, 8, 9, 12, 17
    • Anogenital warts, Laryngeal papilloma, IEN: Type 6, 11 Carcinoma
    • cervix/larynx/esophagus/vulva: Type 16, 18, 31, 33, 45

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: Which mode of transmission of HIV has the maximum risk of transmission?
190.explanation:
• Blood transfusion is the least common mode of transmission but it has the maximum risk.
  • On the other hand, heterosexual intercourse is the most common mode of transmission but it has a minimal risk of transmission.
  • Saliva contains inhibitory substances that prevent transmission of HIV.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 326

190.question_text: HIV enters human cells by binding to CD4 receptors. It also requires a second co-receptor. Maraviroc is an anti-HIV drug that binds to one such co-receptor, CCR5. On which of the following cells is this receptor present?
190.explanation:
• CCR5 receptor is present on macrophages and its lineage of cells.
  • It acts as a second co receptor for fusion of HIV to gain entry into the host cells.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 327

190.question_text: To which genus does HIV-2 belong?
190.explanation:
• Retroviridae family consists of 2 genera, Lentivirus and Delta retrovirus.
  • Lentivirus contains HIV 1 and 2, while Delta retrovirus contains HTLV-1

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 325

190.question_text: Which is the main receptor for HIV to bind to CD4+ cells?
190.explanation:
• Gp120 is the main receptor for HIV to bind to CD4+ cells.
  • Gp41 is the fusion protein
  • P24 is a core antigen
  • P18 is a matrix antigen

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 326

190.question_text: HIV is classified into serotypes based on which protein?
190.explanation:
• Based on sequence differences in env gene, HIV comprises of two serotypes HIV-1 and 2. HIV-1 is divided into three distinct groups (M, N, and O).
  • 'M' is the dominant group worldwide.
  • It comprises of eleven subtypes or "clades" (A-K).
  • Subtype C is the most common and B is transmitted via blood and homosexual contact.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 326

190.question_text: Rita, a 26-year-old presents with a weight loss of 20kgs from her initial weight of 65kgs within 3 months. She also has had intractable diarrhea within this period. She tests positive for HIV infection. Lately, she has been having visual symptoms. Upon fundoscopy, the following appearance is seen. At what CD cell count does this illness manifest?
190.explanation:
• The above fundoscopy image reveals typical pizza pie appearance, seen in CMV retinitis.
  • It shows perivascular hemorrhage with fluffy white exudates.
  • Treatment is IV Ganciclovir and oral therapy till CD count rises to 150cells/uL.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 328

190.question_text: Sheela is an HIV positive primipara. She is worried that her baby will acquire the infection during delivery. You console her that her newborn will be tested for the infection at 6 weeks. Which of the following tests will you perform first?
190.explanation:
• The routine screening methods (ELISA or rapid/simple tests) detect IgG antibodies.
  • They cannot differentiate between baby's IgG or maternally transferred IgG, hence cannot be used for the diagnosis of pediatric HIV.
  • As all maternal antibodies would disappear by 18 months;
  • Therefore, IgG assays can be performed after 18 months of birth. Various methods used for diagnosis of pediatric HIV include:
  1. HIV DNA PCR: This is the most recommended method for diagnosis of pediatric HIV. Baby is tested for HIV DNA PCR at 6 weeks by DBS (Dry Blood Spot) collection. If found positive, then is reconfirmed by a repeat HIV DNA PCR. Then it is reported as positive and the baby is then initiated on lifelong ART
  2. HIV RNA detection
  3. p24 antigen detection
  4. IgG ELISA only after 18 months of age.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 333

190.question_text: What is the best investigation for HIV detection during the window period?
190.explanation:
• Detection of viral RNA is the "gold standard" method for confirmation of HIV diagnosis.
  • It is the most sensitive and specific method, detects even few copies of viral RNA and is the best method for confirmation of HIV.
  • It is the best tool for diagnosis of HIV during window period, detects HIV earlier than all available methods (10-14 days postexposure)

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 333

190.question_text: Given below is the replication cycle of HIV. At which point of replication does the antiviral Dolutegravir act?
190.option_a: Inhibits RNA dependent DNA polymerase activity of reverse transcriptase
190.explanation:
• Dolutegravir is a viral integrase inhibitor and thus prevents viral replication by preventing its genome to be integrated into the host genome.
  • Its congeners are Raltegravir and Elvitegravir.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 334

190.question_text: What is the first line regimen proposed by NACO for the treatment of HIV-2 infection?
190.explanation:
• NACO recommends a combination of 2NRTI+protease inhibitor for treatment of HIV-2 infection.
  • Currently, the first line regimen consists of Tenofovir +Lamivudine +lopinavir -ritonavir

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 335

190.question_text:
A 25-year-old presents to the OBGY labor room at term. She has not had any previous antenatal checkup nor does she have any documented evidence for the same. She claims that her medical history is insignificant and she does not have any reports to support her claim. Her obstetric score is G1P1A0L0. She has a normal vaginal delivery. However, during postnatal routine checkup, she tests reactive for HIV. She is immediately started on HAART. What steps will you take to manage her newborn?
1.HIV DNA PCR of dried blood spot at 6 weeks
2.Nevirapine prophylaxis for 6 weeks
3.Nevirapine prophylaxis for 12 weeks
190.explanation:
• Since the mother is HAART naive, the neonate is given HIV prophylaxis in form of nevirapine syrup for 12 weeks.
  • If the mother has taken HAART for 24weeks or more, the prophylaxis is given for 6 weeks.
  • HIV DNA PCR is the most recommended method for diagnosis of pediatric HIV.
  • Baby is tested for HIV DNA PCR at 6 weeks by DBS (Dry Blood Spot) collection.
  • If found positive, then is reconfirmed by a repeat HIV DNA PCR.
  • Then it is reported as positive and the baby is then initiated on lifelong ART

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 335

190.question_text: Which of the following regimens of HAART is preferred in Children?
190.explanation:
In HIV-1 patients with renal failure or children with body weight <30kg, a regimen of Abacavir-Lamivudine-Efavirenz is given

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 335

190.question_text: A sex worker presents with generalized lymphadenopathy, weight loss of more than 10% in 6 months and fatigue. She also gives history of sharing needles for drug abuse. Which of the following tests will you use as a screening tool in her?
190.explanation:
• Screening for HIV infection is done by antibody detection using 3rd/4th generation ELISA or Rapid test.
  • It gives result within 2-3 hours and has a high sensitivity and specificity. Antigens used are p24, gp120, gp41 and gp160.
  • HIV RT-PCR is the gold standard for confirmation of HIV DNA PCR is used for diagnosis of pediatric HIV

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 330

190.question_text: An intern while drawing blood samples during emergency duty mistakenly injures himself. The patient is later found to be HIV positive. Till what maximum period should he be started on PEP?
190.explanation:
• The first dose of PEP for HIV should be taken as early as possible.
  • Effect is maximum if taken <2 hours and effect is nil if taken after 72 hours of exposure.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 269

190.question_text: What is the duration of PEP for HIV?
190.explanation:
• NACO recommends PEP to be started within 2 hours, maximum upto 72 hours.
  • It should be continued upto 28 days

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 270

190.question_text: Which of the following does not constitute stage 2 of the WHO staging for HIV?
190.explanation: Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 329

190.question_text: Which strain is used for making vaccines against Mumps?
190.explanation:
Mumps belong to the Paromyxoviridae family. It causes parotitis and epididymoorchitis. Period of communicability is 1 week before and after the onset of symptoms. The Jerryl Lynn strain is used for making vaccines against Mumps.

Other Options;

  1. Oka strain: Varicella Zoster vaccine
  2. 17D strain: Yellow Fever vaccine
  3. Edmonston Zagreb strain: Measles vaccine

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: An infant was vaccinated with Measles vaccine at 7th month of age, due to close contact during a Measles outbreak. When should the next doses be administered to this infant?
190.option_b: Only one dose at 9th month of age
190.option_c: Only one dose at 16th month of age
190.explanation:
The Edmonston Zagreb strain is used to prepare vaccines against Measles.

In the National Immunisation Schedule, vaccine for Measles is given at 9th month, followed by one more dose between 16-24th month.

In case of an outbreak of Measles, vaccine can be given anytime after the 6th month. However, the normal vaccination schedule should be followed duly.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: Which of the following strategy is used for Measles immunisation?
190.option_b: Catch up- Keep up- Follow up
190.explanation:
Measles can be eliminated with an efficient immunisation strategy. Hence, WHO came up with a new campaign ?Catch up- Keep up- Follow up.?

  1. Catch up- immunise all children between the ages of 9 months to 10 years irrespective of their previous immunisation status
  2. Keep up- continue the ongoing national immunisation program
  3. Follow up- done every 2-4 years to vaccinate all >9 months of age, who have been born after the last Catch up campaign

Other Options:

a. 90-90-90- For AIDS: 90% of HIV-infected individuals to be diagnosed by 2020, 90% of whom will be on anti-retroviral therapy (ART) and 90% of whom will achieve sustained virologic suppression.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: Majnu, a 24-year old vet clinic worker, comes to the Emergency Department, with a bite mark on his left foot. He complains of being bitten by a rabbit. He has not taken any prophylactic vaccines. How will you manage the patient?
190.option_c: Don't give ARV/Immunoglobulins, manage wound locally
190.explanation:
Anti-Rabies vaccine(ARV) is given for bites from dog, cat, monkey, sheep, goat, buffalo, or any other carnivorous animal.

ARV is not given for bites by squirrel, rabbit or rat.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: Sachin visited the Emergency Department after he had received a Category 3 wound by a cat at his Veterinary centre. He had received pre-exposure prophylaxis. What should be the next line of management?
190.explanation:
In case a person has received Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis, HRIg is not needed to be given. Hence, in this case, Wound management + ARV is only given.

Post-Exposure prophylaxis in a person who has already received Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis:

Cat 1: Wound Management

Cat 2: Wound Management

Cat 3: Wound Management + ARV (only 2 doses are administered on Day 0&3) Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis: 3 doses on Day 0, 7 & 21/28

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: Which of the following rabies vaccine is not commercially available?
190.explanation:
Rabies vaccine can be categorised into 2:

  1. Neural
    1. Semple vaccine
    2. Beta propiolactone vaccine
    3. Infant mouse brain vaccine
  2. Non-neural
    1. Egg-derived
      1. Purified duck embryo vaccine
      2. Live attenuated chick embryo vaccine
    2. Recombinant viral vaccine (in experimental stages)
    3. Cell culture derived vaccine
      1. Purified chick cell embryo vaccine
      2. Purified vero cell vaccine
      3. Human diploid cell vaccine

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: Which of the following is true for IPV (Salk)?
190.option_c: Can be given in immunocompromised patient
190.explanation:
Salk (Injectable Polio Vaccine) is prepared by Formalin killed strain.

  1. No local & herd immunity
  2. Zero chance of VAPP & VDPV
  3. Can be given to immunocompromised patient, pregnant and old aged patients
  4. Short duration of protection
  5. Relatively safer than OPV

Sabin (Oral Polio Vaccine) is prepared from live attenuated strain.

  1. Provides both local & herd immunity
  2. More chances of VAPP & VDPV
  3. Cannot be given to immunocompromised patient, pregnant and old aged patients
  4. Longer duration of protection

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 711

190.question_text: Hospital associated infection can be defined as all of the following except:
190.option_a: The infection should be incubating at the time of admission
190.option_b: The symptoms should appear at least after 48 hours or after admission
190.option_c: The patient should be admitted for a reason other than the infection in context
190.option_d: Infections acquired in hospital, but symptoms present after discharge
190.explanation:
Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) can be defined as- 

  1. The infections acquired in the hospital by a patient admitted for a reason other than the infection in context,
  2. The infection should not be present or incubating at the time of admission, and
  3. The symptoms should appear at least after 48 hours of admission.

This also include:

  • Infections that are acquired in the hospital but symptoms appear after discharge.
  • Occupational infections among staff of the healthcare facility (e.g. needle stick injury transmitted infections).
  • Infection in a neonate that results while passage through the birth canal (in contrast to congenital infections due to transplacental transmission, which are not HAIs).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 229

190.question_text:
The WHO has published standard guidelines describing the situations or opportunities when hand hygiene is indicated in healthcare sectors -known as 'My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene'; which includes:
1) Before you examine a patient for hernia
2) Before you insert a catheter in a patient
3) You accidentally touched patient's bedsheet
4) After aspirating fluid in ascites patient
5) After checking patient's pulse
6) Before inserting an IV line in patient
190.explanation:
The WHO has published standard guidelines describing the situations or opportunities when hand hygiene is indicated in healthcare sectors -known as 'My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene'; which include:

  1. Before touching a patient
  2. Before clean/aseptic procedures
  3. After body fluid exposure/risk
  4. After touching a patient
  5. After touching patient’s surroundings.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 231

190.question_text: Patients with similar infections requiring contact precautions can be placed together if single isolation rooms aren't available. This is called Cohorting. What is the minimum distance for a spatial separation of two patients in a room?
190.explanation:
For infection control: 

Single isolation room with a bathroom facility is preferred. If not available, then cohorting is recommended. Cohorting may be carried out in various ways

  • Patients with similar infections requiring contact precautions can be placed together either in the same isolation room, or in the same cubicle or corner of a ward or
  • Spatial separation of minimum of 3 feet distance between the beds with privacy curtains.

Other measures for infection control are:

  • Hand Hygiene should be maintained.
  • Health care workers should wear PPE.
  • Single-use patient-dedicated equipment.
  • Patient movement should be limited only to medically-necessary purposes.
  • Disinfection of rooms should be carried out frequently and adequately.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 236

190.question_text: Why is an indwelling catheter a risk for UTI?
190.option_c: Increased lateral urethral pressure leading to impaired mucosal blood flow and mucin secretion
190.explanation:
Indwelling urinary catheterization is a risk for UTI because:

  • The presence of a urinary catheter is the single most important risk factor. The risk of developing CAUTI is directly proportional to the duration of catheterization.
  • Urethral pressure: an indwelling catheter exerts lateral urethral pressure causing decreased mucosal blood flow, urothelial mucosal disruption and impaired mucin secretion; All these factors together predispose to infection
  • Incomplete emptying: In catheterized patients, bladder is often incompletely emptied because of pressure differentials created by patient movement or catheter manipulation. A small amount of urine always pools around the balloon which serves as a nidus for infection.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 242

190.question_text: Treatment of catheter associated asymptomatic bacteriuria is recommended in all the following cases except:
190.option_a: In a patient who was operated for cholecystectomy 4 days before due to persistent bacteriuria 24 hours after removal of catheter.
190.option_b: In a primigravida patient who came for an emergency labour  at 38 weeks with asymptomatic bacteriuria.
190.option_c: A patient having bacteriuria planned for transurethral resection of prostate.
190.option_d: In a patient with persistent bacteriuria 4 days after catheter removal.
190.explanation:
Management of CAUTI includes removal of catheter and institution of appropriate antimicrobial therapy based on the susceptibility pattern of the organism isolated.

Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (Ca-aSB) is not recommended except when:

  • Bacteriuria persists for >48 hours after removal of the catheter.
  • In pregnancy, as there is 20–30 fold increased risk of developing pyelonephritis and risk of premature delivery with low birth weight.
  • Prior to traumatic urological procedures such as transurethral resection of prostate where mucosal bleeding is anticipated which may cause bacteremia.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 242

190.question_text: Match the following:
190.explanation:
Depending up on the degree of microbial contamination, wounds are classified as clean, clean contaminated, contaminated, or dirty/infected. The contaminated and dirty wound classes have a higher risk of developing SSI.

  • Class I, Clean Wound: It is an uninfected operative wound in which no inflammation is encountered and the hollow viscus such as respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tract is not entered. SSI rate is usually less than 2% in clean operated wounds.
  • Class II, Clean-contaminated Wound: It is an operative wound in which the hollow viscus such as respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tracts are entered under controlled conditions and without unusual contamination. Surgeries included in this category involve the biliary tract, appendix, vagina, and oropharynx; provided that no evidence of infection or major breach in the technique is encountered SSI rate is about 3% to 11% in clean-contaminated wounds.
  • Class III, Contaminated Wound: Contaminated wound includes the following: Open, fresh, accidental wounds Operations with major breaks in the sterile technique (e.g. open cardiac massage) or Operations with gross spillage from the gastrointestinal tract (colonic surgeries). Entry into biliary or genitourinary tract in the presence of infected bile or urine Incisions in which acute, Non-purulent inflammation is encountered including necrotic tissue without evidence of purulent drainage (for example, dry gangrene). SSI rate is >10% in contaminated wounds even with administration of surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis.
  • Class IV, Dirty/Infected Wound: Surgical procedures performed when active infection is already present are considered dirty wounds. Examples include: Abdominal exploration for acute bacterial peritonitis or perforated viscera Intra-abdominal abscess Old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue. In a dirty wound, the SSI rate can exceed 20-40%.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 246

190.question_text: For prevention of surgical wound infection following should be avoided:
190.option_a: Preoperative bathing using an  antimicrobial soap
190.option_b: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis 60-120 mins before the surgery
190.explanation:
Prevention of surgical site infections (SSIs):

  • Preoperative measures:
    1. Preoperative bathing: It should be performed using a plain soap or an antimicrobial soap to reduce the bacterial load, especially at the site of incision.
    2. For MRSA carriers: Decolonization with mupirocin ointment must be done for patients undergoing surgery who are nasal carriers of MRSA.
    3. Hair removal: For patients undergoing any surgical procedure, hair removal should not be done or, , if it is absolutely necessary, it should be removed only with a clipper. Shaving is strongly discouraged at all times.
  • Intraoperative measures:
  1. SAP: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis (SAP) must be provided for all except for clean surgeries. Timing—SAP must be administered within 60–120 minutes before incision, which usually coincides with the induction of anesthesia. Choice—It depends upon local antibiotic policy. Cefazolin or cefuroxime are usually preferred. Frequency— SAP is usually given as a single dose. Repeat dose may be required only for: Duration of surgery exceeds 4 hours, Cardiac surgeries, Drugs with lower half-lives (redosing required if duration of surgery exceeds 2 half-lives), Extensive blood loss during surgery. For ESBL prevalent area—SAP should not be modified. ESBL screening for patients is not routinely recommended.
  2. surgical hand disinfection- Scrubbing with either antimicrobial soap (chlorhexidine) or with alcohol-based hand rub must be performed before donning sterile gloves, before surgery and in between surgeries.
  3. surgical site preparation should be performed with alcohol-based chlorhexidine antiseptic solution before the commencement of surgery.
  4. Perioperative maintenance of oxygenation (target FiO2 80%), temperature (normothermia), blood glucose level (target level of <200 mg/dL), adequate circulating volume (normovolemia) and nutritional support are necessary during the surgery and immediate 4–6 hours postoperative period.
  • Postoperative measures:
  1. wound dressing—Daily dressing of surgical site and removal of any discharge present at the site must be performed. Perform hand hygiene and use gloves before dressing.
  2. OT disinfection—Thorough postoperative disinfection of the operation theatre must be performed with a high-level disinfectant in between cases and after the last case (terminal disinfection).
  3. Periodic monitoring of the air quality of the operation theatre for various parameters must be performed such as no. of air exchanges, temperature, humidity, pressure and microbial contamination.
  4. SAP prolongation is not recommended in any situations (e.g. presence of a wound drain) for the purpose of preventing SSI as it promotes development of antimicrobial resistance.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 247

190.question_text: An occupational exposure is defined as all of the following except:
190.option_b: Contact with mouth by splash of infected fluid
190.option_c: Contact with skin afflicted with dermatitis by splash of fluid
190.option_d: Contact with the intact skin when the duration is for few seconds
190.explanation:
An occupational exposure is defined as:

  • Percutaneous injury,. needle stick injury (NSI) or other sharp injury.
  • Splash injury:
    • Contact with the mucous membrane (e.g. eye or mouth).
    • Contact with non-intact skin (abraded skin or afflicted with dermatitis).
    • Contact with the intact skin when the duration is prolonged (e.g. several minutes or more).

An occupational injury is often loosely termed as needle stick injury though it includes injury through needle or other sharps and splashes.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 267

190.question_text:
CDC recommends targeted air surveillance, which should be carried out for which of the following indications:
1) Investigation of an outbreak
2) For research purposes
3) Before fogging
4) After reconstruction or newly constructed buildings
5) After fogging
6) For short-term evaluation of a change in infection control practice
7) Routinely at regular intervals
190.explanation:
Routine air sampling (i.e. random or periodic sampling) is not recommended because

  1. HAI rates are not related with levels of general microbial contamination of air or environmental surfaces,
  2. There is no standard guidelines mentioning permissible levels of microbial contamination of environmental surfaces or air.

CDC recommends targeted air surveillance, which should be carried out for the following indications:

  1. Investigation of an outbreak
  2. For research purpose
  3. After reconstruction or newly constructed buildings
  4. After fogging (to monitor the quality)
  5. For short-term evaluation of a change in infection control practice.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 281

190.question_text: Which is the correct method of framing antimicrobial policy by the Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) team?
190.option_a: AMS team discuss with each other and frame the policy based on the standard guidelines
190.option_b: AMS team discuss with each other and frame the policy based on the standard guideline as well as local AMR pattern
190.option_c: AMS team discuss with each other and frame the policy based on the standard guidelines  as well as local AMR pattern, then discuss with each clinicians for their suggestions
190.option_d: AMS team just copy the guidelines  from any other renowned institute of India
190.explanation:
Framing Antimicrobial Policy:

  • Every hospital should frame their own hospital antimicrobial policy which is usually a pocket handbook, consisting of system/syndrome wise indications for antimicrobial choice and their dosage.
  • It should be prepared by the AMS team after discussing with all the clinicians, microbiologists and administrators.
  • The policy must be compliant to the standard national and international antimicrobial guidelines and local antibiogram pattern.
  • Common consensus between all clinicians must be arrived at, before framing the policy; which facilitates better adherence to policy.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 273

190.question_text: Antibiotic stewardship involves all of the following except
190.option_d: Treatment not to be based on culture reports
190.explanation:
A) Prescribing antibiotics only when needed:

  • Justification: Prescribing antibiotics only when needed is a central principle of antibiotic stewardship. Overuse or unnecessary use of antibiotics can lead to antibiotic resistance, making it crucial to prescribe antibiotics judiciously and only when they are warranted.

B) Control of infection:

  • Justification: While controlling infection is a vital aspect of overall patient care, it's not specific to antibiotic stewardship. Antibiotic stewardship primarily focuses on optimizing antibiotic use to combat antibiotic resistance. In contrast, the control of infection is a broader concept that encompasses various infection control measures beyond antibiotic use.

C) Prescribing antibiotics with adequate dosage:

  • Justification: Prescribing antibiotics with the correct dosage is an essential component of antibiotic stewardship. Using an adequate dosage ensures that the antibiotics are effective in treating the infection while reducing the risk of antibiotic resistance due to under-dosing.

D) Treatment not to be based on culture reports:

  • Justification: This practice goes against the principles of antibiotic stewardship. One of the key aspects of antibiotic stewardship is to use culture reports to guide treatment. Culture reports help identify the specific pathogen causing the infection and its susceptibility to antibiotics. Tailoring antibiotic therapy based on culture reports is essential for responsible antibiotic use and reducing the risk of resistance.

In summary, options A, C, and D align with antibiotic stewardship principles, while option B, "Control of infection," is essential for overall patient care but is not specific to antibiotic stewardship.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition,

190.question_text: Which swab material is recommended for collecting specimens to avoid inhibition of bacterial growth, especially for anaerobic cultures?
190.explanation:
Swab Selection for Anaerobic Cultures

  • Calcium Alginate Swab (Option C): Recommended for anaerobic cultures; chemically inert and does not inhibit bacterial growth, preserving specimen integrity during transport.

Other Options:

  • Cotton Swab (Option A): Not recommended due to potential inhibition from fatty acids and other substances that can compromise anaerobic bacterial growth.
  • Wooden Stick Swab (Option B): Unsuitable because wood can introduce inhibitors and contamination, and may absorb moisture, affecting the specimen.
  • Dacron Swab (Option D): Acceptable for many bacterial cultures but not as specifically recommended for anaerobes compared to calcium alginate swabs; suitable where cotton or wooden swab concerns are less significant.

KEY TAKE AWAY:

Calcium alginate swabs are preferred for collecting specimens intended for anaerobic cultures because they do not inhibit bacterial growth, ensuring accurate and reliable culture results. This makes them a better choice compared to cotton or wooden stick swabs, which can introduce substances that might interfere with anaerobic bacterial growth.

Tags: may know

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.)chept -1.3 page no. 36.

190.question_text: Which of the following statements accurately describes transient flora?
190.option_a: Transient flora are microorganisms that permanently reside in a specific body site and are not easily removed
190.option_b: Transient flora are microorganisms that temporarily inhabit a body site and can be easily removed by routine handwashing
190.option_c: Transient flora are microorganisms that cause chronic infections and persist indefinitely in the host
190.option_d: Transient flora are microorganisms that are always present in high numbers in the body and are resistant to antimicrobial treatments
190.explanation:
• A) Transient flora are microorganisms that permanently reside in a specific body site and are not easily removed.
    • Incorrect: This describes resident flora, not transient flora. Resident flora are permanent inhabitants of a body site.
  • B) Transient flora are microorganisms that temporarily inhabit a body site and can be easily removed by routine handwashing.
    • Correct: Transient flora are temporary microorganisms that come and go, often picked up from the environment. They can be removed through routine hygiene practices like handwashing.
  • C) Transient flora are microorganisms that cause chronic infections and persist indefinitely in the host.
    • Incorrect: This describes persistent or pathogenic organisms rather than transient flora.
  • D) Transient flora are microorganisms that are always present in high numbers in the body and are resistant to antimicrobial treatments.
    • Incorrect: Transient flora do not typically persist in high numbers and are not inherently resistant to treatments.

Key Takeaway: Transient flora are temporary microorganisms that are not part of the permanent microbial population of a body site and can be effectively removed by standard hygiene practices.

Tags: may know

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Microbial Flora and Infection Control.

190.question_text: Which of the following statements correctly describes plasmids and their role in bacterial genetics?
190.option_a: Plasmids are linear DNA molecules that integrate into the bacterial chromosome, and they do not replicate independently
190.option_b: Plasmids are circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that replicate independently and can carry genes for antibiotic resistance, toxin production, and cell surface structures
190.option_c: Plasmids are large, single-stranded RNA molecules that are integrated into the bacterial chromosome and are essential for bacterial viability
190.option_d: Plasmids are extra-chromosomal DNA substances that only encode traits essential for bacterial survival and are unable to replicate independently
190.explanation:
Plasmids are circular, double-stranded, extra-chromosomal DNA.

They replicate independently of bacterial chromosomal DNA.

Plasmids carry genes for advantages like:

  • Antibiotic resistance
  • Toxin production
  • Synthesis of cell surface structures (for adherence/colonization)

When plasmids integrate into the bacterial chromosome, they are called episomes.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Plasmids are circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that replicate independently and can carry genes that confer new traits such as antibiotic resistance and toxin production.

Tags: Clinical Question, Moderate

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.). Jaypee Brothers Medical Publishers. Chapter 1.4 : (Plasmids), Page no.40.

190.question_text: Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium, is used to prepare which of the following for PCR?
190.explanation:
1. Option A: Correct
    • Thermus aquaticus provides Taq DNA polymerase, which is crucial for PCR due to its heat resistance during the amplification process.
  2. Option B: Incorrect
    • RNA polymerase is used for transcription and is not derived from Thermus aquaticus, nor is it involved in PCR.
  3. Option C: Incorrect
    • Primers are short DNA sequences used in PCR but are not sourced from Thermus aquaticus.
  4. Option D: Incorrect
    • Restriction endonucleases cut DNA, but they are not related to Thermus aquaticus and aren't used in the PCR process.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Thermus aquaticus is known for providing the heat-stable enzyme Taq DNA polymerase, which is essential for performing PCR.

Tags: must know | fmge 2021

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.). Jaypee Brothers Medical Publishers. Chapter: (PCR Techniques and Applications), Page no. 110-115.

190.question_text: In bacterial conjugation, which of the following accurately describes the role of the HFR (High Frequency Recombination) state in gene transfer?
190.option_a: HFR state involves the integration of the F factor into the bacterial chromosome, leading to high-frequency transfer of chromosomal genes along with the F factor to the recipient cell
190.option_b: HFR state allows the transfer of plasmids with antibiotic resistance genes but does not integrate the F factor into the bacterial chromosome
190.option_c: In the HFR state, only the F factor is transferred to the recipient cell, without any accompanying chromosomal genes
190.option_d: HFR state is characterized by the transfer of F' factors, which carry a full set of chromosomal genes along with the F factor to the recipient
190.explanation:
• Importance of HFR:
    • HFR strains are valuable in genetic studies as they can effectively map bacterial genes based on the frequency of their transfer to recipient cells.
    • Understanding HFR mechanisms aids in researching horizontal gene transfer, an essential process in bacterial evolution and adaptation.

Option A: Correct

  • The HFR (High Frequency Recombination) state occurs when the F factor integrates into the bacterial chromosome. This allows for the transfer of both the F factor and adjacent chromosomal genes to the recipient cell, facilitating high-frequency gene recombination.

Option B: Incorrect

  • In the HFR state, the F factor is integrated into the chromosome, enabling the transfer of chromosomal genes. This state is primarily characterized by the transfer of chromosomal genes, not just plasmids.

Option C: Incorrect

  • The HFR state involves the transfer of chromosomal genes along with the F factor, not just the F factor itself.

Option D: Incorrect

  • The transfer of F' factors is a distinct process where the F' factor carries some chromosomal genes along with the F factor. This scenario is not representative of the HFR state.

KEY TAKE AWAY: The HFR state involves the integration of the F factor into the bacterial chromosome, enabling the transfer of chromosomal genes along with the F factor to the recipient cell, thus facilitating high-frequency gene transfer.

Tags: may know | inicet

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.). Jaypee Brothers Medical Publishers. Chapter: (Bacterial Genetics and Gene Transfer), Page no.45

190.question_text: What is the primary purpose of using biological indicators in sterilization processes?
190.option_a: To measure the temperature of the sterilizer
190.option_b: To check the chemical concentration in the sterilizer
190.option_c: To verify the effectiveness of the sterilization process
190.option_d: To ensure proper packaging of sterile items
190.explanation:
Biological Indicators

Definition:

Biological indicators are essential tools in sterilization monitoring, used to verify the effectiveness of sterilization processes by containing highly resistant bacterial spores.

Purpose and Mechanism:

  1. Verification of Sterilization:
    • Primary Role: To confirm that the sterilization process has effectively eliminated microorganisms.
    • Example: In steam autoclaving, indicators often contain spores of Bacillus stearothermophilus, known for their high-temperature resistance.
    • Post-Cycle Incubation: After sterilization, the indicator is incubated; any growth indicates insufficient sterilization, prompting necessary adjustments.
  2. Process Control:
    • Direct Measurement: Provides a definitive assessment of sterilization effectiveness, as opposed to indirect indicators like temperature or chemical concentration. This ensures that even if parameters are correctly set, the process effectively kills microorganisms.
  3. Quality Assurance:
    • Routine Use: Incorporating biological indicators into a quality assurance program helps identify deviations in the sterilization process, ensuring the sterility of the items being processed.

Key Takeaway:

Biological indicators are essential for confirming that the sterilization process has effectively killed microorganisms. They help ensure that the equipment and procedures used in sterilization are working correctly, thereby safeguarding the sterility of medical and laboratory supplies.

Tags: may know

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection.

190.question_text: Which level of microbial control is usually effective against most fungi, including their spores?
190.explanation:
Intermediate-Level Disinfection and Fungi

  • Effectiveness: Intermediate-level disinfection is generally effective against most fungi, including their spores.
  • Clinical Consideration: In clinical settings where fungi are particularly resistant, sterilization may be preferred for complete assurance.

Key Takeaway: Intermediate-level disinfection is often sufficient for fungi, but sterilization may be necessary for complete elimination in high-risk environments.

Tags: inicet | good to know

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection.

190.question_text: Which of the following is typically used as an intermediate-level disinfectant in healthcare settings?
190.explanation:
Alcohol as an Intermediate-Level Disinfectant

  • Type: Isopropyl alcohol is a widely used intermediate-level disinfectant.
  • Effectiveness: It is effective against a variety of pathogens, including bacteria and viruses.
  • Limitations: It may not effectively kill bacterial spores, which require higher-level disinfection.

Key Takeaway: Isopropyl alcohol is an intermediate-level disinfectant suitable for general disinfection needs but not for sterilization.

Tags: inicet | good to know

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection

190.question_text: Which type of filter is commonly used for the sterilization of heat-sensitive liquids and gases?
190.explanation:
Membrane Filters for Sterilization

Membrane filters, with pore sizes of 0.22 micrometers or smaller, are essential for the sterilization of heat-sensitive liquids and gases, effectively removing microorganisms without the use of heat.

  • A) Sand Filter:
    Incorrect. Used for water purification, sand filters remove larger particles but are ineffective against microorganisms.
  • B) Membrane Filter:
    Correct. Specifically designed to filter out microorganisms, making them ideal for sterilizing heat-sensitive solutions.
  • C) Air Filter:
    Incorrect. Air filters, such as HEPA filters, clean air but are not suitable for liquids.
  • D) Activated Carbon Filter:
    Incorrect. Used for removing organic compounds, activated carbon filters do not sterilize liquids or gases.

Key Takeaway: Membrane filters are crucial for sterilizing heat-sensitive liquids and gases by physically removing microorganisms through fine pores.

Tags: may know | neet

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection.

190.question_text: In the context of CSSD operations, which of the following statements accurately reflects the considerations for choosing an appropriate sterilization method for heat-sensitive instruments?
190.option_a: Ethylene oxide (ETO) sterilization is preferred over steam autoclaving for heat-sensitive instruments due to its ability to penetrate complex devices and its effectiveness at lower temperatures
190.option_b: Hydrogen peroxide plasma is less effective than ETO for sterilizing heat-sensitive instruments because it operates at higher temperatures and has limited penetration
190.option_c: Dry heat sterilization is recommended for heat-sensitive instruments due to its lower temperature requirements and faster cycle times
190.option_d: Boiling water is a suitable method for sterilizing heat-sensitive instruments due to its cost-effectiveness and ease of use
190.explanation:
Analysis of Sterilization Methods for Heat-Sensitive Instruments

  1. A) Ethylene oxide (ETO) sterilization:
    ETO is preferred for heat-sensitive instruments due to its lower operational temperatures (30-60°C) and excellent penetration capabilities, making it suitable for complex devices.
  2. B) Hydrogen peroxide plasma:
    Hydrogen peroxide plasma sterilization is effective for heat-sensitive instruments, operates at low temperatures (50-60°C), and provides good penetration. It is not less effective than ETO; the choice depends on specific needs.
  3. C) Dry heat sterilization:
    Dry heat sterilization requires higher temperatures (160-180°C) and longer exposure times, making it unsuitable for heat-sensitive instruments.
  4. D) Boiling water:
    Boiling water is not a reliable sterilization method as it fails to achieve temperatures necessary to kill all microbial spores, making it inadequate for heat-sensitive instruments..

Key Takeaway: Ethylene oxide (ETO) is the preferred sterilization method for heat-sensitive instruments due to its effective sterilization at lower temperatures and its ability to penetrate complex devices. Understanding the properties and limitations of various sterilization methods is crucial in CSSD operations to ensure appropriate and effective sterilization practices.

Tags: good to know

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection.

190.question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness and a positive anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody test. Which autoimmune disease is most likely in this patient?
190.explanation:
• Myasthenia gravis: Characterized by the presence of anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, leading to muscle weakness due to impaired neuromuscular transmission.
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Involves autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase and does not typically present with anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies.
  • Grave's disease: Involves autoantibodies against the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor, not acetylcholine receptors.
  • Addison's disease: Involves adrenal cortex autoantibodies, not anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

Key Takeaway: Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are indicative of myasthenia gravis.

190.question_text:
An 18-year-old girl presents with a 3-day history of fever, pruritic rash, and bilateral ankle pain and swelling associated with difficulty walking. On arrival, she had a fever of 101.4°F. A rash is present on her lower legs, feet, and her fingers. Her left ankle has diffuse swelling, warmth, redness, tenderness, and a limited range of motion.

After detailed workup, the patient was found to have disseminated gonococcal infection. What is the drug of choice for the same?
190.explanation:
Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI): It occurs rarely following gonococcal bacteremia. DGI is characterized by polyarthritis and rarely dermatitis and endocarditis. It is most commonly associated with PorB.1A serotypes which are also characterized as AHU autotypes.

The drug of choice for DGI is: Ceftriaxone 1g IV every 24 hours + Doxycycline 100mg BID for 7 days and Azithromycin orally 1g in a single dose.

190.question_text: The patient gives a history of low grade fever, skin rash and increased WBC counts. What will you do next?
190.explanation:
For Meningococcal infection:

Asymptomatic colonization is the most common presentation.

Various manifestations include:

  • Rashes: A non-blanching rash (petechial or purpuric) develops in more than 80% of the cases.
  • Septicemia: It is attributed to endotoxin induced endothelial injury leading to increased vascular permeability and intravascular thrombosis.
  • Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: It is a severe form of fulminant meningococcemia, characterized by large purpuric rashes (purpura fulminans ), shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), bilateral adrenal hemorrhage and multiorgan failure.
  • Pyogenic meningitis: it commonly affects young children (3-5 years of age). Presentation includes fever, vomiting, headache, neck stiffness-similar to any other bacterial meningitis, except for the presence of rashes.
  • Chronic meningococcemia: It occurs rarely and is characterized by repeated episodes of petechial rash, fever, arthritis, and splenomegaly.
  • Post Meningococcal reactive disease: Immune complexes (made up of capsular antigens and their antibodies) develop 4-10 days later, lead to manifestations like arthritis, rash, pericarditis, polyserositis, and fever.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition.

190.question_text: Which of the following is the correct method for sterilizing empty glass petri dishes?

190.option_d: Hot air oven at 121°C for 30-60 minutes
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Dry heat sterilization in a hot air oven at 160°C for 2 hours (120 minutes) is the standard method for sterilizing heat-stable, non-aqueous materials that could be corroded by moist heat, such as glassware (petri dishes, pipettes), sharp instruments, and powders. (Option D ruled out)

One of the disadvantage of using hot air is that it has no penetrating power, and hence not suitable for disinfection of bulky Artiles such as mattresses.

Autoclaving uses moist heat (saturated steam under pressure) and is unsuitable for empty glassware as it can cause condensation and wetting, compromising sterility upon opening. (Options A and C ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

  • Dry heat (hot air oven) is for glassware and metal instruments.
  • Moist heat (autoclave) is for culture media, liquids, and waste.
  • Standard dry heat cycle: 160°C for 120 minutes.

190.question_text: Paradoxical carriers are
190.option_a: Person who acquires the microorganism due to his contact with the patient
190.option_b: Person who acquires the microorganism from another carrier
190.option_c: Person who has clinically recovered from an infectious disease and now is still capable of transmitting the infectious agent to others
190.explanation:
Contact carrier - A person can become a contact carrier when he acquires the microorganism due to his contact with the patient.

Paradoxical carrier - A person is a paradoxical carrier when he acquire the microorganism from another carrier.

Temporary carrier - They are those who shed the infectious agents for short period of time. Incubatory, convalescent and healthy carrier are temporary carrier.

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option A) Person who acquires the microorganism due to contact with the patient → This describes a contact carrier, not a paradoxical carrier.
  • (Option C) Person who has clinically recovered but can still transmit the infectious agent → This defines a convalescent carrier, not a paradoxical carrier.
  • (Option D) None of the above → Incorrect, as option B correctly defines a paradoxical carrier.

Key Takeaways:

  • Contact carrier → Acquires infection directly from a patient.
  • Paradoxical carrier → Acquires infection from another carrier, not a patient.
  • Temporary carrier → Only sheds infectious agents for a short time.

190.question_text: WHICH OF THE FOLLOWING RECEPTORS HELPS THE HIV-1 GENOME TO ENTER INSIDE THE HOST CELL?
190.explanation:
• HIV-1 entry into host cells requires interaction between:
    • gp120 (on the viral envelope) and CD4 receptor (on host cells).
    • After CD4 binding, gp120 interacts with a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), facilitating viral entry.
    • CCR5 is the primary co-receptor used in the early stages of infection, allowing HIV to enter macrophages and T cells.
    • Individuals with a CCR5-Δ32 mutation have resistance to HIV infection.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: gp120

  • gp120 is an HIV surface glycoprotein that binds to CD4 and co-receptors (CCR5 or CXCR4).
  • It mediates attachment but does not directly help the viral genome enter the host cell.

Choice B: gp41

  • gp41 is a transmembrane protein responsible for fusion between the viral and host cell membranes.
  • It helps HIV inject its genome into the host cell but does not act as a receptor.

Choice C: CXCR4

  • CXCR4 is a co-receptor used in later stages of HIV infection, mainly in T-tropic (X4) strains.
  • However, CCR5 is used predominantly in initial infection, making it the better answer.

Key Takeaway

CCR5 is the primary receptor that helps HIV-1 enter host cells during early infection.

190.question_text: If numerical aperture of the objective lens of the light microscope is increased then-
190.option_d: Height from where the work can be done increases.
190.explanation:
Basic principle of microscopy - A modern compound microscope has a series of lenses and uses visible light as its source of illumination. With a compound light microscope, we can examine very small specimens as well as some of their fine details.

Magnification is achieved when light rays from an illuminator and the light source are passed through a condenser which has lenses that direct the light rays through the specimen.

From here light rays pass in to objective lens, the lenses closer to the specimen. The image of the specimen is magnified again by ocular or eyepiece.

Magnification - it is the degree of enlargement of the image.

Numerical aperture size has a direct effect on magnification.

So when we increase the numerical aperture of an objective lens of light microscope, we increase the magnification for the microscope.

Incorrect Choices Explanation:

Choice A: The contrast increases – Incorrect
While contrast can be influenced by factors like illumination, staining, and specimen thickness, it is not directly affected by the numerical aperture. Increasing the NA generally improves resolution, but it does not inherently increase contrast. Contrast adjustments are typically achieved by altering the illumination settings or using contrast-enhancing techniques such as phase contrast or differential interference contrast.

Choice B: The magnification increases – Incorrect
Magnification refers to the size of the image relative to the actual size of the specimen. While the numerical aperture plays a role in improving the resolution, it does not directly increase magnification. The magnification is primarily determined by the objective lens power and the eyepiece power. Increasing the NA does not inherently increase magnification, though it can allow you to see more detailed features at the same magnification.

Choice D: Height from where the work can be done increases – Incorrect
Increasing the numerical aperture does not affect the working distance (height from where the work can be done). The working distance is the space between the objective lens and the specimen, and it typically decreases as the NA increases. A lens with a higher NA focuses on a smaller area and thus requires a smaller working distance.

Key Takeaway:

Increasing the numerical aperture of an objective lens improves the resolution of the microscope, allowing for clearer and more detailed images of the specimen, but it does not affect magnification or contrast directly.

190.question_text: Which preparation technique is used to dissolve biopsy specimens that are difficult to process in KOH wet mounts?
190.explanation:
• Tube KOH preparation: This technique involves placing biopsy specimens in a KOH solution for extended periods, facilitating the breakdown of keratin and other components, making it suitable for processing challenging specimens.

Additional Points:

  • Tube KOH preparation allows for a thorough dissolution of samples, making it easier to visualize fungal elements in difficult specimens such as skin or nail biopsies.
  • The incubation time can vary depending on the type of specimen, generally ranging from 30 minutes to several hours, ensuring effective clearing.

Why Not Others:

  • a is incorrect Slide KOH preparation: This method is designed for immediate examination of specimens but is not effective for dissolving tough samples.
  • c India ink stain: Primarily used for visualizing encapsulated fungi, this method does not assist in dissolving specimens.
  • d Nigrosin stain: This negative stain is utilized for highlighting fungal capsules and does not serve the purpose of dissolving biopsy specimens.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tube KOH preparation is the preferred method for dissolving difficult biopsy specimens, enhancing the visualization of fungal elements.
  • This technique is crucial for accurate fungal diagnosis from challenging samples.

190.question_text: A patient presents with a long-standing swelling and discharging sinuses on the foot as shown below. The discharge contains black granules. What is the most likely finding on the KOH mount?
190.option_c: Septate hyphae with 4-5 microns in width
190.explanation:
Explanation:

The above clinical picture of long-standing swelling and discharging sinuses on the foot with black granules is suggestive of eumyectoma caused by Madurella mycetomatis, which has septate hyphae that are 4-5 microns in width.

  • Mycetoma is a chronic subcutaneous infection caused by traumatic implantation of fungi (eumycetoma) or actinomycetes (actinomycetoma) from soil.
  • It is characterised by progressive swelling, draining sinuses, and the presence of granules that represent colonies of the infecting organism.
  • While both forms share similar clinical features, actinomycetoma tends to be more aggressive, spreading from subcutaneous tissues into underlying muscle, though treatment differs between the two types.
  • The fungal agents of mycetoma include P. boydii, M. mycetomatis, Madurella grisea, E. jeanselmei, and Acremonium falciforme.
  • The colour and nature of the granules can distinguish these species:

The granules of M. mycetomatis are hard and compact, containing broad septate hyphae measuring 3-5 µm in width, with the hyphae appearing irregularly distorted and enlarged at the periphery. (Option B ruled out)

Explanation of other answers:

Pseudohyphae (Option A): In a KOH preparation, Candida is identified by the presence of yeast cells or pseudohyphae. The yeast appears as oval budding cells, while pseudohyphae are elongated chains formed when buds grow but do not detach, showing constrictions at the septa. In C. albicans, both yeast cells and pseudohyphae may be seen, and unlike some other Candida species, it can also produce true hyphae.

Filamentous branching bacteria (Option D): Actinomyces are Gram-positive bacteria that show variable morphology, appearing as short club-shaped forms or elongated beaded filaments, which may be branched or unbranched. On agar, they can form colonies with a molar tooth appearance.

Staphylococcus aureus, M. tuberculosis, S. pneumoniae all of these bacteria can be readily cultured on standard or enriched artificial laboratory media (e.g., blood agar, LJ medium, chocolate agar). (Options B, C and D ruled out)

190.question_text: What is the purpose of using cycloheximide in fungal culture media?
190.option_c: To prevent growth of saprotrophic fungi
190.option_d: To support the growth of Cryptococcus species
190.explanation:
• C) To prevent growth of saprotrophic fungi: Cycloheximide is specifically used to inhibit saprotrophic fungi that may overgrow in culture, thereby allowing for better recovery of pathogenic fungi.

Why Not Others:

  • A) To enhance fungal growth: Cycloheximide does not enhance fungal growth; instead, it inhibits the growth of certain fungi.
  • B) To inhibit bacterial contamination: While cycloheximide can inhibit some bacteria, its main role is to target saprotrophic fungi rather than primarily preventing bacterial contamination.
  • D) To support the growth of Cryptococcusspecies: Cycloheximide inhibits several fungi, including Cryptococcus neoformans, so it does not promote their growth.

Key Takeaway: Cycloheximide is crucial in culture media to inhibit saprotrophic fungi, ensuring that pathogenic fungi can be accurately isolated, though it should be used cautiously with certain fungi like Cryptococcus neoformans.

190.question_text: 1,1,1 method is used for:
190.explanation:
There are two principle means of monitoring the microbiological parameters present in the air, passive monitoring and active sampling.

  • Passive Monitoring (Settle plate):
    • Method: Standard Petri dishes containing culture media (e.g. blood agar) are exposed to the air for a given time and then the plates are incubated at 37°C for 24 hours aerobically.
    • 1,1,1 method: The ideal recommendation is the 1,1,1 method where the plates are placed at different locations in the OT one meter away from the side walls, one meter above the floor and for a duration of one hour.
    • Interpretation: Bacteria sediment/settle on the plates which subsequently form colonies on incubation.
    • Maximum acceptable levels in operating theatres with turbulent air flow is:
      • ≤786.4 CFU/m2/h (≤5 CFU/9 cm diameter plate/h) at rest, and
      • ≤3932.1 CFU/m2/h (≤25 CFU/9 cm diameter plate/h) when operational.
    • Disadvantages: (1) It cannot detect smaller particles or droplets suspended in the air, (2) This method cannot quantify the volume of air sampled, (3) This method is not recommended when sampling air for fungal spores, because single spores can remain suspended in air indefinitely.
  • Active Monitoring (Slit Sampler Method): In active monitoring, a microbiological air sampler (e.g. sieve impactor) is used. It has a vacuum pump, and a perforated lid, in which an agar plate can be placed. The vacuum pump physically draws a known volume of air through the perforated lid and allows it to impact on the agar plate (e.g. blood agar) Following incubation, the quantity of microorganisms present in the culture plate is measured in terms of CFU/m3 of air. Active monitoring is applicable when the concentration of microorganisms is not very high, such as in an operating theatre, bone marrow transplant unit, etc.

For water surveillance:

  • Differential Coliform Count (Eijkman Test):
  • Membrane Filtration Method
  • Presence Absence Method
  • Endotoxin detection

For surface surveillance:

  • Moistened sterile swabs (soaked in sterile saline) are used to collect the samples from high-risk areas and then inoculated onto blood agar for the recovery of aerobic bacteria.
  • Newer techniques such as luminometer (expresses bacterial contamination as CFU/mL) and glow gel techniques are available which are easy to perform though expensive.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 282
