190.question_text: Which characteristic of Acid-Fast Bacilli makes them resistant to decolorization during the Ziehl-Neelsen staining process?
190.option_a: High lipid content in the cell wall
190.explanation:
High lipid content in the cell wall: Correct - The unique composition of Acid-Fast Bacilli includes mycolic acids, which contribute to their high lipid content. This property prevents the loss of the primary stain during the Ziehl-Neelsen process, allowing these bacteria to retain the red dye even after exposure to acidic decolorizers.

Why Not Others:

  • Thick peptidoglycan layer: Incorrect - While a thick peptidoglycan layer is a hallmark of Gram-positive bacteria, it does not provide the acid-fast property observed in Acid-Fast Bacilli.
  • Presence of endospores: Incorrect - Endospores are survival structures formed by some bacteria (e.g., Bacillus species) and do not contribute to the acid-fast characteristic of Mycobacterium species.
  • Capsule formation: Incorrect - Although some bacteria can form capsules for protection, this characteristic does not influence the resistance to decolorization seen in Acid-Fast Bacilli during staining.

Key Takeaway: The high lipid content in the cell wall of Acid-Fast Bacilli, particularly mycolic acids, is responsible for their resistance to decolorization during the Ziehl-Neelsen staining process, crucial for their identification in clinical specimens.

Tags: inicet 2020

Reference: Hoffman, P. S., & Srinivasan, S. (2003). The Biology of Acid-Fast Bacteria. Clinical Microbiology Reviews.

190.question_text: Fecal E.coli is detected by which test?
190.explanation:
Differential Coliform Count (Eijkman Test):

  • Detection of coliform bacteria does not always indicate fecal contamination as some of them may be found in the environment. Hence, it is further tested by differential coliform count to detect the fecal E.coli.
  • This is done by sub-culturing the positive tubes (from the multiple tube method) on lactose containing medium such as brilliant green bile broth for: Detection of lactose fermentation with the production of acid and gas at 44°C and Demonstrating a positive indole test at 44°C.

Membrane Filtration Method:

  • This method is based on the filtration of a known volume (e.g. 100 mL) of water through a cellulose membrane of pore size 0.2 or 0.45 µm.
  • Procedure: The bacteria retained on the surface of the membrane filter are transferred into a Petri dish containing a suitable medium (e.g. membrane lauryl sulphate broth) and incubated.
  • Result: Characteristic yellow colonies of coliforms are produced, which can be counted directly to obtain CFU/100 mL of water.

Presence Absence Method:

  • This is a qualitative method, detecting just the presence or absence of the organism in water.

Endotoxin detection:

  • Endotoxins are the component of the cell wall of gram negative bacteria. Dialysis water, devices, etc. contaminated with endotoxin can elicit a variety of inflammatory responses in our body and thereby cause serious toxic effects.
  • Therefore, apart from bacteriological testing, the dialysis water used for hemodialysis is also tested for presence of endotoxin.

190.question_text: What is the primary method for laboratory diagnosis of tetanus?
190.option_b: Culture of blood agar with polymyxin B
190.option_c: Toxin assay using mouse inoculation test
190.explanation:
• B. Culture of blood agar with polymyxin B:
    • Correct; this method is effective because polymyxin B inhibits Gram-negative bacteria, allowing for selective growth of C. tetani.
    • Isolation from clinical specimens (e.g., wound exudates) is critical for diagnosis, especially in cases without classic symptoms.
    • Confirmatory tests can follow culture to ensure species identification.

Why Not Others:

  • A: Gram staining of wound swabs:
    • Useful for initial assessment of bacterial presence but not definitive.
    • Clostridium tetani may not be visible in low numbers or may be overgrown by other flora, leading to false negatives.
  • C: . Toxin assay using mouse inoculation test:
    • While it detects the presence of tetanospasmin, it is not routinely used due to ethical concerns regarding animal use and the time it requires.
    • The mouse bioassay can yield results days after inoculation, delaying diagnosis and treatment initiation.
  • D: Serological testing for antibodies:
    • Not a common diagnostic approach for tetanus, as antibodies may not be present in sufficient quantities during acute infections.
  • This method does not provide immediate diagnostic information, making it impractical for urgent clinical decisions. Serological testing for antibodies:
    • Not a common diagnostic approach for tetanus, as antibodies may not be present in sufficient quantities during acute infections.

Key Takeaway: Culture of blood agar with polymyxin B is the most reliable and practical method for diagnosing tetanus, facilitating the isolation and identification of C. tetani from clinical specimens.

190.question_text: A 38-year-old IV drug user presents with fever, malaise, rigors, and a pansystolic murmur. Three sets of blood cultures are taken. Which organism is most likely to be isolated?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

In intravenous drug users (IVDUs) presenting with acute infective endocarditis, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism. It frequently affects the tricuspid valve, often producing a murmur and septic pulmonary emboli. Its ability to cause bacteremia and adhere to damaged endothelium makes it a prime pathogen in this population.

Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive, non-motile, non-spore forming coccus that typically appears in grape-like clusters.

On nutrient agar, it forms large, convex, smooth, shiny, opaque colonies that are easily emulsifiable and produce a distinctive golden-yellow pigment that does not diffuse into the medium. On blood agar, it exhibits marked hemolysis, and on MacConkey agar, it forms pink colonies due to lactose fermentation. Biochemically, it is coagulase-positive, catalase-positive, and oxidase-negative.

Explanation of other options:

Streptococcus sanguis (Option A): Part of the Viridans group streptococci, which are common causes of subacute endocarditis in patients with underlying valvular disease, not typically in IVDUs.

Enterococcus faecium (Option B): A cause of healthcare-associated or genitourinary tract-related endocarditis, not specifically associated with IV drug use.

Coxiella burnetii (Option C): The cause of Q fever, which can cause culture-negative endocarditis. It is associated with exposure to farm animals, not IV drug use.

Key Takeaways:

  • aureus is the leading cause of acute bacterial endocarditis in IV drug users.
  • Blood cultures are essential for diagnosis.

190.question_text: A patient was catheterized for 8 days. On the 8th day, he started having spikes of fever. Suspecting it to be a catheter associated with UTI, you send a specimen for culture. The bacterium, which was isolated in clinically significant numbers, grows profusely on MacConkey agar, as shown in the accompanying photograph, and ferments lactose. Which of the following cellular attributes is most important in determining virulence and classifying this microbe as a uropathogen?
190.explanation:
P-fimbriae and type-1 fimbriae are significant virulence determinants of uropathogenic strains of Escherichia coli, the most common cause of urinary tract infections. These fimbriae mediate attachment of uropathogenic strains to uroepithelial cells. E. coli, which grows on MacConkey agar and ferments lactose, accounts for 70% to 90% of all the uncomplicated UTIs.

A broad range of bacteria can cause CAUTI, most of which are multidrug resistant.

  • In short-term (<30days) catheterized patients: Most CAUTI are caused by the monomicrobial pathogens such as gram negative bacilli or enterococci. coli is the predominant agent, although it is not as prevalent as in community-associated UTI. Other gram-negative bacilli such as Klebsiella, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter and gram-positive cocci such as Enterococcus account for most of the other infections.
  • In long-term (>30 days) catheterized patients, CAUTI is usually polymicrobial. In addition to the pathogens of short-term catheterization, other organisms such as Proteus, Providencia and Morganella are also encountered.

Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) is the single most common pathogen of UTI, accounting for 70– 75% of all cases. UPEC serotypes O1, O2, O4, O6, O7 and O75 are responsible for most UTIs.

The virulence factors of UPEC include:

  • Cytotoxins (CNF 1–cytotoxic necrotizing factor 1 and SAT: Secreted autotransporter toxin).
  • Hemolysins.
  • Fimbriae (e.g. P fimbriae)–specific for strains causing lower UTI.
  • Capsular K antigen–specific for strains causing upper UTI.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 241

190.question_text: A child presents with high-grade fever, multiple seizures, headache, and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows low glucose, elevated protein, and numerous polymorphonuclear cells. CSF culture reveals pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli. Which of the following statements is true regarding the causative organism?
190.option_b: Produces non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar.
190.option_c: Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies.
190.option_d: It exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar.
190.explanation:
Explanation:

The pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli in CSF culture suggest Haemophilus influenzae, a major cause of bacterial meningitis in children. The statement true regarding H. influenzae is that it exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies.

  • influenzae requires Factor X (hemin) and Factor V (NAD) for growth.
  • Staphylococcus aureus releases NAD, promoting the growth of H. influenzae around its colonies, a phenomenon known as satellitism.
  • The type b capsular polysaccharide (polyribosylribitol phosphate or PRP) is the most virulent serotype, particularly in unvaccinated children under 5 years old, often causing invasive diseases like meningitis.

Clinical features:

  • Meningitis: Fever, irritability, neck stiffness
  • Other invasive diseases: Epiglottitis, pneumonia, septic arthritis
  • Nontypeable strains often cause mucosal infections like otitis media, sinusitis

Diagnosis:

  • CSF analysis in meningitis: elevated protein, low glucose, pleocytosis
  • Gram stain: small gram-negative coccobacilli
  • Culture on chocolate agar
  • Antigen detection tests (latex agglutination) for rapid diagnosis
  • PCR for definitive identification and serotyping

Treatment:

  • Empiric therapy: Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime)
  • Alternative: Chloramphenicol (if cephalosporin allergy)
  • Duration: Usually 10 days for meningitis

Explanation for other options:

It is bacitracin sensitive (Option A): Bacitracin sensitivity is a characteristic of Haemophilus ducreyi, not Haemophilus influenzae.

Produces non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar (Option B): H. influenzae does not grow on MacConkey agar, as it requires Factor X (hemin) and Factor V (NAD), which are absent in this medium.

It exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar (Option D): H. influenzae does not hemolyze red blood cells, whereas Streptococcus pneumoniae (another common cause of meningitis) exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar.

190.question_text: The cell wall is tough because of the presence of:
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Peptidoglycan is the key structural component of bacterial cell walls, particularly in Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. The extensive cross-linking between NAM and NAG molecules is what provides the rigidity and toughness necessary to maintain the shape of the cell, resist osmotic pressure, and protect the bacterium from mechanical stress. Gram positive bacteria have a much thicker peptidoglycan layer as compared to Gram negative cell wall, alowing them to retain the stain during Gram staining.

Explanation of Other Options:

Teichoic acid (Option A):

Teichoic acids are present in the cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria and play a role in cell wall stability, adhesion, and pathogenicity, but they do not contribute directly to the toughness of the cell wall.

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Option B):

LPS is a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, not the cell wall itself. LPS contributes to the bacterial outer membrane's integrity and is important for immune system evasion, but it is not the primary factor that makes the cell wall tough.

Outer membrane (Option C):

The outer membrane is present in Gram-negative bacteria, providing an additional barrier against harmful substances, but it is not the main contributor to the toughness of the cell wall.

Key Takeaway:

The toughness of the bacterial cell wall is primarily due to peptidoglycan, which forms a rigid, protective layer around the cell.

Peptidoglycan is essential for maintaining the shape and stability of the bacterial cell and protecting it from environmental stresses.

190.question_text: What is the primary purpose of using Nigrosin stain in fungal diagnostics?
190.option_a: To visualize internal cellular structures of fungi
190.option_b: To provide a permanent record of fungal specimens
190.option_c: As an alternative to India ink stain for visualizing capsules
190.option_d: To enhance the color contrast of fungal elements
190.explanation:
• As an alternative to India ink stain for visualizing capsules: Nigrosin is effectively used to visualize the capsules of fungi, particularly in organisms like Cryptococcus, serving as a negative stain to highlight the capsule against a dark background.

Additional Points:

  • Nigrosin stain is particularly useful in clinical settings, offering a quick method for identifying encapsulated fungi.
  • The capsule visibility is crucial for diagnosing Cryptococcus neoformans, where the capsule is a key virulence factor.
  • This stain, being a negative stain, helps to outline the capsule by providing a dark background, making the capsule appear as a clear halo.

Why Not Others:

  • a is incorrect as To visualize internal cellular structures of fungi: Nigrosin is not designed for visualizing internal structures; it focuses on the external capsule around the yeast cells.
  • b is incorrect since To provide a permanent record of fungal specimens: While Nigrosin can aid in visualization, it is not used for creating permanent preparations or records.
  • d is incorrect because, although it enhances contrast, its primary role is capsule visualization. To enhance the color contrast of fungal elements: Although Nigrosin provides color contrast, its primary function is to visualize capsules, not just to enhance overall contrast.

Key Takeaways:

  • Nigrosin stain serves as an effective alternative to India ink for visualizing fungal capsules, crucial for identifying encapsulated species.
  • This staining method is vital for the rapid diagnosis of fungi in clinical samples.

Tag Line: Hard

Reference: Textbook of Medical Mycology Hardcover - 1 January 2018, by Jagdish Chander. Appendix B: Fungal Reagents and Stains, PP - 857

190.question_text: Identify the fungus shown in the image given below which is stained by India ink dye.
190.explanation:
Explanation:

  • In the given image the India ink stain a negative staining technique is used to visualize the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans in clinical specimens like cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
  • The stain creates a dark background against which the large, clear, gelatinous capsule surrounding the spherical yeast cell is seen as a prominent "halo." The yeast cells themselves are often seen as budding forms. This capsule is a major virulence factor, allowing the organism to resist phagocytosis.
  • Cryptococcus species are true encapsulated yeasts that act as opportunistic pathogens, primarily causing infection in immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV/AIDS, malignancies, organ transplants, or on immunosuppressive therapy, as well as in individuals at extremes of age.

Management of Cryptococcosis:

  • Microscopy:
    • India ink shows the capsule as a clear halo around budding yeast cells.
    • Mucicarmine stain highlights the carminophilic cell wall of C. neoformans.
  • Culture:
    • Grows on Sabouraud Dextrose Agar as smooth, mucoid, cream-colored colonies.
    • On Niger seed/Bird seed agar, forms brown colonies due to melanin production (phenol oxidase/laccase).
    • Ability to grow at 37°C and hydrolyze urea differentiates C. neoformans from non-pathogenic species.
  • Antigen Detection:
    • Demonstration of capsular antigen by precipitation or latex agglutination tests.
  • Treatment:
    • Initial therapy: Liposomal Amphotericin B + Flucytosine.
    • Maintenance therapy: Fluconazole for 6–12 months depending on immune status.

Explanation of other options:

Aspergillus (Option A): This is a mold characterized by septate hyphae that branch at acute angles (V-shaped). It does not have a capsule and is not a yeast, so it would not be identified with an India ink stain.

Penicillium (Option B): This is a mold, known for its brush-like conidiophores. It lacks a capsule and is not demonstrated using the India ink stain.

Candida (Option D): Candida species are yeasts and may show budding, they do not possess a significant capsule that is visible with India ink staining. They are best visualized with Gram stain, where they appear as Gram-positive budding yeasts with or without pseudohyphae.

Key Takeaways:

  • India ink stain is used to detect the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans.

190.question_text: Which of the following options is considered a high-level disinfectant?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Glutaraldehyde is a chemical sterilant that, with prolonged exposure time (e.g., 10-12 hours), can achieve sterilization. When used for a shorter contact time (e.g., 20-45 minutes), it acts as a High-Level Disinfectant (HLD).

Mechanism: It acts by alkylating proteins and nucleic acids, effectively killing all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, mycobacteria, viruses, and fungi.

Primary Use: It is commonly used for disinfecting semi-critical medical devices like endoscopes, bronchoscopes, and other heat-sensitive instruments that come into contact with mucous membranes.

Explanation of other options:

Isopropyl alcohol (Option A): This is an intermediate-level disinfectant. It is effective against vegetative bacteria, fungi, and most viruses (including enveloped viruses like HIV and influenza), but it is not sporicidal and is less effective against non-enveloped viruses (e.g., norovirus). It is not suitable for HLD.

Iodophores (Option C): Iodophores (e.g., povidone-iodine) are primarily used as antiseptics for skin and tissue. As disinfectants, they are generally classified as intermediate-level. They are not reliable for killing bacterial spores and are therefore not considered high-level disinfectants.

Phenol (Option D): Phenolic compounds are intermediate to low-level disinfectants. They are effective against vegetative bacteria and enveloped viruses but are not sporicidal and have variable activity against non-enveloped viruses and mycobacteria. They are commonly used for environmental surface disinfection.

Key Takeaways:

  • High-Level Disinfectants (HLD): Glutaraldehyde, Ortho-phthalaldehyde, Hydrogen Peroxide, Peracetic Acid. Used for semi-critical items.
  • Intermediate-Level Disinfectants (ILD): Alcohols, iodophores, phenolics. Used for non-critical items or surfaces.
  • Low-Level Disinfectants (LLD): Quaternary ammonium compounds. Used for general environmental cleaning.

190.question_text: Which of the following pathogens is known to be the most resistant to standard sterilization methods?
190.explanation:
Resistance of Microorganisms to Sterilization Methods

  1. A) Bacterial spores: Highly resistant to many sterilization methods, including heat and chemicals, but generally less resistant than prions.
  2. B) Mycobacteria: More resistant to disinfectants and some sterilization methods due to their waxy cell wall, yet not as resistant as prions.
  3. C) Viruses: While lipid-enveloped viruses are susceptible to disinfectants, non-enveloped viruses (like norovirus) can be more resistant but still do not match prion resistance.
  4. D) Prions: Exhibit extreme resistance to standard sterilization methods, resistant to heat, chemicals, and radiation, making them the most challenging to eradicate.

Key Takeaway: Prions are the most resistant to sterilization methods compared to other pathogens, requiring specialized and more aggressive decontamination procedures to ensure their inactivation.

Tags : good to know | inicet

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection.

190.question_text: What is the primary reason that Malassezia species require lipid-supplemented media for culture?
190.option_a: They are resistant to high temperatures
190.option_b: They are lipophilic and need lipids for growth
190.option_c: They produce pigments that inhibit other fungi
190.option_d: They are susceptible to antifungal agents
190.explanation:
• Malassezia species are inherently lipophilic, meaning they thrive on lipid-rich environments, requiring lipids such as oleic acid or olive oil for optimal growth.
  • Their ability to metabolize lipids is crucial for their survival and replication, as they cannot utilize carbohydrates effectively like many other fungi.
  • While Malassezia can tolerate a range of temperatures, the necessity for lipid supplementation is unrelated to temperature resistance; it is purely a nutritional requirement.
  • The production of pigments does occur, but this characteristic does not influence their need for lipid-rich culture media.
  • Malassezia's susceptibility to antifungal agents does not relate to their growth needs, which primarily center around lipid availability.

Why Not Others:

  • a) They are resistant to high temperatures: While temperature tolerance is a factor, it does not explain the need for lipids.
  • c) They produce pigments that inhibit other fungi: Pigment production is not the primary growth requirement for Malassezia; it is secondary and does not necessitate lipid supplementation.
  • d) They are susceptible to antifungal agents: This statement does not address their nutritional requirements or growth conditions.

Key Takeaways:

  • The requirement for lipid-supplemented media is essential for the successful culture of Malassezia due to their lipophilic nature.
  • Understanding this unique growth requirement aids in accurate laboratory diagnostics and effective treatment approaches for Malassezia-related conditions.

Tag Line: Easy

REFERENCE: Textbook of Medical Mycology Hardcover - 1 January 2018, by Jagdish Chander. Chapter 7: Malasseziosis 135

190.question_text: What is the main advantage of using Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO) in KOH solutions for fungal wet mounts?

This allows for immediate microscopic examination without the need for prolonged clearing times.

  • c is incorrect because It increases the pH of the solution: DMSO does not influence the pH of KOH solutions, so this statement is incorrect.

190.question_text: The test shown in the picture works on the principle of?
190.explanation:
The photo shows the immunochromatographic test for COVID-19.

  • Immunochromatographic test (ICT) is based on lateral flow technique.
  • The test system consists of a nitrocellulose membrane (NCM) and an absorbent pad. Two formats are available: cassette or strip. The NCM is coated at two places in the form of lines-a test line, coated with monoclonal antibody targeted against the test antigen and a control line, coated with anti-species immunoglobulin. Specific Ab against the target Ag labelled with chromogenic marker (specific Ab tagged with colloidal gold or silver, a visually detectable marker) is infiltrated in the absorbent pad lining the sample window.
  • Test band: At the test line, the Ag-labelled Ab complex is immobilized by binding to the monoclonal Ab in the test line to form a colored band.
  • Control band: The free colloidal gold labelled Ab can move further and binds to the antihuman Ig to form a color control band. If the control band is not formed, then the test is considered invalid irrespective of whether the test band is formed or not.

Flow-through tests are another type of rapid diagnostic assays which differ from ICT in two aspects:

  1. Protein A is used for labeling antibody instead of gold conjugate and
  2. The sample flows vertically through the nitrocellulose membrane (NCM) as compared to lateral flow in ICT.

Flow-through tests can be used for both antigen and antibody detection. The HIV TRIDOT test is a classic example. It detects antibodies to HIV-1 and 2 separately in the patient's serum.

Chemiluminescence refers to the emission of light (luminescence), as a result of a chemical reaction. The principle of CLIA is similar to that of ELISA; however, the chromogenic substance is replaced by chemiluminescent compounds (e.g. luminol and acridinium ester) that generate light during a chemical reaction (luxogenic). The light (photons) can be detected by a photomultiplier, also called a luminometer.

ELISA is an immunoassay that detects either antigen or antibodies in the specimen, by using an enzyme-substrate chromogen system for detection.

Principle of ELISA:

  • ELISA is so named because of its two components:
    • Immunosorbent: Here, an absorbing material is used (e.g. polystyrene, polyvinyl) that specifically absorbs the antigen or antibody present in serum.
    • Enzyme is used to label one of the components of immunoassay (i.e. antigen or antibody).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 156

190.question_text: A 35-year-old presented with a 7-month history of fever and chronic diarrhea. He, has lost 17 kg of his body weight. He gives a history of multiple encounters of unprotected intercourse. On admission, his temperature was 39.3 °C, pulse was 104/min, and blood pressure was 120/80 mm of hg. The patient was cachectic and appeared chronically ill. Further physical examination was unremarkable. His laboratory parameters are as follows- The CD4 lymphocyte count was 13/μL HIV viral load was 30 000 copies/mL plasma. At what CD4 cell count should Anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) be started in this patient?
190.explanation:
• CD4 Cell Count: CD4 T-lymphocytes play a critical role in the immune system, and their count is often used as a marker of immune function in HIV-infected individuals.
  • Viral Load: The viral load measures the amount of HIV in the blood. A higher viral load is associated with more active viral replication and a greater risk of disease progression.
  • Current Guidelines: According to the current NACO (National AIDS Control Organization) guidelines, HAART should be initiated in an HIV-positive patient irrespective of their CD4 cell count. This approach aligns with the "Test and Treat" strategy, which recommends starting antiretroviral therapy as soon as an HIV diagnosis is confirmed, regardless of the CD4 cell count.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 332

190.question_text: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of psoriasis?
190.option_a: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
190.option_c: Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland
190.option_d: Defective T cell maturation in the thymus
190.explanation:
• Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells: This describes Type 1 diabetes, not psoriasis.
  • Hyperproliferation of keratinocytes: Psoriasis is characterized by the rapid turnover and proliferation of skin cells (keratinocytes), leading to thickened skin and scaling.
  • Immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland: This is seen in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, not psoriasis.
  • Defective T cell maturation in the thymus: This is related to autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, not psoriasis.

Key Takeaway: Psoriasis is primarily due to the hyperproliferation of keratinocytes.

Tags: Good to know

Tag Line: Moderate

Reference: Shastri, A., & Bhatt, S. (2023). Essential Microbiology. Chapter 17: Autoimmunity, pp. 203-207

190.question_text: A 32 year old male presents to his primary care physician with complaints of watery diarrhea approximately 5 times per day, abdominal pain and nausea since 4 days. There is history of travel to Sudan on an educational student exchange programme. Stool culture on BA , MAC and XLD was done. Mac Conkey showed the presence of lactose fermenter colonies. It was found to be Eiken test positive and elongation was seen in Chinese hamster ovary cells. What could be the likely organism and diagnosis?
190.explanation:
LT (heat-labile toxin)

Produced by: Enterotoxigenic E.coli

It resembles cholera toxin in its structure and function.

Detection of LT:

In vivo tests

Ligated rabbit Ileal loop test is positive (fluid accumulation in the loop) only after 18 hours

Adult rabbit skin test is positive

In vitro tests:

Tissue culture tests:

  • Steroid production in Y1 mouse adrenal cell culture
  • Elongation in Chinese hamster ovary cells

Precipitin test (Eiken's test) positive

Reference: Ananthnarayan and Paniker's textbook of Microbiology 12th edition pg no.481

190.question_text: A known case of HIV comes to the OPD for follow up. His CD4 cell count is currently 350 cells/uL. Primary prophylaxis for which opportunistic infection should be started at this stage?
190.explanation:
• Cotrimoxazole preventive therapy for preventing PCP infection (CPT), at a dose of 800 mg/160 mg PO once daily may be initiated in the following scenarios:
  • Primary prophylaxis: It is initiated in HIV patient in any of the conditions- If CD4 count < 350 cells /cm or WHO clinical stage 3 and 4.
  • There is no role for primary prophylaxis of cryptococcal meningitis.
  • MAC infection occurs at CD4 count <50, hence there is no scope for prophylaxis at this stage.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 334

190.question_text: Binary (Secondary) exposure to an antigen result in sudden increase in:
190.explanation:
• IgM is the first antibody produced and secreted by B cells during the primary and secondary immune responses.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 199-200

190.question_text: In respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, which is the most affected immunoglobulin:
190.explanation:
• IgA provides local immunity.
  • IgA is concentrated in secretions and on mucus surfaces and Resistant to digestive enzymes. IgA acts as a mucosa barrier for infection.
  • IgA is the most affected immunoglobulin in respiratory and gastrointestinal tract infections.
    • Inhibits adherence of organism to mucosa
    • Activates - alternate complement pathway
    • Promotes phagocytosis and intracellular killing of microorganism

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 198-199

190.question_text: Immunoglobulin found on B lymphocyte is:
190.explanation:
• Antibodies present on the surface of B cells (surface immunoglobulins) serve as antigen receptors (BCR), or are secreted into the extracellular space where they can bind and neutralize their target antigens.
  • Immunoglobulin D (IgD) is an antibody isotype that makes up about 1% of proteins in the plasma membranes of immature B-lymphocytes where it is usually co-expressed with another cell surface antibody called IgM.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 200

190.question_text: The reaginic antibody is:
190.explanation:
• Reaginic means an antibody that mediates hypersensitive allergic reactions of rapid onset.
  • Reagin, also called homocytotropic antibody, or Prausnitz-Kustner antibody, type of antibody found in the serum and skin of allergically hypersensitive persons and in smaller amounts in the serum of normally sensitive persons. Most reaginic antibodies are the immunoglobulin E (IgE) fraction in the blood.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 200

190.question_text: M band is absent in:
190.explanation:
• Myeloma (M) protein band
    • Monoclonal Ab
    • In multiple myeloma: IgG, IgA, IgD, IgE
    • In Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia: IgM

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 201

190.question_text: Without any therapeutic intervention, the most likely outcome for a transplanted skin graft from an unrelated HLA identical donor to the recipient is:
190.explanation:
• Chronic rejection is most likely to occur, over months to years, in such a situation.
  • Unrelated HLA identical individuals will have numerous mismatches of minor histocompatibility genes.
  • Because the major histocompatibility genes match, hyperacute and acute rejections are unlikely to occur.
  • Skin does not contain immunocompetent tissue and cannot mount a graft versus host response.
  • Even with identical major histocompatibility genes, long-term success of a transplanted skin graft will require immunosuppressive therapy.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

190.question_text: Adenosine deaminase deficiency is seen in:
190.explanation:
Severe combined immunodeficiencies (SCID):

  • SCID represents groups of genetically distinct syndromes; all having in common defects in both humoral and CMI.
  • Types of genetic defect in SCID include:
    • X-linked SCID seen in males - MC type defect (50–60%): Mutation in cytokine receptors (IL-7 mainly and others like IL-2, IL-4, IL-9, and IL-15)
    • Autosomal recessive SCID:
      • Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency
      • Recombinase-activating genes (RAG) mutation
      • Jak3 (intracellular kinase) mutation
      • Class II MHC deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome)
    • Affected infants are susceptible to severe recurrent infections by a wide array of pathogens
    • Treatment: Bone marrow transplantation and gene therapy

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

190.question_text: Binding site of superantigen on T Cell Receptor is:
190.explanation:
Superantigens bind simultaneously to the Vβ domain of a T-cell receptor and to the α chain of a class II MHC molecule.

190.question_text: At what intervals should monitoring of patients on HAART should be done?
190.explanation:

190.question_text: What does "HLA" stand for in the context of MHC molecules?

190.question_text: Identify the cell shown in the image:
190.explanation:

  • Null cells are large granular lymphocytes
  • 5-10% of circulating lymphocytes lack features of either T or B cells and known as Null cell/Natural Killer (NK) cell.
  1. Pan-T cell marker (CD-3) and TCR absent. It does not require thymus for development.
  2. Pan-B cell marker (CD-19) and IgM, IgD are absent

190.question_text: Superantigen causes:
190.explanation:
Superantigens are a class of antigens that cause the activation of a large number of T cells by cross-linking the T-cell receptor (TCR) with the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules, bypassing the normal antigen processing and presenting mechanisms. This results in the polyclonal activation of T cells and subsequent stimulation of B cells.

Superantigens

  • Act on Vβ region of TCR (T cell receptor)
  • Dont require antigen presentation by macrophage, directly stimulate non specific T cells
  • Leads to massive release of cytokines & polyclonal B cell activation

Example:

  • Staphyloccal toxin- TSST, Exfoliative toxin, Enterotoxins.
  • Streptococcal toxin- Str pyrogenic exotoxin A, B, C
  • Mycoplasma arthritidis
  • Yersinia enterocolitica.
  • M.tuberculosis
  • Viral superantigens - EBV, CMV, HIV and Rabies nucleocapsid
  • Fungal superantigens- Malassezia furfur

Key Takeaway: Superantigens bypass normal antigen presentation processes, leading to widespread immune activation.

Tags: INICET 2022 | INICET 2023

Tag Line: Moderate

Reference: Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology, chapter 12 on bacterial antigens - antibody reaction.PP-152.

190.question_text: Phagocytosis enhanced by coating the surface of antigen is called:
190.explanation:
• Opsonins are extracellular proteins that, when bound to substances or cells, induce phagocytes to phagocytose the substances or cells with the opsonins bound.
  • Opsonins act as bridging molecules between the target and the phagocyte, bringing them into contact, and then usually activating the phagocytic receptor to induce engulfment of the target by the phagocyte.
  • Opsonins are related to the two types of immune systems: the adaptive immune system and the innate immune system.
    • Adaptive immune system: The Fab region of antibody is able to bind to a specific epitope on an antigen, and the Fc region is recognized by the Fc Receptor (FcR) on phagocytes.
    • Complement proteins involved in innate opsonization include C4b, C3b and iC3b. C3b is recognized by CR1 on phagocytes. iC3b attaches to apoptotic cells and bodies and facilitates clearance of dead cells and remnants without initiating inflammatory pathways, through interaction with CR3 and CR4 on phagocytes.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 14, Pg 131-133

190.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about hapten?
190.option_b: It needs a carrier to induce immune response
190.option_d: It has no association with MHC
190.explanation:
• A hapten is an incomplete antigen.
  • It is not capable of inducing antibodies due to smaller size (molecular weight).
  • It can be made complete by combining it with a large sized inert carrier particle to induce antibody production.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Page Number 148-150.

190.question_text: The main aim of an adjuvant is to increase:
190.explanation:
• An adjuvant is a substance that increases or modulates the immune response to a vaccine.
  • The word "adjuvant" comes from the Latin word adiuvare, meaning to help or aid.
  • An immunologic adjuvant is defined as any substance that acts to accelerate, prolong, or enhance antigen-specific immune responses when used in combination with specific vaccine antigens.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 192-193

190.question_text: Which of the following is class specific antigenic determinants of an Immunoglobulin?
190.explanation:
• Two terminals in Immunoglobulin structure:
    • Carboxy terminal - constant region- effector functions
    • Amino terminal - amino acid sequence-variable - variable region - antigen recognition
      • Antigen combining site - at amino terminus - composed of both 'H' and 'L' chains
      • Infinite range - antibody specificity
      • Amino acid sequence of variable region of L and H chains
        • Consist of relatively invariable and highly variable zones
        • Highly variable - three in L & four in H
          • Hypervariable - 'hot spots' sites on hypervariable regions that make contact with epitope 'complementary determining region' or CDR

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 197

190.question_text: Variable portion of antibody molecule is:
190.explanation:
• Two terminals in Immunoglobulin structure:
    • Carboxy terminal - constant region- effector functions
    • Amino terminal - amino acid sequence-variable - variable region - antigen recognition
      • Antigen combining site - at amino terminus - composed of both 'H' and 'L' chains
      • Infinite range - antibody specificity
      • Amino acid sequence of variable region of L and H chains
        • Consist of relatively invariable and highly variable zones
        • Highly variable - three in L & four in H
          • Hypervariable - 'hot spots' sites on hypervariable regions that make contact with epitope 'complementary determining region' or CDR

190.question_text: Which of the following statements concerning immunoglobins is wrong?
190.option_b: IgE is increased in parasitic infection
190.option_d: Fetal infection is characterized by increase in IgG
190.explanation:
• IgM is the Earliest immunoglobulin to be synthesized by the fetus at 20 weeks.
  • IgM is Not transported across placenta due to its size.
  • lgM in fetus newborn - indicates intrauterine infections. Fetal infections are characterized by increase in IgM (not IgG).
  • First immunoglobin to appear following infections
  • IgM mediates primary (First) immune/humoral response
  • IgM is the first antibody produced and secreted by B cells during the primary and secondary immune responses.
  • IgE is increased in allergy and parasitic infections.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12 th edition Chapter 13, Pg 199-200

190.question_text: HLA III gene is responsible for:
190.explanation:
MHC= Major Histocompatibility Complex

  • They determine the histocompatibility between the donor graft and the recipient.
  • MHC molecules in humans are human leukocyte antigens (HLA).
  • They are unique identification marker for every person as the genetic sequence of MHC genes is different for every person.
  • In humans, HLA complex coding for MHC proteins/HLA are located on short arm of chromosome-6 (6p).
  • The genes are clustered in three regions named as MHC region-I, II and III
  • MHC I and II help in immune regulation (antigen presentation to T-cells follows MHC restriction):
    1. MHC I
      1. Present on all nucleated cells except sperms.
      2. Consist of two peptide chains
        1. Alpha chain (α1,α2,α3)
        2. Beta-2 macroglobulin (coded from chromosome-15)
      3. Presents intracellular antigen on virus infected/tumor cells to cytotoxic T-cells (CD-8 T-cells)
      4. Determine histocompatibility and acceptance or rejection of allograft
    2. MHC II
      1. Present on all APCs.
      2. Consist of two peptide chains
        1. Alpha chain (α1,α2)
        2. Beta chain (β1,β2)
      3. Regulate immune response: presents extracellular antigen on APCs to helper T-cells (CD-4 T-cells)
  • MHC III does not help in antigen presentation, but codes for various proteins such as
    1. Complement factors : C2, C4, C3 convertase, Factor B, Properdin
    2. Heat shock protein
    3. TNF-α and β
    4. Steroid 21-hydroxylases.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

190.question_text: Runt disease is:
190.explanation:
Graft versus host reaction (GVHR) - called Runt disease in animals.

  • Graft versus host - graft mounts an immune response against antigens of the host.
  • GVH occurs when the following conditions are present:
    • Graft contains immunocompetent cells.
    • Recipients possess transplantation antigens that are absent in the graft.
    • Recipients must not reject the graft.
  • Situations leading to GVH-
    • Allograft in recipient in whom specific immunological tolerance has been induced.
    • Adult lymphocytes injected into an immunologically deficient recipient.
    • F1 hybrid receiving a transplant from any one parental strain.
  • Clinical features of GVHR-
    • Retardation of growth, emaciation
    • Diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly
    • Lymphoid atrophy, anaemia
    • Terminating fatally

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Chapter 19, Page Number 187-190.

190.question_text: Which of the following is the main gene in HIV which undergoes frequent mutations?
190.explanation:
• HIV shows extensive antigenic diversity as it undergoes high rates of mutation.
  • This is believed to be due to the error-prone nature of reverse transcriptase enzyme.
  • Different mutants will be selected under different conditions (host factors, immune responses and tissue types).
  • Although mutations may occur in any gene, most notably it is observed in env gene. Unfortunately, envelope proteins happen to be the major target against which antibodies are produced.
  • Hence mutations in env gene are the main reason which explains why: HIV evades the host's immune response and vaccination against HIV is extremely difficult.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 326

190.question_text: All of the following statements about carbohydrate antigen are true except:
190.option_d: Does not require stimulation by T cells
190.explanation:
Carbohydrate antigens generally have lower immunogenicity and do not induce a memory response as effectively as protein antigens. They can cause polyclonal B cell stimulation and do not require T cell help for stimulation.

Key Takeaway: Carbohydrate antigens typically do not induce a memory response and have lower immunogenicity compared to proteins.

Tag: INICET 2022

Tag Line: Moderate

Reference: Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology, chapter 12 on antigens – antibody reaction.PP-152.

190.question_text: Which antibody is the primary mediator of allergic reactions?
190.explanation:
• IgE: This antibody is central to allergic reactions. It binds to allergens and triggers mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other inflammatory mediators, leading to allergic symptoms such as itching, swelling, and redness.
  • IgM: This antibody is involved in the initial response to infections and does not mediate allergic reactions.
  • IgG: While it can be involved in some allergic responses, IgE is the primary mediator of allergic reactions.
  • IgA: This antibody protects mucosal surfaces but does not mediate allergic responses.

Key Takeaway: IgE is key in mediating allergic reactions by interacting with allergens and triggering inflammatory responses.

Tags: Must know

Tag Line: Easy

Reference: Apurva Shastri, Review of Microbiology and Immunology, chapter 12 on antigens – antibody reaction.PP-152.

190.question_text: A 24-year-old African American man presented to the emergency department (ED) during late summer after multiple visits to health care practitioners with chief complaints of fever and joint pain. The patient described the knee joint pain being diffuse in location with gradual onset persisting for over about a month and described it as a constant ache with similar nature which was worsening in severity. He also endorsed photophobia, malaise, and severe nausea with 1 episode of emesis. He denied any history of neck stiffness or tenderness. He endorsed persistent urinary frequency and urethral discharge over this month, which he had just ignored. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient and its causative agent?
190.option_d: Exacerbation of Rheumatoid arthritis due to inadequate treatment
190.explanation:
Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome):

  • It consists of conjunctivitis, urethritis (or, in females-cervicitis), arthritis, and characteristic mucocutaneous lesions.
  • It occurs in 1-2% of cases of NGU, develops after 1-4 weeks after genital infection.
  • Men are more frequently affected than women (10:1).
  • It is the most common cause of peripheral inflammatory arthritis in young men.
  • Knee, ankle, small joints of feet and sacroiliac joints are commonly affected.
  • Most of the patients possess HLA-B27 haplotype.
  • Mechanism: It is an immune-mediated inflammatory response to an infection at a distant site. C. trachomatis may act as a trigger organism to initiate an aberrant hyperreactive immune response that can produce inflammation of the targeted joints in genetically predisposed individuals.
  • Resolution usually occurs without specific treatment, but relapse is common.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 768

190.question_text: Which is a typical example of second-set rejection?
190.option_b: Revascularization (day 3-7) → cellular infiltration (day 7-8) → decreased vascularization (day 7-10) → necrosis (day 10-12) → rejection (by day 12-14)
190.option_c: In-complete revascularization (day 1-2) → cellular infiltration (day 3-4) → thrombosis and necrosis (day 5-6) → rejection (by day 6)
190.option_d: Decreased vascularization (day 3-7) → Revascularization (day 7-10) → necrosis (day 10-12) → rejection (by day 12-14)
190.explanation:
• Autograft Acceptance: When a skin graft is transplanted to the same individual at a different site, revascularization takes place by day 3-7; followed by healing (within day 7-10) and then resolution and acceptance of the graft (by day 12-14).
  • First-set Rejection: When an allograft is placed for the first time from a donor to a recipient, the type of primary graft rejection that develops is known as first-set rejection. The skin first becomes revascularized between days 3 and 7; as the reaction develops, the vascularized transplant becomes infiltrated with lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and other inflammatory cells There is decreased vascularization of the transplanted tissue by 7-10 days, visible necrosis by 10 days, and complete rejection by 12-14 days.
  • Second-set Rejection If, in a recipient who has rejected a graft by the first set response, another graft from the same donor is transplanted, it will be rejected in an accelerated fashion. Though vascularization starts but is soon interrupted by the inflammatory response Necrosis sets in early and the graft sloughs off by the sixth day.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 215

190.question_text: True statement about negative staining is:
190.option_a: The structure to be demonstrated is stained
190.option_b: The structure to be demonstrated is not stained
190.option_d: The background and structure are stained
190.explanation: Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 2, Pg 12

190.question_text: Which of the following antibody has Pentameric structure?

190.question_text:
True or false:
a. Botryomycosis is caused by cutaneous fungi.
b. Endocarditis in IV drug abusers is most commonly caused by S. Epidermidis
c. Left sided native valve endocarditis is most commonly caused by S. Aureus
d. Honey coloured crusts are seen in impetigo.

Right sided valve endocarditis is caused by staph aureus.

190.question_text: VRSA and VISA are respectively due to:
190.option_a: vanA gene and cell wall thickness
190.option_c: Both due to cell wall thickness
190.option_d: vanA gene and there is no term like VISA
190.explanation:
• Erroneous and overuse of vancomycin has led to the emergence of resistance to vancomycin. It may be of low-grade resistance, known as VISA (vancomycin intermediate S. aureus) or high-grade resistance, known as VRSA (vancomycin-resistant S. aureus).
  • VRSA is mediated by van A gene; whereas VISA is due to increase in cell wall thickness of S. aureus. The van A gene is believed to be acquired from a vancomycin-resistant strain of Enterococcus faecalis by horizontal conjugal transfer
  • Treatment of VRSA should be based on an antimicrobial susceptibility report. Linezolid, telavancin, daptomycin and quinupristin/dalfopristin are the effective drugs.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 518

190.question_text: What type of clostridial wound infection involves muscle invasion and the formation of gas in the muscle compartment?
190.explanation:
• Anaerobic myositis (gas gangrene): This condition involves invasion of muscle tissue, leading to gas formation in the muscle compartment and significant toxin release, resulting in severe symptoms.

Why Not Others:

  • Simple wound contamination: This infection involves surface contamination without underlying tissue invasion, thus not causing muscle issues.
  • Anaerobic cellulitis: Characterized by involvement of the fascial plane with minimal toxin release and no muscle invasion, differentiating it from gas gangrene.
  • Chronic wound infection: This term is too broad and does not specifically describe the muscle invasion and gas formation characteristic of gas gangrene.

Key Takeaway: Anaerobic myositis, or gas gangrene, is marked by muscle invasion, gas formation in the muscle, and significant toxin release, leading to severe clinical manifestations.

Tags: inicet 2022

Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-53, pp-529.

190.question_text: The operating temperature in an ethylene oxide sterilizer is:
190.explanation:
• ETO is a colorless gas that is flammable and explosive.
  • The four essential parameters (operational ranges) are:
    • Gas concentration (450 to 1200 mg/l);
    • Temperature (37 to 63°C);
    • Relative humidity (40 to 80%)(water molecules carry ETO to reactive sites); and
    • Exposure time (1 to 6 hours)

Reference: Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities (2008)

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3 , Pg 28-29

190.question_text: Heat labile surgical instruments can be best sterilized by:
190.explanation:
• 70% isopropyl alcohol is by far better at killing bacteria and viruses than 90% isopropyl alcohol. As a disinfectant, the higher the concentration of alcohol, the less effective it is at killing pathogens. Coagulation of surface proteins proceeds at a slower pace, thereby allowing the alcohol to enter the cell.
  • Nonionizing radiation like infrared and ultraviolet radiations are quite lethal but do not penetrate glass, dirt films, water (250-300 nm wavelength for 30 min) They are used for sterilization of clean surfaces in operation theatres, laminar flow hoods as well as for water treatment.
  • Chlorine releasing compounds are usually corrsive to metal surgical instruments.
  • Heat labile instruments for use in the surgical procedures can be best sterilized by Ethylene oxide gas.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3 , Pg 31-33

190.question_text: Which sterilization agent is commonly used for heat-sensitive materials and requires a gas chamber for application?
190.explanation:
Ethylene Oxide Sterilization

Ethylene oxide is a gaseous agent specifically used for sterilizing heat-sensitive materials. It effectively penetrates various materials, allowing for sterilization without high temperatures.

Key Points:

  • Gaseous Agent: Ethylene oxide is effective in reaching areas that heat cannot.
  • Heat-Sensitive Materials: Ideal for items that would be damaged by traditional sterilization methods, such as plastics and delicate instruments.

190.question_text: Which of the following is true about ethylene oxide (ETO) sterilization?
190.option_a: ETO sterilization requires high temperatures and pressures
190.option_b: ETO is a gas that can penetrate complex items and packaging
190.option_c: ETO is ineffective against spores and bacteria
190.option_d: ETO sterilization is typically used for sterilizing non-metallic items only
190.explanation:
• Option A: Incorrect because ETO sterilization operates at lower temperatures and pressures compared to autoclaving.
  • Option B: Correct because ETO is a gas that can penetrate complex items and packaging, making it suitable for items that cannot withstand high temperatures.
  • Option C: Incorrect because ETO is effective against spores and bacteria.
  • Option D: Incorrect as ETO can be used for both metallic and non-metallic items, including complex and heat-sensitive items.

Ethylene Oxide (ETO) Sterilization

Definition:

Ethylene oxide (ETO) sterilization is a chemical method used to sterilize heat-sensitive and moisture-sensitive medical and industrial equipment by using ethylene oxide gas to kill microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

Operation:

  • Process: Items are placed in a sealed chamber, and ethylene oxide gas is introduced, penetrating the items and disrupting the DNA of microorganisms.
  • Conditions:
    • Temperature: 37°C to 63°C (98.6°F to 145.4°F)
    • Humidity: 40% to 80%
    • Exposure Time: 1 to 6 hours
    • Post-Sterilization: Aeration to remove residual gas.

Uses:

  • Medical Equipment: Sterilizing plastics, electronics, and delicate instruments.
  • Pharmaceuticals: Sterilizing sensitive drugs and materials.

Advantages:

  • Versatility: Effective for materials unsuitable for heat or steam sterilization.
  • Penetration: ETO gas penetrates complex assemblies and packaging for thorough sterilization.

Disadvantages:

  • Toxicity: ETO is toxic and carcinogenic, requiring careful handling.
  • Long Process: Longer sterilization cycle compared to autoclaving; items must be aerated to remove residual gas.

Key Takeaway:

Key takeaways :

ETO sterilization is essential for items that are sensitive to heat and moisture. Safety protocols are critical due to the toxic nature of ethylene oxide.

Tags : good to know

Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). (2020). Sterilization and Disinfection. Retrieved from CDC - Sterilization and Disinfection

  • Option D: Incorrect because 100°C and 2 atm pressure do not apply to ETO sterilization.

Ethylene Oxide (ETO) Sterilization

Definition: Ethylene oxide (ETO) sterilization is a method used to sterilize heat-sensitive and moisture-sensitive medical and industrial equipment. It utilizes ethylene oxide gas to kill microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi, through a process of chemical sterilization.

Operation:

  • Process: Items to be sterilized are placed in a sealed chamber where ethylene oxide gas is introduced. The gas penetrates the items and disrupts the DNA of microorganisms, effectively killing them.
  • Conditions: The typical conditions for ETO sterilization include a temperature range of 37°C to 63°C (98.6°F to 145.4°F), relative humidity of 40% to 80%, and exposure times ranging from 1 to 6 hours. The process also includes a post-sterilization aeration phase to remove residual gas.
  • Uses:
  • Medical Equipment: Sterilizing items that cannot withstand high temperatures, such as plastics, electronics, and delicate instruments.
  • Pharmaceuticals: Sterilizing certain drugs and other sensitive materials.

Advantages:

  • Versatility: Effective for a wide range of materials and items that cannot be sterilized by heat or steam.
  • Penetration: Ethylene oxide gas can penetrate complex assemblies and packaging materials, ensuring thorough sterilization.

Disadvantages:

  • Toxicity: Ethylene oxide is toxic and carcinogenic, requiring careful handling and proper ventilation.
  • Long Process: The sterilization cycle is longer compared to other methods like autoclaving, and items must be aerated after sterilization to remove residual gas.

KEY TAKE AWAY: the most common temperature used for standard ETO sterilization cycles is around 55°C to 60°C (131°F to 140°F).

190.question_text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the process of bacterial transformation?

190.option_b: Transformation is the process where free DNA from one bacterium is taken up by another bacterium, as demonstrated by Griffith's experiment with pneumococcus
190.option_c: Transformation occurs when bacteriophages transfer DNA between bacteria
190.option_d: Transformation is the process of injecting purified DNA into the nucleus of a bacterial cell
190.explanation:
• Option A describes conjugation, not transformation. Conjugation involves the transfer of plasmids through a sex pilus.
  • Option B accurately describes transformation, where free DNA from one bacterium is incorporated into another bacterium. Griffith's experiment with pneumococcus demonstrated this by showing how non-capsulated bacteria could gain the ability to produce a capsule from dead, capsulated bacteria.
  • Option C describes transduction, where bacteriophages mediate DNA transfer between bacteria.
  • Option D describes transfection, a process where purified DNA is introduced into a bacterial cell, but this is not the same as transformation.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Transformation is a process where bacteria take up free DNA from their environment and incorporate it into their genome, as demonstrated by Griffith's experiment.

190.question_text: Which microorganism is commonly used as a biological indicator for monitoring the effectiveness of steam sterilization in autoclaves?

Biological Indicators for Steam Sterilization

  1. Bacillus stearothermophilus as a Biological Indicator:
    • Common Choice: This microorganism is the primary biological indicator for steam sterilization processes.
    • Heat Resistance: Its spores are highly resistant to heat, making them ideal for validating the effectiveness of the autoclaving process.
  2. Purpose of Using Resistant Spores:
    • Survivability: Bacillus stearothermophilus spores withstand steam sterilization conditions (typically 121°C for 15-20 minutes).
    • Assurance of Efficacy: If these spores are killed, it confirms that other microorganisms are also likely destroyed.
  3. Process Verification:
    • Post-Cycle Incubation: After sterilization, the biological indicator is incubated to check for microbial growth.
    • Success Indicator: No growth indicates a successful steam sterilization process.
  4. Alternative Microorganisms:
    • Other Options: While Bacillus subtilis may be used for different sterilization methods, Bacillus stearothermophilus is specifically suited for steam sterilization due to its superior heat resistance.

Key Takeaway:

Bacillus stearothermophilus is the standard biological indicator used to verify the effectiveness of steam sterilization processes in autoclaves due to its high resistance to heat.

Reference: Shastri A. Review of Microbiology and Immunology. 4th Edition. Chapter: Sterilization and Disinfection.

  • This is done by using normal saline as diluent. Distilled water is never used as it is irritant.
  • Once reconstituted; it has to be administered within 1 hour Administration of BCG:0.1 mL (0.1 mg TU) of BCG vaccine is administered above the insertion of left deltoid by intradermal route, using a 26-gauge tuberculin syringe.
  • BCG is directly given to the newborn soon after birth. If not given at birth it can be given later, maximum up to 1 years.

190.question_text: Which of the following is known as Johne's bacilli?

190.question_text:
A 20 year old girl presented to the OPD with complaints of night sweats, fever for 2 weeks. She has lost around 10 kgs since the past 6 months. Her vitals are as follows-

Her sputum is sent for diagnosis and an investigation called CBNAAT is performed.

Which of the following is/are true about CBNAAT?
1. It has the lowest turnaround time
2. It is a type of liquid media
3. It is based on real time PCR
4. It detects antibodies against M.TB
5. It is used for diagnosis of latent TB
6. It also detects rifampicin sensitivity
190.explanation:
• Chip based nucleic acid amplification test, CBNAAT is a real time PCR test.
  • It has the lowest turnaround time (2 hours) among all the diagnostic methods currently available for TB
  • Principle: It is based on real-time PCR technique; It simultaneously detects:
    1. MTB complex DNA, and
    2. Rifampicin resistance (mutations of the rpoB gene).
  • Tests like tuberculin test and Interferon gamma release assay are used for the diagnosis of latent TB
  • Liquid media used for the diagnosis of TB are Kirchner's and Middlebrook 7H9 medium.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 629

190.question_text: A microbiologist is about to run a polymerase chain reaction assay on the specimen of a patient suspected to have TB. He wishes to ensure specificity by using 2 sets of primer. Which of the following PCR should he perform?
190.explanation:
Nested PCR: It is modification of PCR, where two rounds of PCR amplification are carried out by using two primers that are targeted against two different DNA sequences of the same organism.

  • The amplified products of the first round PCR are subjected to another round of amplification using a second primer which targets the same organism but a different DNA sequence.
  • More sensitive: Double round of amplification yields a high quantity of DNA.
  • More specific: Use of two primers targeting two regions of DNA of the same organisms makes the test more specific.
  • Application: Nested PCR is used for detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (targeting IS6110 gene) in samples.
  • Disadvantage: There is more chance of contamination of the PCR tubes, which may lead to false-positive results.

Real-time pcr (rt-PCR): It is based on PCR technology, which is used to amplify and simultaneously detect or quantify a targeted DNA molecule on a real-time basis.

Reverse transcriptase real-time PCR formats can detect and quantify RNA molecules of the test organism in the sample on a real-time basis.

Multiplex PCR: It uses more than one primer which can detect many DNA sequences of several organisms in one reaction.

  • Syndromic approach: Multiplex PCR is useful for the diagnosis of the infectious diseases that are caused by more than one organism.
  • For example, for the etiological diagnosis of pyogenic meningitis, different primers targeting the common agents of pyogenic meningitis, such as pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae can be added simultaneously in the same reaction tube.
  • Contamination issues: There is a risk of the reaction tubes being contaminated with environmental DNA.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 47

190.question_text: Stain used to demonstrate fungal elements are?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Methenamine silver stain (Gomori's methenamine silver stain) is a histochemical stain specifically designed to demonstrate fungal elements in tissue sections.

The stain reacts with polysaccharides in the fungal cell wall, depositing black silver precipitate that clearly outlines fungal structures against a green background.

This method is particularly valuable for detecting fungi in tissue biopsies as it provides excellent contrast and can identify even non-viable fungi. It's considered the gold standard for histopathological diagnosis of invasive fungal infections including aspergillosis, mucormycosis, and pneumocystis.

Gomori methenamine silver stain showing Several fungal colonies are present in the lung. Hyphae show radial organization. The fungi often invade blood vessels.

Explanation of other options:

Acid fast stain (Option A): It is used for Mycobacterium species and Nocardia, not fungi. The acid-fast stain highlights acid-fast bacilli by coloring them red, but it is not useful for fungal elements.

Gabbet's stain (Option B): A modification of Ziehl-Neelsen stain for tuberculosis, not fungal staining

Leifson & Ryu's stain (Option D): This is a staining method for bacteria, especially to highlight flagella in bacterial samples, and it is not used to stain fungal elements.

Key Takeaways:

Detection Methods for Fungi:

190.question_text: An anxious mother bought her 6 year old daughter with complaints of passing loose bulky stools for the past 16 days associated with abdominal pain. On stool examination the following result was obtained on iodine mount. Identify the causative organism.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of G.lamblia infection because of significant history of loose bulky stools and iodine mount shows tetra nucleate oval cyst.

Giardiasis is caused by Giardia lamblia, also known as G. intestinalis or G. duodenalis.

Clinical course of giardiasis can be divided into three stages:

  1. Asymptomatic carriers: Most infected persons are asymptomatic, harbor the cysts in the gut and spread the infection.
  2. Acute giardiasis: Incubation period varies from 1 week to 3 weeks. Common symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, belching, flatus and vomiting Fatty diarrhea (steatorrhea): Diarrhea is often foul smelling with fat, cellular exudate and mucus but no blood.

Giardia is an important cause of traveller's diarrhea.

  1. Chronic giardiasis: It may present with or without a previous acute symptomatic episode with GI symptoms: Include recurrent episodes of foul smelling diarrhea, foul flatus, sulfurous belching with rotten egg taste, and profound weight loss leading to growth retardation Extraintestinal manifestations have been described, such as urticaria, arthritis, anterior uveitis, salt and pepper retinal changes.

190.question_text: Which of the following E. coli strains is most commonly associated with gastroenteritis in children, particularly in developing countries?
190.explanation:
• Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC): Correct - Leading cause of gastroenteritis in children in developing countries. ETEC produces heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins, which cause watery diarrhea by stimulating electrolyte and water loss in the intestines. It is particularly problematic in children due to poor sanitation and limited access to clean water.

Why Not Others:

  • EAEC: More commonly causes persistent diarrhea in malnourished children but is less prevalent than ETEC in acute cases.
  • EIEC: Causes dysentery-like illness but is less commonly associated with childhood gastroenteritis in developing nations.
  • EHEC: Associated with bloody diarrhea and severe complications like HUS, rarely seen in gastroenteritis in developing countries.

Key Takeaway:

Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is the most common cause of gastroenteritis in children in developing countries, primarily due to its production of enterotoxins that cause watery diarrhea.

190.question_text: Cystine lactose enzyme deficient medium CLED is preferred over McConkey agar in UTI because:
190.option_b: Selective medium and differentiates between LF and LNF
190.option_d: Promotes growth of Candida and Staphylococcus spp.
190.explanation:
A) Prevents swarming of Proteus is the correct answer.

Cystine Lactose Electrolyte Deficient (CLED) medium is preferred over McConkey agar in urinary tract infection (UTI) testing for the following reasons:

  1. Prevents swarming of Proteus:
    • Proteus species can swarm on agar plates, which means they exhibit rapid and extensive movement across the surface of the medium, making it difficult to interpret bacterial growth and colony characteristics.
    • CLED agar contains less agar than MacConkey agar and lacks the specific nutrients that support swarming. This inhibits the swarming behaviour of Proteus, allowing for better visualization and identification of other urinary pathogens.

B) Selective medium and differentiates between LF and LNF (Lactose Fermenters and Non-Lactose Fermenters):

  • CLED medium is not primarily a selective medium but a differential one. It allows for the differentiation between lactose-fermenting bacteria (LF) and non-lactose fermenters (LNF) based on the colour change of colonies.
  • McConkey agar is also a differential medium that can differentiate between LF and LNF based on the colour change and the ability to ferment lactose, but it's more commonly used for testing the ability to ferment lactose in enteric bacteria.

C) Promotes growth of Pseudomonas spp.:

  • CLED medium is not specific for promoting the growth of Pseudomonas species. Pseudomonas species have specific growth requirements that are not met by CLED agar.

D) Promotes growth of Candida and Staphylococcus spp.:

  • CLED medium is not intended for promoting the growth of Candida or Staphylococcus species. It is primarily used for culturing and differentiating urinary pathogens, especially Enterobacteriaceae.

In summary, CLED medium is preferred over McConkey agar in UTI testing mainly because it prevents the swarming behaviour of Proteus species, allowing for better identification and differentiation of other urinary pathogens.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition pg 29

190.question_text: Ramesh, a young engineer presented to the ENT OPD with complaints of bilateral nasal obstruction. Suresh, who is his roommate, says that there is a foul smelling discharge from Ramesh's nose, which baffles him since he cannot smell anything. On external examination, the nose is hardened and has a 'woody feel', as shown in the image below. Anterior rhinoscopy shows excessive crusting in both nasal cavities. On removing the crusts, the ENT resident observes wide roomy cavities. Ramesh undergoes an RT-PCR test for COVID-19, which is negative. Based on this history, the doctor orders a biopsy, whose findings reveal 'Miculicz cells'. Which of the following bacteria would you expect to see in the specimen?
190.explanation:
The above clinical vignette, with features of granulomatous diseases of the nose points towards Rhinoscleroma,caused by Klebsiella Rhinoscleromatis. A patient will typically present in 3 stages-

Stage 1- Atrophic- showing typical features of atrophic rhinitis (merciful anosmia, excessive nasal crusting and nasal obstruction and wide roomy cavities.)

Stage 2- Granulomatous- characterised by woody nose/hebra nose.

Stage 3- Cicatricial- presenting as a Tapir shaped nose.

On HPE, characteristic Russel bodies(Plasma cell inclusions) and Mikulicz cells(phagocytized bacteria ) are seen.

Treatment for Rhinoscleroma includes Rifampicin/Tetracycline/Streptomycin/Ciprofloxacin for 6weeks+ Steroids to reduce fibrosis.

Klebsiella ozaenae causes Primary atrophic rhinitis, which does not cause external nasal deformities as in the question above.

Serratia Marcescens is a normal soil saprophyte releasing a non-diffusing red pigment called Prodigiosin, which causes nosocomial UTI and Pneumonia. Due to its red pigment, it leads to pseudohemoptysis.

Klebsiella oxytoca is also implicated in nosocomial infections.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 614.

190.question_text: An 18-year girl was playing in a slowly moving stream when she cut her foot on a sharp object. Three days later, she was brought to the emergency room because of pain and swelling at the site of the wound and drainage of pus from it. The most likely cause of the infection is
190.explanation:
• Vibrio vulnificus: Cutaneous Infection Apart from sepsis, V. vulnificus can also cause primary wound infection (Vulnificus is Latin word for "wound maker"). Characterized by painful erythematous swelling or cellulitis or even vesicular, bullous or necrotic lesions. It generally affects people without underlying disease, in contrast to sepsis, which is usually observed in patients with underlying disease such as liver disease, iron overload or immunosuppression.
  • Wound infections can also be produced by Vibrio parahaemolyticus. Other options are less likely in comparison to vibrio vulnificus to cause wound infection.

190.question_text: A 61-year-old person reactive to HIV, presented with altered mental status, seizures, neck stiffness, fever, photophobia and myalgia. On investigations, the CD4 count was 196/microliter. Negative staining was used for CSF specimens which demonstrated refractile capsules around round budding yeast cells and white mucoid colonies were obtained on SDA at 37°C. All of the following tests are used to confirm the likely organism except:

Cryptococcosis is most likely the diagnosis in this patient. The points towards the diagnosis are: CSF specimens examined by negative staining for direct demonstration showed refractile capsules around round budding yeast cells, white mucoid colonies on SDA and CD4 count less than 200/microliter in HIV is a risk factor for cryptococcosis.

Confirmation of Cryptococcus species is made by:

  • Niger seed agar and bird seed agar: They are used to demonstrate melanin production (brown colored colonies).
  • Growth at 37°C.
  • The Urease test is positive.

190.question_text: Reidel-Walker co-efficient is related with:
190.explanation:
Phenol coefficient (Rideal Walker) test:

  • It is determined by the dilution of the test disinfectant to sterilize the suspension of Salmonella Typhi in a given time divided by the dilution of phenol (standard disinfectant) to sterilizes the suspension in the same time.
  • Phenol coefficient of > 1 is taken as satisfactory.
  • Disadvantages:
    • Only the phenolic disinfectants can be assessed
    • It does not evaluate the disinfectant ability to act in presence of organic matter.

190.question_text: All of the following are the tests to assess the efficiency of disinfectant EXCEPT:
190.explanation:
Hugh Leifson test is used to differentiate micrococci from staphylococci.

  1. Phenol coefficient (Rideal Walker) test:
    • It is determined by the dilution of the test disinfectant to sterilize the suspension of Salmonella Typhi in a given time divided by the dilution of phenol (standard disinfectant) to sterilize the suspension in the same time.
    • Phenol coefficient of > 1 is taken as satisfactory.
    • Disadvantages:
      • Only the phenolic disinfectants can be assessed
      • It does not evaluate the disinfectant ability to act in presence of organic matter.
  2. Chick Martin test (Modified rideal and walker test):
    • Here the disinfectants are tested in the presence of organic matter (e.g. dried yeast, feces, etc.) to simulate the natural conditions.
  3. Capacity (Kelsey-Sykes) test:
    • It assesses the capacity of a disinfectant to retain its activity when repeatedly used microbiologically.
  4. In-use (Kelsey and Maurer) test:
    • It determines whether the test disinfectant is effective in actual use in hospital practice.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3, Pg 31-33

After 48 h, he had a sudden onset of painless watery diarrhea that quickly became voluminous and was followed by vomiting. He vomits if he eats or drinks anything.
