190.question_text:
A 25-year old Sindhi woman with repeated episodes of jaundice and fatigue presented with chief complaints of pain in her left knee joint and fever for 3 days. On eliciting further history, she revealed having an acute ischemic stroke at age 5 years and has received monthly, simple red cell transfusions since the stroke. Her last transfusion was approximately four months ago. Her vitals are as follows- temperature- 99.8° C, pulse - 112 bpm and RR-19/min. On examination, the patient is icteric.local examination of the left knee joint reveals a warm, tender and painful to touch knee joint with restricted range of motion. Her blood counts are as follows-
Hb- 7.5g/dl
WBC 9300/mm3
Platelets- 202,000/mm3
Hct- 24%
S. bilirubin - 2.3mg/dL
Indirect bilirubin- 1.2 mg/dL
Hb electrophoresis- 92%
HbS, 6%
HbF, 2%
HbA2
The doctor suspects that the patient's underlying haematological disorder has precipitated an episode of acute osteomyelitis. Which of the following bacteria is most commonly implicated in acute osteomyelitis when the patient suffers with such anemias?
190.explanation:
Patients with underlying hemoglobinopathies, such as sickle cell disease, are at increased risk of developing osteomyelitis, especially caused by Salmonella spp. Here's why:

  • Patients with sickle cell disease, like the patient described, are prone to vaso-occlusive crises, which can lead to ischemia in various tissues, including the bone.
  • Salmonella spp. is known to have a predilection for bones and joints in patients with sickle cell disease. This predilection is attributed to the impaired blood flow in the bone, making it more susceptible to infection.
  • Salmonella osteomyelitis is a well-recognized complication in patients with hemoglobinopathies, and it often involves long bones, such as the femur and tibia.
  • Staphylococcus aureus (Option B) is a common cause of osteomyelitis, but in the context of sickle cell disease, Salmonella spp. is more commonly implicated.
  • Eikenella spp. (Option C) and Pseudomonas (Option D) are less commonly associated with osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease.

Therefore, in a patient with sickle cell disease and acute osteomyelitis, Salmonella spp. (Option A) is the most commonly implicated bacteria, as it has a particular propensity for causing bone and joint infections in these individuals.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 406.

190.question_text: A 30 year old male developed arthritis type knee pain 7 months after an episode of dysentery with Shigella. A diagnosis of reactive arthritis was made. Which HLA is commonly associated with this syndrome?

The clinical features include early morning arthritis, ocular inflammation and urethritis, classically remembered as can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree.

HLAB54 is associated with Behcet's disease and HLADR04 with Rheumatoid arthritis.

190.question_text: What is the primary route of transmission for Shigella infections?
190.explanation:
• Contaminated food and water: Correct - Shigella primarily spreads through the ingestion of food or water contaminated with fecal matter. This often occurs in areas with poor sanitation, where water sources may be contaminated. It can also spread through food prepared by infected individuals who do not practice proper hand hygiene.

Why Not Others:

  • Airborne droplets: Incorrect - Shigella is not transmitted through the air; its transmission requires close contact with an infected person or contaminated material.
  • Direct contact with contaminated surfaces: Incorrect - While contact with surfaces contaminated with Shigella (such as toys or bathroom fixtures) can facilitate transmission, this is typically secondary to oral ingestion of contaminated food or water. Proper sanitation can mitigate this risk.
  • Insect bites: Incorrect - Shigella is not transmitted through insects; it requires human-to-human or fecal-oral transmission routes, emphasizing the importance of hygiene in preventing infections.

Key Takeaway:

Shigella infections are primarily transmitted through contaminated food and water, highlighting the importance of sanitation and hygiene in preventing outbreaks.

Tags: Fmge 2020

Tag Line: EASY

Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher, Chapter 41, pp 404

Manjeet, a 6-year-old boy, presented with mild fever, lethargy and flu-like symptoms since past few days. His past history was suggestive of Sickle Cell Disease. His laboratory parameters were as follows:

190.question_text: A 6-month old baby was brought with a severe diaper rash. The parents gave a history of recurrent infections since birth. This time the baby was brought to hospital having a rash with centripetal distribution and of different stages. The biopsy of the thymus showed remnants of Hassall's corpuscles. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
190.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). The biopsy of the thymus showing remnants of Hassall's corpuscles indicates it is due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. SCID is a defect in both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.

Affected infants present with prominent thrush (oral candidiasis), extensive diaper rash, and failure to thrive. Some patients develop a morbilliform rash shortly after birth because maternal T cells are transferred across the placenta and attack the fetus, causing graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including:

  • Candida albicans
  • Pneumocystis jiroveci
  • Pseudomonas
  • Cytomegalovirus
  • Varicella

There are 2 types of SCID based on inheritance:

  1. X-linked SCID is the most common form and hence it is more common in boys than in girls. The genetic defect is the mutation in the common y-chain (yc) subunit of cytokine receptors. Tcell numbers are greatly reduced, and although B cells may be normal in number, antibody synthesis is impaired because of the lack of T-cell help. The thymus contains lobules of undifferentiated epithelial cells resembling fetal thymus.
  2. Autosomal recessive is most commonly caused due to deficiency of the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). The deficiency of ADA leads to the accumulation of deoxyadenosine and its derivatives (e.g., deoxy-ATP). They are toxic to rapidly dividing immature lymphocytes, especially those of the T-cell lineage. Hence, there may be a greater reduction in the number of T lymphocytes. In the two most common forms (yc mutation and ADA deficiency), the thymus is small and devoid of lymphoid cells. In SCID caused by ADA deficiency, remnants of Hassall's corpuscles can be found.

Note: X-linked SCID is the first human disease in which gene therapy has been successful.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 208

190.question_text:
A 27 year old female patient was rushed to ER for high fever and shortness of breath. Her symptoms started a week before presentation with diarrhea followed by high-grade fever for three days. She has a recent history of traveling to Phuket for her honeymoon 3 weeks before. Her husband has no symptoms. On clinical examination: bilateral crepitations were heard. She also had skin ulcers as shown in the photo

What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
190.explanation:
The above clinical scenario is most likely suggestive of melioidosis.

Points in favour of diagnosis are:

Travel history, skin ulcers and pneumonia-like picture. Presence of purple wrinkled colonies on Ashdown media also aids in diagnosis.

  • Melioidosis can present with an array of manifestations (hence called as 'great mimicker');
  • Grouped into four types of clinical presentations:
  • Acute, localized infection: Presents as localized nodule, fever, general muscle aches, and may progress rapidly to infect the bloodstream
  • Sub-acute (Pulmonary) infection: Ranges from mild bronchitis to severe tuberculosis-like pneumonia with cellulitis and lymphangitis.
  • Acute bloodstream infection: Seen in patients with underlying illness such as HIV, renal failure and diabetes and presents as septicemia (septic shock) with metastatic pus-filled skin lesions and disorientation.
  • Chronic suppurative infection forming abscesses: Involves various organs such as joints, viscera, lymph nodes, skin, brain, liver, lung, bones, and spleen.
  • Incubation period may range from 2 days to many years. Some cases may have long latency; presented long time after the exposure; hence melioidosis is also known as 'Vietnam time-bomb disease'. B. pseudomallei is the causative agent of melioidosis.
  • Habitat: B. pseudomallei is a saprophyte of soil and water and has a large number of animal reservoirs. Melioidosis also occurs in rats, rabbits and guinea pigs.
  • Mode of transmission: Humans and animals are infected by various routes such as inoculation, inhalation, aspiration or ingestion.
  • Virulence factors:B. pseudomallei is perhaps the most virulent among the non-fermenters. Several virulence factors are described such as polysaccharide capsule, lipopolysaccharide, toxins, enzymes and proteins (such as hemolysin, lipases and proteases)
  • Ashdown's medium is used as a selective medium, where it produces wrinkled purple colonies

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 644

A 63 year old diabetic patient presents with following clinical picture:

What is the most likely diagnosis?

The photo is indicative of Necrotizing otitis externa known as malignant otitis externa.

It is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Ear infections:

For infections caused by Pseudomonas, remember:

'BE PSEUDo'

190.question_text:
A 9 year old girl came to your OPD with complaints of:
i. Itchiness in the ear
ii. Pain
iii. Trouble hearing
iv. Pus draining out of the ear
She has a habit of putting keys in her ear.
On external examination the ear appeared as shown in the figure:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
Swimmer's ear, which has the medical name of otitis externa, is an infection in your ear canal.

Usually, swimmer's ear is caused by bacteria (mcc: pseudomonas), but it can sometimes be brought on by a virus or fungus.

Symptoms are:

  • Itchiness in the ear
  • Pain, which can become severe
  • Trouble hearing (sound may seem muffled as your ear canal swells)
  • Fluid or pus draining out of the ear

Common reasons to get swimmer's ear are:

  • Sticking stuff in your ear.
  • Moisture trapped in your ear.
  • Humid weather and sweat can cause the same problem.
  • While swimmer's ear can happen to anyone, it's most common in kids and early teenagers.
  • Narrow ear canals. Kids often have ear canals that are small and don't drainas well as it does in adults.
  • Skin reactions and conditions.

Ear infections by Pseudomonas:

The infections are either mild, such as Swimmer’s ear (among children) or serious necrotizing form designated as malignant otitis externa (in elderly diabetic patients).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 643

190.question_text:
A 2nd degree deep burn patient on the 3rd day of admission had the following clinical picture.

Identify the selective media for its causative organism
190.explanation:
Burn infection in the photo appears to be greenish yellow. The most common cause of burn wound infections is Pseudomonas. They secrete pyocyanin and pyoverdin leading to the colour of the wound.

For infections caused by pseudomonas, remember:

'BE PSEUDO'

  • Burns
  • Endocarditis
  • Pneumonia
  • Sepsis
  • External malignant otitis
  • UTI
  • Diabetic osteomyelitis

Culture media for pseudomonas:

  • Peptone water: Pseudomonas forms uniform turbidity with a surface pellicle formation, due to more oxygen tension at surfaces Nutrient agar: It produces large, opaque, irregular colonies with a metallic sheen.
  • Pigments: Most strains produce diffusible pigments which are either blue-green (pyocyanin), or yellow green (pyoverdine). Some strains are nonpigmented Mostly colonies of Pseudomonas have a characteristic sweet ether or alcohol-like fruity odor.
  • Blood agar: It produces β-hemolytic gray moist colonies on blood agar.
  • MacConkey agar: It produces pale non-lactose fermenting colonies.
  • Selective media such as cetrimide agar can be used to isolate the organism from mixed growth in purulent specimens.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 643

190.question_text: A 3-month-old male infant has recurrent infections. He is found to have an impaired ability to kill microbes by the positive nitroblue tetrazolium test. The most likely diagnosis is:
190.explanation:
• Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by defects in a degradative enzymes or other molecules involved in the oxidative burst.
  • Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by an inability to fuse lysosomes with phagosomes.
  • HIV/AIDS results from progressive destruction of CD4+ T cells. Although HIV can infect macrophages and dendritic cells, they remain capable of normal phagolysosome function.
  • Waldenstrüm's macroglobulinemia is caused by excessive production of IgM.

Chronic granulomatous disease

  • CGD is a genetic disease that has two forms:
    • X-linked form (more common, 70%): membrane component of phagocyte oxidase is defective.
    • Autosomal recessive form: cytoplasmic component of phagocyte oxidase is defective.
  • Inherited defects in the gene encoding NADP oxidase of phagocyte which breaks down hydrogen peroxide leads to decreased oxidative burst. This predisposes to
    • recurrent infections by catalase positive bacteria
    • inflammatory reactions that result in gingivitis, swollen lymph nodes, etc.

Diagnosis: Nitroblue tetrazolium reduction test (NBT) is positive.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

190.question_text: Seema, a mother, has brought her 10-month-old infant into the hospital. She mentions that the baby has been unwell for several weeks, starting with what she thought was a cold, with a runny nose and dry cough. However, in the past two weeks, a more definite cough has developed, and the baby has had to be kept home from Day-care. When checking the baby's history, you notice that he has not received his standard childhood immunisations. When you mention this to the Mother of the child, she states that she is very 'anti-vaccination' due to all the toxic products that are included in vaccines today. Tests confirm your suspicions that the baby has a whooping cough. What is the drug of choice for this patient?
190.explanation:
As pertussis is mainly toxin mediated, antibiotics are less useful once the infection is established.

However, they play a vital role in eliminating the bacteria from nasopharynx.

Macrolides are the drugs of choice (Azithromycin for 5 days or Erythromycin for 7-14 days).

Cotrimoxazole is recommended as an alternative in macrolide resistance or allergy. Isolation in a quiet environment may inhibit the stimulation of paroxysms. Cough suppressants are not very effective.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 640

190.question_text: A 29-year-old woman who worked as a research assistant in a veterinary microbiology laboratory complained of intermittent fever, anorexia, profuse sweating, malaise, headache, normo-tensive and muscle pain especially of the neck and shoulder, and arthralgia for 3 d. She was one of the 7 laboratory workers who were involved in a research on isolation of B. melitensis from goats for the past 6 months. Which of the following is not the mode of transmission of this organism?
190.explanation:
B.melitensis is the most pathogenic species, followed by B. abortus and B. suis. Human infection with other species is extremely rare.

Transmission: Brucellosis is zoonotic, transmitted from infected animals to man by various modes:

  • Direct contact: The most common route is direct contact of abraded skin or mucosa with the infected animal tissue, blood, urine, vaginal discharge or placenta
  • Food-borne: By ingestion of unpasteurized milk or dairy products or undercooked meat from infected animals or rarely vegetables or water contaminated with animal excreta
  • Air-borne: By inhalation of dust or aerosols in the infected cowshed or slaughterhouses
  • Person-to-person spread is extremely rare; through breast milk or by tissue transplantation or blood transfusions.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 316

190.question_text: Which of the following methods are not used for diagnosing brucellosis in animals?
190.explanation:
Brucellosis is diagnosed in animals by various methods such as: Milk ring test and Rose Bengal card test; detecting antibodies in infected milk.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 318

190.question_text: What is the WHO regimen for Brucellosis?
190.explanation:
Various regimens are recommended for the treatment of brucellosis.

  • Standard regimen in adults: Gentamicin for 7 days plus doxycycline for 6 weeks. Streptomycin can be given alternative to gentamicin.
  • WHO regimen in adults: Rifampicin for 6 weeks plus doxycycline for 6 weeks Relapse or treatment failure occurs in 5–10% of cases.
  • For CNS involvement: Ceftriaxone is added to the regimen and treatment is prolonged for 3–6 months.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 319

190.question_text: Match the correct option with the layers of a mask as shown in figure:
190.explanation:
The mask shown in figure has three layers

  1. Outer fluid repellent layer: Hydrophobic layer that can repel water, blood and body fluids.
  2. Middle filter layer: It is made up of melt-blown material; filters bacteria/viruses and also filters out the water droplets. In contrast to N95 respirator, the filter pore size of a surgical mask is not standardized.
  3. Inner hydrophilic layer: Absorbs water, sweat and spit; made up of non-woven fabric.

When using a surgical mask, the following measures should be considered:

  • Shelf-life: Disposable (single-use); should be discarded or changed after 4-6 hours of use or earlier if it becomes soiled or wet.
  • Donning: Place the mask carefully, ensuring it covers the mouth and nose, adjust to the nose bridge, and tie it securely to minimize any gaps between the face and the mask.
  • Hanging mask syndrome: Masks should not be left dangling around the neck, a common practice observed among doctors, doing so may contaminate the inner side of mask.
  • Touching the front of the mask while wearing should be avoided.
  • Mask should not be worn with beard or unshaven face.
  • Hand hygiene should be performed before donning the mask, upon touching or discarding a used mask.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 232

190.question_text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the modifications of PCR and its applications in bacterial genetics?
190.option_a: Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) is used to amplify DNA from bacteria, whereas Real-Time PCR (rt-PCR) is used for detecting fastidious microorganisms
190.option_b: Nested PCR involves a single round of amplification with two different primers to increase specificity and sensitivity, while Multiplex PCR uses multiple primers to detect different pathogens in one reaction
190.option_c: Real-Time PCR allows real-time visualization of the amplification process, providing quicker results and quantification of DNA, and is useful for detecting genetic diseases and monitoring disease progression
190.option_d: Multiplex PCR can amplify DNA from very few copies, making it useful for detecting drug resistance genes, but is not applicable for detecting uncultivable microorganisms
190.explanation:
Option A: Incorrect

  • Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) is used to amplify RNA (not DNA), especially from RNA viruses.
  • Real-Time PCR (rt-PCR) is used for real-time visualization and quantification of DNA, not specifically for detecting fastidious microorganisms.

Option B: Incorrect

  • Nested PCR involves two rounds of amplification with two sets of primers to increase specificity and sensitivity.
  • Multiplex PCR uses multiple primers to detect various pathogens in a single reaction.

Option C: Correct

  • Real-Time PCR allows real-time visualization of the amplification process.
  • It provides quicker results and quantification of DNA and is used for detecting genetic diseases and monitoring disease progression.

Option D: Incorrect

  • Multiplex PCR is used to detect multiple pathogens in one reaction.
  • Amplifying very few DNA copies is a general feature of PCR, not exclusive to multiplex PCR.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Real-Time PCR provides real-time data on the amplification process, allowing for quicker results, quantification, and applications in detecting genetic diseases and monitoring disease progression. Each PCR modification has unique applications suited to different needs in genetic analysis.

Tags: must know | neet 2020

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.). Jaypee Brothers Medical Publishers. Chapter: (PCR Techniques and Applications), Page no.43

Glutaraldehyde as a High-Level Disinfectant

190.question_text: Which of the following is not a Macrophage?
190.explanation:
• Macrophages originate from blood monocytes that leave the circulation to differentiate in different tissues.
  • There is a substantial heterogeneity among each macrophage population, which most probably reflects the required level of specialisation within the environment of any given tissue.
  • This heterogeneity is reflected in their morphology, the type of pathogens they can recognise, as well as the levels of inflammatory cytokines they produce (i.e. IL-1, IL-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha).
  • In addition, macrophages produce reactive oxygen species, such as nitric oxide, that can kill phagocytosed bacteria.The heterogeneous nature of these cells may not solely be the result of their differentiation process, but it is likely to be inherited from their monocyte precursors.
  • Macrophages migrate to and circulate within almost every tissue, patrolling for pathogens or eliminating dead cells.
  • The table below describes the location and function of a few different macrophage populations.

190.question_text: While performing the following staining for a patient presenting with leonine facies, you happen to count both live and dead bacteria per oil immersion field. Which index will you be measuring?
190.explanation:
• Bacteriological index (BI): It is based on the total number of bacilli (live and dead) seen per oil immersion field.
  • The bacteriological index (BI) is calculated by totalling the number of pluses scored in all the smears and divided by the number of smears examined.
  • Morphological index (MI): It is expressed as the percentage of uniformly stained bacilli out of the total number of bacilli counted.
  • MI is a better marker to monitor the treatment response.
  • Following clinical improvement by treatment, the MI should fall down, whereas the BI may remain the same.
  • SFG percentage (solid, fragmented granular rod percentage): Since the percentage of solid, fragmented granular rods are recorded separately, this method gives better picture of bacterial morphology and is a more sensitive indicator of monitoring the treatment response than MI

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 538

190.question_text: Which of the following is true about urease producing bacteria?
190.option_a: Urease acidifies the urine creating neutrophils inactive
190.option_b: Acidification of the urine can lead to precipitation of struvite stones
190.option_c: Morganella morganii is a urea-splitting bacteria
190.option_d: Are commensals that prevent hepatic encephalopathy
190.explanation:
• Bacterial urease alkalises urine, and urease-producing bacteria are implicated in the development of infection-induced urinary stones.
  • The formation of struvite stones occurs when urine pH increases and ammonia production increases, decreasing the solubility of phosphate.
  • Proteus spp., M. morganii and Klebsiella pneumoniae are urea-splitting bacteria
  • E.coli is the most common cause of lower urinary tract infections, it is not associated with significant alkalinisation, nor is infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  • The production of excessive amounts of ammonia by bacterial urease, and its subsequent re-absorption into the systemic circulation, can result in hyperammonaemia, a condition associated with hepatic encephalopathy.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition pg 33

190.question_text: All of the following indicates chlamydia to be a bacteria except:
190.option_c: Is susceptible to a wide range of antibacterial agents
190.explanation:
Chlamydiae were once thought to be viruses because of possessing a few viral properties, such as:

  • They are obligate intracellular.
  • They cannot be grown in artificial media.
  • Filterable - small enough to pass through bacterial filters.
  • Produce intracytoplasmic inclusions.

However, chlamydiae are now confirmed to be bacteria, because they have many other properties similar to that of bacteria, as follows:

  • Possess both DNA and RNA.
  • Their cell wall is similar to that of gram-negative bacteria (although they lack peptidoglycan layer).
  • Multiply by binary fission.
  • Susceptible to a wide range of antibacterial agents.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 766

190.question_text: Acid-fast bacilli can be stained by:
190.explanation:
Acid-fast stain: Differentiates bacteria into Acid-fast (red) and Nonacid-fast (blue) groups. It was discovered by Ehrlich and later on modified by Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) which is mot commonly used now.

  • Primary stain: ZN Carbol fuchsin (Basic fuchsin + Phenol) for 1 minute.
  • Mordant: Intermittent Heat until fumes rise from slide.
  • Decolorization: 20% H2SO4 (sulphuric acid) or acid-alcohol for 10 sec with immediate wash. Decolorizer removes the primary stain from non-acid-fast bacteria while the Acid-fast bacteria retain the primary stain due to mycolic acid in the cell wall.
  • Counter stain or Secondary stain: Methylene blue or Malachite Green or Picric acid for 30 sec.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition Chapter 2, Pg 14-15

190.question_text: Which of the following is NOT included in the composition of ZN stain:
190.explanation:
ZN stain components:

  • Primary stain: Basic fuchsin + Phenol
  • Mordant: Heat
  • Decolorizer: Sulfuric acid or acid-alcohol
  • Counter stain: Methylene blue or Malachite Green

Acid-fast stain: Differentiates bacteria into Acid-fast (red) and Non-acid-fast (blue) groups.

  • Primary stain: ZN Carbol fuchsin (Basic fuchsin + Phenol) for 1 minute.
  • Mordant: Intermittent Heat until fumes rise from slide.
  • Decolorization: 20% H2SO4 (sulphuric acid) or acid-alcohol for 10 sec with immediate wash. Decolorizer removes the primary stain from non-acid-fast bacteria while the Acid-fast bacteria retain the primary stain due to mycolic acid in the cell wall.
  • Counter stain or Secondary stain: Methylene blue or Malachite Green or Picric acid for 30 sec.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition , Pg 14-15

190.question_text: The cytoplasmic membrane of bacteria is responsible for:
190.explanation:
Cytoplasmic membrane of bacteria act as an osmotic barrier being a semipermeable membrane.

  • Essential for survival
  • Fluid mosaic model:
    • 5-10 nm thick
    • Phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins (peripheral & integral proteins)
    • Carbohydrates attached to outer surface of plasma membrane proteins.

But many bacterial cell membrane have pentacyclic sterol like molecules called hopanoids

Functions:

  1. Semipermeable membrane: Osmotic barrier
  2. Transport system: by proteins and enzymes in cell membrane
  3. Site of metabolism: Respiration, Lipid synthesis, Cell wall synthesis, Chromosome segregation
  4. Special receptor for chemical detection in surroundings.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 19

190.question_text: Mesosomes are:
190.explanation:
• Mesosomes are invagination of plasma membrane (not cytoplasm).
  • Mesosomes are sites of bacterial respiration: have respiratory enzymes (analogous to mitochondria in eukaryotes)
  • Location: next to septa in dividing bacteria or attached to bacterial chromosome.
  • More prominent in Gram positive bacteria.

190.question_text: The bacteria which are able to grow at 0°C but which grow optimally at 10°C to 30°C, are known as

190.question_text: An 20 year-old male with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) has recurrent staphylococcal infection. What is the mechanism behind this?
190.explanation:
• Phagocytes use nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase to generate reactive species of oxygen.
  • CGD is caused by mutations resulting in loss of function in this process.
  • Neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages are unable to phagocytose bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus leading to recurrent bacterial infections.

Chronic granulomatous disease

  • CGD is a genetic disease that has two forms:
    • X-linked form (more common, 70%): membrane component of phagocyte oxidase is defective.
    • Autosomal recessive form: cytoplasmic component of phagocyte oxidase is defective.
  • Inherited defects in the gene encoding NADP oxidase of phagocyte which breaks down hydrogen peroxide leads to decreased oxidative burst. This predisposes to
    • recurrent infections by catalase positive bacteria
    • inflammatory reactions that result in gingivitis, swollen lymph nodes, etc.
  • Diagnosis: Nitroblue tetrazolium reduction test (NBT) is positive.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 19, Pg 187-190

190.question_text: Antimicrobial stewardship program is required for all the following reasons except:
190.option_c: Use of antibiotics more in humans as compared to animal industry
190.explanation:
• Antimicrobial stewardship program (AMSP) provides strategies for rationalizing the use of antimicrobials in the hospital.
  • Centers for disease control and prevention (CDC) has defined antimicrobial stewardship as use of the right antimicrobial agent, for the right patient, at the right time, with the right dose, route and frequency, causing the least harm to the patient and future patients. Why is AMSP needed? Antimicrobial stewardship program in a hospital is required for the following reasons.
    • Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR): AMR is a rising threat across the globe. The multidrug resistant organisms (MDROs) are prevalent in every country though the extent and the severity of the problem varies. Extensive use of antimicrobials is the single most important factor for the bacteria to undergo mutation, which leads bacteria to become resistant to antimicrobials and then the resistant strain flourish exponentially in the presence of selective pressure of antimicrobials.
    • Misuse and Overuse of Antimicrobials: The last eight decades since the discovery of penicillin witnessed the saving of millions of lives due to use of antimicrobials in treating infections. However, at the same time, this has also led to their misuse through various ways—(1) use without a prescription, (2) overuse for self-limiting infections, nonbacterial infections and (3) treatment of colonizer/contaminants.
    • Widespread Use of Antimicrobials in Other Sectors: World’s largest antimicrobial use occurs for animal non-therapeutic purpose (70%), followed by animal therapeutic purpose (15%). Human use accounts for only 15%.
    • Poor Antimicrobial Research: Research in the development of new antimicrobials is a huge investment for the pharmaceutical industry. More so, soon after the discovery of an antimicrobial, the bacteria develop resistance mechanisms to tackle the antimicrobial. As a result, investment goes to waste. It is also hypothesized that there could be a return to the pre-antibiotic era, where many people could suffer or die from untreatable bacterial infections.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 272

190.question_text: Which method is best suited for antibiotic sensitivity testing?

190.question_text: Pour-plate culture is primarily used for which purpose?

190.question_text: Which medium is NOT commonly used for anaerobic culture?

Media for Anaerobic Bacteria:

190.question_text: Which media is used to maintain the viability of bacteria during transport in a liquid state and is also utilized for the preservation of specimens?
190.explanation:
A) Buffered Glycerol Saline:

  • Usage: Preserves bacterial viability during transport.
  • Mechanism: Contains glycerol and buffering agents to prevent desiccation and maintain a stable ph.

B) Pike's Media:

  • Usage: Transport medium for clinical specimens, especially anaerobes.
  • Mechanism: Preserves specimen integrity for short-term transport but lacks long-term preservation capabilities.

C) Autoclaved Sea Water:

  • Usage: Transport medium for marine bacteria and Vibrio species.
  • Mechanism: Provides a saline environment but lacks buffering capacity and is not suitable for all bacterial types.

D) Mischulow's Charcoal Agar:

  • Usage: Enriched medium for culturing Bordetella pertussis and some other bacteria.
  • Mechanism: Absorbs toxins and provides nutrients for growth, not intended for transport or long-term preservation.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Buffered glycerol saline is critical for long-term specimen preservation during transport, ensuring bacterial viability. Other media serve different functions such as short-term transport or culturing specific bacteria.

190.question_text: Which specimen serves to be the best for the culture of Bordetella Pertussis?
190.explanation:
The best specimen for the culture of Bordetella pertussis is Nasopharyngeal swab (Option A). 

A) Nasopharyngeal swab (Option A):

  • Preferred method for diagnosing pertussis.
  • Targets the primary site of infection in the respiratory tract.
  • More likely to contain the bacterium Bordetella pertussis.

B) Cough plate culture (Option B):

  • Can be used but not the primary choice.
  • Requires the patient to cough into a plate to collect respiratory secretions.
  • Less reliable and may result in false-negative results if the patient is not actively coughing.

C) Per oral (Option C):

  • Not a common or recommended method for diagnosing pertussis.
  • Sample collected from the mouth is less likely to contain the bacterium.

D) Endotracheal aspirate (Option D):

  • Used when the patient is intubated or ventilated.
  • Not the first-line choice for diagnosing pertussis.
  • May be considered in specific clinical situations, such as when the patient is in critical condition and requires intubation for other reasons.

In summary, Nasopharyngeal swab (Option A) is the preferred and most reliable method for diagnosing pertussis, primarily because it targets the primary site of infection in the respiratory tract. Options B, C, and D are alternative methods, each with specific limitations and use cases.

190.question_text: Which is the highly infective stage of 100 days fever disease?
190.explanation:
100 days fever is commonly known as whooping cough caused by Bordetella Pertussis.

The clinical course of whooping cough (or pertussis or 100 days fever) passes through three stages following an incubation period of 7–10 days.

  • Catarrhal phase: It lasts for 1–2 weeks, and is characterized by common cold-like nonspecific symptoms, such as coryza, lacrimation, mild cough, low-grade fever and malaise. It is a highly infectious stage. In this stage, both smear and culture are likely to be positive .
  • Paroxysmal phase: This stage lasts for 1–6 weeks. Patients are less infectious; smear and culture may become negative. It is characterized by specific symptoms, such as whooping cough and post-tussive vomiting.
  • Convalescent stage: This stage lasts for 1–3 months. It occurs following the paroxysmal stage, during which the frequency and severity of coughing gradually decreases. Antibodies may appear in serum.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 638

190.question_text: A 19 year old college student presents with sudden onset fever, headache, vomiting, and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash. He appears confused, and his BP is measured to be 80/50 mmHg, HR 120/min, and Temp 39.5°C. On examination, he has petechiae and purpura over his lower limbs and trunk. He succumbs to his illness, and an autopsy is carried out. The gross specimen of the brain is shown below. Which of the following pathogens is the most likely cause of his condition?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely causative pathogen in a patient with features of meningitis and petechial rashes progressing to shock and a gross specimen of the brain showing pus in the subarachnoid space is Neisseria meningitidis.

  • Neisseria are aerobic, Gram-negative, nonmotile, kidney-shaped diplococci arranged in pairs.
  • They can be cultured on sheep blood agar, chocolate agar, and selective media such as Thayer-Martin agar, which contains antibiotics to inhibit commensal organisms.
  • Colonies are convex, glistening, and mucoid, measuring 1-5 mm, with species variations in pigmentation and texture.
  • In N. meningitidis, at least 13 serogroups exist, with A, B, C, X, Y, and W-135 most important in human disease.
  • The capsule, composed of polysaccharides, aids immune evasion, while outer membrane proteins (Por A, Por B) and opacity proteins (Opa) contribute to virulence by interacting with host cells.
  • Lipooligosaccharide endotoxin, especially its lipid A, causes severe toxic effects.
  • Pathogenesis begins in the nasopharynx, where organisms adhere via pili and may remain asymptomatic or progress to invasive meningococcal disease (IMD).
  • Bacteremia can lead to meningitis or meningococcemia, presenting with fever, headache, vomiting, photophobia, stiff neck, and sometimes rapid progression to coma.
  • In meningococcemia, numerous small blood vessels across various organs undergo thrombosis, accompanied by surrounding infiltration and petechial bleeding.
  • Fulminant cases may involve hemorrhagic rash, DIC, shock, and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome due to adrenal haemorrhage.
  • Lesions may also occur in the heart, joints, skin, and meninges, where thrombosis and purulent exudate develop.
  • Diagnosis involves blood and CSF cultures, Gram staining showing Gram-negative diplococci within leukocytes, and growth on selective media.
  • Serological tests measure antibodies to meningococcal polysaccharides.
  • Prevention includes vaccines targeting epidemic serogroups, chemoprophylaxis of close contacts with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone, and public health measures such as reducing crowding.

Explanation of other options:

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A): Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive spherical bacterium that typically appears in pairs or chains. Clinically, pneumococcal pneumonia begins abruptly with fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain, and bloody or rusty sputum, with bacteremia occurring in up to one-fifth of cases. Complications include empyema, meningitis, endocarditis, and septic arthritis. The presence of petechial rashes is more consistent with Neisseria meningitidis infection.

Haemophilus influenzae type B (Option B): Haemophilus influenzae type b typically spreads through the respiratory tract and can extend locally to involve the sinuses or middle ear, causing otitis media and sinusitis. It is also responsible for bronchitis and pneumonia, especially in individuals with impaired mucociliary clearance, and may lead to severe conditions such as septic arthritis, meningitis in children, or obstructive laryngotracheitis with epiglottitis.

Listeria monocytogenes (Option D): Exposure to Listeria monocytogenes in food may cause no illness or only a brief, mild febrile gastroenteritis with fever, chills, myalgia, abdominal pain, and diarrhoea, usually appearing 6-48 hours after ingestion. In immunocompromised individuals, it can progress to meningitis, meningoencephalitis, bacteremia, or rarely localised infections.

190.option_a: Crystal violet (1 min) > Gram's iodine (1 min) > acetone (2-3 seconds) > safranin (30 seconds)
190.option_b: Crystal violet (1 min) > Gram's iodine (2 mins) > acetone (20-30 seconds) > safranin (30 seconds)
190.option_c: Gram's iodine (2 mins) > Crystal violet (1 min) > acetone (20-30 seconds) > safranin (30 seconds)
190.option_d: Crystal violet (1 min) > Gram's iodine (1 min) > acetone (2-3 seconds) > basic fuchsin (2 mins)
190.explanation:
Smear is examined under oil immersion objective.

  • Gram-positive bacteria resist decolorization and retain the color of primary stain i.e. violet.
  • Gram-negative bacteria are decolorized and, therefore, take counterstain and appear pink.

Decolorization is the most crucial step of Gram staining. If the decolorizer is poured for more time, even gram-positive bacteria lose color (over decolorization) and if poured for less time, the gram-negative bacteria do not lose the color of primary stain properly (under decolorization).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 27

190.question_text: In the clinical classification of leprosy, which of the following is true for Multibacillary (MB) leprosy?
190.option_a: It is characterized by 1 to 5 skin lesions, no nerve involvement, and a negative slit-skin smear
190.option_b: It is characterized by >5 skin lesions, possible nerve involvement, or a positive slit-skin smear
190.option_c: It has no involvement of the peripheral nerves
190.option_d: It is always caused by a single skin lesion
190.explanation:
PAUCIBACILLARY VS MULTIBACILLARY

  • It is characterized by 1 to 5 skin lesions, no nerve involvement, and a negative slit-skin smear: This describes Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, not Multibacillary (MB) leprosy.
  • It is characterized by >5 skin lesions, possible nerve involvement, or a positive slit-skin smear: Correct; MB leprosy is defined by having more than 5 skin lesions, potential nerve involvement, or a positive slit-skin smear.
  • It has no involvement of the peripheral nerves: Incorrect; MB leprosy can include nerve involvement, which is a significant feature of the disease.
  • It is always caused by a single skin lesion: Incorrect; MB leprosy involves multiple skin lesions rather than just one.

Why Not Others:

  • Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy: Defined by fewer lesions and no nerve involvement, contrasting with MB leprosy.
  • Nerve involvement: A hallmark of MB leprosy, making this option inaccurate.
  • Single skin lesion: Mischaracterizes the nature of MB leprosy, which involves multiple lesions.

Key Takeaway: Multibacillary (MB) leprosy is characterized by multiple skin lesions, possible nerve involvement, or a positive slit-skin smear, indicating a more severe form of the disease.

Tags: fmge 2023

Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-54-Leprosy , pp-536.

190.question_text: What is the reason for decolourisation in gram negative bacteria in Gram staining?
190.option_a: Due to the two dyes used in staining
190.explanation:
Gram negative bacteria gets decolorized easily due to 2 reasons:

  • Thin peptidoglycan layer and less cross linking
  • Presence of lipid rich lipopolysaccharide layer which gets easily removed by decolorizer

Gram stain: Differentiates bacteria into Gram-positive (violet) and Gram-negative (pink) groups

  • Primary stain: crystal violet (or gentian violet or methyl violet) for 1 minute.
  • Mordant: Gram's iodine for 1 minute.
  • Decolorization: acetone (for 1-2 sec) or ethanol (20-30 sec) with immediate wash. Decolorizer removes the primary stain from Gram-negative bacteria due to loss of lipid layer of cell wall while the Gram-positive bacteria retain the primary stain.
  • Counterstain or Secondary stain: safranin or diluted carbol fuchsin for 30 sec.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 2, Pg 13

190.question_text: True statement in reference to Gram staining is:
190.option_a: Heating is done to promote entry of stain into cell wall of both Gram positive and Gram-negative bacteria
190.option_b: If observed staining technique and microscopy before decolorization, both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria appear same.

Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria appear same.

  • In Gram stain:
    • Declorization is the critical step.
    • If observed staining technique and microscopy before decolorization, both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria appear same.
    • Under decolorization: Everything will look gram-positive (violet)
    • Over decolorization: Everything will look gram-negative (pink)

190.question_text: True about Teichoic acids is:
190.option_a: They are found in the cell walls of many gram-positive bacteria
190.option_b: They contain several enzymes for antibiotic destruction.
190.option_d: They influence the permeability of membrane
190.explanation:
• Teichoic acid are polymers of ribitol or glycerol joined by phosphate groups. They are present in Gram positive bacteria.
    • Cell wall teichoic acid: Covalently linked to NAM of cell wall.
  • Lipoteichoic acid: attached to lipids of cell membrane Outer membrane proteins (OMP) in Gram negative bacteria serve as specific receptors for some bacteriophages.
  • Periplasmic space in Gram negative bacteria contains several enzymes for antibiotic destruction.
  • Teichoic acid does not affect permeability of cell membrane.

190.question_text: A 30-year-old male presents with a ruptured dental abscess. A swab of the pus is sent. Which of the following antimicrobials is commonly used to make the media selective for obligate anaerobes?
190.explanation:
• The addition of neomycin inhibits facultative anaerobes (such as many of the Enterobacteriales), without inhibiting the growth of obligate anaerobes (such as Bacteroides spp.).
  • Colistin is often combined with nalidixic acid (CNA) to suppress the growth of gram-negative organisms (such as the Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas), enabling gram positive organisms and yeasts to grow.
  • Chloramphenicol (Rose Bengal) agar is used to suppress all bacterial growth, enabling identification of fungi - it is particularly used in food investigation.
  • Vancomycin can be added to agar for screening for glycopeptide resistant Enterococci.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 10th Edition, Chapter 4, Page Number 40-45.

190.question_text: Empirical antibiotic therapy in a suspected case of Toxic Shock Syndrome mediated by superantigens of Gram-positive cocci should include a beta lactam agent and:

190.question_text: A patient with complains of a step ladder pattern of fever for 2 weeks comes to the medicine OPD. Which of the following investigations is the most sensitive for culture?
190.explanation:
Let's justify each option:

Option A) Blood:

  • Blood cultures are commonly performed to detect bacterial or fungal infections in the bloodstream.
  • They are often used as the first-line diagnostic test for patients with fever of unknown origin or suspected sepsis.
  • Blood cultures can detect a wide range of pathogens that may be causing the fever, including bacteria and fungi.
  • However, they may not always yield positive results, especially if the pathogen is not present in the bloodstream or if the patient is receiving antibiotics that suppress bacterial growth.

Option B) Stool and Urine:

  • Stool and urine cultures are essential for diagnosing gastrointestinal and urinary tract infections, respectively.
  • They are typically used when the clinical presentation and symptoms suggest these specific types of infections.
  • Stool cultures are important for identifying enteric pathogens responsible for conditions like infectious diarrhea.
  • Urine cultures can help diagnose urinary tract infections (UTIs).
  • While these cultures are valuable for their respective purposes, they may not be the primary choice for investigating a step ladder pattern of fever unless gastrointestinal or urinary tract infections are suspected.

Option C) Bone Marrow Aspirate:

  • Bone marrow aspirate is an invasive procedure that involves collecting a sample of bone marrow from the patient's bone.
  • It is used in various clinical scenarios, including the evaluation of prolonged or undiagnosed fever.
  • Bone marrow cultures can detect pathogens that have entered the bloodstream and reached the bone marrow, making it a valuable tool for diagnosing infections that may not be readily detected in peripheral blood.
  • In some cases, bone marrow aspirate can provide a more sensitive diagnostic approach, especially when other cultures, like blood cultures, may be negative.

Option D) Duodenal Aspirate:

  • Duodenal aspirate may be collected for various diagnostic purposes, including the evaluation of gastrointestinal infections.
  • It is typically used to detect infections or abnormalities in the upper gastrointestinal tract, such as infections with Helicobacter pylori.
  • Duodenal aspirates can be valuable for diagnosing specific gastrointestinal infections, but they are not typically the first-line investigation for patients with a step ladder pattern of fever, as other sources of infection are usually explored first.

In summary, the choice of which culture to perform depends on the clinical presentation and suspected source of infection. While blood cultures are commonly used for fever of unknown origin, bone marrow aspirate cultures may offer higher sensitivity in certain cases, especially when other cultures are negative and an underlying infection is suspected. Stool and urine cultures are essential for diagnosing gastrointestinal and urinary tract infections, respectively, and duodenal aspirates are specific to upper gastrointestinal evaluations.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 298

190.question_text:
You come across the following culture media for gram negative bacilli, wherein bacteria which ferment the substance present in the media produce bright pink colonies while non fermenters produce pale colonies. Which type of agar would this be?

i. Simple media
ii. Enrichment media
iii. Differential media
iv. Enriched media
v. Selective media
190.explanation:
The given image is of the Mac conkey agar, whose constituents can be remembered by the mnemonic PLANT

P-Peptone

L-Lactose

A-Agar

N-Neutral Red

T-Taurocholate

It is used to differentiate between lactose fermenters (bright colonies on the left) and lactose non fermenters (pale colonies on the right). Hence it is a differential media

It is also a selective media since it contains taurocholate, which is a selective substance for the growth of Gram negative bacteria.

Simple media are those in which non fastidious bacteria can grow. Eg- Peptone water, Nutrient agar

Selective media inhibit the growth of unwanted organisms. Eg- TCBS, Mac conkey

Enrichment media are typically liquid and inhibit unwanted growth of commensal organisms. Eg- Alkaline Peptone Water, Selenite-F broth

Differential media are those where distinct visual distinction between bacteria is seen. Eg- Mac conkey

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 31

190.question_text: Raju, a 5 year old boy presents to the OPD with complaints of abdominal cramps associated with classical rice water diarrhea. On examination, his skin pinch test went back slowly. His vitals were as follows- temperature - 100.2°C, Pulse 120bpm, RR- 32/min. Upon eliciting further history, it turns out his neighbours, who used the same well as his family, had also developed similar complaints. What is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis for his family members?
190.explanation:
• This clinical vignette describes a classical case of diarrhea caused by V.Cholera. It is a Gram negative rod, which is a halophile, meaning it grows in optimum salt concentration.
  • It is transmitted mainly by the feco-oral route.
  • It acts by increasing cAMP in intestinal villous cells, mediated by receptor GM 1 ganglioside, which is responsible for the secretory diarrhea caused by Vibrio.
  • It has 2 main serotypes, O1 and O139. O1 further has 2 biotypes, classical and El Tor.
  • The mainstay for treatment is hydration and antibiotics based on antibiograms.
  • The drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis is Doxycycline, 500mg B.D in adults and 125mg in children, for 3 days.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 416

190.question_text: A 63-year-old male with the complaints of breathlessness and chest discomfort was referred to the emergency department of our hospital for medical stabilization. He was a known case of rheumatic heart disease with severe mitral stenosis and moderate atrial regurgitation with bilateral pleural effusion.On examination, the patient was afebrile with:?	Body temperature 98.4°F?	Pulse rate of 48/min?	Blood pressure 100/60 mmHg.The patient was admitted and shifted to cardiac care unit (CCU) where he was put on oxygen support and later on the ventilator. Since there was no improvement, the patient was taken up for mitral valve replacement following which the patient was weaned off from the ventilator. Two days later, the patient became febrile and the general condition also deteriorated, so he was put on a ventilator again.?	CT scan of thorax revealed bilateral pleural effusion with basal lung collapse.?	The patient's laboratory investigations revealed leukocytosis with the TLC of 16,000/mm3.Blood samples were sent for culture on two separate occasions where both times, the culture showed pure growth of non-lactose fermenting, mucoid, smooth colonies on MacConkey agar. On Gram staining, the colonies were found to be Gram-negative rods which were motile and they decarboxylated lysine but did not hydrolyze arginine.The causative organism in the above clinical scenario is intrinsically resistant to which of the following drugs?
190.explanation:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of infection with B. cepacia.

The points favouring the diagnosis are:

  • Respiratory failure
  • Leukocytosis
  • Decarboxylation of lysine
  • Non lactose fermenters on MacConkey agar

Various clinical manifestations of B. cepacia include:

  • Cepacia syndrome: It is characterized by a rapidly fatal respiratory infection and septicemia in patients with cystic fibrosis.
  • Nosocomial pathogen: It is resistant to multiple antibiotics, hence has been emerging as an important nosocomial pathogen in ICUs causing pneumonia, wound infections, etc.

B.cepacia is intrinsically resistant to: Ampicillin, Amoxicillin, Ampicillin-sulbactam, Amoxicillin-clavulanate, Ertapenem, Polymyxins and Fosfomycin. Therefore, these drugs should not be used in the treatment regimen.

The effective drugs are:

  • Cotrimoxazole, meropenem, and doxycycline are the most effective agents.
  • Levofloxacin, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam are the alternatives.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 646

190.question_text: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, multiple episodes of watery diarrhea and vomiting over the past 24 hours. During his trip, 5 days ago, he drank water from the river. The patient is up to date with all childhood vaccinations. Which of the following best describes the offending pathogen?
190.option_b: Motile, acid labile, encapsulated, gram-negative bacilli
190.explanation:
This patient is presenting with evidence of viral gastroenteritis, such as watery, non-bloody diarrhea, vomiting, lack of high fever (i.e., > 40°C), and absence of extra intestinal infections (e.g., UTI, pneumonia, and meningitis). Given patient age, vomiting, and vaccination status, the most likely viral culprit of infection is Norovirus, which is a naked, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus.

Norovirus is the most common cause of outbreaks of viral gastroenteritis for patients across all ages. In countries with regular childhood rotavirus immunization, norovirus is also quickly replacing rotavirus as the most common cause of viral gastroenteritis in children.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 424

190.question_text: A 62 year old male patient presented with rash all over the body sparing palms, soles and face. He had severe muscle pain and was in a body posture of ease. He was treated with doxycycline for 5 days. The patient was discharged without any complaints. 7 years later, the patient was diagnosed with oesophageal cancer. The patient presented with the same clinical symptoms of rash and myalgia. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
190.explanation:
The patient initially had epidemic typhus.

Points towards the diagnosis are:

  • Rash all over the body except face, sole and palm.
  • Myalgia and position of ease.

Epidemic typhus is an acute febrile disease; accompanied by headache, myalgia, eye discharge and rashes occurring after an incubation period of 1-2 weeks.

  • Rash begins on the upper trunk, usually on the fifth day, and then becomes generalized, involving the entire body except for the face, palms and soles.
  • Myalgia is usually severe, was referred to as sutama ("crouching") in Burundi outbreak, a designation reflecting the posture of the patients attempting to alleviate the pain.
  • Complications include interstitial pneumonitis, CNS involvement manifests as mental confusion and coma ('typhus' name comes from the Greek word typhos meaning smoky or hazy, describing the state of mind of the affected patients).

Brill-Zinsser disease: It is a recrudescent illness occurring years after acute epidemic typhus. R. prowazekii remains latent for years; its reactivation occurs due to waning immunity, which leads to sporadic infection or outbreaks.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 311

190.question_text: Cell lines are classified according to the number of cell divisions they can undergo. Which of the following is not an example of a continuous cell line, which is capable of indefinite growth?
190.explanation:
• Monkey kidney cell line is a primary cell line which is derived from normal cells thus has limited replicative potential
    Secondary or diploid cell lines are those which can divide up to 10-50 times.
  • g.- Human fibroblast cell line
  • Continuous cell lines.
  • They are derived from cancerous cell lines, hence are capable of indefinite growth.
  • They also possess altered haploid chromosome.
    They are easy to maintain in the laboratories by serial subculturing for indefinite divisions.
  • This is the reason why continuous cell lines are the most widely used cell lines.

Common examples include-

HeLa cell line (Human carcinoma of cervix cell line)

HEp-2 cell line (Human epithelioma of larynx cell line)-widely used for RSV, adenoviruses and HSV

KB cell line (Human carcinoma of nasopharynx cell line) McCoy cell line (Human synovial carcinoma cell line)-useful for isolation of viruses, as well as Chlamydia

Vero cell line (Vervet monkey kidney cell line)-used for rabies vaccine production BHK cell line (Baby hamster kidney cell line).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 92

190.question_text: A 17-year-old male presents with painful genital sores, malaise, and fever for 3 days. He is sexually active with 3 female partners. Examination shows tender lymphadenopathy in the left inguinal region and multiple, punched-out ulcers over the penile shaft and glans. Microscopic examination of a smear from the ulcer is most likely to show which of the following?
190.explanation:
• Eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions on a smear of an ulcer or opened vesicle describe the Cowdry A inclusion bodies seen in infections by herpesviruses such as HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, and CMV.
  • These intranuclear inclusions are formed during herpesvirus replication within the nucleus.
  • Another microscopic characteristic of herpesvirus infection is the formation of multinucleated giant cells as a result of the fusion of multiple infected cells (seen on Tzanck smear).
  • Other Options:
    • Bipolar-staining intracytoplasmic inclusions means Donovan bodies, seen in Granuloma Inguinale caused by Klebsiella granulomatis
    • Basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions mean Reticulate bodies, seen in LGV infection caused by Chlamydia
    • Basophilic intranuclear inclusions are seen in Adenovirus infections

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 30-year-old male, Ramesh, presented with a complaint of dysuria and painful rashes on his penis, shown in the image below. What is the most likely causative organism?
190.explanation:
• The image on correlating with history is suggestive of a STD by Herpes simplex virus.
  • Genital lesions are common in HSV2 infection, which are bilateral, painful, multiple, tiny, vesicular lesions.
  • Associated fever and inguinal lymphadenopathy may also be seen.

Approaching a case of STD (Keywords):

  • Painful lesions: Herpes simplex, Hemophilus ducreyi
  • Painless lesions: Treponema palladium, Klebsiella granulomatis, Chlamydia serovar L1-3
  • Vesicles: Herpes simplex
  • Groove sign: Chlamydia serovar L1-3
  • Pseudo-bubo: Klebsiella granulomatis

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: The colonies of mycoplasma are examined by which of the following stains?
190.explanation:
For mycoplasma:

  • In liquid medium (containing PPLO broth): M. pneumoniae growth is detected by turbidity and a color change.
  • In solid medium (containing PPLO agar): The colonies appear very small (200-500 μm size), embedded on agar surface described as fried egg appearance colonies.
  • The colonies can be examined by hand lens or use of special stain such as Dienes' staining (nonspecific stain that imparts color to Mycoplasma colonies on agar).

190.question_text: What is the most common manifestation of the organism showing following picture on HeLa cell lines and McCoy cell culture respectively:

190.option_b: Vaginosis in female; urethritis in males
190.option_c: Salpingitis in female; proctitis in male
190.option_d: Cervicitis in female; urethritis in male

The above cell lines and culture show chlamydia infection.

Chlamydia most commonly causes Cervicitis in females and non-gonococcal urethritis in males.

The most common cause of epididymitis in males is Chlamydiae but the most common manifestation of Chlamydia in males is urethritis.

190.question_text: Which of the following is not a recommended specimen for chlamydia infection:
190.explanation:
For chlamydia:

  • Scrapings or swabs from infected sites: As chlamydiae are intracellular, the sample must contain cells. Hence, firm scraping or swabbing of the site is required.
  • Recommended specimens are:
    • Urethral swab for NGU
    • Endocervical swab for cervicitis
    • Conjunctival swabs for ocular infections-upper conjunctiva for trachoma and lower conjunctiva for ophthalmia neonatorum.
    • First catch urine samples in the morning contain the highest amount of urethral secretions, hence it is the preferred specimen for urethritis or cervicitis.
    • Nasopharyngeal aspirate and respiratory secretions for suspected chlamydiae pneumoniae.
    • Bubo aspirate for LGV.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 768

190.question_text: The following image depicts a schematic diagram of an embryonated egg used for viral cultivation. Which of the following sites will you use to cultivate vaccines for someone travelling to an endemic area for yellow fever?
190.explanation:
Yolk sac inoculation: Used for arboviruses (e.g., JE virus) and some bacteria such as Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Hemophilus ducreyi
Amniotic sac: Used for the isolation of influenza virus
Allantoic sac: It is a larger cavity, hence is used for better yield of viral vaccines such as influenza vaccine, yellow fever (17D) vaccine
