190.question_text: A 30-year-old male with multiple sexual partners, presented with a single, painless ulcerative lesions on his genitals. The lab test results of patient is shown in number 2 circle below. The test shown in the image is an example of:
190.explanation:
• RPR (rapid plasma reagin) is a screening test for syphilis.
  • It measures antibodies that are present in the blood of people who may have the disease.
  • It is a type of Slide flocculation test.
  • The serum or plasma of syphilitic patients contains an antibody-like substance called reagin.
  • The principle of the RPR test is a flocculation reaction between the RPR antigen and the reagin.
  • The reaction can be seen macroscopically on the test slide as clumping of the carbon particles.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 12, Pg 107-115

190.question_text: A previously healthy 27-year-old man presents with fever, chills, headache, and severe muscle aches for the past 3 days. He also has dry cough and some difficulty breathing today. He returned from Korea 2 weeks ago, where he was involved in monitoring agricultural barns. Physical examination shows basilar lung crackles bilaterally and use of accessory muscles of respiration. Calves are tender to palpation bilaterally. An X-ray of the chest shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. His creatinine is 2.4mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely infectious agent?
190.explanation:
Hantavirus infection is associated with two febrile illnesses, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS).

This patient's potential exposure to infected rodents while working in barns in Korea, the prodromal phase (e.g., fevers, chills, and myalgias) after a latency period of 2–3 weeks with progression to respiratory failure, and his AKI (e.g., elevated creatinine, proteinuria, and hematuria) are suggestive of HFRS.

As HFRS progresses, thrombocytopenia and disseminated intravascular coagulation develop, causing diffuse hemorrhage, hemoptysis, petechiae, and melena. The treatment is supportive care.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 336

190.question_text: RBC form the inclusion bodies of C. trachomatis. These inclusion bodies can be stained with:
190.explanation:
Lugol's iodine: The inclusion bodies of C.trachomatis can be stained with Lugol's iodine because of the presence of glycogen matrix.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 768

190.question_text: All of the following statements are true for the technique shown in photo except:
190.option_a: It is known as hybridoma technique.
190.option_b: The mouse cells are the source of immortal cells whereas the myeloma cells are the source of antibodies.
190.option_c: Aminopterin blocks the de novo pathway for purine synthesis.
190.option_d: Chimeric mAb: It is prepared by recombination of 34% mouse proteins (variable region) and 66% human proteins (constant region).
190.explanation:
Monoclonal antibodies are produced by Hybridoma technique.

A clone of B cell stimulated against a single epitope of antigen is fused with an immortal cell, e.g. myeloma cell (capable of multiplying indefinitely) to produce a hybridoma cell. This hybridoma cell has two unique properties:

  1. Produces monoclonal antibodies of same antigen specificity (due to B cell component)
  2. Multiplies indefinitely producing clones of identical cells (due to immortal myeloma cell component).

Procedure:

The steps of hybridoma technique are as follows:

  • Mouse splenic B cells: The mouse is injected with an antigen containing the desired epitope. After an interval, the mouse splenic B cells are obtained which are activated against the epitope of the antigen injected.
  • Myeloma cells are used as a source of immortal cells. They are cancerous plasma cells. They closely resemble mouse B cells; hence are compatible for fusion.

HAT medium:

It contains hypoxanthine, aminopterin and thymidine Purine synthesis in mammalian cells (e.g. splenic B cell) occurs by either de novo or salvage pathways.

  • Aminopterin blocks the de novo pathway so that the cell has to perform the salvage pathway to synthesize purines for its survival.
  • Salvage pathway requires two important enzymes- HGPRT (hypoxanthine guanine phosphoribosyl- transferase) and thymidine kinase So any cell (e.g. myeloma cell) that lacks HGPRT cannot grow on HAT medium.

Fate of three types of cells on HAT media:

  1. Unfused splenic B cells: They can grow, but do not survive long as they are not immortal
  2. Unfused myeloma cells: They cannot grow as they lack HGPRT enzyme to perform the salvage pathway of purine synthesis
  3. Hybridoma cells: They can grow and survive long.

Types of Monoclonal Antibodies

  • Mouse mAb: It contains 100% mouse derived proteins.
  • Chimeric mAb: It is prepared by recombination of 34% mouse proteins (variable region) and 66% human proteins (constant region).
  • Humanized mAb: Here, only the antigen binding site (i.e. CDR-complementarity determining region) is mouse derived (10%) and the remaining part of mAb is human derived.
  • Human mAb: It contains 100% human derived amino acids. It is the best accepted mAb in humans.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 149

190.question_text: Which of the following does NOT affect the resolving power of a microscope?
190.option_d: Focal length of the objective lens
190.explanation:
In a microscope, the resolution depends upon the wavelength and numerical aperture, which in turn is influenced by the refractive index and angular aperture.

Resolving power of a microscope:

  • Resolving power denotes the smallest detail that a microscope can resolve when imaging a specimen. It is a function of the design of the instrument and the properties of the light used in image formation.
  • The smaller the distance between the two points that can be distinguished, the higher is the resolving power.
  • Thus, according to the formula, d = 0.61 λ / NA, the resolving power can be increased in two ways:
    • Decreasing the wavelength, λ (i.e. by using filters).
    • Increasing the NA (numerical apertures). As stated earlier, NA = n sin u. Thus, NA can be increased in the following ways:
      • Increasing the refractive index, n (this can be done by adding oil to the object).
      • Increasing the angle of light coming from the object.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology, 12th Edition, Page Number 7.

190.question_text: A 34-year old male died after being in a coma. Prior to coma, he showed bizarre behaviour, hydrophobia and aerophobia. On a PM examination of a brain section, the following image was observed. Identify the condition and given image.
190.explanation:
In Rabies, following an animal bite, there is an incubation period of 20-90 days. There are 3 phases:

  1. Short Prodromal Phase: for 2-10 days, nonspecific symptoms
  2. Acute Neurologic Phase: for 2-7 days, shows hyperexcitability, hydrophobia, aerophobia, autonomic dysfunction, paralysis
  3. Coma & Death

Negri bodies: intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusion bodies with basophilic inner granules. Most common sites are neurons of the hippocampus and cerebellum.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: Inclusion bodies are aggregates of viral proteins or virions that confer altered F staining properties to host cells. You find the following inclusion body in a particular cell and are asked whether the given inclusions are intracytoplasmic, intranuclear, or both. Which of the following cases will show inclusion bodies at a similar site to the one you identified above?
190.option_a: A 12-year-old with a dog bite experiencing hydrophobia
190.option_b: A patient with travel history to Africa presenting with fever and jaundice
190.option_c: A 7-year-old with coryza and Koplik's spots
190.explanation:
• The above image shows owl eye inclusions, seen in CMV infections.
  • These inclusions are both intracytoplasmic and intranuclear.
  • Another virus which shows both these inclusions is Measles, a member of Paramyxoviridae.
  • Koplik's spots are pathognomonic of measles infection and hence C is the best answer.
  • Other options
    A- describes Rabies infection. Rabies infection shows Negri bodies, which are intracytoplasmic
    B- describes yellow fever, caused by Flaviviridae. They show Cowdry A inclusion bodies called Torres bodies, which are intranuclear.
    D- describes rotavirus infection, which belongs to family Reoviridae. They show perinuclear intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 89

190.question_text: By which phenomenon does the OPV vaccine prevent an outbreak of wild polio strains?
190.explanation:
• Viral interference is when two viruses infect a host line or a cell line and one of the viruses leads to an inhibition of the other.
  • Genetic reassortment is seen in segmented viruses, such as influenza.
  • Genetic recombination occurs between related viruses of the same family infecting a host cell simultaneously.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 86

190.question_text: Which application of PCR is most appropriate for detecting drug-resistant genes in pathogens?
190.option_a: Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) - Used for amplifying RNA viruses
190.option_b: Nested PCR - Enhances specificity and sensitivity by using two rounds of amplification
190.option_c: Multiplex PCR - Allows simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens or genes in a single reaction
190.option_d: Real-Time PCR (rt-PCR) - Provides real-time quantification and monitoring of DNA amplification
190.explanation:
Option A: Incorrect

  • RT-PCR is for amplifying RNA viruses, not specifically designed for detecting drug-resistant genes.

Option B: Incorrect

  • Nested PCR increases specificity and sensitivity for a single target but isn't ideal for detecting multiple drug-resistant genes simultaneously.

Option C: Correct

  • Multiplex PCR allows detection of multiple genes (including drug resistance genes) in a single reaction, making it very useful for identifying multiple drug-resistant pathogens.

Option D: Incorrect

  • Real-Time PCR is for quantification and real-time monitoring of DNA amplification, but not specifically for detecting multiple drug-resistant genes at once.

KEY TAKE AWAY: Multiplex PCR is particularly useful for detecting multiple drug-resistant genes in pathogens simultaneously, which can aid in the effective management and treatment of infections.

Tags: good to know | inicet

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.). Jaypee Brothers Medical PublishersPage no. 43

190.question_text: Which diagnostic test is used to identify monkeypox?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is the preferred and most reliable diagnostic method for monkeypox. It detects the viral DNA in clinical samples like skin lesions, blood, or respiratory secretions, enabling an accurate diagnosis.

Explanation for other options:

ELISA (Option A): Although ELISA can detect antibodies or antigens, it is not the gold standard for monkeypox diagnosis. It might be used to identify antibodies in some cases, but PCR remains more definitive.

Hemagglutination assay (Option B): This test is typically used for viruses that cause red blood cell agglutination, like influenza, and is not commonly employed to diagnose monkeypox.

Hybrid Capture assay (Option D): Primarily used to detect viral DNA in infections like HPV, this assay is not used for diagnosing monkeypox.

Reference:

  1. Poxviruses - Medical Microbiology - NCBI Bookshelf
  2. Chickenpox - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics

190.question_text: Exposure to which of the following viral infections show better results with combined immunization with Immunoglobulins and Vaccination?
190.explanation:
• Combined vaccination with IG's and Vaccine is generally not recommended.
  • However, for neonates born to HBV infected mother and unvaccinated cases of dog bites, these are given together.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 485

190.question_text: Which of the following is known as Australia antigen?
190.explanation:
• HBsAg is also known as Australia antigen.
  • It is the first to be elevated following an infection.
  • HBsAg is a protein on the surface of HBV.
  • Continuous presence of HBsAg indicates carrier state.
  • Without HBsAg, Anti-HBs indicates immunity to HBV due to resolved infection or vaccination.
  • Usually appears ∼ 1-3 months after infection or vaccination.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

190.question_text: Which of the following has the highest risk of transmission following a needlestick injury?
190.explanation:
• HBV, HCV and HIV are the 3 major blood borne viruses transmitted through a needlestick injury.
  • The highest risk of transmission is HBV>HCV>HIV.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 268

190.question_text: Nitin, a 6-year old boy, presented to the Paediatric OPD, with complaints of weakness in his hips 5 days ago, followed by weakness in his feet 2 days ago. He was partly immunized. Which sample should be taken in order to diagnose it as Poliomyleitis paralysis?
190.explanation:
Poliovirus may be detected from throat swabs (upto 1 week of illness) or from stool samples (upto 6-8 weeks of illness). However, longer excretion rates are observed in case of immunocompromised patients.

Virus isolation from CSF or blood is very rare.

Reverse cold chain (RCC) technique is used to transport stool samples from site of collection to laboratory.

Other Options:

d. Slit skin smear is used to detect M. leprae (Leprosy)

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 711

190.question_text: What is the site of action of poliovirus after entering human body?
190.explanation:
Poliovirus is transmitted by feco-oral route. It multiplies locally in Peyer's patches in the intestines, tonsils and other lymphoid tissue. Entry into the host cell is via CD155 receptor.

Spread to spinal cord is via hematogenous route or neural route. Final site of action is the Anterior Horn Cell of the spinal cord which leads to muscle weakness and flaccid paralysis.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 710

190.question_text: A 17 year old patient presented with weakness and numbness in both lower limbs. He is unable to move his legs, has fasciculations and absent DTRs (Deep Tendon Reflexes). His temperature is 98.4° F, BP is 112/70. On asking history, patient says, "I ate undercooked food 4 days ago, but I frequently do that and I am usually fine. However, 2 days ago, I had blood in my stool and I panicked. Will I be okay, doctor?" The doctor puts a peripheral demyelinating disease in his differential. Which microbiological organism is most likely associated with this patient?
190.explanation:
This is a case of Gullain Barre Syndrome (GBS) following a Campylobacter jejuni infection.

  • C. jejuni is a microaerophilic, thermophilic gram-negative organism.
  • It causes bloody diarrhea, which is self-limiting in nature.
  • Transmission is by undercooked food/unpasteurized milk/untreated water.
  • Lab techniques used are:
  • Gram staining shows gull-wing shaped organism
  • Dark Ground Microscopy shows Darting motility
  • Skirrow's/ Campy BAP media
  • C.jejuni can also act as a trigger for GBS, which causes ascending paralysis with LMN-like features (loss of reflexes/fasciculations).
  • GBS is usually an afebrile condition and self-limiting in nature.

Other Options:

A, B, C, D: They can also act as a trigger to GBS, but are not associated with bloody diarrhea.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 419

190.question_text: Pleurodynia is caused by?
190.explanation:
Coxsackie virus belongs to Enterovirus group of Picornaviridae.

Coxsackie A causes:

  1. Herpangina
  2. Aseptic Meningitis
  3. Hand-Foot-Mouth Syndrome
  4. Acute Hemorrhagic conjunctivitis

Coxsackie B causes:

  1. Aseptic Meningitis
  2. Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease)
  3. Myocarditis, Pericarditis
  4. Pneumonia
  5. Pancreatitis (Juvenile DM)

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 708

190.question_text: A 5-year-old boy is brought by his mother with a 3-day history of low-grade fever and sore throat. Today, she noticed a rash on his buttocks, hands, and feet without pruritus. Physical examination shows oral vesicles. A photograph of the rash on the feet is shown. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen?
190.explanation:
A rash on the hands, feet, and mouth is typical of this pediatric febrile exanthem.

Coxsackie A virus can cause hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD), which presents with a nonpruritic papulovesicular rash on the palms, soles, and oral cavity. Oral vesicles can easily rupture and cause painful ulcers. In some cases, the arms, legs, and buttocks are also affected. The illness is typically self-limiting. Coxsackie A virus can also cause pharyngitis and herpangina.

Coxsackie A causes:

  1. Herpangina
  2. Aseptic Meningitis
  3. Hand-Foot-Mouth Syndrome
  4. Acute Hemorrhagic Conjunctivitis

Coxsackie B causes:

  1. Aseptic Meningitis
  2. Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease)
  3. Myocarditis, Pericarditis
  4. Pneumonia
  5. Pancreatitis (Juvenile DM)

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 563-564,707

190.question_text:
Brain biopsy of a patient showed following:

He had complaints of difficulty in swallowing liquids, loss of appetite and restlessness. His history is significant for a dog bite a week ago. Which of the following schedules is not a part of the PEP regimen for this disease.
190.option_a: 1-site IM vaccine given on days 0, 3, 7 and the fourth dose between days 14 to 28.
190.option_b: 2-site IM vaccine given on day 0 and 1-site IM on days 7 and 21
190.option_c: 2-site ID vaccine given on days 0 and 7
190.option_d: 2-site ID vaccine is given on days 0, 3 and 7
190.explanation:
• The photo shows Negri bodies ( intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusion with characteristic basophilic inner granules, composed of rabies virus proteins and viral RNA).
  • The patient is most likely to have Rabies infection considering the dog bite and Negri bodies in brain biopsy.

There are various vaccination schedules for Rabies:

  • For post exposure prophylaxis:
    • ID regimens are cost effective; dose-sparing and time-sparing and therefore are preferred over IM regimens
    • ID PEP regimen (2-2-2): 2-site ID vaccine is given on days 0, 3 and 7 - IM PEP regimens: Total four doses are given. Two schedules are available:
      • 1-site IM vaccine given on days 0, 3, 7 and the fourth dose between days 14 to 28 or
      • 2-site IM vaccine given on day 0 and 1-site IM on days 7 and 21.
  • PEP for Individuals Previously Vaccinated (PrEP or PEP):
    • 1-site ID vaccine given on days 0 and 3 or
    • 1-site IM vaccine given on days 0 and 3 or
    • 4-site ID vaccine given on day 0 only (left and right deltoids, thigh or suprascapular areas).

Note: If repeat exposure occurs within 3 months of receiving PEP, only local wound treatment is required; neither vaccine nor RIG are needed.

  • Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP):
    • 2-site ID vaccine given on days 0 and 7 or
    • 1-site IM vaccine given on days 0 and 7.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 723

190.question_text: Which serotype of HPV results in the following disease?
190.explanation:
The photo shows plantar warts, caused by HPV serotype 1.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a DNA virus belonging to the Papillomaviridae family. It has selective tropism for epithelium of skin and mucous membranes. It has >100 serotypes, which produce an array of infections ranging from benign warts, to malignant neoplasia of the cervix.

  • Benign warts: They are small, hard, rough growth on the skin. They are of following types:
    • Common skin warts (verruca vulgaris) and flat warts (verruca plana) are common in children (seen with serotypes 2, 4, 27, 57).
    • Plantar warts (verruca plantaris)-benign lesion, widely prevalent among adolescents (seen with serotype 1).
    • Anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum): It is a sexually transmitted infection, seen among adults and is associated with HPV serotypes 6 and 11.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 557

190.question_text: Identify the etiology in an 8 year old girl presenting to your OPD with such skin lesions.
190.explanation:
• Diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum is based on clinical appearance.
  • Molluscum contagiosum manifests as pink pearly wart-like lesions with a characteristic dimple at them center (umbilicated), not associated with inflammation and necrosis.

Varicella zoster represents as shingle or rash in centripetal distribution in form of macules/papules/vesicular on erythematous.

Herpes simplex one usually presents as herpes labialis.

Kaposi's sarcoma is an AIDs defining ailment presenting with red purple macules and plaques.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 559

190.question_text: Which of the following organism causes Sixth disease?
190.explanation:
• Sixth Disease, also known as Erythema subitum/ Roseola infantum, is caused by HHV6.
  • Sixth Disease is transmitted by infected oral secretions and presents with high grade fever and skin rashes.
  • HHV6 infects the T-cells by binding to CD46 receptors.
  • Other options:
    • Tetani causes Congenital Tetanus (Eighth Day Disease)
    • Parvovirus causes Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Day Disease)
    • Measles (First Day Disease)
    • Second day disease- Scarlet fever by Streptococcus
    • Third day disease- Rubella
    • Fourth day disease- Ritter's disease/Staphylococcus Scalded Skin Syndrome by S. aureus

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 15-year-old girl came to Medicine OPD with complaints of headache, fever, pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly. A local quack prescribed her an antibiotic, following which she developed rashes. On taking proper history, her doctor also notes that her boyfriend is also suffering from similar symptoms. Which is the most likely cause of this infection?
190.explanation:
• The girl is most likely having Infectious Mononucleosis, caused by Ebstein-Barr Virus (EBV).
  • Infectious Mononucleosis (Kissing Disease) is spread by salivary contact.
  • Presentation includes headache, fever, pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly.
  • Rashes following Ampicillin therapy is also seen.
  • Lab Diagnosis is done by Paul Bunnell test/ Monospot test by detecting heterophile antibodies against sheep RBCs.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of headaches, facial numbness, recurrent epistaxis, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. He recently immigrated from Hong Kong. Examination shows right-sided cervical lymphadenopathy. Endoscopy shows an exophytic nasopharyngeal mass. Histologic examination of a biopsy specimen of the mass shows sheets of undifferentiated cells with nuclear pleomorphism and abundant mitotic figures. The patient most likely acquired the causal pathogen of his nasopharyngeal mass via which of the following routes of transmission?
190.explanation:
• Headache, facial numbness (due to cranial nerve involvement), recurrent epistaxis, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy are suggestive of malignancy.
  • The biopsy of this patient's mass shows undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which is endemic in Southern China.
  • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the primary causative agent in the pathogenesis of this condition.
  • EBV is mainly transmitted through saliva and respiratory secretions.
  • In addition to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, EBV is associated with the development of infectious mononucleosis (“kissing disease”), oral hairy leukoplakia, primary CNS lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and Burkitt lymphoma.
  • Most individuals have a latent EBV infection, but malignant complications typically occur only after reactivation in immunocompromised individuals (e.g., patients with HIV).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 49-year-old woman had a routine Pap smear that showed atypical squamous cells. Colposcopy shows an area of white discoloration of the cervix with application of acetic acid solution. Biopsy of this area shows carcinoma-in-situ. Activation of which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
190.explanation:
• HPV 16 and HPV 18, are responsible for the majority of cervical cancers.
  • These pathogens facilitate the transcription of proteins that alter tumor suppression upon successful infection of cervical cells.
  • eF2 transcription factors that promote G1 to the S phase transition are normally inhibited by the retinoblastoma protein (Rb).
  • High-risk types of HPV induce production of the oncoprotein E7, which binds and inactivates Rb protein, thereby increasing G1 to S phase transition and cell proliferation.
  • High-risk HPV also induces the production of the oncoprotein E6, which binds and inactivates the tumor suppressor protein p53.

Other Options:

  1. P53 is main tumor suppressor gene
  2. p24 is a component of HIV virus
  3. JAK2 mutations lead to Polycythemia vera, Essential thrombocythemia, etc.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmologist with the complaint of redness and photophobia in her right eye for the past 2 days. She says that she noticed these changes after her young nephew accidentally brushed the end of a hockey stick directly into her eye when they were playing in the backyard, although she was surprised to feel an ABSENCE of significant eye pain during the incident or afterwards. On slit lamp examination, the ophthalmologist finds a large corneal abrasion with fluorescein staining. The patient is found to have an absent corneal reflex in her right eye. Which of the following conditions would be most likely be present in her past medical history?
190.explanation:
• This patient presenting with a corneal abrasion and evidence of repeated corneal trauma without corneal sensation likely has had damage to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which can occur after herpes zoster infection affecting the trigeminal nerve.
  • Herpes zoster infection, or shingles, manifests as a reactivation of a latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection in a specific nerve and typically presents as a painful skin rash along a dermatome.
  • About 10-20% of herpes zoster cases involve the eye (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) and can result in keratitis that often is associated with corneal denervation and subsequent loss of corneal sensation.
  • Patients with loss of corneal sensation are susceptible to repeated corneal abrasions from trauma and corneal scarring.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 3-year old boy, Sumit, presented to Pediatric OPD with complaints of fever and white spots in his mouth, following which he developed rashes behind his ear that spread to his entire body. On taking detailed history, his mother said that she did not vaccinate him as it was against her beliefs. What is the child most likely infected with?
190.explanation:
The child is most likely infected with Measles virus. Measles belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family.

Three stages of Measles infection:

  1. Prodromal stage: Fever + Koplik spots (white/blue spot in mouth against 2nd lower molar tooth) + non-specific symptoms(cough/coryza/diarrhea) 2. Eruptive stage: Rashes appear behind the ear and spread to face, trunk & legs. Fade in the same order as they appear.
  2. Post-measles stage: weakness + weight loss

Complications:

  1. Secondary bacterial infection
  2. Giant cell pneumonitis
  3. Subacute sclerosing pan-encephalitis (SSPE)
  4. Post-measles encephalomyelitis
  5. Measles inclusion body encephalitis

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: What is the period of communicability observed in Measles?
190.explanation:
Measles belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family. Period of communicability is 4 days before and after the onset of rash.

Three stages of Measles infection:

  1. Prodromal stage: Fever + Koplik spots(white/blue spot in mouth against 2nd lower molar tooth) + non-specific symptoms(cough/coryza/diarrhea)
  2. Eruptive stage: Rashes appear behind the ear and spread to the face, trunk & legs. Fade in the same order as they appear.
  3. Post-measles stage: weakness + weight loss

Complications:

  1. Secondary bacterial infection
  2. Giant cell pneumonitis
  3. Subacute sclerosing pan-encephalitis (SSPE)
  4. Post-measles encephalomyelitis
  5. Measles inclusion body encephalitis

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text:
A 17-year old boy presented with confusion and disorientation. He was failing in his school exams. Her mother noticed his reduced attention and poor memory. His mother states that he is normally a "bright student" and is in all honors classes. The patient was not vaccinated as a child and developed measles at age 6. Since then, he has been healthy.
MRI of the brain is obtained, as shown in image. Within 3 days of hospital admission, the patient develops unilateral, slow-myoclonic jerks. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a slowly progressive, neurodegenerative disorder caused by a persistent measles virus infection.

Most patients will have a history of measles at an early age with a latent period that can range from 6-15 years. Initial symptoms include memory loss and changes in behavior/personality that progress to disturbances in motor function (e.g., myoclonic jerks, ataxia, paralysis, and seizures).

Brain imaging will show multiple white matter hyperintensities, scarring, and cerebral atrophy. The prognosis is poor with patients deteriorating to coma and/or death within 1-3 years of diagnosis.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: A 7-year-old boy presents with several days of high fever accompanied by a runny nose, cough, and red itchy eyes. The vaccination history is undocumented. Upon physical examination you see a red, slightly bumpy rash extending from the head to the mid-chest level. If you had examined this child before the rash, which of the following signs may you have observed?
190.option_d: White bluish spots in buccal mucosa
190.explanation:
This scenario is most consistent with an infection of Rubeola (Measles). The classic presentation of measles is a prodrome of high fever with the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis) and Koplik spots followed by a maculopapular rash that begins on the head and then descends to the trunk and the extremities.

In Measles, Koplik spots (White bluish spots in buccal mucosa) are sometimes seen in the buccal mucosa prior to the development of the rash.


Measles is a highly contagious infectious disease. However, it is important to consider that in populations that do not have regular access to preventive health services, an outbreak of Measles is observed.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: A 26-year-old teacher presents to his primary care physician for a low-grade fever and severe groin pain. He had a swollen cheek 4 days ago. He teaches at an elementary school, where many parents decline vaccination for their children. On examination, he does not recall if he had been vaccinated prior. What might be the reason for the patient's presentation?
190.option_a: Bulging of soft tissue through the inguinal canal
190.option_b: Inflammation of the testicles due to a viral infection
190.option_c: Malignant growth of germ cells at the testicle
190.explanation:
This patient is experiencing orchitis secondary to infection with the mumps virus (fever, severe testicular pain, and parotitis 4 days prior). He is, therefore, experiencing inflammation of the testicles due to a viral infection.

Mumps is a contagious viral illness that is largely preventable by vaccination. It is highly infectious and is transmitted via respiratory droplets, direct contact, or fomites. Patients usually present with a few days of fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, and salivary gland swelling within 48 hours of symptom onset. The disease is self-limited, and most individuals recover within a few weeks.

In post pubertal males, orchitis is the most common complication of mumps infection and typically occurs 5-10 days after the onset of parotitis. Symptoms include abrupt onset of fever, and severe testicular pain with swelling and erythema of the scrotum. Management of patients is supportive.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: What is the best specimen for antigen detection of Rabies?
190.option_b: Hair follicle of nape of neck
190.explanation:
Various samples can be taken for diagnosis of Rabies virus:

For rtPCR: Saliva

For Antigen detection: Hair follicle of nape of neck

For antibody detection: CSF > Serum

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: A 27-year-old man presents with persistent fever, nausea, and vomiting for the past 3 days. He quickly becomes disoriented and agitated. He has visible signs of difficulty breathing with copious oral secretions and generalized muscle twitching. When the nurse tries to place a nasal cannula, the patient becomes fearful and combative. The patient is sedated and placed on mechanical ventilation. Which of the following is a risk factor for the patient's most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
The patient is presenting with fever, agitation, excess salivation, and aerophobia, which is suspicious for the diagnosis of rabies. Exploring caves with bats may be a risk factor for rabies.

Rabies is caused by a virus that is transmitted through exposure to common reservoirs including bats, raccoons, skunks, and dogs. The incubation period is from weeks to months.

Patients will present with fever and a flu-like prodrome that can progress to agitation, disorientation, hallucination, seizures, paralysis, coma, and death secondary to respiratory dysfunction. Other classic symptoms include pharyngeal spasm (which causes drooling, 'foaming' at the mouth, and dysphagia), hydrophobia (i.e., fear of water), photophobia, and aerophobia (i.e., fear of air).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: Which category of waterborne pathogens is most commonly associated with fecal contamination of drinking water and causes diarrheal outbreaks?
190.explanation:
• Category 1 (Enteric Pathogens): Correct, includes E. coli, Salmonella, and Rotavirus, which are commonly transmitted via fecally contaminated water, causing diarrheal outbreaks.

Why Not Others:

  • B. Category 2 (Common Hospital Pathogens): Incorrect, these pathogens (e.g., multidrug-resistant organisms) are more associated with healthcare settings, not fecal contamination.
  • C. Category 3: Emerging pathogens are not specifically linked to fecal contamination.
  • D. Category 4: Not a valid classification in this context.

Key Takeaways: Category 1 (Enteric Pathogens), transmitted via fecal contamination, is responsible for diarrheal outbreaks caused by drinking contaminated water.

Tags: fmge 2023

Reference: Shastri, A. (2021). Essentials of Medical Microbiology (3rd ed.). Publisher. Chapter-27 .pp-278.

190.question_text: Virus-mediated transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another is known as:
190.explanation:
• Transduction is defined as the transmission of a portion of DNA from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria).
  • This mechanism allows horizontal gene transfer and plays a role in genetic diversity among bacteria.

Related important points and concepts (if needed and/or relevant):

  • Transduction can be generalized (any part of the bacterial genome transferred) or specialized (only specific genes near the prophage).
  • It is a common mechanism for antibiotic resistance gene transfer in bacterial populations.
  • This process requires bacteriophages as mediators and does not involve direct contact between bacteria (unlike conjugation).

Explanation of other options:

Transformation (Option B): Refers to the random uptake of free/naked DNA from the environment by a bacterial cell and its incorporation into the genome.

Transcription (Option C): The process of forming mRNA from DNA, part of gene expression, not gene transfer.

Integration (Option D): Involves insertion of a DNA segment into chromosomal DNA, but does not specify viral mediation or gene transfer between bacteria.

Key Takeaways:

  • Transduction = Bacteriophage-mediated gene transfer
  • Distinct from transformation, transcription, and integration
  • Important in horizontal gene transfer and bacterial evolution

Reference Standard Microbiology Textbooks

190.question_text: Which of the following best describes the nucleic acid of the smallest virus?
190.explanation:
• The smallest virus is parvovirus, which is a ssDNA viru
  • It has a linear DNA.
  • The largest virus is poxvirus, which has a dsDNA.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 81

190.question_text:
Human herpes virus 4 is associated with many other diseases. From the following list, it is not associated with?
a) A teenager having kissing disease
b) Duncan syndrome in an 8 year old boy
c) A 64 year old male with Kaposi's sarcoma
d) A chronic tobacco chewer with oral submucous fibrosis
e) A HIV positive man with hairy leukoplakia
f) A 47 year old female with cervical cancer
190.explanation:
• Herpes virus 4 is also known as Ebstein barr virus.
  • Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) causes infectious mononucleosis and is also associated with several human tumors, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt's lymphoma, Hodgkin's disease, and B cell lymphoma.

Other associations are:

  • Lymphoproliferative disorder: It is seen among immunodeficient patients, e.g. Duncan syndrome which is an X-linked recessive disease affecting young boys.
  • Oral hairy leukoplakia: Wart-like growth of epithelial cells of the tongue developed in some HIV-infected patients and transplant recipients. - Chronic fatigue syndrome.

Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV 8.

HPV is associated with cervical cancer.

There is no viral association with oral submucous fibrosis.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 673

190.question_text:
34-week late preterm female child who was born to a 29-year-old primi mother delivered by an emergency lower segment caesarean section due to the intrauterine growth retardation of the baby had following findings:
The birth weight of the baby was 1165 g, length was 37cm, and the head circumference was 26.5cm and remained below the fifth percentile. On examination, the child had pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Mild subcostal retractions were present bilaterally, and there were no added breath sounds. S1 and S2 were heard, and apex beat was present in the fourth intercostal space, medial to the midclavicular line. A pan systolic murmur of grade 3 was heard. Blood investigations revealed thrombocytopenia (64000/μL of blood). Ophthalmic evaluation revealed bilateral cataract in the eyes. Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly and osteopenic ribs. The child is most likely to have?
190.explanation:
Rubella is a highly teratogenic virus. The risk of transmission of infection to the fetus and the severity of congenital infection-both are maximum if the mother acquires the infection during the first trimester of pregnancy.

Rubella is a RNA virus, belonging to the Togaviridae family.

Clinical manifestations of CRS can be grouped into permanent congenital defects and transient reversible congenital changes.

  • Permanent Congenital Defects:
    • The classical triad consists of:
      1. Ear defect: Sensorineural deafness (most common defect of CRS.
      2. Ocular defects: The most common ocular defect is salt-and-pepper retinopathy, followed by cataract.
      3. Cardiac defect: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is the most common cardiac defect followed by pulmonary artery stenosis and ventricular septal defect.
      4. Other features include-CNS defects may occasionally be seen such as microcephaly, mental retardation, motor delay and autism.
  • Transient Congenital Changes
    • Transient changes such as hepatosplenomegaly, bone lesions and intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) may be seen. Occasionally, thrombocytopenia with petechiae (Blueberry muffin syndrome) may also be seen.
  • In congenital CMV infection:
    • Petechial rash
    • Jaundice
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Microcephaly
    • Deafness
    • Chorioretinitis
    • IUGR
    • Periventricular calcification and ventriculomegaly

In congenital toxoplasmosis:

  • The classical triad comprises chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications.

In neonatal herpes:

  • Local lesions involving skin, eye and mouth (SEM) are the most frequent manifestations; typically present at 9-11 days of life.
  • Disseminated: Presents with septic appearance, with deranged liver function tests; typically presents at 9-11 days of life.
  • CNS infections: Among HSV infected people neonates are at higher risk of CNS infections (encephalitis).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 795

190.question_text: A 28 week preterm baby was born with weight 1.5kg, Cicatricial skin lesion and limb hypoplasia. The infant had an episode of seizure after 5 hours of being born. On USG, kidneys were enlarged suggestive of hydronephrosis. Which maternal infection leads to these findings in a newborn?
190.explanation:
Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is highly teratogenic.

Risk of transmission is maximum when mother: Acquires primary infection during pregnancy Acquires infection at early pregnancy.

Congenital varicella syndrome is characterized by:

  • Cicatricial skin lesions and limb hypoplasia (most characteristic anomalies).
  • CNS defects: Microcephaly, mental retardation and seizures.
  • Ocular defects: Chorioretinitis, microphthalmia, and cataract.
  • Renal system defects: Hydroureter and hydronephrosis.
  • Autonomic system defect: Neurogenic bladder.
  • Low birth weight.

Congenital zika syndrome:

  • It is characterized by microcephaly and other neurological manifestations.

Congenital syphilis:

  • Earliest manifestations occur within 2 years of age.
  • Affected children are infectious and they suffer from rhinitis (or snuffles), mucocutaneous lesions, bone changes, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy.
  • Late congenital syphilis occurs after 2 years and is noninfectious. It is characterized by interstitial keratitis, eighth nerve deafness, bilateral knee effusions (Clutton's joints).
  • Residual stigmata may remain for a long time such as: Hutchinson's teeth (notched central incisors) Mulberry molars (molars with poorly developed cusps) Saddle nose, and saber shins.

Congenital trypanosomiasis:

  • Low birth weight
  • Stillbirth
  • Rarely myocarditis
  • Neurological alterations.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 797

190.question_text: A 27-year old female presents to your clinic with such lesions. Identify the causative organism.
190.explanation:
The photo shows herpes labialis caused by HSV 1.

HSV4 is varicella zoster virus causing chickenpox.

HSV8 is associated with Kaposi's sarcoma.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 552

190.question_text: You are asked to investigate a possible act of terrorism using Hanta virus. Which of the following is true regarding this category of bioterrorism agent?
190.option_c: Are readily available and easily produced
190.explanation: Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 821

190.question_text: Prions are best removed by:
190.option_a: Autoclave at 121°C for 15 min at 15 lbs pressure
190.option_b: 5% formalin followed by autoclave at 121°C for 30 min
190.option_c: Sodium hydroxide for 1 hr followed by autoclave at 121°C for 60 min
190.option_d: Sodium hypochlorite for 10 min followed by autoclave at 121°C for 30 min
190.explanation:
• Prions are the most resistant structure to sterilization and disinfection.
  • Prions can be sterilized by either steam sterilization or using a combination of sodium hydroxide and autoclaving, using 1 of the 4 following options:
  • Option 1. Autoclave at 134°C for 18 minutes in a prevacuum sterilizer.
  • Option 2. Autoclave at 132°C for 1 hour in a gravity displacement sterilizer.
  • Option 3. Immerse in 1 N NaOH (1 N NaOH is a solution of 40 g NaOH in 1 L water) for 1 hour; remove and rinse in water, then transfer to an open pan and autoclave (121°C gravity displacement sterilizer or 134°C porous pre-vacuum sterilizer) for 1 hour.
  • Option 4. Immerse in 1 N NaOH for 1 hour and heat in a gravity displacement sterilizer at 121°C for 30 minutes, then clean and subject to routine sterilization.
  • However, as it remains unclear which of the above options is best for completely eradicating prions from medical equipment.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 3, Pg 31

190.question_text: Rajneesh, an 8-year-old boy, was detected with polio virus in his stool sample. He has maximum chances of developing which of the following?
190.explanation:
Poliovirus is transmitted by feco-oral route. Incubation period is usually 7-14 days. Manifestations may vary from -

  • Inapparent infection (90-96%): Asymptomatic
  • Abortive infection (~ 5%): Minor symptoms such as fever, malaise, sore throat, anorexia, headache etc.
  • Non-paralytic poliomyelitis (~1%): Similar to aseptic meningitis.
  • Paralytic poliomyelitis (<1%): Descending, asymmetric, acute flaccid poliomyelitis (AFP).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number-710.

190.question_text: Rajeev, a 5-year-old kid presented with fever, coryza, red eye and sore throat. He had participated in a summer camp organized by his school, a few days ago, after which other kids also presented with similar complaints. Which of the following virus is most likely to be associated with this kid?
190.explanation:
• A history of fever, coryza, red eye and sore throat along with similar complaints in other kids suggests a typical pharyngoconjuctival fever caused by Adenovirus.
  • Adenovirus is a dsDNA, non-enveloped, space ship shaped virus.
  • Other manifesatitons of Adenovirus are:
    Epidemic Keratoconjuctivitis - Serotype 8, 19, 37 (also known as Shipyard Eye)
    1. Pharnygoconjuctival fever - Serotype 3, 4, 7
    2. Hemorrhagic cystitis - Serotype 11, 21
    3. Infantile diarrhea - Serotype 40, 41
    4. ARDS

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 672

190.question_text: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of a red, itchy, burning rash on her vulva. She has had three similar episodes over the last two years that have all self-resolved. Genitourinary examination shows a small area of erythema with an overlying cluster of vesicles on the inside surface of the vulva. Latent infection of which of the following is most likely responsible for this patient's recurrent symptoms?
190.explanation:
• This patient with acute onset of itchy, burning rash and grouped vesicles on genital examination has recurrent genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection.
  • Latency and reactivation in the dorsal root ganglion of host sensory neurons is the mechanism underlying the recurrent symptoms seen in herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 infection.
  • Under certain conditions (e.g., immunodeficiency, stress, trauma), HSV may reactivate and multiply in the dorsal root ganglia of the trigeminal (HSV-1) or sacral (HSV-2) nerves, producing recurrent flares, as are seen in this patient.

Other Options:

  1. TB undergoes latency in Macrophages
  2. HIV goes into latency in Lymphocytes
  3. JC virus undergoes latency in Astrocytes

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 2-day history of dysuria and increased urinary frequency. Vital signs are within normal limits. Urinalysis shows cloudy, red urine. This patient's clinical presentation is best explained by an infection with a virus with which of the following features?
190.explanation:
• Adenovirus is a dsDNA, non-enveloped, space vehicle-shaped icosahedral virus.
  • Manifestations of Adenovirus are:
  1. Epidemic Keratoconjuctivitis - Serotype 8, 19, 37 (also known as Shipyard Eye)
  2. Pharnygoconjuctival fever - Serotype 3, 4, 7
  3. Hemorrhagic cystitis - Serotype 11, 21
  4. Infantile diarrhea - Serotype 40, 41
  5. ARDS
  • Serotypes 7, 11, 21, and 35 cause acute viral hemorrhagic cystitis.
  • This condition occurs most frequently among male children and typically manifests with dysuria and hematuria that resolves within days to weeks after onset.
  • Adenovirus infection is also associated with febrile pharyngitis, pneumonia, conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis, and myocarditis.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 672

190.question_text:
A 37-year-old female suffering from Multiple Sclerosis presents with complaints of headache, behavioural changes, seizures and ataxia. She was taking drug Natalizumab for managing MS. An MRI scan was done and image is shown below.
Which class of DNA virus is responsible for this condition?
190.explanation:
• This woman with headache, behavioral changes, seizures and ataxia with history of consuming Natalizumab is suffering from Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PMLE), caused by JC virus which belongs to Polyomavirus.
  • Risk factors: transplant patients, AIDS patients, drugs Rituximab or Natalizumab, malignancy
  • MRI shows focal non-enhancing white matter lesions without any specific boundaries.
  • PMLE occurs due to reactivation of latent JC virus, due to setting of immunocompromised state.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 97

190.question_text: Identify the correct organism causing this type of presentation.
190.explanation:
• This pearly, flesh-colored rash with a central umbilication occurs due to Molluscum contagiosum virus (Poxvirus family).
  • It is usually asymptomatic, but maybe associated with pruritus or tenderness.
  • On histology, it shows Molluscum bodies (aka Henderson-Peterson bodies) which are large cells with granular eosinophilic cytoplasm that contain accumulated virions, as shown in image below.
  • It is self-limiting in nature, heals by itself or Ritonavir can be given in severe cases.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: HIV Virus Has 3 structural genes, Gag, Pol, Env. which of these encodes for antigen P24, which is used to diagnose the infection?
190.explanation:
• Gag gene encodes for the core and shell of the virus. Its precursor, p55 dissociates into 3 proteins, p18, p24 and p15.
  • Pol encodes for the viral enzymes.
  • Env encodes for the envelope glycoprotein.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 325

190.question_text: Which of the following accurately describes the characteristics of Orthomyxoviridae?
190.explanation:
Orthomyxoviridae(Influenza virus) is a ssRNA, -ve sense, Helical shaped and 8 segmented virus.

Influenza has 3 types: A(causes pandemics), B(causes epidemics in humans) & C(causes sporadic disease).

It has 2 surface proteins: HA(Hemagglutinin) and NA(Neuraminidase). HA helps in viral entry via sialic acid receptors. NA is a receptor destroying enzyme, which helps in elution(viral release).


Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: A 1-year old girl, Sushma, arrived at the Pediatric OPD with respiratory distress. On examination, she was found to have inspiratory stridor, barking cough, and hoarseness. Which organism is most commonly responsible for this condition?
190.explanation:
Inspiratory stridor, barking cough, and hoarseness along with respiratory distress is suggestive of Croup. Most common organism causing croup is Parainfluenza virus.

Croup is inflammation of the larynx, trachea and bronchus. X-ray shows a Steeple sign.

Other Options:

  1. Hemophilus influenza causes Epiglottitis
  2. Mumps causes parotitis and orchitis
  3. Bordetella pertussis causes Whooping cough

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: Which virus is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants?
190.explanation:
Respiratory Syncytial Virus is a Paramyxovirus.

It is spread by direct contact and large droplets inhalation.

RSV replicates in epithelial cells of nasopharynx and spreads to the lower respiratory tract to cause pneumonia and bronchiolitis.

RSV shows a characteristic cytopathic effect of syncytium formation.

In adults, RSV causes influenza-like upper respiratory tract infection. RSV may exacerbate COPD.

Drug of choice is Ribavirin and prophylactic drug of choice is Palivizumab.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 648

190.question_text: Anti-Rabies vaccine is prepared from?
190.explanation: Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: A 43-year-old male comes 4 weeks after getting bitten by a bat during a cave diving trip. After cleansing the wound with water, the patient reports that he felt well enough not to seek medical attention immediately following his trip. He does endorse feeling feverish in the past week but a new onset of photophobia and irritability led him to seek help today. What would the post-mortem pathology report show if the patient succumbs to this infection?
190.explanation:
A patient presenting with a latent fever along with photophobia, hydrophobia, and/or agitation following an animal bite is most likely infected by the rabies virus. With more time, the patient will likely advance to paralysis, coma, and eventually, death.

Rabies virus is a bullet shaped (-) linear ssRNA virus often found in raccoons and bats; domesticated dogs or cats are rarely the vector. Further, the rabies virus is helical in shape with a surrounding envelope. Once bitten by the vector organism, rabies virus will migrate up to the central nervous system to form distinctive "Negri bodies" in the Purkinje cells.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: A 35-year-old spelunker presents to the emergency room complaining of one week of worsening malaise, after he came back from exploring bat caves. On examination he appears tremulous and agitated. He is oriented to person and place but not time. Which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
190.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this patient is rabies. Rabies is a (-) single-strand RNA virus.

RV is a rhabdovirus that travels in retrograde fashion from peripheral nerves to the CNS, where it replicates and spreads neurally to other organs. The virus is commonly found in the cerebellum of infected patients, where it produces cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons called Negri bodies. However, once the virus has disseminated from the CNS to other organs, it is believed that vaccination does not alter the course of the disease.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 715

190.question_text: Which WHO region has not been able to eradicate Polio virus?
190.explanation:
Wild polio virus is still transmitted in Afghanistan and Pakistan, which belong to Eastern Mediterranean Region of WHO.

India belongs to South East Asia Region of WHO, whose headquarters is located in New Delhi. India eradicated Polio in 2014 successfully, as the last case of Polio was discovered in 2011 in Howrah.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 713

190.question_text: What is the most common mode of Polio virus transmission?
190.explanation:
Poliovirus is transmitted by feco-oral route(most common), respiratory droplets via inhalation and rarely by conjuctival route. It multiplies locally in Peyer's patches in the intestines, tonsils and other lymphoid tissue. Entry into the host cell is via CD155 receptor.

Spread to spinal cord is via hematogenous route or neural route. Final site of action is the Anterior Horn Cell of the spinal cord which leads to muscle weakness and flaccid paralysis.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, Page Number 710

190.question_text: A 30-year-old woman delivers a baby with microcephaly, spasticity, sensorineural hearing loss and retinal mottling at 38 weeks by vaginal delivery. During her first trimester, she went on a trip to Puerto Rico in 2015-16 and had multiple mosquito bites. Following which, she had a fever, itchy maculopapular rash, and conjunctivitis that resolved within 10 days. A serum sample from the baby is collected. Which pathogen might be expected on the basis of travel history?
190.explanation:
Microcephaly, spasticity, sensorineural hearing loss and retinal mottling in this newborn indicate Congenital Zika syndrome.

The newborn's mother most likely contracted the Zika virus (in the first trimester of pregnancy) during her visit to Puerto Rico in 2015-16.

The pathogen responsible for this newborn's condition was the cause of an ongoing outbreak in the USA, Caribbean islands and Pacific Islands in 2015-16.

It was recommended that pregnant women postpone travel to affected countries. If such travel is necessary during pregnancy, the use of mosquito repellent, mosquito nets, and long-sleeved, light-colored clothing help to prevent transmission.

For individuals with known Zika infection, barrier contraception should be used to prevent virus transmission via semen.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 793

190.question_text: A 45-year-old man presents with hematuria, dysuria and suprapubic pain. He reports that he had a renal transplant 3 months ago and is currently on many immunosuppressants. Urinalysis is positive for blood but is negative for nitrates or leukocyte esterase. A nucleic acid amplification test of his urine is positive for a polyomavirus. Identify the virus causing this condition.
190.explanation:
BK virus belongs to Polyomavirus, is a dsDNA circular virus. BK virus is transmitted via airborne route.

Polyomavirus-associated nephropathy under immunosuppression: occurs in up to 10% of all kidney transplant patients due to JC virus.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 745

190.question_text: Munna, a 7-year-old boy presents with a rash that began approximately 2 days ago. According to his mother, it began as a pink rash on his face and has subsequently spread to his trunk. Physical exam is notable for the rash shown in image and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
190.explanation:
This patient is presenting with a low-grade fever, cold-like symptoms, a characteristic rash (with macules and papules), and is well appearing suggesting a diagnosis of rubella.

Rubella is caused by the rubella virus (a togavirus) that is transmitted via respiratory droplets following an incubation period of 14-21 days. Prior to the appearance of the rash, patients typically experience the prodrome of malaise, mild conjunctivitis, low-grade fever, adenopathy, and cold symptoms. The rash begins on the face as pink macules. After 1 day, the rash typically spreads to the trunk and extremities.

In contrast to measles, these patients are usually well appearing and have symptoms that begin to resolve around day 3.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 562

190.question_text: A 2-week-old boy is brought to the Pediatric Department. His mother says that is not awakened by loud noises. She shows his eyes which appear 'cloudy' as shown in the image. On a physical exam, a continuous murmur with machine-like consistency over the precordium is heard. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this child's problems?
190.explanation:
This child has the classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome: patent ductus arteriosus, congenital cataracts, and deafness.

Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) is one of the "TORCH" infections, which are infective organisms that can pass from mother to fetus.

If contracted early during pregnancy (within 16 weeks), maternal rubella infection results in a serious congenital syndrome that includes the classic triad of cardiac defects, eye defects, and auditory defects.

The presentation is variable and may include hepatosplenomegaly and/or "blueberry muffin rash'' (petechiae and purpura).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 563

190.question_text: A 27-year-old comes for her first antenatal visit. Examination shows a pink maculopapular rash that started from face and now all over her body, sparing her palms and soles. Postauricular lymphadenopathy is present. Knee joints are mildly swollen. USG shows a uterus with a 24-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
190.explanation:
An itchy maculopapular rash that started on the face and spread to the rest of the body but spares the palms and soles with postauricular lymphadenopathy and polyarthritis, is suggestive of Rubella infection.

If a rubella infection occurred before 16 weeks of gestation, the patient should be counselled about the potentially devastating effects on the fetus and the possibility of terminating the pregnancy, due to Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS).

But after 16th week of gestation, the risk of developing congenital defects is very low. Hence, reassurance and symptomatic therapy are usually recommended.

MMR vaccine should be administered to all nonpregnant women of childbearing age who have an unknown vaccination history or are seronegative for rubella-specific IgG.

190.question_text: An 8-month-old girl has fever, vomiting, and diarrhea for 3 days. Her immunizations are incomplete. Her temperature is 101.3°F, pulse is 145/min, and blood pressure is 92/54 mm-Hg. 190.explanation:
The presence of acute watery diarrhea containing neither mucus nor blood and dehydration in an unimmunized child without abdominal pain should raise suspicion for Rotavirus infection.

Although the incidence of rotavirus infection has decreased due to routine rotavirus vaccinations, it is still a common cause of diarrheal illness in children under 5 years of age. This child may not have received the complete schedule, making her vulnerable to the infection. Rapid diagnosis is important because rotavirus is highly contagious and infected patients need to be isolated.

Children with rotavirus infection need adequate hydration. ORS can be given to restore potential electrolyte imbalance as well as to hydrate a child with mild to moderate dehydration. If dehydration is severe, as is the case with this patient, intravenous fluid therapy is appropriate.

190.question_text: pH of Sabourauds dextrose agar is adjusted to:

• Sabourauds Dextrose Agar (SDA) is used for the isolation, cultivation, and maintenance of non-pathogenic and pathogenic species of fungi and yeasts.

  • The pH is adjusted to approximately 5.6 in order to enhance the growth of fungi, especially dermatophytes, and to slightly inhibit bacterial growth in clinical specimens.

    • Dextrose is added as the energy and carbon source.

    • Chloramphenicol and/or tetracycline may be added as broad spectrum antimicrobials to inhibit the growth of a wide range of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

• Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. Pulmonary mucormycosis is the second most common form.
  • Mucormycosis is an invasive disease caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia.
  • The disease is often characterized by hyphae growing in and around the blood vessels. It can turn fatal on cerebral involvement and development of septicaemia.

Risk factors for the infection include:

  • Elevated levels of free iron.
  • Defects in phagocytic function. (e.g. neutropenia or steroid therapy).
  • Organ or hematopoietic stem transplantation.

  • Patients taking iron therapy or deferoxamine (iron chelator)

190.question_text: A HIV positive female presents with complaints of fever and shortness of breath for 4 days. On CT scan of lungs: ground glass opacities are found. Histopathological examination of lung tissue obtained by bronchoscopy shows the following result. Identify the etiology in this patient.
190.explanation:
• The photo shows ping pong balls on methenamine silver stain which indicates the etiology to be pneumocystis jirovecii along with ground glass opacities on CT and HIV being a risk factor.
  • Pneumocystis pneumonia (PcP) has been increasingly reported after the discovery of HIV/AIDS.
  • Histopathological examination of lung tissue or fluids obtained by bronchoscopy, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), or open lung biopsy reveals cysts.
  • Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) staining is the method of choice to demonstrate the cysts of P. jirovecii. The cysts resemble black colored crushed ping-pong balls, against the green background.
  • Pneumocystis is not cultivable and there is no serological test available.
  • Radiology: Chest X-ray depicts classical finding of bilateral diffuse infiltrates. CT of the lung may reveal ground-glass opacities at the early stage.

190.question_text: A 65 year old female diagnosed with COVID 19, was admitted to a private hospital, with chief complaints of shortness of breath for 3 days. On examination the vitals were: BP: 156/108mmHg, SpO2: 88%, PR: 98/min and temperature: 101.8°F. The patient has been on anti-diabetic drugs for 10 years and on antihypertensive drugs for 6 years. On the 10th day of her admission, she noticed sudden blackening of skin near the nose and eye, had complaints of purulent discharge from nose, facial swelling and rapid deterioration of general condition and On nasal examination black necrotic mass was seen occupying the nasal cavity as shown in figure. What is the probable diagnosis of the condition the patient is having and what will be the best next step in order to save the life of the patient?
190.option_a: Orbital cellulitis; Antibiotics and supportive therapy
190.explanation:
Mucormycosis is an uncommon but serious infection that complicates the course of severe COVID-19.

  • Mucormycosis, previously termed as zygomycosis, is a rare fungal ailment, instigated by the mucormycetes mould, that occurs extensively in soil, leaves, decayed wood and putrefied manure.
  • Besides darkening of skin, inflammation, redness, ulcers, fevers, this dangerous sickness can also invade the lungs, eyes and even the brain, proving to be fatal if left unattended to.
  • Therefore, it is crucial to understand the causative factors and prominent symptoms associated with Mucormycosis, to quickly identify any possible warning signs arising in both, COVID-19 patients and other individuals.
  • These must be promptly conveyed to the healthcare professional so that timely medical treatment can be provided and the affected individual recovers completely.

190.question_text: A 62 year old male patient comes to the ER with features of meningoencephalitis. Wet mount examination of his CSF shows the presence of motile unicellular organisms. The organism is most likely to be?
190.explanation:
Encephalitis is an acute inflammation of the brain parenchyma by invasion of infectious agents, most often the viruses.

  • Manifestations: The common manifestations include altered consciousness, behavioural changes, seizures, focal neurological deficits and sometimes, extrapyramidal signs such as involuntary movements.
  • Agents: The common etiological agents of encephalitis include viruses, followed by parasites.
    • Viruses: Include rabies, herpes, and arboviruses such as Japanese encephalitis and West Nile viruses
    • Parasites: Such as Toxoplasma gondii and Naegleria fowleri. The cellular infiltrate present in the CSF is typically lymphocytic rather than neutrophilic .
  • Very often, encephalitis is associated with concomitant meningitis; called as meningoencephalitis (e.g. primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, caused by a free-living amoeba called Naegleria fowleri).

Trypanosoma cruzi is the causative agent of South American trypanosomiasis or Chaga's disease.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 689

190.question_text: A 34-year-old man presents with 2-day history of progressively blurred vision. He also reports seeing flashing lights in his visual field. Examination shows right conjunctival injection. Visual acuity is 20/20 in the left eye and 20/100 in the right eye. Funduscopic examination of the right eye is shown. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 46/mm3. Which of the following is responsible for this patient's eye condition?
190.explanation:
• Fundoscopy in this patient, who’s depressed CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is almost certainly secondary to infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), shows fluffy, hemorrhagic, perivascular retinal lesions that radiate out from the optic disc (pizza-pie appearance).
  • These symptoms and findings are characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis.
  • Valgancyclovir is the first-line therapy for CMV retinitis, a condition that can cause blurring, vision loss, floaters, and photopsia (flashing lights).
  • Other first-line systemic therapies include ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir.
  • Patients with acutely sight-threatening disease (e.g., lesions < 1.5 mm from the fovea or adjacent to the optic nerve head) should also receive intravitreal therapy with ganciclovir or foscarnet.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

190.question_text: A 45-year-old female from a village of Bihar came to the hospital with a history of fever on and off for the past one year and recently developed unilateral swelling of the left lower limb. Her blood sample was sent for peripheral blood smear examination which revealed microfilariae, 240 μm in length, tail tip pointed free of nuclei. What is the etiological diagnosis?
190.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of Elephantiasis by W.bancrofti.

Lymphatic Filariasis:

Lymphatic filariasis passes through four stages.

  • Endemic normal
  • Asymptomatic Microfilaremia
  • Acute Filariasis (acute adenolymphangitis)
  • Chronic Filariasis

The manifestations in descending order of occurrence are:

  1. Hydrocele (most common manifestation): Accumulation of clear straw colored fluid in the cavity of tunica vaginalis of testes.
  2. Elephantiasis (swelling of lower limb or less commonly arm, vulva or breast)
  3. Lymphedema is initially pitting type (stage-1) which becomes non pitting and irreversible on limb elevation (stage-2) followed by brawny lymphedema with thickening of the skin (grade-3), finally lead to fibrosis and fissuring (grade-4)
  4. Chronic funiculitis and epididymitis.
  5. Chyluria: Excretion of chyle, a milky white fluid in urine may occur rarely. This is due to rupture of lymph vessels into the urinary system.

Both lymphatic filariasis and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia syndrome are observed in brugian filariasis.

  • Clinical features are similar to bancroftian filariasis except: More frequent episodes of acute adenolymphangitis, adenitis (femoral nodes), and filarial abscesses.
  • Chronic manifestations (lymphedema and elephantiasis) occur less frequently.
  • The genital involvement is not seen.
  • Elephantiasis: Swelling is limited to legs below the knee.
  • Chyluria does not occur.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 376

190.question_text: Plasma sterilization is primarily achieved using which of the following?
190.explanation:
Explanation:

Plasma sterilization involves sterilizing medical instruments and equipment by exposing them to vaporized hydrogen peroxide in a low-pressure environment. The vapor is then energized into a plasma state, producing highly reactive ions and free radicals that efficiently destroy microorganisms.

Explanation of Other options:

Ethylene oxide (Option A): Used for gas sterilization of heat- and moisture-sensitive equipment but not part of plasma sterilization.

Gamma rays (Option B): Utilized in radiation sterilization, effective for deep sterilization of certain medical items, but unrelated to plasma sterilization.

Ultraviolet radiation (Option D): Effective for surface sterilization but cannot penetrate materials deeply enough to achieve plasma sterilization.

Standard precautions are a set of infection control practices used to prevent transmission of diseases that can be acquired by contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin (including rashes), and mucous membranes. These measures should be followed when providing care to or handling:

Standard precautions are a set of infection control practices used to prevent transmission of diseases that can be acquired by contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin (including rashes), and mucous membranes. These measures should be followed when providing care to or handling:

191.question_text: Most potent stimulator of Naive T-cells -
191.explanation: Mature Dendritic cells Mature B-cells and T-cells before antigenic exposure are called naive-B and T cells respectively. Sequence of events in activation of naive T cells. Immature dendritic cells in the epidermis are called langerhans cell. These immature dendritic cells (langerhans cells) capture the antigen in the epidermis. After capturing the antigen these cells secrete cytokines. These cytokines cause loss of adhesiveness of langerhans cells. Langerhans cells separate from each other and migrate into lymphatic vessels. In lymphatic vessel, maturation of langerhans cells takes place. Then these mature langerhans dendritic cells reach to naive T cells in the lymph nodes and present antigen to these cells and activate them.

191.question_text: All are features of HLA-A molecules, EXCEPT:
191.explanation:

  • MHC Class I molecules are always associated with B2-microglobulin.
  • MHC-I molecules act as a target for elimination of infected or tumor-transformed host cells by CD8-bearing cytotoxic T cells.
  • The MHC class I molecules bind endogenous peptides during their synthesis by host cells.
  • The MHC class II molecules bind exogenous peptides produced during lysosomal enzyme degradation of ingested proteins internalized by antigen-presenting cells.
