191.question_text: Which of the following accurately describes a key difference between MHC class I and MHC class II molecules?
191.option_a: MHC class I molecules present endogenous antigens to CD8+ T cells, while MHC class II molecules present exogenous antigens to CD4+ T cells.
191.option_b: MHC class I molecules are found only on professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs), whereas MHC class II molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells.
191.option_c: MHC class I molecules present exogenous antigens, whereas MHC class II molecules present endogenous antigens.
191.option_d: MHC class I molecules are involved in activating helper T cells, while MHC class II molecules are involved in activating cytotoxic T cells.
191.explanation:
• MHC class I molecules present endogenous antigens to CD8+ T cells, while MHC class II molecules present exogenous antigens to CD4+ T cells: This is correct. MHC class I molecules present peptides from intracellular (endogenous) proteins to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, while MHC class II molecules present peptides from extracellular (exogenous) proteins to CD4+ helper T cells.
  • MHC class I molecules are found only on professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs), whereas MHC class II molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells: This is incorrect. MHC class I molecules are expressed on all nucleated cells, while MHC class II molecules are restricted to professional APCs (such as dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells).
  • MHC class I molecules present exogenous antigens, whereas MHC class II molecules present endogenous antigens: This is incorrect. MHC class I molecules present endogenous antigens, while MHC class II molecules present exogenous antigens.
  • MHC class I molecules are involved in activating helper T cells, while MHC class II molecules are involved in activating cytotoxic T cells: This is incorrect. MHC class I molecules activate cytotoxic T cells (CD8+), and MHC class II molecules activate helper T cells (CD4+).

Key Takeaway: MHC class I molecules present endogenous antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and are expressed on all nucleated cells, whereas MHC class II molecules present exogenous antigens to CD4+ helper T cells and are primarily expressed on antigen-presenting cells.

191.question_text: Where would the eggs/ova of helminths be concentrated by the formol-ether technique shown in the figure?
191.explanation:
Formal ether technique is a widely used technique for stool examination. Concentration procedure separate parasite from fecal debris and increase the chances of detecting parasitic organisms when these are in small numbers.

They are divided into flotation technique and sedimentation technique.

Procedure mix small portion of stool about the size of marble, in 10 ml 5 -10 % formalin in a test tube. Allow to stand 30 min for fixation. Strain about 10 ml of this suspension through a small funnel containing wet gauze into a 15 ml centrifuge tube. Use two layers of gauze.

The suspension should yield about 0.75 ml of sediment for fresh specimens and 0.5 ml for formalinized feces.

Decant the supernatant and wash the sediment with 10 ml of saline solution. Centrifuge again and repeat washing until supernatant is clear.

After the last wash, decant the supernatant and add 10 ml of 10 % formalin to the sediment. Mix and let stand for 5 min to effect fixation.

Add 1 to 2 ml of ethyl acetate, stopper the tube and shake vigorously,

Centrifuge at 450 g RCF ( about 1500 rpm) for 10 min. Four layers should result as follow

  1. A top layer of ethyl acetate
  2. Plug of debris
  3. Layer of formalin
  4. Sediment
  5. Free the plug of debris from the side of the tube by ringing with an applicator stick. Carefully decan the top three layers

The 4th layer has parasitic eggs.

Key Takeaway:

The Formol-Ether Concentration Technique separates stool components into four layers after centrifugation. Helminth eggs and protozoan cysts concentrate in the sediment layer (Layer 4), making it the correct choice for microscopic examination.

191.question_text: ParvoB19 infection is associated with all except?
191.option_b: Transient aplastic crisis with hemolytic anemia
191.explanation:
Explanation:

  • A plastic anemia is not the most typical presentation of Parvovirus B19 infection in immunocompromised individuals.
  • While Parvovirus B19 can cause transient aplastic crises in patients with underlying hemolytic disorders, immunocompromised patients usually develop chronic anaemia or persistent infection due to impaired viral clearance, rather than true aplastic anaemia.

Clinical Manifestations of Parvovirus infections:

  • Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease) (Option A ruled out)
    • Children: "Slapped cheek" rash on the face followed by a lacy rash on the trunk and limbs.
    • Adult women: Symmetrical polyarthropathy, especially in the hands and knees.
  • Transient Aplastic Crisis (Option B ruled out)
    • Causes severe acute anemia in patients with pre-existing hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell anemia, thalassemia).
  • Pure Red Cell Aplasia (Characteristic in immunocompromised individuals)
    • Leads to chronic anemia due to persistent Parvovirus B19 infection.
  • Non-Immune Hydrops Fetalis (Option D ruled out)
    • Occurs via transplacental transmission (~30% of cases).
    • Causes severe fetal anemia and death; highest risk during the second trimester.
  • Papular-Purpuric Gloves and Socks Syndrome
    • Painful, itchy, symmetric swelling and erythema of the hands and feet.
    • May mimic acute meningococcemia.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • PCR: Highly sensitive, detects viral DNA (VP1, VP2 genes) in serum, tissue, or respiratory secretions.
  • ELISA: Detects IgM antibody (early indicator, elevated 2-3 months) and IgG against VP1 and VP2 antigens.
  • Immunohistochemistry: Detects viral antigens in fetal tissues and bone marrow.
  • Bone marrow cytology shows Giant pro-erythroblasts with multiple cytoplasmic projections that look like "dog ears" or "pseudopodia".

191.question_text: A 35-year-old patient presents with frequent bacterial infections and is found to have a genetic deficiency in complement component C3. Which aspect of innate immunity is most directly affected by this deficiency?
191.explanation:
Complement component C3 is crucial for opsonization, a process where pathogens are tagged for easier recognition and engulfment by phagocytes like macrophages and neutrophils. A deficiency in C3 impairs this process, leading to increased susceptibility to bacterial infections. While C3 is important for opsonization, it does not directly affect interferon production, T cell activation, or the barrier function of the skin.

Key Takeaway: Deficiency in complement component C3 primarily affects the phagocytosis of pathogens due to impaired opsonization.

191.question_text: Which test is used to assess long-term glucose control?
191.explanation:
Explanation:

HbA1C (glycated hemoglobin) is the test used to evaluate long-term glucose tolerance by measuring the average blood sugar levels over the previous three months. It indicates the percentage of hemoglobin molecules that have glucose bound to them, offering a reliable marker of overall blood sugar control.

Explanation for other options:

Fasting blood glucose (Option A): This test measures blood sugar levels after at least 8 hours of fasting. While helpful for diagnosing diabetes, it does not offer a long-term assessment of glucose tolerance.

Random blood glucose (Option B): This measures blood sugar at any time of day, regardless of the last meal. It can aid in diagnosing diabetes but does not reflect long-term glucose control.

CBC (Complete Blood Count) (Option D): This test evaluates components of the blood such as red and white blood cells and platelets, but it is unrelated to glucose metabolism.

Reference:

The A1C Test & Diabetes - NIDDK

191.question_text: A 30 year old man reports four hours after acquiring a clean wound without laceration. He had received TT vaccination 10 year back. What do you advice regarding tetanus prophylaxis?
191.explanation:
As it is clean wound without laceration, Person has taken TT before 10 years.

So as per guideline, he should take single dose of TT

Prevention of tetanus after injury.

All wounds must be thoroughly cleaned soon after injury- Removal of foreign body, soil, dust, necrotic tissue. This procedure abolish anaerobic conditions which favour germination of tetanus spore.

Further management depend on the immune status, type of wound and duration of wound.

A - He had complete course of toxoid or a booster dose within the past 5 years

B - Had a complete course of toxoid or a booster dose more than 5 years ago and less than 10 year ago

C - Had a complete course of toxoid or a booster dose more than 10 years ago.

D - Has not had a complete course of toxoid or immunity status is unknow.

All wound surgical toilet

1) Would less than 6 hr old, clean, non penetrating and with negligible tissue damage

  • IF A - nothing more required
  • IF B - Toxoid 1 dose
  • IF C- toxoid 1 dose
  • IF D - Toxoid complete course

2) Other wounds

  • IF A - nothing more required
  • IF B- toxoid 1 dose
  • IF C - Toxoid 1 dose plus human immunoglobulin
  • If D - Toxoid complete course plus human immunoglobulin

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option B) Full course of TT → Incorrect.
    • Full TT course is only needed if the last dose was >10 years ago or if the patient has never been vaccinated.
  • (Option C) 1 dose TT + TIG → Incorrect.
    • Tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) is only required for high-risk wounds (dirty, deep, or crush injuries) in patients whose last TT dose was more than 10 years ago or unknown.
  • (Option D) No vaccination needed → Incorrect.
    • Since the last dose was 10 years ago, a booster dose is required.

Key Takeaways:

  • Clean minor wound + last TT dose 5-10 years ago → Single booster TT dose required.
  • Dirty wound + last TT dose >10 years ago → TT + TIG.
  • No prophylaxis if last TT dose was within 5 years.

191.question_text: What is a primary advantage of Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) in fungal molecular diagnostics?
191.option_c: Use of two fluorophores to measure DNA distance
191.explanation:
• Use of two fluorophores to measure DNA distance: This is a key feature of FRET; it detects changes in fluorescence based on the proximity of two fluorophores, allowing for sensitive measurement of molecular interactions and presence of fungal pathogens.

Why Not Others:

  • A: FRET is complex and not simply about detecting DNA, as it involves multiple components and requires precise calibration. Simplicity in detecting DNA: FRET is not a simple technique; it requires careful setup and calibration due to its reliance on two fluorophores for effective detection, making it more complex than basic DNA detection methods.
  • B: High specificity for fungal DNA: While FRET can be designed to target specific sequences, its primary advantage lies in measuring distances between fluorophores rather than exclusively ensuring high specificity for fungal DNA.
  • D: Non-quantitative results: This statement is incorrect; FRET is inherently quantitative as it provides measurements based on the intensity of fluorescence signals, offering insights into the concentration of target nucleic acids.

Key Takeaway: FRET utilizes the distance between two fluorophores to detect fungal DNA, providing valuable insights into the presence of fungal pathogens through quantitative fluorescence measurements.

191.question_text: What is the primary advantage of using galactomannan and glucan tests in fungal infection diagnosis?

Why Not Others:

Specificity: Galactomannan and glucan tests are not designed to identify individual fungal species; rather, they detect components associated with a broad range of fungal pathogens, making them less specific.
  • C: Complementary Role: While these tests are informative, they do not replace the need for traditional fungal cultures, which remain the gold standard for definitive identification.
  • D: Bacterial Detection: The galactomannan and glucan tests are specifically tailored for fungal infections and do not provide accurate information about bacterial infections.

Key Takeaway: Galactomannan and glucan tests are instrumental for early detection of fungal infections and effective therapeutic monitoring, aiding in the timely management of patients at risk.

191.question_text: What is the purpose of warming the slide in the KOH wet mount preparation?
191.option_a: To dissolve the fungal elements more effectively
191.option_b: To prevent the formation of air bubbles
191.option_c: To enhance the color contrast of the fungal elements
191.option_d: To speed up the clearing process
191.explanation:
• To speed up the clearing process: Warming the slide accelerates the clearing of the specimen by increasing the kinetic energy of the KOH solution, leading to more rapid penetration and breakdown of the sample components.
  • Warming enhances the effectiveness of KOH in clearing the specimen, allowing for quicker visualization of fungal elements.
  • This technique is especially useful in clinical settings where rapid diagnosis is essential.
  • The warming process can also help to reduce viscosity, facilitating the movement of the KOH solution throughout the preparation.

Why Not Others:

  • a is incorrect To dissolve the fungal elements more effectively: Warming does not significantly enhance the dissolution of fungal elements; the KOH is already effective at dissolving keratin and other debris.
  • b is partially correct but not the main purpose; air bubbles can be minimized through careful handling and technique. To prevent the formation of air bubbles: Although warming can help reduce air bubbles, it is not the primary purpose of warming the slide.
  • c is incorrect To enhance the color contrast of the fungal elements: Warming does not affect the color contrast of fungal structures under the microscope.

Key Takeaways:

  • Warming the slide in KOH preparation primarily serves to speed up the clearing process of the specimen.
  • This method ensures efficient visualization of fungal elements for accurate diagnosis.

191.question_text: NK cells kill the viral infected cells due to:
191.option_a: Increased expression of MHC class I molecules
191.option_b: Decreased expression of MHC class I molecules
191.option_c: Increased expression of MHC class II molecules
191.option_d: Decreased expression of MHC class II molecules
191.explanation:
• While on patrol NK cells constantly contact other cells. Whether or not the NK cell kills these cells depends on a balance of signals from activating receptors and inhibitory receptors on the NK cell surface.
  • Activating receptors recognise molecules that are expressed on the surface of cancer cells and infected cells, and 'switch on' the NK cell. Inhibitory receptors act as a check on NK cell killing.
  • Most normal healthy cells express MHC I receptors which mark these cells as 'self'. Inhibitory receptors on the surface of the NK cell recognise cognate MHC I, and this 'switches off' the NK cell, preventing it from killing. Cancer cells and infected cells often lose their MHC I, leaving them vulnerable to NK cell killing. Once the decision is made to kill, the NK cell releases cytotoxic granules containing perforin and granzymes, which leads to lysis of the target cell.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 14, Pg 131-133

    • Serum immunoglobulins
    • Serum protein electrophoresis
    • IgG subclasses
    • B cell phenotype
    • Specific antibody levels pre and post immunization with polysaccharide and conjugate vaccines (e.g., Pneumovax and Menitorix)

Common variable immunodeficiency

  • The clinical manifestations (secondary infection, autoimmune diseases) are superficially similar to those of Bruton diseases; but differ in the following aspects:
    • Both sexes are affected equally
    • Onset of symptoms is much later, in the second or third decade of life.
    • It is also B-cell development defect; B-cells may be present in circulation in normal numbers, but they appear defective in their ability to differentiate into plasma cells and secrete immunoglobulins.
    • The diagnosis is usually one of exclusion (after other causes of immunodeficiency are ruled out); the basis of the immunoglobulin deficiency is variable (hence the name).
    • The defect in the antibody production has been variably attributed to intrinsic B-cell defects, deficient T-cell help, or excessive T-cell suppressor activity.

  • Development of memory cells: Memory cell development is a feature of acquired immunity.
  • Production of antibodies: Antibody production is primarily a function of acquired immunity.

Key Takeaway: The innate immune system is known for its immediate and non-specific response to pathogens.

191.question_text: Antigen binding to MHC I activates
191.explanation:
There are 3 types of MHC. MHC I, MHC II and MHC III

MHC stands for Major histocompatibility complex.

It is also known as HLA ( human leucocyte antigen).

It has major role in graft rejection. All cells have MHC I or MHC II except RBCs.

Antigen binding and processing done by MHC I and MHC II depending on whether the intracellular antigen is there or extracellular antigen is there.

For MHC I Cytotoxic T cell are involved, for MHC II B cells are involved.

MHC I or II does not stimulate Helper T cell or NK Cells.

Incorrect Choices Explanation:

Choice A: B cell B cells are primarily involved in humoral immunity and recognize antigens via their surface immunoglobulin receptors. They are activated by MHC II-restricted antigen presentation, not MHC I, which is associated with cytotoxic T cell activation.

Choice C: Helper T cell Helper T cells (CD4+ T cells) are activated by antigens presented on MHC II molecules, which are expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells. MHC I does not activate Helper T cells.

Choice D: NK cell Natural Killer (NK) cells do not require antigen presentation through MHC I for activation. Instead, they target cells that lack MHC I expression, a characteristic feature of some virally infected or cancerous cells. Their activation is regulated by inhibitory and activating signals rather than antigen-MHC interactions.

Key Takeaway:

MHC I presents intracellular antigens to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, leading to targeted cell destruction. In contrast, MHC II presents extracellular antigens to CD4+ helper T cells, which aid in immune response coordination.

191.question_text: Apart from NK cells, which cells can recognize and kill antibody-coated target cells in antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)?
191.explanation:
Explanation:

ADCC is a defense mechanism where immune cells lyse target cells coated with antibodies.

  • Mechanism: Antibodies (IgG or IgE) bind to target cell → Fc portion engages Fc receptors on effector cells → cytotoxic release kills the target.
  • Cells involved:
    • NK cells (major role).
    • Neutrophils and eosinophils (especially important in parasitic infections).
    • Macrophages also participate to some extent.
  • Target cells: Tumor cells, virus-infected cells, and large parasites.

Explanation of other options:

NK cells only (Option A): NK cells are important but not the only effectors.

Macrophages only (Option B): Participate in ADCC but not exclusively.

Neutrophils only (Option D): Both neutrophils and eosinophils are important contributors.

Key Takeaways:

  • ADCC = antibody + Fc receptor → immune cell-mediated killing.
  • NK cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, and macrophages can all mediate ADCC.
  • Eosinophils + IgE → key in parasite defense.

191.question_text: Delayed hypersensitivity reaction is mediated by:
191.explanation:
Delayed Hypersensitivity Reaction:

  • Delayed hypersensitivity reactions are a type of immune response that occurs 24 to 72 hours after exposure to an antigen.

Mediating Cells:

  • T lymphocytes (T cells) play a central role in delayed hypersensitivity reactions.
    • Specifically, T helper cells (CD4+ cells) are involved in orchestrating this immune response.
    • These cells release cytokines that activate other immune cells and initiate an inflammatory response.

Immune Response Mechanism:

  • In delayed hypersensitivity reactions, T cells recognize and respond to antigens presented by antigen-presenting cells (e.g., dendritic cells or macrophages).
  • T helper cells release cytokines that activate macrophages and other immune cells in the affected tissue.

Result:

  • This activation of immune cells results in inflammation and tissue damage at the site of antigen exposure.
  • The inflammatory response contributes to the characteristic signs and symptoms of delayed hypersensitivity reactions.

Other Options:

  • B lymphocytes (Option A) are responsible for the production of antibodies in humoral immunity, not delayed hypersensitivity.
  • NK cells (Option B) are associated with innate immunity and are not the primary mediators of delayed hypersensitivity reactions.
  • Mast cells (Option C) are primarily involved in immediate hypersensitivity reactions, specifically type I hypersensitivity reactions, and are not the main mediators of delayed hypersensitivity.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

191.question_text: NK cells provide direct immunity against which of the following microorganism?
191.explanation:
• Functions of NK cell
  1. Kills virus infected cells and cancer cells.
    • They are called “natural” killer cells because
      • They are active without prior exposure to the virus
      • They are not enhanced by exposure.
      • They are not specific for any virus.
    • Killing is nonspecific and not dependent on antigen presentation by MHC-I/II proteins.
    • However, NK cells have receptors that detect the presence of class I MHC proteins on the cell surface. If a cell displays sufficient class I MHC proteins, that cell is not killed by the NK cell. Virus-infected cells and tumor cells have reduced amount of class I MHC proteins, and it is those cells that are recognized and killed by the NK cells.
    • NK cells detect MICA protein that is found on the surface of cancer cells but not normal cells. Interaction of MICA with a receptor on NK cells triggers the production of cytotoxins by the NK cell and death of the tumor cell.
    • They kill by secreting cytotoxins (perforins and granzyme) like Cytotoxic T cells and by participating in Fas-Fas ligand-mediated apoptosis

192.question_text: A newborn female has a malformed jaw, cardiac abnormalities, and hypocalcemia and diminished cell-mediated and B cell responses. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
192.explanation:
• The defects in jaw, heart and calcium metabolism (due to abnormal parathyroid development) point to defect in development of structures derived from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
  • None of the other diseases given are associated with these accompanying features.
  • This individual is likely to have an underdeveloped thymus, which is a hallmark of DiGeorge syndrome.

DiGeorge syndrome (Thymic hypoplasia)

  • It results from a congenital defect in thymic development leading to defect in T-cell maturation.
  • Infants are extremely vulnerable to viral, fungal, intracellular bacterial and protozoan infections.
  • Pathogenesis: In 90% of cases, there occurs a deletion affecting chromosome 22q11 → leads to malformation of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches in embryonic life
  • As a result, all the structures that develop from third and fourth pharyngeal pouches such as thymus, parathyroid glands, and portions of the face and aortic arch become defective.
  • Thus, in addition to the thymic defects, there may be associated:
    • Parathyroid gland hypoplasia resulting in neonatal tetany and hypocalcemia
    • Anomalies of the heart and the great vessels (Fallot’sTetralogy).
    • Characteristic facial appearance
  • B-cells and serum immunoglobulin levels are generally unaffected.
  • Treatment: Thymus transplantation

192.question_text: DNA hybridization, where DNA is detected using specific probes, is called:
192.explanation:
Applications of Southern Blotting:

  • Genetic Testing: To detect specific mutations related to genetic diseases.
  • Forensic Analysis: In criminal investigations to match DNA samples.
  • Gene Cloning: To confirm the presence of specific gene sequences in recombinant DNA studies.
  • Option A: Southern blot
    • Correct: This technique detects specific DNA sequences through hybridization with labeled probes. It involves digesting DNA with restriction enzymes, separating the fragments by gel electrophoresis, transferring them to a membrane, and hybridizing with a complementary labeled probe.
  • Option B: Northern blot
    • Incorrect: The Northern blot is used for detecting RNA sequences. It follows a similar process as the Southern blot but focuses on RNA instead of DNA.
  • Option C: Eastern blot
    • Incorrect: The Eastern blot is used for detecting glycoproteins. It is not related to nucleic acids but instead focuses on analyzing post-translational modifications.
  • Option D: Western blot
    • Incorrect: The Western blot is used for detecting proteins. This technique involves separating proteins by gel electrophoresis, transferring them to a membrane, and probing with specific antibodies.

KEY TAKE AWAY: The Southern blot technique is used for DNA hybridization to detect specific DNA sequences using labeled probes.

Tags: must know | neet

Reference: Sastry, A. S., & Bhat, S. K. (2022). Review of Microbiology & Immunology (With DVD) (4th ed.). Jaypee Brothers Medical Publishers. Chapter: (Blotting Techniques), Page no. 95-100.

192.question_text: Select the correct statement regarding the organism shown in the image.
192.option_b: Patient is at high risk with CD4<900
192.option_c: Lung is the primary site of infection
192.explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows an India ink preparation with cells surrounded by a clear halo, indicating Cryptococcus, whose primary site of infection is the lungs.

Cryptococcus

  • Cryptococcus is a true yeast with a polysaccharide capsule that protects against phagocytosis.
  • The capsule allows serotyping:
    • Serotypes A, D, and AD correspond to Cryptococcus neoformans
    • Serotypes B and C correspond to Cryptococcus gattii.
  • Birds and bats serve as natural reservoirs. (Option A ruled out)
  • Humans acquire the fungus by inhaling spores from contaminated environments, such as bird or bat droppings.
  • Infection risk increases in immunocompromised individuals, those exposed to bird droppings or decaying wood, and people in tropical or subtropical regions.
  • Cryptococcus is the most common cause of meningitis in HIV-positive individuals.
  • It causes infection in immunocompromised individuals, when CD4 counts < 100. (Option B ruled out)

Virulence factors

  • Polysaccharide Capsule
    • The primary virulence factor.
    • It helps the pathogen evade phagocytosis and suppresses the host’s local immune responses, enabling the organism to survive and spread.
  • Melanin Production
    • Cryptococcus produces melanin via the enzyme phenol oxidase, which the pathogen from oxidative stress and immune defenses.
  • Enzyme Production
    • The fungus secretes several enzymes, including:
  • Phospholipase
    • Aids in tissue invasion and damage.
  • Urease
    • Helps the fungus survive in the host environment by neutralizing acidic conditions, enhancing its ability to colonize and spread.

Infections Caused by Cryptococcus

  • Pulmonary Cryptococcosis
    • Primary infection in the lungs after inhalation of spores; may be asymptomatic or cause pneumonia-like symptoms.
  • Cryptococcal Meningoencephalitis
    • Most common disseminated form, especially in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS), leading to headache, fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status.
  • Cutaneous Cryptococcosis
    • Skin lesions, often secondary to disseminated infection.
  • Other Disseminated Disease
    • May involve bones, prostate, or other organs in severely immunocompromised individuals.



Treatment

  • Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine
  • Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status.
  • Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes.
  • Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk.

Explanation of other options:

Pseudohyphae and budding is seen (Option D): These features are characteristic of Candida species. In contrast, Cryptococcus typically appears as encapsulated yeast cells without pseudohyphae.

Reference:

  1. Cryptococcus gattii - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics.

192.question_text: Which of the following helps in bacterial adhesion?
192.explanation:
Role of fimbriae is adhesions. Fimbriae can have other role as sex pilus, which helps in transfer of genetic material between two bacteria.

Role of flagella is locomotion. It can be monotrichous, peritrichous, Lophotrichous, amphitrichous

LPS is lipopolysaccharide it is present in Gram negative bacteria, it has role in septic shock production.

Mesosome supports respiration and secretion and enhance plasma membrane surface area and enzyme .

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option A) Cytoplasmic membrane → Incorrect
    • The cytoplasmic membrane controls transport of molecules in and out of the bacterial cell.
    • It does not play a direct role in adhesion.
  • (Option B) Mesosomes → Incorrect
    • Mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane.
    • Their proposed functions include respiration, DNA replication, and secretion, not adhesion.
  • (Option D) LPS (Lipopolysaccharide) → Incorrect
    • Found in Gram-negative bacteria, it is a component of the outer membrane.
    • Plays a role in immune evasion and septic shock, but not in adhesion.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fimbriae (pili) are the primary bacterial structures responsible for adhesion.
  • They allow bacteria to attach to host cells and establish infections.
  • LPS and mesosomes serve other functions but do not help in bacterial adhesion.

192.question_text: Opsonisation is directly mediated by:

192.question_text: A 2-year-old male child with an X-linked defect in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene is impaired in:
192.option_b: Formation of the membrane attack complex
192.option_c: IFN-γ secretion by CD4+ T cells
192.option_d: T cell precursor migration to the thymus
192.explanation:
• Bruton's agammaglobulinemia results in a near or total absence of B cells and immunoglobulins; hence antibody-mediated responses to microbes are severely impaired.
  • Even without antibodies and the classical pathway of complement activation, the membrane attack complex (MAC) can be formed through the MBL and alternative pathways.
  • Antibodies are not involved in the other options.

Bruton disease (X-linked agammaglobulinemia)

  • It is characterized by failure of pre-B-cells to differentiate into immature B-cells in the bone marrow- due to absence of an enzyme called Bruton’s tyrosine kinase leading to total absence of B-cells, plasma cells and all classes of Ig.
  • The B-cell maturation stops at pre B cell stage; after the synthesis of heavy-chain without forming the light chains.
  • Hence the cytoplasm of pre B cell have incomplete immunoglobulins.
  • X linked disorder: hence seen primarily in males; rarely in females.
  • Onset -after 6 months of life.
  • Secondary infection:
    • Recurrent bacterial infections,
    • Viruses (enteroviruses) and
    • Parasites (Giardia lamblia)
  • Autoimmune diseases (such as SLE and dermatomyositis) also occur in up to 20% of cases.

192.question_text: Antibody diversity is due to:
192.explanation:
• Antibody diversity is the phenomenon of immense variability characteristic of antibodies, which enables the immune system to react specifically against the essentially unlimited kinds of antigens it encounters.

  • The large number of inherited V, J, and D gene segments available for encoding antibody chains makes a substantial contribution on its own to antibody diversity, but the combinatorial joining of these segments (called combinatorial diversification) greatly increases this contribution.

192.question_text: Which of the following is a crucial element involved in activating the complement through the alternative pathway?
192.explanation:
Explanation:

C3 is the central and crucial component for alternative pathway activation. The pathway initiates through spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 to form C3(H₂O) in a process called "tickover."

This hydrolyzed C3 then binds Factor B, which is cleaved by Factor D to form the initial C3 convertase (C3bBb). This enzyme amplifies the pathway by cleaving more C3 molecules into C3a and C3b, creating a powerful positive feedback loop.

C3b deposited on pathogen surfaces forms additional C3 convertase molecules, making C3 essential for both initiation and amplification of the alternative pathway.

Complement System

A complex network of over 30 plasma and membrane-bound proteins that play a key role in both innate and adaptive immunity.

Functions:

  • Lysis: Destroys pathogens by forming membrane attack complexes (pores).
  • Opsonization: Coats microbial surfaces to enhance phagocytosis.
  • Immune Clearance: Removes immune complexes and apoptotic cells from circulation.
  • Inflammation: Promotes release of inflammatory mediators and recruitment of immune cells.

Pathways of Activation:

  1. Classical Pathway – Triggered by antigen–antibody complexes.
  2. Alternative Pathway – Activated directly by pathogen surfaces.
  3. Lectin Pathway – Initiated by mannose-binding lectin binding to microbial carbohydrates.

Explanation of other options:

C1 (Option A ): Component of the classical pathway, activated by antigen-antibody complexes.

C2 (Option B): Involved in both classical and lectin pathways as part of their C3 convertase complexes.

C4 (Option D): Required for classical and lectin pathways but not for alternative pathway initiation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Alternative pathway initiates via spontaneous C3 hydrolysis (tickover)
  • C3 serves as both the initiator and amplifier of the pathway
  • Forms C3 convertase (C3bBb) that creates a positive feedback loop

192.question_text: How might the use of azole fungicides in agriculture contribute to antifungal resistance in clinical settings?
192.option_a: By causing cross-resistance in environmental fungi, which can then infect humans.
192.option_b: By increasing the production of antifungal agents in the environment, leading to resistance.
192.option_c: By reducing the overall efficacy of all antifungal drugs through environmental contamination.
192.option_d: By directly affecting human immune response to fungal infections.
192.explanation:
• By causing cross-resistance in environmental fungi, which can then infect humans: This statement is correct. The use of azole fungicides in agriculture can lead to the development of resistant fungal strains, which may then infect humans and show resistance to medical azoles, complicating treatment options.

Why Not Others:

  • Option b: By increasing the production of antifungal agents in the environment, leading to resistance: This statement is incorrect. Azole fungicides do not increase the natural production of antifungal agents; instead, they exert selective pressure on fungal populations, contributing to the emergence of resistance.
  • Option c: By reducing the overall efficacy of all antifungal drugs through environmental contamination: This statement is incorrect. Environmental contamination does not universally reduce the efficacy of all antifungal drugs; rather, it may lead to specific resistance in certain fungal strains.
  • Option d: By directly affecting human immune response to fungal infections: This statement is incorrect. Azole fungicides do not have a direct impact on the human immune response; their primary concern is the emergence of resistant strains in the environment.

Key Takeaway:

  • The use of azole fungicides in agriculture can contribute to antifungal resistance in clinical settings by creating resistant fungal strains in the environment, which can then infect humans.

Tag Line: Moderate

Reference: Textbook of Medical Mycology Hardcover - 1 January 2018, by Jagdish Chander. Chapter 6: Antifungal Therapy 115.

192.question_text: How can drug interactions impact the effectiveness of antifungal therapy?
192.option_a: By increasing the absorption of antifungal drugs, leading to reduced efficacy.
192.option_b: By altering the metabolism of antifungal drugs, potentially reducing their effectiveness.
192.option_c: By enhancing the excretion of antifungal drugs, leading to increased efficacy.
192.option_d: By directly modifying the structure of the antifungal drugs, causing resistance.
192.explanation:
• By altering the metabolism of antifungal drugs, potentially reducing their effectiveness: This statement is correct. Drug interactions can significantly impact the metabolism of antifungal medications, leading to reduced drug levels and decreased efficacy.

Why Not Others:

  • Option a: By increasing the absorption of antifungal drugs, leading to reduced efficacy: This statement is incorrect. Increased absorption would generally enhance drug efficacy, not reduce it.
  • Option c: By enhancing the excretion of antifungal drugs, leading to increased efficacy: This statement is incorrect. Enhanced excretion typically reduces drug levels in the body, which can lead to a decrease in efficacy.
  • Option d: By directly modifying the structure of the antifungal drugs, causing resistance: This statement is incorrect. Drug interactions do not usually modify the chemical structure of drugs but can affect their levels and efficacy.

Key Takeaway:

  • Drug interactions can impact the effectiveness of antifungal therapy by altering the metabolism of the drugs, potentially leading to reduced efficacy.

192.question_text: Condyloma acuminata is most commonly associated with which HPV types?
192.explanation:
Explanation:

Condyloma acuminata, also known as anogenital warts, are characterized as small papules or growths that may be light brown, grey, or the same color as the surrounding skin, and they are caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV). These warts are generally not painful but have the potential to grow to a larger size, which may result in itching (pruritus) and bleeding (hemorrhage). The two most frequent strains of HPV responsible for inducing anogenital warts are types 6 and 11. The virus is capable of causing infection in the skin located on the genitalia, anus, mouth, and throat.

Condyloma Acuminata (Anogenital Warts)

  • This condition involves a benign, moist, soft, and pedunculated (stalk-like) wart located on the external genitalia, and it possesses a low malignant potential. The lesions are caused by HPV 6 and 11.
  • Location (Site): These warts are found in the genital region, which includes the penile shaft, the scrotum, the labia majora of the vagina, or in the anal area.
  • Gross Features (Appearance): They generally appear pink and project outward from the skin's surface. Although their size can vary, they often start small but can merge to form extensive, large masses.
  • Histopathology (Microscopy):
    • The structure is a branching villous architecture with a supporting connective tissue stroma.
    • The epidermis exhibits hyperkeratosis and acanthosis (which denotes thickening).
    • A hallmark feature is the cytoplasmic vacuolization of the squamous cells, known specifically as koilocytosis.
    • Crucially, there is no evidence of dysplasia.
  • Oncogenic potential: Rarely malignant, unlike HPV 16/18.

Explanation of other options:

HPV 31, 33 (Option A): High-risk types associated with intraepithelial neoplasia and carcinomas.

HPV 16, 18 (Option C): Oncogenic strains strongly linked to cervical and oropharyngeal cancers.

HPV 16, 11 (Option D): Incorrect pairing; HPV 11 is low-risk while HPV 16 is high-risk.

Key Takeaways:

  • HPV 6 & 11 → benign genital warts.
  • HPV 16 & 18 → cervical carcinoma.
  • Koilocytosis is the diagnostic histological feature.

192.question_text: Maternal antibodies do not provide protective immunity to neonate in-
192.explanation:
Maternal antibodies can protect in Diphtheria, Pertussis and Tetanus Not in Polio,

Maternal antibodies to polio may impair the immune response of infants to the polio vaccine.

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option A) Diphtheria → Protected by maternal antibodies.
    • IgG antibodies from the mother cross the placenta, providing passive immunity.
    • Newborns are protected for several months, but vaccination is still required.
  • (Option B) Pertussis → Partial protection by maternal antibodies.
    • Maternal IgG offers some protection, but wanes early in infancy.
    • Infants rely on DTaP vaccination for full protection.
  • (Option C) Tetanus → Protected by maternal antibodies.
    • Maternal IgG antibodies protect neonates if the mother is vaccinated.
    • Neonatal tetanus is preventable if the mother receives tetanus toxoid vaccination during pregnancy.

Key Takeaways:

  • Polio is NOT effectively protected by maternal antibodies.
  • Diphtheria, Pertussis, and Tetanus have some degree of protection via maternal IgG.
  • Polio vaccination is essential in early infancy due to lack of natural passive immunity.

192.question_text: A female from a tribal area of Jharkhand reports with fever for last 3 days. Peripheral blood is collected and stained with Giemsa. A diagnosis of malaria is made. The smear is shown in the figure. What is the likely cause?
192.explanation:
Given case is of Malaria. Blood picture shows ring structure. Ring of P vivax and P falciparum are different. Gametocyte are also different in shapes.

In vivax in RBC one ring is seen and Falciparum multiple rings are seen.

VIvax ring is bigger than falciparum ring.

Because gametocyte of P Falciparum is banana shaped. Or sausage shaped with pale blue or pink cytoplasm, large diffuse nuclear,

Macrogamete are - crescentic deep blue cytoplasm, compact nuclear

While p Vivax Microgamate are Spherical, compact pale blue cytoplasm diffuse nucleus

Macrogamate large spherical deep blue cytoplasm

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option B) P. vivax → Usually a single large ring per RBC
    • P. vivax shows a single ring per RBC, which is larger and more prominent than P. falciparum's multiple small rings.
    • Schüffner's dots (stippling in infected RBCs) are seen in vivax, which are absent in P. falciparum.
    • The gametocytes of P. vivax are round, not crescentic.
  • (Option C) P. malariae → Band form trophozoites
    • P. malariae trophozoites show a characteristic "band form" across the RBC, which is not seen in the given image.
    • The gametocytes of malariae are round, not crescentic.
  • (Option D) P. ovale → Rare and has oval RBCs
    • P. ovale is rare in India.
    • Infected RBCs appear oval-shaped with fimbriated edges, which are not described in the given case.

Key Takeaways:

  • Multiple ring forms per RBC → P. falciparum.
  • Banana-shaped (crescentic) gametocytes → P. falciparum.
  • Schüffner's dots and a single ring form → P. vivax.
  • Band-form trophozoites → P. malariae.
  • Oval RBCs with fimbriated edges → P. ovale.

192.question_text: The HIV genome requires which of the following to initiate the process of entering the host cell membrane?
192.explanation:
Explanation:

gp120, an envelope glycoprotein, is the first viral protein involved in HIV entry.

It attaches to the CD4 receptor on host CD4+ T-helper cells, macrophages, and dendritic This binding induces a conformational change in gp120.

Co-receptor Interaction

  • The conformational change exposes sites on gp120 that allow it to bind co-receptors:
    • CCR5 → used by R5-tropic HIV (dominant in early infection).
    • CXCR4 → used by X4-tropic HIV (often seen in late-stage infection, more aggressive).

Membrane Fusion

  • Once gp120 binds CD4 + co-receptor, gp41 (transmembrane glycoprotein) is activated.
  • gp41 mediates the fusion of viral and host membranes, allowing viral RNA and enzymes to enter the host cell.

Thus, gp120 starts the process, while CCR5/CXCR4 and gp41 act later.

HIV Structure Overview

  • Size: 80-110 nm; belongs to the Lentivirus subgroup of Retroviridae.
  • Envelope:
    • Lipid coat from the host cell.
    • Proteins: gp120 (surface spikes), gp41 (anchoring fusion protein).
  • Core (Nucleocapsid):
    • Icosahedral symmetry with a dense cylindrical inner core.
    • Contains two copies of ssRNA (+ sense).
    • Associated enzymes: Reverse transcriptase, Integrase, Protease.

HIV Genes

Structural genes (3):

  • gag → codes core proteins (p24, p18, p15).
  • Pol → enzymes (RT, Integrase, Protease).
  • env → gp160 (cleaved into gp120 + gp41).

Regulatory & accessory genes (6):

  • Tat (transcription activator), rev (RNA splicing/transport), nef (virulence regulator).
  • vif, vpr, vpu → replication, infectivity, viral release.

Explanation of other options:

CCR5 (Option B): Co-receptor required after gp120-CD4 binding.

gp41 (Option C): Fusion protein activated later, not the initiator.

CXCR4 (Option D): Alternative co-receptor, also secondary to gp120 binding.

192.question_text: What is wrongly matched
192.option_b: PIR - lag period - 4 to 7 days; SIR- lag period- 1-2 days
192.option_c: PIR-antibody affinity high ;  SIR-antibody affinity low
192.explanation:
There are many differences between Primary immune response and Secondary immune response.

In primary immune response IgM are increased.

In secondary immune response IgG are increased.

In primary immune response there is a lag period of 4-7 days. In secondary immune response there is a lag of 1-2 days.

Primary immune response is short lived, While secondary immune response is prolonged.

Option C is wrong that in primary immune response antibody affinity is high and in secondary immune response antibody affinity is low.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

  • Choice A: PIR-IgM; SIR-IgG This is correct. In primary immune response, IgM is the first antibody produced. In secondary immune response, IgG predominates due to memory B cell activation.
  • Choice B: PIR - lag period - 4 to 7 days; SIR- lag period- 1-2 days This is correct. The primary immune response has a longer lag phase (4-7 days) as naive B cells require activation. In contrast, the secondary immune response has a shorter lag period (1-2 days) due to the presence of memory B cells.
  • Choice D: PIR-Short lived; SIR - Prolonged. This is correct. The primary immune response is weaker and short-lived, whereas the secondary immune response is stronger and long-lasting due to memory cell activation.

Key Takeaway:

The primary immune response is characterized by a longer lag phase, production of IgM, and lower antibody affinity, whereas the secondary immune response has a shorter lag phase, predominantly involves IgG, and results in higher antibody affinity due to affinity maturation.

192.question_text: Isotype switching occurs in which of the following cells?
192.explanation:
Isotype switching is when B cell starts produces Ig M first then after some time switch to produce IgG.

This process occurs once infection converts from acute to chronic.

This type of isotype switching does not occur for T cells. It has no role in cell mediated immunity.

Incorrect Choices Explanation:
Choice A: Helper T cells – Incorrect
Helper T cells (CD4+ T cells) play an indirect role in isotype switching by releasing cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, IFN-γ, which guide B cells in selecting the appropriate antibody class. However, they do not undergo isotype switching themselves.

Choice B: Cytotoxic T cells – Incorrect
Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+ T cells) are involved in cell-mediated immunity, directly killing infected or cancerous cells. They do not produce antibodies and do not undergo isotype switching.

Choice C: B cell – Incorrect
Naïve B cells initially produce IgM and IgD but do not undergo class switching until they are activated by an antigen and receive signals from helper T cells. Only activated B cells switch antibody classes.

Key Takeaway:
Isotype switching occurs only in activated B cells, allowing them to switch from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE, depending on the immune response needed. This process is crucial for producing more effective antibodies against different pathogens.

192.question_text: Immunocompromised patient after renal transplantation c/o chronic diarrhoea. On staining the stool by Kinyoun stain, 4-6 microns. Which is true?
192.option_a: Globally the most common species among them to cause diarrhea is C. parvum
192.option_b: Oocyst is infective immediately after coming out in stool
192.option_d: They do not have the property of internal autoinfection
192.explanation:
This is opportunistic organism causing diarrhea in immuno compromised case. And the structure in stool is acid fast.

Cryptospora, cyclospora, isosporas can cause this.
They can be differentiated by size of oocyst. All are equally acid fast, 1 % H2so4 is required for doing modified zn staining .

Globally the most common species among them to cause diarrhea is not C parvum.

They are not obligate intracellular.

They have the property of internal autoinfection.

Oocyst coming out in stool is effective immediately. So option B is correct.

Incorrect Choices Explanation:

Choice A: Globally the most common species among them to cause diarrhea is C. parvum – Incorrect
While C. parvum is a well-known cause of diarrhea, the most common species causing cryptosporidiosis globally is actually C. hominis. C. parvum is more commonly associated with zoonotic transmission, while C. hominis is more frequently transmitted human-to-human.

Choice C: Obligate intracellular – Incorrect
Cryptosporidium species are not strictly obligate intracellular parasites. While they attach to and invade intestinal epithelial cells, they remain extracytoplasmic, enclosed within a specialized parasitophorous vacuole that allows them to survive while still interacting with the host cell.

Choice D: They do not have the property of internal autoinfection – Incorrect
Cryptosporidium does exhibit internal autoinfection, which is a key feature allowing persistent infection in immunocompromised patients. This occurs when thin-walled oocysts rupture within the host intestine, leading to reinfection without the need for external transmission.

Key Takeaway:

Cryptosporidium species, particularly C. hominis and C. parvum, cause severe chronic diarrhea in immunocompromised patients. The oocysts are immediately infective upon excretion, contributing to rapid transmission. Unlike Cyclospora, they do not require maturation in the environment and can undergo internal autoinfection, making infections difficult to clear in immunosuppressed individuals.

192.question_text: Which antibody is primarily responsible for mucosal immunity?
192.explanation:
• IgA: This antibody is primarily found in mucosal areas, such as the gut, respiratory tract, and urogenital tract. It plays a crucial role in mucosal immunity by preventing pathogens from adhering to and penetrating mucosal surfaces. It is present in secretions such as saliva, tears, and breast milk.
  • IgM: This antibody is primarily found in the blood and lymphatic fluid. It is the first antibody produced in response to an infection but is not involved in mucosal immunity.
  • IgG: This is the most abundant antibody in the blood and extracellular fluid, providing systemic protection but not specifically targeting mucosal areas.
  • IgE: This antibody is involved in allergic reactions and defense against parasitic infections, not mucosal immunity.

Key Takeaway: IgA is essential for mucosal immunity, protecting the body's entry points against infections.

  • IgA: While important for mucosal immunity, it is not the primary antibody involved in the initial response to infections.
  • IgD: Found mainly on B cell surfaces and does not play a significant role in the initial immune response.
  • IgG: Although crucial for long-term immunity, it is not the primary antibody produced during the initial response to infections.

192.question_text: Examine the image of an antibody structure provided below. Which region of the antibody binds to the antigen?
192.explanation:
• Fab Region: The Fab (Fragment antigen-binding) region is the part of the antibody that binds to the specific antigen. It contains the variable regions of both heavy and light chains that are responsible for antigen specificity.
  • Fc Region: This is the constant region that interacts with cell receptors and complements but does not bind directly to the antigen.
  • Hinge Region: This provides flexibility to the antibody but is not directly involved in antigen binding.
  • Variable Region:While crucial for antigen binding, it is not a distinct part like the Fab region.
