193.question_text: Ayushee's grandfather was 80 years old and he had complaints of drooping of eyelid, double vision and progressive muscular weakness towards the end of day. His condition was improved on giving edrophonium. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for the disease in Ayushee's grandfather?
193.explanation:
• Type I hypersensitivity reaction: It is IgE-mediated, which causes mast cell degranulation following a contact with soluble antigen
  • Type II hypersensitivity reaction: It is IgG (or rarely IgM) mediated, which causes complement activation or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) in response to cell surface bound antigens.
  • Type III hypersensitivity reaction: It is immune complex-mediated; which are formed due to interaction between soluble antigen and antibody (usually IgG), resulting in an abnormal inflammatory response.
  • Delayed Hypersensitivity Reaction: Delayed hypersensitivity reaction occurs after a few days of antigen contact, as a result of abnormal cell mediated immune response. This is also called type IV hypersensitivity reaction. It is mediated by a specific subset of TH cells called delayed hypersensitivity T cells or TDTH cells.

In type II reactions, the host injury is mediated by antibodies (IgG or rarely IgM) which interact with various types of antigens, such as:

  • Host cell surface antigens (e.g. RBC membrane antigens like blood group and Rh antigens)
  • Extracellular matrix antigens or
  • Exogenous antigens absorbed on host cells (e.g. a drug coating on RBC membrane).
  • Complement Mediated Type II Reactions: ABO incompatibility, Rh incompatibility.
  • Autoantibody Mediated (Antibody-dependent Cellular Dysfunction or ADCD):
    • In this condition, the host produces certain antibodies which bind and disturb the normal function of human self-antigens.
    • Anti-receptor Ab: Antibodies may be directed against human receptors, resulting in either inhibition or excessive activation of the receptors leading to host injury.
    • Activation of receptor, e.g. Grave's disease: Here, the autoantibodies produced are called LATS (long-acting thyroid stimulators), which stimulate the thyroid cells to upregulate the production of thyroid hormones.
    • Inhibition of receptors, e.g. myasthenia gravis: In this condition, anti-acetylcholine (ACh) receptor antibodies are produced; which block the Ach receptors, leading to profound muscular weakness.
    • Other examples of ADCD:
      • Goodpasture syndrome (antibody produced against type IV collagen)
      • Pernicious anemia (antibody directed against intrinsic factor)
      • Rheumatic fever (antibody against streptococcal antigens cross reacting with heart)
      • Myocarditis in Chagas disease.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 197

193.question_text: A 65-year-old male is evaluated in clinic approximately six months after resolution of a herpes zoster. Despite lesions having resolved, he still experiences constant burning and hypersensitivity to touch in the distribution of the old rash. You explain that vaccination with the shingles vaccine in individuals 60-70 years of age can reduce the incidence of this complication. What is the complication?
193.explanation:
• This patient is experiencing post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN), which occurs in 20-30% of people who experience a herpes zoster outbreak.
  • Post-herpetic neuralgia is described as alterations in skin sensation in a unilateral dermatomal distribution that persists for a minimum of 6 months after the resolution of herpes zoster lesions.
  • Patients may complain of continuous or intermittent burning, stabbing, or sharp pain, as well as areas of anaesthesia and allodynia (hypersensitivity).
  • The mainstays of treatment include tricyclic antidepressants, opioids, and GABA analogues.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

193.question_text: Tuberculin test response is due to:
193.explanation:
• Delayed type hypersensitivity (occurs after 48-72 hours of antigen exposure)
  • Cell mediated hypersensitivity (Characteristic cells called TDTH cells are the principal mediators): T-lymphocytes mediated hypersensitivity
  • Characterized by Chronic Granuloma formation: Tissue injury occurs predominantly due to activated macrophages.
  • Mechanism of Type-IV Reactions
    • Sensitization phase (occurs 1-2 weeks following Ag exposure): APCs process and present the antigenic peptides to TH cells. TH cells are differentiated to TH1 cells which further differentiates to form TDTH cells
    • Effector phase: The TDTH cells, on subsequent contact with the antigen, secrete variety of cytokines such as: Interferon γ,IL-2, MCAF (Monocyte chemotactic and activating factor), TNF-β, MIF (migration inhibitory factor), IL-3, GM-CSF (granulocyte-monocyte colony stimulating factor).
    • Cytokines in turn perform various functions which may be either protective type or tissue damage type.
  • Types :
    • Tuberculin type
      • Tuberculin (Mantoux test)
    • Contact dermatitis type

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 10th edition Chapter 16, Pg 164-168

193.question_text: Match the following test with its most appropriate condition
193.option_a: i- c, ii- d, iii- b, iv- a
193.option_b: i- a, ii- d, iii- b, iv- c
193.option_c: i- d, ii- c, iii- b, iv- a
193.option_d: i- b, ii- d, iii- c, iv- a
193.explanation:
Explanation:

Patch test:

  • A patch test is used to diagnose contact dermatitis, which is a hypersensitivity reaction to allergens.
  • It involves applying potential allergens to the skin and observing for any allergic reactions.

KOH mount

  • KOH mount is used in the detection of fungi in clinical specimens such as skin scrapings, nails, hair, sputum, urine, CSF, and tissue.
  • Differentiates fungal elements from host cells by dissolving tissue and debris.

Biopsy

  • Biopsy is done when tissue-level changes need to be examined, such as in granulomatous diseases like Lupus vulgaris.
  • It involves the removal of a tissue sample for histological examination.

Slit skin smear

  • The diagnostic and specific test used in the diagnosis of leprosy.
  • It involves scraping skin lesions and examining them under a microscope for the presence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) to confirm the diagnosis.

Reference:

  1. Contact dermatitis - Diagnosis - NHS
  2. Leprosy Workup: Laboratory Studies, Other Tests, Procedures.
  3. A Clinico-Histopathological Study of Lupus Vulgaris at a Tertiary Care Centre - PMC
  4. Skin scraping and a potassium hydroxide mount - Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology

194.question_text: Necrotizing fascitis is caused by -
194.explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Beta hemolytic streptococci The spectrum of infections of the deep soft tissues ranges from localized bacterial, viral and parasitic lesions to rapidly spreading, tissue destructive infections such as necrotizing fascitis and myonecrosis. A) Pyomyositis :- It is common in tropics, therefore also called tropical pyomyositis. It is a localized infection of skeletal muscles. It is caused most commonly by staphylococcus aureus. B) Necrotizing fascitis Necrotizing fascitis is an infection of the deeper layers of skin and subcutaneous tissues, easily spreading across the fascial plane within the subcutaneous tissues. There are two types of necrotizing fascitis :? i) Type 1:- It is a polymicrobial infection, i.e. mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection. It occurs most commonly after surgical procedures in diabetic patients or in those who have peripheral vascular disease. ii) Type 2 :- It is caused most commonly by streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta hemolytic streptococci). C) Clostridial myonecrosis (Gas gangrene) :- It is characterized by rapid and extensive necrosis of muscle accompanied by gas formation and systemic toxicity. It is caused by C. perfringens (most common), C. novyi, C. septicum and C. histolyticum. It is also called type III necrotizing fascitis.

194.question_text: Which among the following is a superantigen?
194.explanation:
Choice A: Streptococcus pyogenic exotoxin (SPE)

  • Superantigens re toxins that cause excessive activation of T-cells by binding directly to MHC-II and T-cell receptors, leading to a massive cytokine release ("cytokine storm").
  • Streptococcus pyogenic exotoxins (SPE-A, SPE-B, SPE-C) are produced by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) and cause:
    • Scarlet fever(SPE-A, SPE-C).
    • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS)(SPE-A).
    • Necrotizing fasciitis(SPE-B).
  • Mechanism: Activates ~20% of T-cells, leading to massive cytokine release (IL-1, IL-2, TNF-α, IFN-γ), causing shock and multi-organ failure.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Clostridium difficile exotoxin

  • difficileproduces Toxin A (enterotoxin) and Toxin B (cytotoxin).
  • These are NOT superantigens but act by:
    • Glucosylating Rho proteins, disrupting the cytoskeleton of intestinal epithelial cells, leading to diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis.

Choice C: Corynebacterium diphtheriae diphtheria toxin

  • Diphtheria toxin is an AB toxin that inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylation of EF-2, leading to cell death.
  • Causes pharyngeal pseudomembranes, myocarditis, and neuropathy, but does not function as a superantigen.

Choice D: Pseudomonas exotoxin (Exotoxin A)

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosaproduces Exotoxin A, which also ADP-ribosylates EF-2, leading to cell death.
  • It acts similarly to diphtheria toxin but is not a superantigen.

Key Takeaway

The superantigen among the options is Streptococcus pyogenic exotoxin (SPE-A, SPE-C), which triggers massive immune activation and cytokine release, leading to toxic shock-like syndrome and necrotizing fasciitis.

194.question_text: Group A Streptococcus is the most common cause of bacterial pharyngitis in school-aged children. Which of the following bacterial components is primarily responsible for its attachment to fibronectin on the epithelial lining of the pharynx?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the lipoteichoic acid of the Group A streptococcus is responsible for its attachment to fibronectin on the epithelial lining of the pharynx.

  • Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A streptococcus) attaches to the pharyngeal epithelium using surface pili coated with lipoteichoic acid, while fibronectin on epithelial cells likely serves as the binding ligand for this lipoteichoic acid, facilitating adherence and colonisation.
  • Gram-positive cell walls are rich in teichoic and teichuronic acids, which may form up to half the dry weight of the wall and significantly contribute to its negative charge.
  • These acids exist as wall teichoic acid (linked to peptidoglycan) or lipoteichoic acid (linked to membrane glycolipids), forming a polyanionic network that influences elasticity, porosity, and electrostatic properties.
  • Teichoic acids serve as major surface antigens, sometimes bearing specific determinants like the Forssman antigen, and in Streptococcus pyogenes, they associate with M protein fibrils to aid bacterial attachment to host cells.
  • Additionally, Gram-positive walls may contain polysaccharides made of neutral or acidic sugars, although their precise origin is uncertain.
  • The differentiating features of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria are summarised in the table and illustration below.

Explanation of other options:

Capsule (Option A): Bacteria produce extracellular polysaccharide material called glycocalyx, which may appear as a capsule when firmly attached or as a slime layer when loosely associated. Capsules protect bacteria from phagocytosis and enhance virulence.

Flagella (Option B): Bacterial flagella function as helical rotors that enable motility by rotating through proton or ion-driven motors, allowing the cell to swim in liquid environments. They facilitate chemotaxis, where cells adjust movement toward attractants or away from repellents.

Lipoprotein (Option D): Lipoprotein in Gram-negative bacteria is a unique protein that links the outer membrane with the peptidoglycan layer. Its main role is to stabilise the outer membrane and firmly attach it to the underlying peptidoglycan layer.

194.question_text: A 10-year-old child presents to the pediatric clinic with joint pain, swelling, and difficulty walking. On examination, the knee joint is tender and swollen. The child also has a recent history of sore throat. Laboratory investigations show elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers. A renal biopsy demonstrates glomerular changes indicative of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Which organism is most likely responsible for both acute rheumatic fever and PSGN in this patient?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is the causative organism for both acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). It commonly infects the throat and skin, triggering immune-mediated sequelae in susceptible individuals.

Diseases caused by Streptococcus pyogenes:

Explanation of Other Options:

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A): Causes pneumonia, otitis media, meningitis, and sepsis, but not ARF or PSGN.

Streptococcus agalactiae (Option C): Group B Streptococcus; associated with neonatal sepsis and meningitis, not post-streptococcal immune complications.

Streptococcus mutans (Option D): Found in the oral cavity; primarily causes dental caries, unrelated to rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis.

194.question_text: Griffith typing of beta-hemolytic streptococci is based on
194.option_d: Based on biochemical and physiological properties
194.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Griffith typing is a method of classifying beta-hemolytic streptococci based on the M protein present on the bacterial cell surface.
  • The M protein is a major virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes, providing resistance to phagocytosis.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • A) Group specific C carbohydrate antigen:
    • Basis of Lancefield classification, not Griffith typing.
    • Used to classify streptococci into groups (A, B, C, etc.).
  • B) Group specific T antigen:
    • Used in T-typing, another epidemiological method, but not Griffith typing.
  • D) Based on biochemical and physiological properties:
    • This refers to biotyping, not Griffith typing.
    • Involves metabolic and growth characteristics, not surface antigens.

194.question_text: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, a "strawberry tongue," and a rash that feels like sandpaper. A throat swab is cultured on blood agar, with the resulting growth shown in the image. Identify the type of hemolysis seen and the virulence factor responsible.
194.explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is classic for Scarlet Fever, caused by toxigenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus). The image shows clear, transparent zones around the bacterial colonies, which represents the complete lysis of red blood cells. This is known as beta (β) hemolysis.

This powerful hemolytic activity is caused by exotoxins called streptolysins. S. pyogenes produces two types:

  • Streptolysin O (SLO): Oxygen-labile and antigenic (ASO test).
  • Streptolysin S (SLS): Oxygen-stable and responsible for the surface hemolysis seen.

Types of Hemolysis on Blood Agar:

Explanation of Other Options:

Alpha hemolysis (Option A): The image shows complete, clear hemolysis, not the greenish partial hemolysis characteristic of alpha-hemolytic streptococci.

Gamma hemolysis (Option C): The image clearly shows hemolysis, whereas gamma hemolysis is the absence of any hemolytic activity. Hyaluronidase is a "spreading factor," not a hemolysin.

Alpha hemolysis : M protein (Option D): This option incorrectly pairs the type of hemolysis with the virulence factor. M protein is a major anti-phagocytic virulence factor of S. pyogenes, not a hemolysin.

194.question_text: A patient presents with fever and fatigue for 3 days. Echocardiography shows valvular vegetations. Blood culture reveals an organism producing alpha-hemolysis on blood agar, resistant to optochin and bile. Which organism is most likely responsible?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

The findings are consistent with subacute bacterial endocarditis (SABE) caused by viridans streptococci such as Streptococcus sanguis.

  • Characteristics: Part of oral and pharyngeal flora, alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant, bile insoluble.
  • Epidemiology: Entry often follows dental procedures.
  • Pathogenesis: Forms biofilms and extracellular polysaccharides, aiding adherence to damaged valves.
  • Clinical features: Fever, malaise, new murmur, embolic signs (splinter hemorrhages, petechiae).
  • Complications: Heart failure, embolization, valvular destruction.

Explanation of other options:

Mycoplasma (Option A): No cell wall; causes atypical pneumonia, not endocarditis.

Enterococcus (Option C): Can cause endocarditis but shows gamma hemolysis; different profile.

Streptococcus agalactiae (Option D): Group B strep, causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Viridans streptococci (esp. S. sanguis) → subacute endocarditis.
  • Alpha-hemolysis, optochin resistance, bile insolubility.
  • Dental procedures are a major risk factor.

194.question_text: A patient diagnosed with Enterococcus infective endocarditis has a history of penicillin allergy. Which of the following antibiotics would be the most appropriate treatment?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Enterococcal infections, including Enterococcus infective endocarditis, are commonly treated with vancomycin, particularly in patients with a penicillin allergy.
  • Vancomycin is effective against penicillin-resistant Enterococcus species and works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis.

Treatment and Antibiotic Resistance in Enterococci

  • Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to:
    • Cephalosporins (E.g; Ceftriaxone) (Option B ruled out)
    • Penicillinase-resistant penicillins
    • Monobactams

Resistance mechanisms: Penicillin and Aminoglycoside

  • Decreased affinity of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) for β-lactams.
  • Enterococci have low-level intrinsic resistance to aminoglycosides due to poor cellular uptake.
  • Synergy occurs when a β-lactam (penicillin/ampicillin) damages the cell wall, allowing the aminoglycoside (streptomycin/gentamycin) to enter and inhibit ribosomal protein synthesis.
  • Some strains exhibit high-level aminoglycoside resistance via ribosomal mutations or aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes, eliminating this synergy.

Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococci (VRE)

  • Enterococcus faecium is the species that is most commonly vancomycin resistant.
  • Vancomycin resistance in enterococci occurs when Van gene mutations modify the terminal dipeptide of peptidoglycan precursors.
    • D-alanine-D-alanine to D-alanine-D-serine or D-alanine-D-lactate
  • This resultant effect is decreased vancomycin binding and causing resistance.

Drug of Choice: Enterococcal infection

Explanation of other options:

Piperacillin (Option C): Piperacillin is a penicillin-class antibiotic, and since the patient has a penicillin allergy, this would not be the most appropriate treatment option.

Aztreonam (Option D): Aztreonam is a monobactam antibiotic, which is effective against Gram-negative bacteria but not typically against Enterococcus. Therefore, it would not be the most appropriate treatment for enterococcal endocarditis.

194.question_text: Which of the following is the test used for antibiotic sensitivity?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

  • The E test (Epsilometer ) determines bacterial antibiotic sensitivity by measuring the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the drug.
  • The test uses a strip with a gradient of antibiotic, placed on an agar plate seeded with bacteria.
  • MIC is read where bacterial growth intersects the strip, useful for detecting resistant subpopulations.

Antibiotic Susceptibility Testing

  • Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (AST) helps clinicians choose appropriate antibiotics by determining which drugs are effective against the specific bacteria causing the infection.
  • Minimal Inhibitory Concentration (MIC)
    • The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that prevents visible growth of the microorganism in a standardized growth medium.
    • If MIC > breakpoint value, then there is resistance
    • If MIC < breakpoint value, then there is sensitivity
  • Minimal Bactericidal Concentration (MBC)
    • The lowest concentration of an antibiotic that kills the bacteria in a medium.

Different Methods of Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing

Explanation of other options:

Camp test (Option B): Detects enhanced hemolysis of Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B strep) in the presence of Staphylococcus aureus; not for antibiotic sensitivity.

Elek test (Option C): Identifies toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae by detecting diphtheria toxin; unrelated to antibiotic sensitivity.

Latex agglutination (Option D): Detects specific bacterial antigens or antibodies using latex beads coated with antibodies; used for rapid identification, not for antibiotic sensitivity.

Key Takeaways

  • Minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC): The lowest concentration of the antibiotic inhibits the pathogen's growth in the medium.
  • Minimal bactericidal concentration (MBC): The lowest concentration of antibiotic that kills the bacteria in a medium.

194.question_text: What is a primary risk factor for the development and spread of Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus (VRE) in hospitalized patients?
194.explanation:
• A. High-fiber diet: This option is unrelated to VRE development. Dietary fiber does not impact antibiotic resistance mechanisms.
  • B. Long-term use of vancomycin: Prolonged administration of vancomycin can select for resistant strains, leading to VRE, making it a significant risk factor.
  • C. Routine hand hygiene: Proper hand hygiene is vital for infection control and does not increase the risk of VRE; instead, it reduces the likelihood of spreading resistant bacteria.
  • D. Non-invasive diagnostic procedures: These procedures typically do not involve the use of antibiotics and therefore do not contribute to the risk of developing VRE.

Key Takeaway: Long-term use of vancomycin is the primary risk factor for the development of VRE in hospitalized patients, while the other options do not promote resistance and instead aid in infection control.

Tags: inicet 2022

Reference: WHO Guideline, Risk factors for VRE development and spread in healthcare settings.

194.question_text: Which of the following is a key strategy to reduce the risk of VRE transmission in a hospital setting, particularly in high-risk areas?
194.option_b: Ensuring rigorous environmental cleaning and disinfection
194.option_d: Increasing the use of invasive procedures
194.explanation:
• B. Ensuring rigorous environmental cleaning and disinfection: This is crucial for controlling VRE as it reduces the environmental reservoirs where the bacteria can survive and be transmitted.

Why Not Others:

  • A. Implementing broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy: This can exacerbate resistance issues by promoting the survival of resistant strains, which does not effectively address VRE transmission.
  • C. Using only single-use medical devices: While helpful in minimizing infection risks, relying solely on this strategy does not significantly impact the broader issue of VRE transmission and may lead to waste and increased costs.
  • D. Increasing the use of invasive procedures: This approach can increase the risk of VRE infections, as invasive procedures create opportunities for bacteria to enter the body and facilitate the spread of infections.

Key Takeaway: Rigorous environmental cleaning and disinfection is crucial for controlling VRE transmission in healthcare settings.

Tags: inicet 2020

Reference: WHO Guideline, Risk factors for VRE development and spread in healthcare settings.

194.question_text: A neonate is admitted with clinical features of meningitis. CSF culture grows bacteria that are bacitracin resistant. Neonatal meningitis in this case is most likely caused by which organism?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Group B Streptococcus (GBS) / Streptococcus agalactiae is a leading cause of neonatal meningitis and sepsis, especially within the first week of life.
  • GBS is commonly carried asymptomatically in the maternal genital tract and transmitted during delivery.
  • Bacitracin resistance is a distinguishing feature of Group B Streptococcus (whereas Group A Streptococcus is bacitracin sensitive).

Clinical Course:

  • Early-onset GBS disease (0-6 days): presents with respiratory distress, poor feeding, lethargy, and sepsis.
  • Late-onset GBS disease (7-89 days): more commonly presents as meningitis (fever, irritability, bulging fontanelle).
  • Diagnosis: Blood cultures, CSF analysis, PCR.
  • Treatment: Ampicillin + gentamicin (or cefotaxime).

Prevention:

  • Pregnant women are screened at 35-37 weeks gestation.
  • GBS-positive mothers are given intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (usually penicillin/ampicillin).
  • In Pregnant Women: UTI, chorioamnionitis, postpartum endometritis
  • In Adults: Skin/soft tissue infections, bacteremia, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis

Explanation of Other Options:

Pneumococcus (Option A):

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major cause of meningitis in children and adults, but it is not a common neonatal cause.
  • Unlike GBS, it is not characteristically transmitted during delivery and is not bacitracin resistant.

Streptococcus pyogenes (Option B):

  • Group A Streptococcus causes pharyngitis, scarlet fever, necrotizing fasciitis, and rheumatic fever, but it is rarely implicated in neonatal meningitis.
  • It is also bacitracin sensitive, helping to differentiate it from GBS.

Meningococci (Option D):

  • Neisseria meningitidis is an important cause of meningitis in adolescents and young adults.
  • It is not typically associated with early neonatal infections or bacitracin resistance.

194.question_text: Which of the following is positive by Indian ink staining?
194.explanation:
Negative staining:

  • The background stains black whereas unstained bacteria stand out in contrast.
  • It is used for the demonstration of capsules which do not take up simple stains.
  • Example: India ink or nigrosine
  • Capsulated bacteria: Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae), Meningococcus (Neisseriae meningitidis), Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Capulated fungus yeast: Cryptococcus neoformans

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 12

194.question_text: A 54-year-old female with a history of rheumatic heart disease underwent prosthetic valve replacement surgery 6 months ago. She now presents with fever, fatigue, worsening dyspnea, a new heart murmur, and splinter hemorrhages. What is the most likely causative organism responsible for her infective endocarditis?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus (CoNS) and is the most common cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis within the first year after valve replacement surgery.
  • It is part of normal human skin flora but becomes pathogenic when it breaches host defenses (e.g., surgery, prosthetic devices).
  • Pathogenesis is strongly linked to biofilm formation, which allows persistence on prosthetic material and resistance to antibiotics.
  • It also commonly causes stitch abscesses and device-associated infections (catheters, prosthetic joints, heart valves).

Explanation of Other Options:

Streptococcus viridans (Option B):

  • Classically causes subacute infective endocarditis on native valves, particularly in patients with pre-existing valvular damage (e.g., rheumatic heart disease, congenital defects).
  • It is strongly associated with poor dental hygiene or dental procedures, not with prosthetic valve infections within the first year.

Enterococcus faecalis (Option C):

  • A common cause of nosocomial infections and can cause infective endocarditis, especially in elderly patients with genitourinary or gastrointestinal manipulation.
  • However, it is not the most common cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis within the first year; epidermidis is more typical in this early postoperative period.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus (Option D):

  • A coagulase-negative staphylococcus but is almost exclusively associated with urinary tract infections in young women.
  • It does not cause endocarditis, particularly not prosthetic valve infections.

Key Takeaway:

  • <12 months after prosthetic valve replacement → Staphylococcus epidermidis (CoNS) is the leading cause.
  • >12 months → Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus viridans become more common culprits.

194.question_text: Which among the following is the most specific disease of Streptococcus agalactiae?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

Neonatal sepsis is the most specific disease of Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) because it is a leading cause of bloodstream infections in newborns.

β-haemolytic Streptococci:

Classified into Groups A-V based on the carbohydrate C antigen present in the cell wall (Lancefield classification).

  • Group A: Streptococcus pyogenes
  • Group B: Streptococcus agalactiae
  • Group D:Enterococcus

Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus)

  • It is a normal commensal organism found in the vaginal and birth canal flora.
  • It is the most common cause of neonatal meningitis and can also cause early- or late-onset neonatal sepsis.
  • The organism is bacitracin-resistant and CAMP test positive.
  • Transmission occurs from mother to baby during childbirth, especially if the mother's status is unknown.
  • Early-onset disease occurs within the first 24-48 hours of life.
  • Clinical Features
    • Respiratory distress, lethargy, poor feeding.
  • Diagnosis
    • Blood culture shows gram-positive cocci in chains, consistent with GBS.
  • Prevention
    • Screening pregnant women at 35-37 weeks and providing intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to GBS-positive mothers reduces the risk of neonatal infection.

Conditions caused by Group B Streptococcus:

  • In neonates
  • In pregnant women:
    • Urinary tract infections
    • Chorioamnionitis
    • Postpartum endometritis
  • In adults:
    • Skin and soft tissue infections
    • Bacteremia
    • Pneumonia
    • Osteomyelitis
    • Endocarditis

Explanation of other options:

Infective endocarditis (Option B): While S. agalactiae can cause infective endocarditis, it is not the most common or specific pathogen for this condition. Other bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus viridians are more commonly associated with infective endocarditis.

Dental caries (Option C): Dental caries are primarily caused by Streptococcus mutans and not Streptococcus agalactiae.

Pharyngitis with or without tonsillitis (Option D): Pharyngitis is most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), not Streptococcus agalactiae.

194.question_text: A patient diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever presents to the outpatient department. On examination, gram-positive cocci arranged in chains are observed. Which organism is the likely causative agent?
194.explanation:
Explanation:

The causative organism of acute rheumatic fever is Streptococcus pyogenes, also referred to as Group A Streptococcus (GAS). It appears as gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. This bacterium is commonly responsible for infections such as pharyngitis (strep throat), and if left untreated, especially in children, it can lead to acute rheumatic fever a post-infectious inflammatory condition that can affect the heart, joints, skin, and central nervous system.

Diseases caused by Streptococcus pyogenes:



Hence option A,C and D are incorrect

Reference: Clinical Guidance for Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis | Group A Strep | CDC

194.question_text: A known case of AIDs with productive cough and fever was found to have consolidation in the right infrascapular area with X ray showing right lower lobe consolidation with CD4 count of less than 55 per microlite. What is the most common cause of this?
194.explanation:
In AIDS when CD 4 cell count goes below 55 per microlitre. Many opportunistic infection can occur.

Here patient has consolidation in right infrascapular area and x ray showing right lower lobe consolidation. So patient has pneumonia.

This pneumonia is commonly caused by Pneumocystis jiroveci

Streptococcus pneumoniae is also right option, but incidence is less.

mycoplasma is wrong option.

S aureus is wrong option.

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • Option A: Staphylococcus aureus - While S. aureus can cause pneumonia, it is more commonly seen in post-viral pneumonia or in association with lung abscesses and cavitary lesions. It is not the most common cause of pneumonia in advanced AIDS patients with a very low CD4 count.
  • Option B: Streptococcus pneumoniae - S. pneumoniae is a leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. However, in AIDS patients with severe immunosuppression (CD4 < 55), PCP is more common than bacterial causes, making Pneumocystis jiroveci the more likely answer.
  • Option C: Mycoplasma - Mycoplasma pneumoniae typically causes atypical pneumonia with diffuse interstitial infiltrates rather than lobar consolidation. It is more common in young, immunocompetent individuals and is not a frequent cause of pneumonia in advanced AIDS cases.

Key Takeaways:

  • Pneumocystis jiroveci is the most common cause of pneumonia in AIDS patients with CD4 < 200, especially below 55.
  • While PCP typically presents with diffuse interstitial infiltrates, it can sometimes show lobar consolidation.
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae remains a possible cause of pneumonia in AIDS but is less common than PCP in advanced cases.
  • Staphylococcus aureus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae are less likely in this scenario.

194.question_text: Quellung reaction is associated with:
194.explanation:
Capsule swelling (delineation) or Quellung reaction :

  • It was described by Neufeld (1902)
  • It was widely employed for the typing of pneumococci in the pre-sulphonamide days when lobar pneumonia used to be treated with specific anticapsular sera.
  • Swollen, refractile and delineated capsules are seen on adding antisera mixed with methylene blue.

Reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 12th edition, Pg 20

194.question_text: Which of the following is positive by India-ink staining on a CSF sample for demonstration of capsule of yeast?
194.explanation:
Negative staining:

  • The background stains black whereas unstained bacteria stand out in contrast.
  • It is used for the demonstration of capsules which do not take up simple stains.
  • Example: India ink or nigrosine
  • Capsulated bacteria: Pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae), Meningococcus (Neisseriae meningitidis), Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Capsulated fungus yeast: Cryptococcus neoformans

Negative staining:
