209.question_text: Needle prick in a HCW, patient HBV reactive, anti-HBs >90mIU for HBV prophylaxis. What is to be done?
209.explanation:
An occupational exposture is defined as

Percutaneous injury - Needle stick injury or other sharp injury

Splash injury - contact with mucus membrane ( Eye or mouth)

Contact with non intact skin ( abraded skin or afflicted with dermatitis)

Contact with the intact skin when the duration is prolonged ( several minutes or more)

HIV,, HCV, HBV can be transmitted by needle stick injury.

When needle stick injury occurs, a person must report to the head of that unit and then to infection control nurse or officer.

Basic tests to be performed for patient as well as health care worker,

If his Anti HBS title is more than 90 MlU then nothing is to be given as per standard guidelines.

If the titre is less than anti serum and vaccines both need to be started.

Incorrect Choices Explanation:

Choice B: Hep B vaccine and IG - Incorrect
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and the vaccine are not needed for a healthcare worker with a protective anti-HBs titre (>90 mIU/mL). The immune status is already sufficient, so administering the vaccine and immunoglobulin would be unnecessary.

Choice C: Only immunoglobulin - Incorrect
Since the HCW has a protective anti-HBs titre, administering only immunoglobulin is not required. The immune system is already protected against HBV.

Choice D: Only vaccine - Incorrect
Administering only the vaccine is not necessary when the HCW already has a protective titre (>90 mIU/mL). The person is already immune to HBV, and additional vaccination would be redundant.

Key Takeaway:

If a healthcare worker has a protective anti-HBs titre greater than 90 mIU/mL, no further prophylaxis (such as vaccine or immunoglobulin) is required after exposure to an HBV-positive patient.

209.question_text:
Sheela, a 28-year-old female presents to the medicine OPD with a 10-day history of flu-like symptoms, including anorexia and malaise. She has a history of blood transfusion, which had not been screened for any infectious etiology. Her vital signs are temperature of 99.9°F, pulse 78/minute, respirations of 18/minute, and blood pressure of 121/78 mm Hg. upon general examination, mild scleral icterus is noted. Heart sounds are regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, and lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen is soft and nontender, except the liver which is tender when palpated and extends 8 cm below the costal margin, with a smooth edge.

Which of the following is not the use of HBV DNA titers?
209.explanation:
HBV DNA detection-

  1. Indicates active viral replication and high infectivity
  2. Viral DNA load helps in monitoring treatment response

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 27th Edition, Pg:133

209.question_text: When hepatitis D was injected into an immunocompromised mouse, there was no detectable hepatitis D RNA in the blood at any time point during the next several months. When co-injected with hepatitis B, hepatitis D RNA was detected in the blood. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
209.explanation:
• Hepatitis B complements hepatitis D, a defective virus, and assists the latter in virion assembly and secretion.
  • Hepatitis D is a small enveloped, circular RNA hepatitis virus.
  • Although HDV can replicate on its own, it requires co-infection with HBV to produce viable HDV virions and for proper secretion.
  • Thus, to acquire HDV, a persons must have a preexisting HBV infection.
  • An interesting but not fully elucidated mechanism is the suppression of HBV replication during HDV replication.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 80

209.question_text: Hepatitis B virus exists in 3 morphological forms. What form does the image given below represent?
209.explanation:
• The given image represents the complete form of HBV, or DANE Particle.
  • They are 42nm in size, spherical virions made up of Outer surface envelope, HBsAg and an inner nucleocapsid made of core antigen, pre-core antigen and a partially double stranded DNA.
  • Spherical Forms: Most numerous, small form measuring 22 nm in diameter.
  • These particles are exclusively made up of HBsAg
  • Tubular or filamentous forms: They Also Have the Same diameter, but 200 nm long. They are also exclusively made up of HBsAg

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 479

209.question_text: Lamivudine is a Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI), which has proven antiviral activity against HIV and HBV. However, some patients infected with HBV are resistant to Lamivudine. Which mutation confers this property of drug resistance?
209.explanation:
• Hepatitis B virus infected patients on lamivudine therapy may develop resistance to the drug due to mutation in the YMDD locus present in the HBV reverse transcriptase region of polymerase gene.
  • Pre-core mutants have mutations in pre-core region (which abolishes HBeAg production) or basal core promoter region (down regulates HBeAg production).
  • The escape mutants of HBV have mutations in the S gene ("a" antigen region) which leads to alteration of HBsAg.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 20, Pg: 279

209.question_text:
What would the given serological markers depict?
HBsAg -
Anti HBs +
Anti HBc -
HBeAg -
Anti-HBe -
Liver enzymes normal HBV DNA -
209.explanation: Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 271

209.question_text: Which of the following is used as an epidemiological marker of HBV infection?
209.explanation:
• HBsAg is the first marker to be elevated following infection; appears within 1-12 weeks (usually between 8 and 12 weeks of infection).
  • It appears during incubation period; 2-6 weeks before the biochemical and clinical evidence of hepatitis.
  • Presence of HBsAg indicates onset of infectivity (i.e. patient is capable of transmission of HBV)
  • It remains elevated in the entire duration of acute hepatitis; becomes undetectable 1-2 months after the onset of jaundice.
  • However, it persists rarely beyond 6 months if the disease progresses to chronic hepatitis or carrier state.
  • HBsAg is used as an epidemiological marker of hepatitis B infection (i.e. to calculate prevalence of infection).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 482

209.question_text: Which of the following best describes Hepatitis D Genome?
209.explanation:
• Hepatitis D virus is taxonomically unclassified though it resembles viroids. It is small in size (35 nm), consisting of: Circular, negative-sense ssRNA.
  • Protein coat is made up of single protein called hepatitis D antigen (HDAg).
  • Surrounded by an envelope protein derived from HBsAg from hepatitis B virus; hence, it is called defective virus.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, byApurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page 487

209.question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents to your office with decreased appetite, malaise, and fever. Serologic tests reveal positive Anti-HBsAg and Anti-HAV IgM antibodies. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this patient's presentation?
209.explanation:
• IgM antibodies to hepatitis A (HAV) are indicative of recent or acute infection. HAV can be acquired via contaminated shellfish.
  • Hepatitis A is an ssRNA Picornavirus, transmitted via the fecal-oral route, through contaminated food, water, and shellfish.
  • The patient has also been immunized against hepatitis B, as seen by her positive Anti-HBsAg serology.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: A 24-year-old Primi comes to Medicine OPD. Her serology testing shows that hepatitis B surface antibody and hepatitis C antibody are both positive. Hepatitis B core antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis A antibody are negative. Polymerase chain reaction of hepatitis C RNA is positive for genotype 1. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation at this time?
209.option_a: Give Hep B immunoglobulins to newborn
209.option_d: Treatment with IFN alpha and Ribavirin
209.explanation:
• This pregnant patient has a positive hepatitis C antibody and is hepatitis C RNA positive for genotype 1, indicating "chronic liver disease" due to an active hepatitis C infection.
  • The presence of the hepatitis B surface antibody and absence of hepatitis core and surface antigens indicate she has immunity acquired by vaccination.
  • Individuals with chronic liver disease such as hepatitis C can develop fulminant hepatitis if infected with hepatitis A.
  • It is imperative that this pregnant patient, who has chronic hepatitis C infection and has been vaccinated against hepatitis B but not against hepatitis A (no anti-HAV IgG antibodies), receives the hepatitis A vaccine to prevent such complications.
  • Individuals who are HCV-positive usually receive combination treatment with ribavirin and interferons such as interferon α.
  • However, ribavirin has known teratogenic effects on the fetus and interferons have been shown to cause abortion in animal models.
  • Therefore, combination antiviral therapy is not recommended in pregnant women infected with HCV.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: To which family does Hepatitis A virus family belong to?
209.explanation:
• Hepatitis A is an ssRNA Picornavirus, transmitted via the fecal-oral route, through contaminated food, water, and shellfish.
  • Patients are often asymptomatic, but they can develop symptoms 2 to 6 weeks after exposure, with a course of several weeks of symptoms.
  • Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, fever, and right upper quadrant pain. Very few patients progress to acute liver failure.
  • Anti-HAV IgM can be used to detect acute hepatitis A infection, and anti-HAV IgG can be used to detect prior HAV infection or prior immunization.
  • Supportive treatment is recommended for nausea and diarrhea, but the majority of infections resolve without chronic liver disease.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: Hepatitis C virus belongs to which family?
209.explanation:
• Hepatitis C is Hepacivirus from the Flaviviridae family.
  • It is a linear, positive-sense single-stranded RNA with an icosahedral capsid.
  • Hepatitis C is an infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV), which attacks liver cells and causes liver inflammation.
  • The virus is mainly transmitted parenterally, especially through IV drug use or needlestick injuries in healthcare settings.
  • Most patients are asymptomatic in the acute phase, but may develop fever, malaise, fatigue, or jaundice.
  • Transition to chronic infections occurs in up to 85% of cases since asymptomatic patients are rarely diagnosed and treated.
  • Chronic infection is associated with increased mortality due to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: Which of the following is the most common outcome of an Acute Hepatitis C infection?
209.explanation:
• Chronic progressive hepatitis is the most likely natural disease course of acute HCV infection. Between 50 and 85% of patients develop chronic hepatitis.
  • Both viral and individual host factors (e.g., genetic polymorphisms) contribute to the overall risk of viral persistence.
  • Up to one-third of chronically infected individuals develop liver cirrhosis within 20 years.
  • As chronic HCV infection and even liver cirrhosis are frequently asymptomatic or present with nonspecific symptoms until late stages, diagnosis and treatment are often delayed.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of malaise, nausea, vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain after eating contaminated food. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and right upper quadrant tenderness. The liver is palpated 1.5 cm below the right costal margin. A biopsy specimen of this patient's liver would most likely show which of the following findings?
209.option_b: Ground glass hepatocytes and periportal inflammation
209.option_c: Necrosis with neutrophilic infiltrate and Mallory bodies
209.explanation:
• Acute onset of nausea, vomiting, fever, scleral icterus, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly following recent history of eating contaminated food are suggestive of acute hepatitis A infection.
  • Ballooning degeneration (swelling of hepatocytes due to depletion of ATP) and bridging necrosis (confluent necrosis spanning adjacent lobules) are histopathological findings seen in acute viral hepatitis.
  • Other typical findings include Councilman bodies (reflecting shrunken hepatocytes that underwent apoptosis) and periportal infiltration with helper T cells, B cells, and plasma cells.


Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: Which type of hepatitis virus is primarily transmitted through contaminated food and water?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis A is transmitted mainly through the ingestion of contaminated food and water, making it an enteric virus. It causes acute hepatitis and is preventable by vaccination.

  • Hepatitis A : Transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food and water.
  • Hepatitis B: Primarily transmitted through blood and bodily fluids.
  • Hepatitis C: Transmitted mainly through blood-to-blood contact, such as through needle sharing.
  • Hepatitis D: Requires the presence of Hepatitis B to be transmitted, typically through blood and body fluids.
  • Hepatitis E: Transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food and water.


Tags: fmge 2020 | fmge 2023

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For more information on Hepatitis A, see CDC Hepatitis A.

209.question_text: Which hepatitis virus is known for causing chronic liver disease and can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis C is a leading cause of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). It is known for its potential to become a chronic infection.

  • Hepatitis A: Usually causes acute illness and rarely leads to chronic infection.
  • Hepatitis B: Can also cause chronic liver disease and increase the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.
  • Hepatitis C: Most commonly leads to chronic infection, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.
  • Hepatitis E: Typically causes acute disease and is less commonly associated with chronic liver disease.

Tags: inicet 2020

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For detailed information on Hepatitis C, see CDC Hepatitis C.

209.question_text: Which hepatitis virus requires the presence of Hepatitis B virus for its replication?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis D Virus (HDV) is a defective virus that can only replicate in the presence of Hepatitis B Virus (HBV). It requires HBV for its envelope proteins.

  • Hepatitis A: Does not require Hepatitis B for replication.
  • Hepatitis B: Can exist independently and does not require Hepatitis D.
  • Hepatitis C: Does not require Hepatitis B for replication.
  • Hepatitis D: Dependent on Hepatitis B Virus for its replication and expression.

Tags: good to know

Tagline: HARD

Reference: For more information on Hepatitis D, visit CDC Hepatitis D.

209.question_text: Which hepatitis virus is primarily transmitted through sexual contact and can be prevented by vaccination?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis B is transmitted through sexual contact, as well as through blood and other bodily fluids. It is preventable by vaccination.

  • Hepatitis A: Transmitted via the fecal-oral route, not primarily through sexual contact.
  • Hepatitis B: Transmitted through sexual contact, blood, and bodily fluids; preventable by vaccination.
  • Hepatitis C: Primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood contact; no vaccine available.
  • Hepatitis E: Transmitted through contaminated water; not preventable by a vaccine currently available.

Hepatitis B Vaccination (NOTES)

  • Overview: The Hepatitis B vaccine is essential for preventing Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, which can lead to chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. It is highly effective and recommended for infants, children, and adults at risk.
  • Key Points:
  • Vaccine Schedule:

Infants: Typically administered in a series of three or four doses starting at birth, with subsequent doses given at 1-2 months and 6-18 months of age.

  • Adults: A series of three doses is given, with the second dose administered 1 month after the first and the third dose 6 months after the first.
  • Effectiveness: The vaccine is approximately 95% effective in preventing Hepatitis B infection in healthy individuals.
  • Administration: The vaccine is given as an intramuscular injection, typically in the deltoid muscle of the arm.
  • Safety: The Hepatitis B vaccine is safe and well-tolerated. Common side effects include soreness at the injection site and mild fever. Serious side effects are rare.
  • CDC Recommendations: The CDC recommends Hepatitis B vaccination for all infants, children, and adults who are at increased risk of HBV infection, including healthcare workers, people with chronic liver disease, and those with high-risk behaviors.
  • Nonresponders:
  • Definition: A "nonresponder" is an individual who does not develop detectable antibodies to Hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs) after completing the full vaccination series.
  • Prevalence: Approximately 5-10% of healthy adults may be nonresponders to the Hepatitis B vaccine.
  • Possible Causes: Nonresponse can be due to factors such as older age, obesity, immune system disorders, or specific genetic factors affecting vaccine efficacy.
  • Management: Nonresponders can receive additional doses of the vaccine. If they remain nonresponsive, further evaluation for underlying health issues or alternative methods of prevention and monitoring may be needed.
  • CDC Guidance: The CDC advises testing for anti-HBs after the completion of the vaccine series, especially for individuals at high risk of Hepatitis B. For those who remain nonresponsive, consultation with a healthcare provider is recommended to discuss further vaccination strategies or possible alternative interventions.

Tags: inicet 2020 | neet 2021

Tagline: EASY

Reference: For more information on Hepatitis B vaccination and nonresponders, visit CDC Hepatitis B Vaccine.

Reference: For information on Hepatitis B and its vaccine, see CDC Hepatitis B.

209.question_text: Which type of hepatitis is most commonly associated with travelers to areas with poor sanitation?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis A is commonly associated with poor sanitation and is prevalent in areas with inadequate hygiene and sanitation practices. It is often contracted by travelers visiting these regions.

  • Hepatitis A: Commonly contracted through contaminated food and water in areas with poor sanitation.
  • Hepatitis B: More common in areas with higher rates of infection through blood and body fluids, not typically related to sanitation issues.
  • Hepatitis C: Primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood contact; sanitation is less of a factor.
  • Hepatitis D: Requires Hepatitis B for infection; not associated with sanitation.

Tags: fmge 2020

Tagline: Moderate

Reference: For details on Hepatitis A and travel, see CDC Hepatitis A.

209.question_text: What is the primary method of diagnosing Hepatitis C infection?
209.option_a: Blood tests for antibodies and viral RNA
209.explanation:
The diagnosis of Hepatitis C is primarily made through blood tests. Initial tests detect antibodies to the virus (anti-HCV), and follow-up tests detect the viral RNA to confirm the presence of the virus.

  • Blood tests for antibodies and viral RNA: Key for diagnosing Hepatitis C infection.
  • Liver biopsy: Used to assess liver damage, not for initial diagnosis of Hepatitis C.
  • Ultrasound imaging: Can assess liver condition but not used to diagnose Hepatitis C infection directly.
  • Urine tests: Not used for diagnosing Hepatitis C.

Tags: good to know

Tagline: Hard

Reference: For more information on Hepatitis C diagnosis, see CDC Hepatitis C Testing.

209.question_text: Which hepatitis virus is most commonly associated with acute liver failure in pregnant women?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis E is known to cause acute liver failure, particularly in pregnant women, especially during the third trimester. This is more common in areas with poor sanitation.

  • Hepatitis A: Causes acute liver disease but is less commonly associated with acute liver failure in pregnancy.
  • Hepatitis B: Can cause acute liver failure but is less specifically associated with pregnant women.
  • Hepatitis C: Generally causes chronic disease; acute liver failure is less common.

Key takeaways:

Hepatitis E: Notably associated with acute liver failure in pregnant women.

Tags: must know

Tagline: Easy

Reference: For information on Hepatitis E, see CDC Hepatitis E.

209.question_text: Which hepatitis virus is known for its ability to rapidly mutate, making it difficult to develop a vaccine?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis C is known for its high mutation rate, which complicates the development of a vaccine. The virus has multiple genotypes and subtypes that evolve quickly, making it challenging to create a universal vaccine.

  • Hepatitis A: Has a stable genome and an effective vaccine.
  • Hepatitis B: Has a vaccine and less genetic variability compared to Hepatitis C.
  • Hepatitis C: Rapidly mutates, complicating vaccine development.
  • Hepatitis D: Dependent on Hepatitis B; does not have a separate vaccine.

Key takeaways: Hepatitis C's high mutation rate and diverse genotypes make developing a universal vaccine challenging.

Tags: good to know

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For more on Hepatitis C and its mutation, see CDC Hepatitis C Vaccine Research.

209.question_text: Which marker is the first to become elevated after Hepatitis B virus infection?
209.explanation:
HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is the first marker to appear after Hepatitis B virus infection, typically within 1-12 weeks of infection.

  • Anti-HBs: Appears after clearance of HBsAg.
  • Anti-HBc IgG: Indicates chronic infection and appears later than HBsAg.
  • HBsAg: First marker to be elevated.
  • HBeAg: Appears concurrently with or shortly after HBsAg but not first.

Hepatitis B Viral Markers(NOTES)

  1. Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg)
    • Description:
      • First marker to become elevated: Appears within 1-12 weeks of infection, usually between 8-12 weeks.
      • Timing: Can appear 2-6 weeks before biochemical evidence of hepatitis during the incubation period.
      • Presence: Detected in acute, chronic, and carrier states of Hepatitis B.
      • Usage: Serves as an epidemiological marker for establishing Hepatitis B infection.
      • Escape Mutants: Some variants, due to mutations in the S gene, cannot form detectable HBsAg. These are seen in infants born to HBeAg-positive mothers or in liver transplant recipients receiving combined HBV vaccine and immunoglobulin.
      • Detection Window: Becomes undetectable 1-2 months after the onset of jaundice and rarely persists beyond 6 months.
  2. Hepatitis B e-Antigen (HBeAg) and HBV DNA
    • Description:
      • Timing: Appears concurrently with or shortly after HBsAg.
      • Role: Marker of active viral replication and infectivity.
      • Presence: Found in acute, chronic, and carrier states of Hepatitis B.
  3. Hepatitis B Core Antigen (HBcAg)
    • Description:
      • Detection: Hidden antigen due to the surrounding HBsAg coat, not detected in blood.
      • Observation: Can be detected on hepatocytes using immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy.
  4. Anti-HBc IgM (Hepatitis B Core Antibody IgM)
    • Description:
      • First Antibody to Elevate: Indicates acute viral infection.
      • Timing: Begins within the first 1-2 weeks after HBsAg appearance and lasts for about 6 months. It is replaced by Anti-HBc IgG after this period.
      • Presence: Also present during the window period (when HBsAg is not detectable, but infection is ongoing).
  5. Anti-HBc IgG (Hepatitis B Core Antibody IgG)
    • Description:
      • Indicates Chronic Infection: Signifies a past or chronic infection.
      • Usage: Epidemiological marker that typically precedes detectable levels of Anti-HBs by weeks to months.
  6. Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B Surface Antibody)
    • Description:
      • Appearance: Appears after the clearance of HBsAg.
      • Duration: Remains indefinitely after the resolution of infection.
      • Role: Marker of vaccination, recovery from Hepatitis B, immunity, and non-infectivity.

Summary of Hepatitis B Markers

  • HBsAg: Indicates current infection; first marker elevated; can be undetectable within 1-2 months post-jaundice.
  • HBeAg: Indicates active viral replication and high infectivity; appears concurrently with HBsAg.
  • HBcAg: Hidden antigen; not detected in blood but visible in liver cells.
  • Anti-HBc IgM: Indicates acute infection; first antibody to rise; present for about 6 months.
  • Anti-HBc IgG: Indicates chronic infection; appears after Anti-HBc IgM.
  • Anti-HBs: Indicates recovery or vaccination; persists indefinitely; confirms immunity and non-infectivity.

Key takeaways:

High yield table:


Tags: inicet

Tagline: Easy

Reference: For more details, see CDC Hepatitis B Diagnosis.

209.question_text: Which marker indicates active viral replication and is a marker of infectivity in Hepatitis B infection?
209.explanation:
HBeAg (Hepatitis B e-antigen) is a marker of active viral replication and infectivity in Hepatitis B infection.

  • HBsAg: Indicates infection but not specifically active replication.
  • Anti-HBs: Indicates immunity or recovery.
  • HBcAg: Hidden antigen, not detected in blood.
  • HBeAg: Marker of active replication and infectivity.

Key takeaways:



Tags: Inicet 2022

Tagline: Moderate

Reference: For information on markers of active infection, see CDC Hepatitis B Markers.

209.question_text: What is the significance of the presence of Anti-HBc IgM in a Hepatitis B infection?
209.explanation:
Anti-HBc IgM (Hepatitis B core antibody IgM) is the first antibody to elevate and indicates an acute viral infection. It is also present during the window period.

  • Indicates chronic infection: Anti-HBc IgG is associated with chronic infection.
  • Indicates vaccination: Anti-HBs indicates vaccination.
  • Indicates acute viral infection: Anti-HBc IgM is specific for acute infection.
  • Indicates past infection: Anti-HBc IgG indicates past or chronic infection.

Tags : inicet 2020

Tagline: Hard

Reference: For more on Hepatitis B antibodies, see CDC Hepatitis B Testing.

209.question_text: How long does HBsAg typically remain detectable in a patient after the onset of jaundice?
209.explanation:
HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) usually becomes undetectable 1-2 months after the onset of jaundice. It rarely persists beyond 6 months.

  • 1-2 weeks: Too short a period for HBsAg to remain detectable.
  • 1-2 months: Correct duration.
  • 6 months: HBsAg can be detectable longer, but typically becomes undetectable within 1-2 months.
  • Indefinitely: HBsAg does not remain indefinitely.

Tags: good to know

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For details on HBsAg persistence, see CDC Hepatitis B Diagnostic Testing.

209.question_text: Which Hepatitis B marker is hidden due to the surrounding HBsAg coat and not detected in the blood?
209.explanation:
HBcAg (Hepatitis B core antigen) is hidden by the HBsAg coat and thus not typically detected in the blood. It may be detected in hepatocytes by immunofluorescence microscopy.

  • HBcAg: Hidden antigen, not in blood.
  • HBsAg: Surface antigen detected in blood.
  • HBeAg: Detected in blood as a marker of infectivity.
  • Anti-HBc IgM: Detected in blood during acute infection.

Tags: inicet 2021 | must know

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For information on Hepatitis B antigens, see CDC Hepatitis B Markers.

209.question_text: What does the presence of Anti-HBs indicate?
209.explanation:
Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B surface antibody) appears after the clearance of HBsAg and indicates either vaccination or recovery from Hepatitis B infection.

  • Ongoing Hepatitis B infection: Indicated by HBsAg.
  • Vaccination or recovery: Correct interpretation of Anti-HBs.
  • Active viral replication: Indicated by HBeAg.
  • Chronic Hepatitis B infection: Indicated by Anti-HBc IgG.

Tags: good to know

Tagline: Easy

Reference: For details on Anti-HBs, see CDC Hepatitis B Immunization.

209.question_text: What is the role of the Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) in diagnosing Hepatitis B infection?
209.option_a: It confirms the resolution of the infection
209.option_c: It shows the presence of antibodies
209.option_d: It marks the beginning of vaccination
209.explanation:
HBeAg is a marker of active viral replication and high infectivity in Hepatitis B infection. It is used to assess the level of viral activity.

  • Confirms the resolution of the infection: Not correct; HBeAg indicates ongoing replication.
  • Indicates active viral replication:
  • Shows the presence of antibodies: HBeAg is not an antibody; it is an antigen.
  • Marks the beginning of vaccination: Not relevant to HBeAg.

Tags: must know

Tagline: Moderate

Reference: For more on HBeAg and its role, see CDC Hepatitis B Diagnostic Testing.

209.question_text: What is the significance of Anti-HBc IgG in Hepatitis B infection?
209.explanation:
Anti-HBc IgG (Hepatitis B core antibody IgG) indicates past or chronic Hepatitis B infection and serves as an epidemiological marker.

  • Indicates current acute infection: Anti-HBc IgM indicates acute infection.
  • Indicates past or chronic infection:
  • Indicates recent vaccination: Not related to Anti-HBc IgG.
  • Indicates active viral replication: Not relevant for Anti-HBc IgG.

Key takeaways:


Tagline: Hard

Reference: For details on Anti-HBc IgG, see CDC Hepatitis B Testing.

209.question_text: Which Hepatitis B marker appears concurrently with or shortly after HBsAg?
209.explanation:
HBeAg (Hepatitis B e-antigen) appears concurrently with or shortly after HBsAg and indicates active viral replication and infectivity.

  • Anti-HBs: Appears after HBsAg clearance.
  • Anti-HBc IgM: Appears after HBsAg but specifically indicates acute infection.
  • HBeAg: Correct, appears around the same time as HBsAg.
  • Anti-HBc IgG: Appears later, usually after Anti-HBc IgM.

Tagline: Moderate

Reference: For more on Hepatitis B markers, see CDC Hepatitis B Markers.

209.question_text: What is the interpretation when both HBsAg and Anti-HBs are positive?
209.explanation:
• HBsAg Positive: Indicates ongoing infection.
  • Anti-HBs Positive: Indicates that the body has developed antibodies, usually after recovery or vaccination. However, if both are positive simultaneously, it suggests an acute phase where the body is transitioning from acute infection to recovery.
  • Acute hepatitis B: Correct, as the presence of HBsAg indicates current infection, and Anti-HBs could be detected if there is a transition phase or due to heterotypic anti-HBs.
  • Chronic hepatitis B, high infectivity: This would typically have Anti-HBs negative.
  • Precore-mutant hepatitis B: Not indicated by the simultaneous presence of HBsAg and Anti-HBs.
  • Early acute hepatitis (Incubating): Early acute typically does not show Anti-HBs.
  • KEY TAKEAWAY

Tags: neet 2020

Tagline: Easy

Reference: For more details, see CDC Hepatitis B Diagnosis

209.question_text: What does the presence of HBsAg and Anti-HBc IgM indicate?
209.explanation:
• HBsAg Positive: Indicates current infection.
  • Anti-HBc IgM Positive: Indicates acute infection as IgM appears first during the early stages.
  • Acute hepatitis B, high infectivity: Correct, as the combination indicates acute infection with high infectivity.
  • Chronic hepatitis B, low infectivity: Would not have Anti-HBc IgM but Anti-HBc IgG.
  • Precore-mutant hepatitis B: Typically associated with HBeAg-negative status.
  • Window period of acute hepatitis: Anti-HBc IgM would not be detectable in the window period.
  • KEY TAKEAWAY

Tags: must know | neet 2021

Tagline: Moderate

Reference: For details on acute hepatitis B, see CDC Hepatitis B Testing.

209.question_text: When HBsAg is positive and Anti-HBc IgM is positive, but Anti-HBs is negative, what is the most likely interpretation?
209.explanation:
• HBsAg Positive: Indicates ongoing infection.
  • Anti-HBc IgM Positive: Indicates acute infection as it appears first.
  • Anti-HBs Negative: Indicates no previous recovery or vaccination.
  • Acute hepatitis B: Correct, as this combination suggests an acute phase of infection.
  • Chronic hepatitis B: Would not show Anti-HBc IgM.
  • Recovery: Would show Anti-HBs as positive.
  • Vaccination: Would not have HBsAg.
  • KEY TAKEAWAY

Tags: must know | inicet

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For acute Hepatitis B infection, see CDC Hepatitis B Testing.

209.question_text: What is a characteristic marker combination for a supercarrier of Hepatitis B?
209.explanation:
• HBsAg Positive: Indicates ongoing Hepatitis B infection.
  • HBeAg Positive: Indicates high viral replication and high infectivity.
  • Supercarrier: Typically has HBsAg and HBeAg positive, with normal liver enzymes, suggesting a carrier state with high viral load but asymptomatic.
  • HBsAg positive, Anti-HBs positive: Indicates transition or recovery phase, not supercarrier.
  • HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs positive: Indicates recovery or vaccination, not supercarrier.
  • HBsAg positive, Anti-HBc IgM positive: Indicates acute infection, not supercarrier.
  • KEY TAKEAWAY

Tags: must know

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For details on Hepatitis B carrier states, see CDC Hepatitis B Overview.

209.question_text: What is the primary goal of antiviral therapy in chronic Hepatitis B infection?
209.option_b: To reduce liver inflammation and decrease viral load
209.option_c: To eliminate HBsAg from the bloodstream
209.option_d: To prevent the development of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
209.explanation:
• Antiviral Therapy: The main goal is to manage chronic Hepatitis B by reducing liver inflammation and lowering the viral load to minimize liver damage and prevent progression to cirrhosis or liver cancer.
  • To reduce liver inflammation and decrease viral load: Correct, as antiviral therapy aims to manage the infection and its effects rather than providing a complete cure.
  • To cure the infection completely: Not always achievable with current treatments; goal is often management.
  • To eliminate HBsAg from the bloodstream: Complete elimination of HBsAg is not always the goal or achievable with current treatments.
  • To prevent the development of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC): While antiviral therapy can reduce the risk, it is not the primary goal of treatment.

Key takeaways: The primary goal of antiviral therapy for chronic Hepatitis B is to reduce liver inflammation and viral load, not to cure the infection.

Tags: good to know

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For more information on Hepatitis B treatment goals, see CDC Hepatitis B Treatment.

209.question_text: Which medication is commonly used for treating chronic Hepatitis B and works by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase?
209.explanation:
• Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate: An antiviral medication that works by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase, effectively reducing the viral load in chronic Hepatitis B patients.
  • Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate: Correct, as it is a nucleotide analog that inhibits HBV DNA polymerase, reducing viral replication.
  • Interferon-alpha: Works by boosting the immune system and is used for treating Hepatitis B, but it does not inhibit viral DNA polymerase.
  • Adefovir Dipivoxil: Also an antiviral that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, but less commonly used compared to Tenofovir.
  • Lamivudine: An antiviral medication used to treat Hepatitis B, but Tenofovir is preferred in many cases due to better efficacy and resistance profile.

Tags: may know | inicet

Tagline: Text-Based

Reference: For information on Hepatitis B antiviral medications, see CDC Hepatitis B Treatment.

209.question_text: Which gene of the Hepatitis B virus is responsible for coding the DNA polymerase enzyme?
209.explanation:
• P gene: This gene codes for the DNA polymerase enzyme, which is essential for viral replication.
  • S gene: Codes for Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), not for DNA polymerase.
  • Core gene: Codes for Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg), not for DNA polymerase.
  • Pre-core gene: Codes for Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg), not for DNA polymerase.

Short Explanation Data:

  • S gene: Codes for HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen).
  • Core gene: Codes for HBcAg (Hepatitis B core antigen).
  • Pre-core gene: Codes for HBeAg (Hepatitis B e antigen).
  • P gene: Codes for DNA polymerase, which is crucial for viral replication.
  • X gene: Acts as a regulatory gene in the Hepatitis B virus lifecycle.

Tags: good to know | inicet

Reference: For more detailed information on Hepatitis B virus genes and their functions, see CDC Hepatitis B Overview.

209.question_text: According to the CDC guidelines, which of the following is an effective method for preventing Hepatitis B virus (HBV) transmission in healthcare settings?
209.option_a: Administering the Hepatitis B vaccine to healthcare workers
209.option_c: Performing routine disinfection with hydrogen peroxide
209.option_d: Avoiding the use of sharps in patient care
209.explanation:
• A. Administering the Hepatitis B vaccine to healthcare workers: The CDC recommends this as it provides immunity against HBV, reducing transmission risk.

Why Not Others:

  • B. Using alcohol-based hand sanitizers exclusively: While effective for general hand hygiene, it is not sufficient to prevent HBV after blood exposure; soap and water are necessary.
  • C. Performing routine disinfection with hydrogen peroxide: Not the best agent for HBV; other disinfectants like bleach are more effective.
  • D. Avoiding the use of sharps in patient care: Impractical in healthcare; safe sharps handling and disposal is the correct approach.

Key Takeaway: The Hepatitis B vaccine is crucial for protecting healthcare workers from HBV infection.

Tags: neet 2022

Reference: CDC Hepatitis B guidelines for healthcare settings.

209.question_text: A traveller is moving from Nigeria to the United States. Which vaccine must he receive as per International Health Regulations?
209.explanation:
Explanation:
According to International Health Regulations (IHR), travelers from yellow fever endemic zones (such as Nigeria and many parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South America) are required to receive the 17D live-attenuated yellow fever vaccine before entering countries like the United States. The vaccine certificate (International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis) is mandatory and valid for life after a single dose. This measure prevents the international spread of yellow fever.

Yellow fever:

  • A viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus.
  • Symptoms include jaundice, hemorrhagic fever, and conjunctival effusion
  • Yellow fever is endemic in parts of Africa and South America and is transmitted to humans primarily through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly Aedes aegypti.

17 D vaccine:

  • The 17 D vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine against yellow fever.
  • It provides effective and long-lasting immunity against the yellow fever virus infection and is recommended for individuals traveling to or residing in areas where yellow fever is endemic.
  • Vaccination with the 17 D vaccine is the most effective preventive measure against yellow fever and could have potentially prevented the patient's death if administered before travel to Africa.

Explanation of other options:

Hepatitis B (Option A): Important for individual protection, especially in healthcare workers, but not required under IHR for international travel.

Typhoid (Option C): Recommended for travelers to typhoid-endemic regions but not mandated under IHR.

Japanese encephalitis (Option D): Recommended for travelers to endemic areas in Asia, not Africa-to-US travel, and not part of IHR requirements.

209.question_text: A patient tested HBsAg and IgM Anti-HBc +ve. What is the likely diagnosis?
209.explanation:
Explanation:

A positive HBsAg and IgM Anti-HBc antibody are indicative of acute hepatitis infection.

Key Takeaway:

The combination of HBsAg and IgM Anti-HBc positivity is most consistent with acute Hepatitis B infection.

IgM Anti-HBc is a key marker for identifying recent or acute infection, while HBsAg indicates the presence of an active infection.

Reference: WHO. Hepatitis B. World Health Organization.

209.question_text: A patient's serum sample is positive for Infectious Hepatitis B. Which of the following markers would be positive?
209.explanation:
Explanation :

The presence of HBsAg indicates current infection. Anti-HBsAg antibodies protect against infection

The presence of HBeAg indicates active viral replication and high infectivity. Anti-HBeAg antibodies reduce infectivity but do not eliminate infection

So active and infectious hepatitis B is indicated by presence of HBsAg and HBeAg

Explanation of Other Options:

HBcAg (Option C)

  • HBcAg (Hepatitis B core antigen) is not detectable in serum because it is intracellular, found inside hepatocytes.
  • Instead, Anti-HBc (IgM or IgG) is used to detect core antigen exposure.

Key Takeaways:

Active and infectious Hepatitis B is confirmed by HBsAg and HBeAg

HBcAg is NOT detectable in serum, and Anti-HBe appears later when infectivity decreases. Identifying serological markers for Hepatitis B is crucial for diagnosing the infection status, determining immunity, and guiding patient management.

Reference: WHO. Hepatitis B. World Health Organization.

209.question_text: Shown in the figure is the HBV card test. Which of the following is the principle of this test?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis B can be diagnosed by many ways, rapid card test, principle is chromatography test.

ELISA is one of method to diagnose hepatitis B inf

PCR is also used for diagnosis of Hepatitis B inf.

Rapid chromatography is easy and cost effective, it has good sensitivity and specificity.

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option B) Chemiluminescence → NOT used in HBV card test
    • Chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIA) detect antigens using enzyme-labeled antibodies that produce light emission upon reaction.
    • Used in automated lab tests, NOT in rapid card tests.
  • (Option C) ELISA → Used for HBV detection, but NOT the principle of card test
    • Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) is a sensitive lab-based method for detecting HBsAg.
    • Requires 96-well microplates, enzyme-linked antibodies, and colorimetric detection.
    • More sensitive than rapid tests, but not the same principle.
  • (Option D) Immunofluorescence → NOT used in HBV rapid tests
    • Uses fluorescent-labeled antibodies to detect antigens under a fluorescence microscope.
    • Used in viral diagnostics, but NOT in rapid card tests.

Key Takeaways:

  • HBV card test uses immunochromatography (lateral flow assay).
  • It is rapid, cost-effective, and detects HBsAg.
  • ELISA, CLIA, and immunofluorescence are lab-based methods, NOT the principle of the card test.

209.question_text:
Which of the following cancers can be prevented by vaccination?
i.Cervical cancer
ii.Burkitt lymphoma
iii.Merkel cell carcinoma
iv.Hepatocellular carcinoma
209.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hepatocellular carcinoma and cervical cancer are the only malignancies preventable by vaccination.
  • Hepatitis B virus and sometimes Hepatitis C virus is linked to hepatocellular carcinoma, while HPV is associated with cervical cancer.
  • Merkel cell carcinoma is caused by Merkel cell polyomavirus and Burkitt's lymphoma is caused by Ebstein-bar virus in combination with other factors.
  • There are no vaccine available for Merkel cell polyomavirus and EBV.

HPV-associated cancer

  • HPV is the major cause of cervical cancer in women worldwide as well as anal and genital cancers in men.
  • It is also known to cause oropharyngeal cancer.
  • More than 80% of the HPV-associated cancers are caused by HPV 16 and 18, whereas 12% by HPV 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.

HPV Vaccine

  • HPV Gardasil-9 vaccine is recommended for routine immunization between 11- and 12-year-old girls and boys but can be given until age 26 years and in some cases up to 45 years.

Hepatitis B virus associated cancers

  • Chronic hepatitis B virus infection, in some cases, hepatitis C virus can lead to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
  • Hepatitis B vaccine, prevents chronic HBV infection, thereby reduces HCC risk.
  • Hepatitis B vaccine
    • Currently used vaccine: Recombinant Vaccine (prepared in yeast)
    • Dosing interval: 0, 1, 6 months

209.question_text: Hepatitis B subunit vaccine is derived from which antigen
209.explanation:
HBV contains two different antigenic components

  1. Common group reactive antigen a
  2. Two pairs of type specific antigen d-y and w-r only one member of each pair being present at a time.

HBV can be divided into four major antigenic types.

  1. Adw
  2. Adr
  3. Ayw
  4. Ayr

For vaccine production HBsAg antigen is used. It starts antibody production after vaccine as this antigen is highly immunogenic.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

Choice A (HBeAg): HBeAg (Hepatitis B e-antigen) is a marker of active viral replication and high infectivity. It is not used in vaccine production as it does not induce protective immunity.

Choice C (HBcAg): HBcAg (Hepatitis B core antigen) is an internal antigen of HBV and does not circulate freely in the blood. It primarily stimulates cell-mediated immunity but does not induce protective antibodies, making it unsuitable for vaccine production.

Choice D (HBV DNA): HBV DNA is the genetic material of the virus and is used for diagnostic purposes (e.g., PCR testing for HBV viral load). It is not used in vaccines.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Hepatitis B vaccine is a subunit vaccine derived from HBsAg, which induces protective immunity.
  • HBsAg is highly immunogenic and stimulates the production of anti-HBs antibodies, conferring immunity.
  • The vaccine is produced using recombinant DNA technologyin yeast or mammalian cell cultures.
  • HBeAg, HBcAg, and HBV DNA are not used in vaccine production.

209.question_text: Which of the following hepatitis viruses is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route?
209.explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus from the Picornaviridae family, transmitted predominantly via contaminated food and water.
  • Infection occurs through the fecal-oral route, leading to acute hepatitis, but HAV does not cause chronic infection.

Hepatitis Viruses and Their Features


Hepatitis G Virus (HGV)

  • HGV is a bloodborne virus from the Flaviviridae family, related to HCV.
  • Transmitted via blood transfusions, shared needles, less commonly sexually or vertically.
  • Usually asymptomatic, rarely causes liver inflammation.
  • Some studies suggest HGV may slow HIV progression in co-infected patients.
  • Diagnosis: PCR for HGV RNA.
  • Treatment: Specific antiviral therapy is generally not required.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554549/

209.question_text: Which of the following hepatitis viruses is transmitted through contaminated water?
209.explanation:
Explanation:

Hepatitis A virus is primarily spread through contaminated water and food via the faecal-oral route.

Hepatitis A Virus (HAV)

  • Also known as Enterovirus-72, it belongs to the:
    • Family: Picornaviridae
    • Genus: Hepatovirus.
  • Hepatitis A virus has single serotype with six genotypes, of which I, II, and III infect humans.

Viral Morphology:

  • Small, non-enveloped virus
  • Icosahedral symmetry
  • Single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome (+ssRNA)
  • Encodes four capsid proteins (VP1-VP4)

Epidemology and Transmission:

  • Transmission primarily via the faecal-oral route, especially in areas with poor sanitation.
  • Spread occurs through direct contact, contaminated food or water, fomites, or person-to-person contact with inadequate hygiene.
  • Rarely transmission can occur through blood transfusion or sexual contact.
  • It shares transmission patterns with poliovirus.
  • Cases show seasonal peaks during warmer months.

Cultivability:

  • Can be cultivated in specific cell cultures, such as human or primate diploid cell lines.
  • Only Hepatitis virus which can be cultured

Manifestations:

  • Incubation: 15-45 days (mean 25 days)
  • Symptoms: Fever, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant pain, vomiting
  • Jaundice: Appears within several days; dark urine and clay-colored stool may precede jaundice by 1-5 days
  • Most cases self-limiting; chronic infection does not occur

Diagnosis:

  • Serology:
    • IgM anti-HAV: Indicates acute infection; detectable early and for several weeks/months
    • IgG anti-HAV: Appears during convalescence; persists for life, indicates past infection or immunity
  • Molecular: RT-PCR can detect HAV RNA

Treatment:

  • Supportive care only: Adequate nutrition, rest, and hydration
  • No specific antiviral therapy.
  • Inactivated hepatitis A virus vaccine confers long-term protection.
    • Two doses are given 6 to 12 months

209.question_text: Lipidator sanitizer is a non-ionic surfactant that is used to disrupt the lipid membranes of cells. This disruption of the lipid membrane results in the release of all of its cytoplasmic contents. Which of the following viruses would not be disrupted if treated with this detergent?
209.explanation:
A) Herpesvirus:

  • Herpesviruses have lipid envelopes composed of host cell-derived lipids. These lipid envelopes make them susceptible to disruption by Lipidator sanitizer.
  • Lipidator sanitizer is a non-ionic surfactant that targets lipid membranes of cells and can effectively disrupt the lipid envelope of herpesviruses.
  • When the lipid envelope is disrupted, it results in the release of the virus's cytoplasmic contents.

B) Hepadnavirus:

  • Hepadnaviruses, including hepatitis B virus, have a unique viral envelope primarily composed of lipids derived from the host cell's membrane. The envelope is different from the lipid envelopes of many other viruses.
  • As a result, hepadnaviruses may not be effectively disrupted by Lipidator sanitizer, as their envelope is different in composition and may be more resistant to this type of treatment.
  • Lipidator sanitizer primarily targets lipid membranes, and hepadnavirus's envelope composition may not make it susceptible to disruption.

C) Flavivirus:

  • Flaviviruses have lipid envelopes containing host-derived lipids, which are vulnerable to disruption by Lipidator sanitizer.
  • Lipidator sanitizer effectively targets the lipid membranes of cells and viruses, causing the release of cytoplasmic contents when applied to flaviviruses.

D) Picornavirus:

  • Picornaviruses have lipid envelopes that can be disrupted by Lipidator sanitizer.
  • The lipid envelope of picornaviruses is susceptible to the action of Lipidator sanitizer, leading to the release of cytoplasmic contents when treated with this detergent.

In summary, the correct answer is B) Hepadnavirus. Hepadnaviruses, with their unique viral envelope composition, are less likely to be disrupted by Lipidator sanitizer, while the other viruses listed have lipid envelopes that are effectively disrupted by this detergent.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 80

209.question_text: HBV and HCV are known to be oncogenic viruses. Which of the following genes in the HBV genome is postulated to cause carcinogenesis?
209.explanation:
Hepatitis B virus genome is compact and consists of four overlapping genes:

  1. S gene: It has three regions-
    1. S gene,
    2. pre-S1
    3. pre-S2.
      They code for surface antigen (HBsAg)
  2. C gene: It consists of pre-C and C-regions, which code for two nucleocapsid proteins
    1. Pre-C region-codes for HBeAg
    2. C-region-codes for HBcAg.
  3. X gene: It codes for HBxAg, which can activate the transcription of cellular and viral genes. It may contribute to the pathogenesis of carcinogenesis by binding to p53
  4. P gene: It is the largest gene and codes for polymerase (P) protein, which has three enzymatic activities-
    1. DNA polymerase activity,
    2. RNase H activity
    3. Reverse transcriptase activity.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 17, Pg: 259

209.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of nausea, diarrhea & vague abdominal pain after eating at a roadside stall few days ago. He also had loss of appetite and started developing a fever to 102.0°F. The patient appears jaundiced with scleral icterus & has RUQ tenderness. His labs have elevated transaminases, with an ALT of 10,000 U/L and AST of 8,000 U/L. Which of the following best describes the causative agent of this patient's disease?
209.explanation:
Patient Presentation:

  • A 35-year-old man with 2 weeks of symptoms, including nausea, diarrhea, vague abdominal pain, and fever (102.0°F).
  • Loss of appetite, jaundice, scleral icterus, and right upper quadrant (RUQ) tenderness.

Laboratory Findings:

  • Elevated transaminases: ALT of 10,000 U/L and AST of 8,000 U/L.

Causative Agent:

  • The patient likely has Hepatitis A infection.

Characteristics of Hepatitis A Virus (HAV):

  • HAV is a single-stranded, positive-sense, non-enveloped RNA virus.
  • It has an icosahedral capsid.
  • Transmission occurs through the fecal-oral route, often due to contaminated food or water or contact with an infectious person.

Clinical Presentation of Hepatitis A:

  • Patients with Hepatitis A may be asymptomatic.
  • Symptoms typically develop 2 to 6 weeks after exposure and last for several weeks.
  • Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, fever, and right upper quadrant pain.
  • Severe cases can progress to acute liver failure, although this is rare.

Diagnostic Tests:

  • Anti-HAV IgM is used to detect acute hepatitis A infection.
  • Anti-HAV IgG is used to detect prior HAV infection or prior immunization.

Treatment:

  • Supportive treatment is recommended for nausea and diarrhea.
  • The majority of infections resolve without causing chronic liver disease.

Justification:

  • The causative agent of this patient's disease is Hepatitis A, which is characterized by the clinical presentation and laboratory findings.
  • Hepatitis A virus is a single-stranded, positive-sense, non-enveloped RNA virus.

So, the best description of the causative agent of this patient's disease is C) Single-stranded, positive-sense, non-enveloped RNA virus (Hepatitis A virus).

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 32-week's gestation presents with severe abdominal pain, fatigue, and nausea. Physical examination shows jaundice and RUQ tenderness. Infection with which of the following organisms would portend the worst prognosis with the highest mortality rate for this patient?
209.explanation:
• Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection is typically self-limited in men and non-pregnant women; however, the disease is more severe in pregnant patients, often leading to fulminant hepatic failure.
  • The mortality rate of HEV infected women in their 3rd trimester is 20%.
  • HEV is a positive, single-stranded RNA virus that is transmitted primarily via a fecal-oral route.
  • In non-pregnant patients who suffer relatively mild disease, the presentation is similar to that of hepatitis A virus, with nausea, vomiting, and mild jaundice.


Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page 487

209.question_text: The image shown here is used for the diagnosis of
209.explanation:
Explanation:

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a member of the Herpesviridae family and demonstrates the following structural and biological features:

  • Capsid symmetry: Icosahedral
  • Size: 150–200 nm (the second largest virus)
  • Genome: Double-stranded DNA
  • Envelope: Derived from the modified host cell nuclear membrane as the naked virion buds during replication
  • Tegument: An amorphous layer situated between the envelope and nucleocapsid
  • Unique property: Ability to establish latency in neurons with periodic reactivation

Classification of Human Herpesviruses (HHVs):


Explanation of Other Options:

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (Option A):

  • Member of the Retroviridae family.
  • Contains two copies of positive-sense RNA within a cone-shaped capsid.
  • Requires reverse transcriptase for replication.
  • Unlike HSV, it is an RNA virus without a tegument or a nuclear membrane–derived envelope.

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) (Option B):

  • Belongs to the Hepadnaviridae family.
  • Contains a partially double-stranded DNA genome enclosed in the Dane particle.
  • Replicates through reverse transcription but lacks a tegument.
  • Structurally much smaller than HSV.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) (Option C):

  • Non-enveloped virus from the Papillomaviridae family.
  • Small DNA virus with icosahedral symmetry.
  • Lacks an envelope and tegument.
  • Causes epithelial proliferations (warts, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia) instead of neuronal latency.

209.question_text: The occupational health department at a hospital implements new safety precaution which includes disinfecting the microbiology laboratory benches with 70% ethanol before and after use. This measure is most likely to be effective in preventing the transmission of which of the following viruses?
209.explanation:
Let's justify each option in terms of its susceptibility to disinfection with 70% ethanol:

Option A) Parvovirus:

  • Parvovirus is a non-enveloped virus.
  • Non-enveloped viruses like Parvovirus have a protein capsid but lack a lipid envelope.
  • Ethanol-based disinfection is generally less effective against non-enveloped viruses because it primarily targets the lipid envelope.
  • Parvovirus is relatively resistant to ethanol-based disinfection.
  • Therefore, disinfecting with 70% ethanol is less likely to be effective in preventing the transmission of Parvovirus (Option A).

Option B) Polyomavirus:

  • Polyomavirus is also a non-enveloped virus.
  • Like Parvovirus, it lacks a lipid envelope and has a protein capsid.
  • Non-enveloped viruses tend to be more resistant to ethanol-based disinfection.
  • Therefore, disinfecting with 70% ethanol is less likely to be effective in preventing the transmission of Polyomavirus (Option B).

Option C) Herpes simplex virus:

  • Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is an enveloped virus.
  • Enveloped viruses, including HSV, have a lipid bilayer envelope surrounding their protein capsid.
  • Ethanol-based disinfection is effective against enveloped viruses because it disrupts the lipid envelope.
  • Disinfecting with 70% ethanol is likely to be effective in preventing the transmission of Herpes simplex virus

Option D) Hepatitis A virus:

  • Hepatitis A virus is also a non enveloped virus.
  • It lacks a lipid envelope and therefore disinfecting with 70% ethanol is less likely to be effective .

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd Edition, Page Number 550

209.question_text: A 45-year-old man comes with progressively increasing multiple lesions on his chest and lower extremities. He was diagnosed with HIV seven years ago. A photograph of the lesions is shown. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 450/mm3. A skin biopsy shows multiple spindle-shaped cells and lymphocytic infiltrate. Which virus is responsible for this?
209.explanation:
