213.question_text: An HIV positive patient with a CD4 count of 300/cumm presents with mucosal lesions in the mouth as shown in the figure. On microscopy budding yeasts and pseudo-hyphae are seen. What is the likely diagnosis?
213.explanation:
Given is case of opportunistic infection in AIDS. As HIv virus infection progress patients CD4 cell count starts decreasing.

And patient starts having opportunistic infections.

In given case, CD4 cell count is 300/cumm and pt has mucosal lesions in mouth , from microscopy finding it is candida infection.

Incorrect Answer Explanations:

  • (Option B) Oral hairy leukoplakia → Incorrect
    • Caused by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).
    • Characterized by white, non-scrapable plaques on the lateral tongue (unlike candidiasis, which is scrapable).
    • More common in CD4 count <200/mm³.
  • (Option C) Lichen planus → Incorrect
    • Characterized by Wickham’s striae (fine white lace-like pattern) on the buccal mucosa.
    • Does not show budding yeasts or pseudo-hyphae on microscopy.
  • (Option D) Aphthous ulcer → Incorrect
    • Presents as painful, round ulcers with a red halo and yellowish base.
    • Not associated with budding yeasts or pseudo-hyphae on microscopy.

Key Takeaways:

  • Oral candidiasis is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS.
  • CD4 count <500/mm³ increases susceptibility to fungal infections like Candidiasis.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of budding yeasts and pseudo-hyphae on microscopy.

213.question_text:
Which of the following statements about Cryptococcus are true?
i.Pathogenic species are urease-positive
ii.Cryptococcus gattii is associated with bird guano
iii.Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis is an AIDS-defining illness
iv.Opportunistic infection occurs in AIDS when CD4 counts fall below 500
213.explanation:
Explanation:

Cryptococcus species are urease-positive and cause cryptococcosis, an AIDS-defining illness, usually when CD4 < 100. Cryptococcus gattii is linked to eucalyptus trees.

Cryptococcus

  • Cryptococcus is a true yeast with a polysaccharide capsule that protects against phagocytosis.
  • The capsule allows serotyping:
    • Serotypes A, D, and AD correspond to Cryptococcus neoformans
    • Serotypes B and C correspond to Cryptococcus gattii.
  • Birds and bats serve as natural reservoirs.
  • Humans acquire the fungus by inhaling spores from contaminated environments, such as bird or bat droppings.
  • Infection risk increases in immunocompromised individuals, those exposed to bird droppings or decaying wood, and people in tropical or subtropical regions.
  • Cryptococcus is the most common cause of meningitis in HIV-positive individuals.
  • It causes infection in immunocompromised individuals, when< 100.

Infections Caused by Cryptococcus

  • Pulmonary Cryptococcosis
    • Primary infection in the lungs after inhalation of spores; may be asymptomatic or cause pneumonia-like symptoms.
  • Cryptococcal Meningoencephalitis
    • Most common disseminated form, especially in immunocompromised patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS), leading to headache, fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status.
  • Cutaneous Cryptococcosis
    • Skin lesions, often secondary to disseminated infection.


Treatment

  • Initial Treatment with liposomal Amphotericin B and Flucytosine
  • Maintenance Therapy with Fluconazole for 6-12 months, depending on immune status.
  • Monitoring: Regularly check CSF for fungal clearance, renal function, and electrolytes.
  • Management of Underlying Conditions: Optimize ART to reduce recurrence risk.

Reference:

Cryptococcus gattii - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics.

213.question_text: A patient is tested positive for rk39ag test. Choose the correct treatment.
213.explanation:
Rk39 test is used to diagnose invasive fungal disease.Invasive fungal disease are caused by candida albicans, aspergillus fumigatus, cryptococcus neoformans, pneumocystis jiroveci, endemic dimorphic fungi, mucormycetes.

Treatment of invasive fungal disease echinocandin ( Caspofungin, micafungin or anidulafungin) given through IV.

Fluconazole, amphotericin B and other antifungal medications may also be appropriate in certain situations.

Incorrect Choices Explanation:

Choice A: Fluconazole - Fluconazole is an antifungal medication primarily used for Candida infections and cryptococcal meningitis, not for visceral leishmaniasis. It is ineffective against Leishmania donovani.

Choice C: Miltefosine - Although miltefosine is an oral drug used for treating visceral leishmaniasis, it is not the preferred first-line therapy in all cases. Liposomal Amphotericin B remains the treatment of choice, especially in severe cases or where resistance to miltefosine is a concern.

Choice D: Sodium Stibogluconate - While sodium stibogluconate was historically used for visceral leishmaniasis, resistance to this drug has emerged in many regions, particularly in India, making it less favorable compared to Liposomal Amphotericin B.

Key Takeaway:

The rk39 antigen test is a specific diagnostic test for visceral leishmaniasis, not an invasive fungal disease. Liposomal Amphotericin B is the preferred treatment due to its efficacy, lower toxicity, and widespread recommendation by WHO.

214.question_text: A young adult female having profuse yellowish green offensive vaginal discharge, dysuria and dyspareunia has come to the STI clinic. Upon physical examination, mucosa has an erythematous, punctate and papilliform appearance. (Strawberry mucosa). Which rapid test/technique helps to find out etiological agent.
214.option_a: Wet mount examination for characteristic jerky motility
214.option_b: Gram stain demonstration of intracellular diplococci
214.option_d: Demonstration of clue cells by gram stain
214.explanation:
Option A – This is a case of Trichomonas vaginalis infection which can be diagnosed by examining saline wet mount of vaginal discharge. As characteristic jerky and twitching motility of trophozoite is rapidly lost outside the body, it should be examined immediately upon collection. Offensive yellowish green profuse discharge along with Strawberry mucosa is characteristic of infection.

Other causes of vaginitis are : fungal Candida species (demonstrated by KOH preparation) in which thick, white, curdy or cheesy discharge is produced. Bacterial by Gardnerella vaginalis (demonstrated by clue cells) has profuse, thin, watery discharge with fishy smell. N.gonorrhoeae typically causes cervicitis and not vaginitis. (Gram stain demonstration of intracellular diplococci).

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -37

214.question_text: Which of the following statement is NOT accurate for Microsporidia species -
214.option_b: Reproduce in cell by spore formation
214.option_d: Demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin stain
214.explanation:
• Option D - Microsporidia are unicellular obligate intracellular parasites. They reproduce in host cells by producing spores. 3 genera and 13 species are associated with human disease particularly, in HIV and other immuno-compromised patients. Infection is caused by an inhalation or ingestion of spores. Though commonly causes diarrhea, it may also lead to extra intestinal infections like sinusitis, cholangitis, bronchiolitis and kerato- conjunctivitis. Because of its intracellular locations, they are not routinely demonstrated by hematoxylin and eosin stain.
  • Modified trichrome stain, gram stain and modified acid-fast stain are usually used to demonstrate them.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -106

214.question_text: Intestinal re-infection (Hyper infection syndrome) is seen in -
214.explanation:
Option B - in S.stercoralis infection, if patient has defective cellular response - AIDS patient, lepromatous leprosy, corticosteroid therapy or severe malnutrition, rhabditiform larva which are released in intestinal lumen instead of passing into feces develop into filariform larva in intestine which penetrate intestinal mucosa and lodge into lungs and various tissue and organs - condition called as intestinal re-infection or Hyper infection syndrome.

Option A & D - intestinal re-infection usually does not occur in these parasites.

Option C - auto-infection and retro-infection is a feature of E. vermicularis in which eggs deposited in perianal skin, autoinfects person due to itching and unhygienic habits or larva hatched in perianal skin moves retrograde through anus causing retrograde autoinfection.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -184

214.question_text: A sample of sputum from a patient with a parasitic lung infection is examined microscopically. The slender, bipyramidal hexagonal crystals seen in the image are noted. These crystals are formed from the breakdown of which type of inflammatory cell?
214.explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image displays Charcot-Leyden crystals. These are distinct, microscopic crystals with a characteristic slender, bipyramidal hexagonal shape.
  • These crystals are composed of an enzyme called galectin-10, which is a primary constituent of the cytoplasmic granules of eosinophils.
  • When eosinophils congregate at a site of allergic or parasitic inflammation and subsequently break down, the galectin-10 is released and crystallizes. Therefore, the presence of Charcot-Leyden crystals in a sample (e.g., sputum, stool, tissue) is a hallmark of an eosinophil-rich inflammatory process, strongly suggesting an underlying allergic reaction or a helminthic infection.

Explanation of Other Options:

Options A, C, and D: Neutrophils, macrophages, and basophils have different enzymatic contents in their granules, and none of them form these specific bipyramidal crystals upon degranulation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Charcot-Leyden crystals are microscopic crystals formed from the breakdown products of eosinophils.
  • Their presence indicates an eosinophilic inflammatory response.
  • This is a classic finding in samples from patients with conditions like allergic asthma and parasitic worm infections.

Reference:

Paniker's Textbook of Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page Number: 22.

214.question_text: Which stain can demonstrate the oocysts of Cryptosporidium best:
214.explanation:
Option C - For better demonstration of protozoa, stool samples are stained with various stains like Iron-Hematoxylin and Trichrome stain. Trichrome stain has 3 reagents - Chromotrope 2R, Light green SF & Phosphotungstic acid. Modified trichrome stain is used for Microsporidia which are intracellular in location for which higher concentration along with longer duration is required to stain them. For oocyst of Cryptosporidium and Isospora, modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain using 0.5-1% sulfuric acid as decolorizing agent is used.

214.question_text: Regarding T.cruzi, which of the following is most accurate :
214.option_c: Exists as both amastigote and trypomastigote in humans
214.option_d: Complications of chronic diseases are common in children
214.explanation:

Some of them, after converting through epimastigote form, convert to trypomastigote forms inside blood. Reduviid bug is a vector which when feeds on human blood, acquires infection.

Option A - Tsetse fly is a vector which transmits T.brucei

Option B - Armadillo, cat ,dog and pigs are major reservoir

Option D - complications of chronic diseases are common in adults, while in children acute disease is common.

214.question_text: Quantitative Buffy coat examination for identification of malarial parasite is :
214.explanation:
• Option D - In QBC test, 50-100 μl blood is collected in capillaries coated with acridine orange dye (fluorescent dye). It is then centrifuged in a special centrifuge at high speed - 12000 rpm for 5 min.
  • Blood is separated in columns in layers of plasma, buffy coat containing platelets & WBC and RBC. Principle is that infected RBC are less dense than uninfected RBC and concentrate just below the buffy coat at top of the RBC column. As RBC do not contain any nuclear material (DNA & RNA) they are not stained, while nuclei (DNA) of parasites are stained by acridine orange as fluorescing greenish yellow against dark background.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -82

214.question_text: The most consistent finding about intestinal amoebic ulcer -
214.option_c: Many discrete ulcers with pinhead center
214.option_d: Healing of ulcer without scar formation
214.explanation:
Option C – Most frequent location is caecum, not ileum. Usually, many discrete ulcers are produced with pinhead center and raised edges. Rarely, multiple ulcers coalesce to form large ulcers. As most ulcers are extending deep in submucosa, they heal with scar formation. Superficial aphthous ulcers heal without scar formation.

214.question_text: An intermediate host whose presence may be required for the completion of a parasite's life cycle but in which no development of the parasite occurs is -
214.explanation:
Paratenic host : An organism that harbors the sexually immature parasite (larva) but is not necessary for the parasite's developmental cycle to progress.

Reservoir host : an organism that harbors a pathogen but suffers no ill effects, responsible for continued existence of parasite in area

Accidental host : an organism that generally does not allow transmission to the definitive host, thereby preventing the parasite from completing its development.

Definite host : An organism in which the parasite reaches the adult stage and reproduces sexually

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -1

214.question_text: A first-year pathology resident is given exercise to demonstrate various parasitic infections from peripheral blood smear (PBS). He should look for following parasites in PBS EXCEPT

214.question_text: Match following skin test used in parasitology with their disease
214.explanation:
Option B - these are various skin tests which are useful for detection of parasitic infection. Antigen is administered intradermally, if a patient has a previous infection, either an immediate reaction with wheal and flare or delayed hypersensitivity reaction with erythema and induration takes place. Bachman test for T.spiralis and Casoni's reaction for E.granulosus are immediate hypersensitivity reaction developing in 15-30 minutes. Frenkel's test for Toxoplasma and Montenegro's test for Leishmania donovani are examples of delayed type of response in infected persons developing in 48-72 hours.

214.question_text: Which genus of protozoa is responsible for malaria, and how is it classified within the Phylum Apicomplexa?
214.option_a: Plasmodium, classified under the class Coccidia
214.option_b: Plasmodium, classified under the class Hematozoa
214.option_c: Babesia, classified under the class Hematozoa
214.option_d: Toxoplasma, classified under the class Piroplasmida
214.explanation:
• Plasmodium, classified under the class Hematozoa: This is correct; Plasmodium is indeed classified under the class Hematozoa, which includes blood parasites.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: Misclassifies Plasmodium under Coccidia, which is inaccurate for malaria-causing protozoa. Plasmodium, classified under the class Coccidia: This is incorrect; Plasmodium is not classified in Coccidia, which includes other protozoa like Toxoplasma.
  • Option C: While Babesia is a blood parasite, it is not responsible for malaria. Babesia, classified under the class Hematozoa: This is incorrect; while Babesia is classified under Hematozoa, it is not responsible for malaria but rather causes a similar disease known as babesiosis.
  • Option D: Toxoplasma, classified under the class Piroplasmida: This is incorrect; Toxoplasma is classified under Coccidia, and it does not cause malaria.

Key Takeaway: The genus Plasmodium, responsible for malaria, is classified under the class Hematozoa within the Phylum Apicomplexa, highlighting its specific role as a blood parasite.

Tags: good to know

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter-: Malaria and Babesia,pp - 66

214.question_text: In the life cycle of malaria parasites, what is the term used to describe the asexual phase that occurs in the human host?
214.explanation:
• Schizogony: Correct; it refers to the asexual multiplication phase of the malaria parasites that occurs in the liver and blood of the human host, leading to the production of merozoites.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: Sporogony: Incorrect; this is the sexual phase occurring in the mosquito where gametes fuse to form sporozoites.
  • Sporogony is related to the mosquito lifecycle, not the human phase.
  • Option C: Gametogony: Incorrect; this phase involves the formation of gametocytes and occurs in the mosquito after the human host has been infected.
  • Gametogony is a mosquito-specific process, unrelated to the human asexual phase.
  • Option D: Oocyst Formation: Incorrect; this occurs in the mosquito after fertilization of the gametes, not in the human host

Key Takeaway: Schizogony is the critical asexual phase of the malaria parasite's life cycle that occurs in the human host, responsible for the disease's symptomatic manifestations.

Tags: fmge 2023

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter-: Malaria and Babesia,pp - 69

214.question_text: What is the infective stage of the malaria parasite injected into the human bloodstream by the female Anopheles mosquito?
214.explanation:
• Sporozoites: Correct; they are the infective forms injected by the female Anopheles mosquito into the human bloodstream during a bite.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: Merozoites occur after infection and are not injected by the mosquito. Merozoites: Incorrect; these are produced after sporozoites infect liver cells and are released into the bloodstream to invade red blood cells.
  • Option C: Gametocytes: Incorrect; these are the sexual forms of the malaria parasite found in the blood but not injected by the mosquito.Gametocytes are not involved in the initial infection process as they are produced in humans.
  • Option D: Schizonts: Incorrect; these are formed within liver or red blood cells after sporozoites have infected them, not injected directly.
  • Schizonts result from asexual reproduction inside host cells and are not the initial infective form.

Key Takeaway: Sporozoites are the infectious agents injected into humans by the female Anopheles mosquito, initiating the malaria infection.

Tags: inicet 2023

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter-: Malaria and Babesia,pp- 69

214.question_text: What is the term for the process by which malaria parasites multiply in the liver cells of the human host?
214.explanation:
• Exoerythrocytic Schizogony: Correct; this process involves the asexual multiplication of malaria parasites in liver cells, leading to the formation of thousands of merozoites.

Why Not Others:

  • Option B: Erythrocytic Schizogony: Incorrect; this occurs in red blood cells after the liver stage and is part of the subsequent cycle of multiplication.
  • Option C: Sporogony: Incorrect; this refers to the sexual phase of the malaria life cycle that occurs in the mosquito vector Sporogony is specific to the mosquito's reproductive cycle and does not involve the human host.
  • Option D: Gametogony: Incorrect; this is the stage where gametes are formed in the mosquito, not in the human host .

Key Takeaway: Exoerythrocytic schizogony refers to the multiplication of malaria parasites in liver cells, a crucial step in the malaria life cycle before they enter the bloodstream.

Tags: neet 2023

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter-: Malaria and Babesia,pp - 69.

214.question_text: Infective form of E.histolytica for humans is -
214.explanation:
Option D – E.histolytica passes its life cycle in single species of host (man). However, transfer to another host is required for propagation of species. Man excretes trophozoite and uninucleate cyst in feces. Trophozoites gets killed within short time in environment due to drying and heat. Cyst is able to survive for a long time in the environment. Uninucleate cyst convert into binucleate and finally quadrinucleate cyst. Mature quadrinucleate cyst is infective form, which when ingested along with food or water undergoes excystation in lower part of ileum or caecum.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -17

214.question_text: Conversion of uninucleate cyst into mature quadrinucleate cyst in E.histolytica is accompanied by all EXCEPT -
214.explanation:
Option C – Uninucleate cyst is spherical about 10-20 µ in size. It has a single nucleus, large glycogen mass and 1-4 chromatoid bodies. With successive nuclear division, glycogen mass is reduced in size and the chromatoid body disappears and the cyst is surrounded by refractile cyst wall.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -16

214.question_text: Match the virulence factors of E. histolytica with their mode of action -
214.explanation:
Option B has correct match of virulence factors with their mode of action. Lectin helps in adhesion, followed by mucosal penetration by motility. Once in submucosa, histolysin leads to tissue lysis and amoebapores leads to insertion of ion channels into liposomes causing lysis of target cell membrane.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -18

214.question_text: E.histolytica trophozoites multiplies by :
214.explanation:
Option A – Protozoa reproduce by asexual and sexual methods. Asexual method like binary fission, multiple fission and endodyogeny. E.histolytica, Leishmania and Trypanosomes multiplies asexually by binary fission. Plasmodia multiplies by multiple fission (Schizogony). Some protozoa like Toxoplasma multiply by internal budding (Endodyogeny).

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -16

214.question_text: Etiological agent of granulomatous amoebic encephalitis is :
214.explanation:
Option B -Acanthamoeba causes primary amoebic granulomatous meningo-encephalitis. E.histolytica cause brain abscess secondary to infection in intestine. Naegleria causes acute suppurative inflammation. D.fragilis though classified as amoeboflagellate like Naegleria, causes gastro-intestinal symptoms like diarrhea, flatulence, abdominal pain, anorexia and fatigue.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -29

214.question_text: Infective form of acanthamoeba is -
214.explanation:
Option C – Acanthamoeba is a free-living amoeba which exists in soil and water, as trophozoite and cysts forms. Both are infective forms. Humans acquire infection by inhalation of cyst or trophozoite, ingestion of cysts or through traumatized skin or eyes. Naegleria occurs in 3 forms. Cyst, amoeboid trophozoite and flagellated trophozoite. Cysts are not infectious. Infection is acquired by trophozoites ( both amoeboid and flagellated).

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -28

214.question_text: Schizont of P.falciparum are not found in peripheral blood because of :
214.option_a: Schizonts are absent in life cycle
214.option_c: Develop only in capillaries of internal organs
214.explanation:
• Option C - Merozoites released from liver cells infects RBS’s. Inside RBC, they convert into early trophozoite- late trophozoite and Schizont. Late trophozoite, early and mature schizonts are not found in peripheral blood as this stage occurs inside capillaries of internal organs like spleen, liver and kidney. Thus, only trophozoite (ring forms ) and gametocytes are diagnostic forms present in peripheral blood smear.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Page no : 73

214.question_text: Young RBCs are preferentially infected by :
214.explanation:
• Option B - P.vivax merozoites after entering into RBC convert into early trophozoite(ring form) about 2.5 -3 in diameter which remains in middle of RBC. This early ring form further convert to late trophozoite form having size of 6-7 . In order to accommodate such a large ring, RBC has to enlarge. RBCs infected with P.vivax became pale, enlarged, irregular and became mottled having Schuffner's dots.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -72

214.question_text: Which form of malarial parasite is present in the saliva of infective mosquitoes?
214.explanation:
• Option B - Sporozoite is an infective form developed in the female anopheles mosquitoes after external incubation period. It is formed when introduced inside the human body through mosquito bite. It undergoes asexual development inside liver cells (pre-erythrocytic schizogony).
  • Merozoites released from pre-erythrocytic schizogony infects RBCs and undergoes a developmental cycle of trophozoite-schizont-merozoite.

Reference: Paniker's Textbook of Parasitology, 8th Edition, Page Number-67.

214.question_text: The most conclusive evidence of previous malarial infection in peripheral blood smear is -
214.explanation:
• Option C - In malaria, when parasitized RBC ruptures, they release malarial pigment. The parasite feeds on hemoglobin of the RBC. It does not metabolize hemoglobin completely and therefore leaves behind a hematine pigment called hemozoin. This is when released in circulation due to destruction of RBC at end of erythrocytic schizogony, taken up by reticuloendothelial cells. Such pigment laden cells provide evidence of previous malarial infection.
  • Left shift is an increase in the number of immature cell types among the blood cells particularly neutrophils.
  • The term right shift describes increased numbers of hypersegmented neutrophils, with five or more nuclear lobes. This occurs in pernicious anemia.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -69

214.question_text: The characteristics of merozoite induced malaria are all EXCEPT :
214.explanation:
• Option D - Natural malaria is sporozoite induced, transmitted by female anopheles mosquitoes. Injection of merozoite as occurs due to blood transfusion can lead to direct infection of RBCs. As there is absence of pre erythropoietic schizogony and hypnozoites, relapses do not occur and incubation period is short. However, the parasite can be transmitted transplacentally from mother to baby.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -80

214.question_text: Following statement about a thick smear for diagnosis of plasmodia is INCORRECT -
214.explanation:
• Option C - As the thick smear concentrates 20-30 layers of RBC in a small area, it is more sensitive and requires more blood. Fixation is not required. As the RBCS are destroyed due to the dehemoglobinaztion, the characteristics like RBC enlargement and stippling cannot be seen. So, species identification is difficult.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -82

214.question_text: Toxoplasmosis in man is acquired by all EXCEPT :
214.explanation:
• Option C - There are many ways by which humans acquired Toxoplasma infection. Consumption of oocyst in cats faces through contaminated food or water is a common mode of infection. Ingesting contaminated pork or lamb containing tissue cyst can also lead to infection.
  • As the parasite resides inside reticuloendothelial cells, humans can also acquire infection through blood transfusion & organ transplant. The parasite is also able to cross the placenta, producing congenital infection.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -93

214.question_text: INCORRECT about Babesia -
214.option_d: Severe infection can occur in asplenic persons
214.explanation:
• Option C - There is no exo-erythrocytic schizogony in Babesia. Relapse does not occur in babesia. Sporozoites are the infective forms present in the salivary glands of ticks (definite host). Man, and other mammals are the intermediate host. Humans acquire infection by bite of infected ticks. They are causing malaria-like illness and can lead to severe anemia with hemoglobinuria in asplenic persons.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -86-88

214.question_text: INCORRECT about infection with Isospora belli :
214.option_a: Mode of infection is ingestion of oocyst
214.explanation:
• Option D - In Isosopora belli infection, diarrhea is usually watery and does not contain blood or mucus. Most infections are asymptomatic in immunocompetent persons. However, diarrhea can be protracted, lasting for several years in immunocompromised persons like AIDS patients.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -97

214.question_text: Match the following parasite with their oocyst :
214.explanation:
• Option D - All the four protozoan parasites mentioned above, share certain common characteristics. All are causing diarrhea in AIDS patients and all of them are partial acid fast in modified acid-fast stains. So the only way to identify the species is through the microscopic examination of the oocyst through modified acid-fast stain.
  • Species differentiation is important because the treatment is different. Isosopra belli and Cyclsopora are treated with cotrimoxazole. Specific and effective drugs for microsporidia and Cryptopsoridia are not available. Cryptosporida are treated with paromomycin and micropsoria with metronidazole and albendazole.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -96-100

214.question_text: Stool in Isospora belli infection may contain all EXCEPT
214.explanation:
• Option D - Stool in case of Isospora belli infection contains high fecal content, fatty acid crystals and Charcot-Leyden crystals. Stool does not contain blood or mucus. As eosinophilia is one of the features of this infection unlike other protozoal infections, C-L crystals which are derivatives of eosinophils are seen in stool.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -97

214.question_text: An 8 -year-old child living in a rural area of Africa, contracts an illness that is initially characterized by vomiting and periods of moderate fever. Over the next few days, his condition dramatically worsens, he becomes markedly lethargic, and his fever intensifies to the point of delirium and convulsions. Peripheral blood smear reveals the infective agent (shown in the image). What is the cause of this child's illness?
214.explanation:
• Option B - The double ring trophozoites (stereo headphone) and Accole formation due to attachment of ring to RBC margin along with lack of erythrocytic Schuffner's dots are consistent with P.falciparum infection. Infected RBCs are not enlarged, unlike P.vivax.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology-8th Edition, Pg No: 73

214.question_text: Worms shown below in picture were recovered from stool specimens of several dogs that work in sheep ranches. Examination reveals tapeworms that measure <10 mm (shown in the image). Which medically important disease is linked to this worm?
214.explanation:
• Option A - D.latum and Taenia are very long worms measuring in meters. Dipylidium caninum is a common tapeworm of dogs. However, its size is 10-70 cm and it has a number of segments. E.granulosus is having size of 3-6 mm and has 3-4 segments.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 129-130

214.question_text: Regarding E.granulosus, which of the following is most accurate?
214.option_c: Mode of infection for humans is ingestion of contaminated eggs along with food and water
214.explanation:
• Option C - Hydatid cyst in humans is due to ingestion of contaminated eggs excreted in dog feces, along with food and water. Thus, humans are intermediate hosts, while dogs are definitive hosts. E.granulosus is one of the smallest tapeworms.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 129-130

214.question_text: A 67-year-old man undergoes a cholecystectomy, and during the procedure a liver cyst is discovered (shown in the image). During surgical removal of cyst, an error allows for a significant amount of cyst fluid (contents shown) to spill out into the abdominal cavity. Epinephrine averts an anaphylactic attack, and his immediate recovery proves uneventful. But, what is his long-term prognosis as a result of the surgical mishap ?
214.option_a: Good but only if he undergoes long-term therapy for visceral larva migrans
214.option_b: Guarded because of the development of secondary Echinococcosis
214.option_c: He will die in less than a month as a result of spread of cryptosporidiosis
214.option_d: Poor because of likelihood of disseminated ameobiasis.
214.explanation:
• Option B - This is a case of Hydatid cyst caused by E.granulosus. Hydatid fluid present in cyst is antigenic. When cyst ruptures, it can lead to severe anaphylactic reactions due to prior sensitization of antigen, due to seepage of minute amounts of fluid through the capsule. Because of presence of brood capsule containing protoscolices, secondary Echinococcosis develops leading to dissemination of hydatid cyst and it is a difficult situation to treat.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 135

214.question_text: Match the following :
214.explanation:
• Option C - P. westermani is lung fluke. C.sinensis, Opisthorchis and F.hepatica are liver flukes. F.buski is a giant intestinal fluke and Schistosoma species are blood flukes.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 142

214.question_text: Intestinal bilharziasis (Schistosomal dysentery) is commonly seen in infection with -
214.explanation:
• Option B - S.mansoni resides in venules of inferior mesenteric vein in sigmoido-rectal region. Because of the presence of characteristic eggs having lateral spine, eggs deposited in the intestinal wall leads to erosion, microabscesses, granuloma and dysentry.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 148

214.question_text: The larval stage of Schistosomes infective to human is -
214.explanation:
• Option D - Cercariae are infective forms to humans, which enter through skin penetration. Once inside the blood vessels, they lose their tails and convert into schistosomules. When they reach mesenteric venous plexuses, they convert into adult forms.
  • Living in copula, females produce eggs, which passes along with feces or urine, and reach water. Eggs containing ciliated embryo (miracidium) hatch immediately and release miracidium. Miracidium enters snails and successively pass through stages of first and second generation sporocyst. Sporocyst convert into cercariae which escape from snails in water. Stage of redia is not found in Schistosomes.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 143

214.question_text: Identify the Schistosome egg which is passed in stool. These eggs are acid fast in nature, having size of 130 x 75 μ.
214.explanation:
• Option D - Terminal spine eggs are characteristic of S.haematobium. However, eggs are present in urine and size is 150 x 50 μ.intercalatum produces similar eggs having terminal spine but their eggs are acid fast, slightly smaller in size and are produced in feces.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 150

214.question_text: A Korean visitor came to India is admitted to hospital because of chest pain and night sweats. He has had a productive cough since arriving in India, now he has a few episodes of hemoptysis too. The sputum sample is speckled with brown granules, which upon microscopic examination are identified as parasite ova. These same ova are present in the stool (shown in the image). What is the diagnosis?
214.explanation:
• Option B - P.westermani is a lung fluke which causes peribronchial granuloma and pneumonitis. The patients usually presented with cough, chest pain and hemoptysis.
  • Viscous septum is speckled with golden brown eggs. Presence of operculated, golden-brown, 100 x 50 μ size eggs are diagnostics.
  • Infection occurs due to consumption of raw or undercooked crab or crayfish which is practiced in parts of Southeast Asia like Korea, Taiwan, China & Japan.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 161

214.question_text: A resident of India who was employed as a river guide for a safari and adventure enterprise in a central African nation returns to the country for treatment of hepatic disease and dysentery. Surgical biopsy of the colon reveals granulomas (shown in the first image). Parasite ova are also noted in the stool examination (shown in the second image). What is the most likely parasite agent responsible for this condition ?
214.explanation:
• Option B - This is a case of S.mansoni infection. Eggs having lateral spines are characteristic. Patient has manifestation of Schistosomal dysentery (intestinal bilharziasis), Katayama fever and periportal fibrosis. Egg granulomas are found in the distal part of the colon and rectum.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. 148

214.question_text: A 45-year-old patient with AIDS presents to a clinic with chronic, intractable, debilitating diarrhea. He gave a history of returning from a camping trip recently. He admits to drinking water from a stream without using a filter or boiling it. Smear prepared from stool was positive with modified acid-fast stain. What is the likely diagnosis?
214.explanation:
• Option D - parvum is an opportunistic parasite in AIDS patients which produce chronic intractable diarrhea lasting for more than 1 month.
  • Option A & C - produces acute dysentery
  • Option B - acute watery diarrhea with mucus and/or fat

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -100

214.question_text: Which of the following uses cilia for locomotion?
214.explanation:
Option B -Cilia are normally organs of adhesion in micro-organism. However, in certain protozoa like B.coli, they can act as an organ of locomotion.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -107

214.question_text: Sabin - Feldman dye test is used for diagnosis of :
214.explanation:
Option C - Sabin – Feldman dye test is the first serological test for detection of Toxoplasma antibody. The test is based on the principle that in presence of antibodies, trophozoites of Toxoplasma lose affinity for alkaline dye – methylene blue. Patient serum is mixed with live trophozoites and complement and incubated at 37 degree celsius for one hour. Then methylene blue dye is added. If > 50 % of trophozoites remain unstained, the test is considered as positive. Widely used once, this test is now rarely used due to low sensitivity, false positive reactions and technical complexity. With the availability of molecular techniques and better serological tests, it has become obsolete now, having historical significance only.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -95

214.question_text: In which of the following parasites, the cysts form is not seen.
214.explanation:
Option C - T.vaginalis exist only in one form - Trophozoite. There is no cyst stage. As trophozoite cannot survive in the outside environment, infection has to be transmitted directly from person to person. As habitat of parasite is genital tract, sexual transmission is usual mode of infection. E.histolytica, E.coli & Giardia lamblia have both trophozoite and cyst forms. Cyst forms are also absent in Dientamoeba fragilis and Entamoeba gingivalis.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -35

214.question_text: Which of the following is true about Entamoeba coli?
214.option_a: It has a cyst stage with a single nucleus
214.option_b: The trophozoite form is larger than that of Entamoeba histolytica
214.option_c: It causes severe gastrointestinal disease in humans
214.option_d: The cystic form lacks a prominent glycogen mass
214.explanation:
• Entamoeba coli trophozoites are significantly larger, measuring 20-50 µm in diameter, which distinguishes them from the smaller E. histolytica.
  • The cyst stage of E. coli features multiple nuclei (up to eight), which aids in identification and classification; thus, option A is incorrect.
  • E. coli is a nonpathogenic commensal, meaning it typically resides in the intestines without causing disease, contradicting option C.
  • The cystic form of E. coli indeed contains a prominent glycogen mass, particularly during the early stages, making option D incorrect.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: The cyst stage has multiple nuclei (up to eight), not a single nucleus, indicating a critical identification feature of E. coli.
  • Option C: As a commensal organism, E. coli does not cause gastrointestinal diseases in humans; this is a key distinction from E. histolytica, which is pathogenic.
  • Option D: The presence of a prominent glycogen mass in the cystic form is a characteristic feature of E. coli, not absent as suggested.

Key Takeaway: Entamoeba coli is a larger, nonpathogenic intestinal ameba with unique features in its cyst and trophozoite forms, especially in comparison to Entamoeba histolytica.

Tags: fmge 2020

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter 3: Amebae pp.-26

214.question_text: Following is NOT true about E.histolytica
214.option_a: Ingested RBCs are seen in trophozoites
214.option_b: Cause flask shaped ulcer in large intestine
214.option_c: Ingestion of trophozoites do not cause infection
214.explanation:
Option D – Metastatic lesions are features of E.histolytica infection. Amoeba invades intestine and it penetrates various tissue forming metastatic lesions like liver abscess and abscess in various other organs like kidney, brain, and spleen.

Option A - Trophozoites which have ingested RBCs is a feature by which pathogenic amoeba can be differentiated from commensal amoeba like Entamoeba coli, Entamoeba hartmanni and Endolimax nana which do not have RBCs in their cytoplasm.

Option B - Characteristic feature of amoebic intestinal ulcer is flask shape due to migration of amoeba laterally to healthier tissue for lysis.

Option C - Trophozoites passed in the stool are rapidly destroyed once outside the body, and if ingested would not survive exposure to the gastric environment. Thus, ingestion of trophozoite does not cause infection.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -21

214.question_text: A young adult after a visit to an endemic area, developed dull aching epigstric pain, belching, flatulence and diarrhea after 10-14 days. Macroscopic examination of stool shows pale colored, offensive, fatty, and float in water, containing mucus but not blood. Microscopic examination revealed trophozoite of 14 μ size with slow oscillatory motion. Most likely organism will be -
214.explanation:
Option D - Giardia lamblia causes steatorrhea. Stool contains excess mucus and fat due to malabsorption. It adheres to intestinal mucosa by its large sucking disc and causes abnormalities in villous architecture. Loss of brush border epithelium leads to deficiency of enzymes causing above mentioned symptoms. As it doesn't invade, blood is absent in stool.

Option A & B - they cause dysentery with the presence of blood in stool. E.histolytica trophozoites are 20-30 in size having gliding motility. B.coli trophozoites are very large 60-70 in size having rapid revolving motility.

Option C - though clinical picture resemble that of G.lamblia, it may also contain blood in stool. However, there will be the presence of characteristic barrel shaped eggs and not trophozoites in stool.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -34

214.question_text: Size of cyst shown in picture is :
214.explanation:
Option A – this is cyst of Giardia lamblia having size of 12 x 7 µ

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -33

214.question_text: Many parasitic life cycles are complex, requiring more than one host to complete development. Which of the following parasites has a direct life cycle, requiring only a single host (humans) to complete its development?
214.explanation:
Explanation:

Entamoeba histolytica is protozoan has a direct life cycle (monoxenous), meaning it completes its entire development within a single host. Humans become infected by ingesting the mature cysts (e.g., in contaminated food or water), and the organism multiplies and encysts within the human gut, passing infective cysts in the feces.

The other parasites listed all have indirect life cycles (heteroxenous), requiring both a definitive host (where sexual reproduction occurs) and an intermediate host or vector (where asexual development occurs).

Comparison of Parasitic Life Cycles:

Explanation of Other Options:

Leishmania donovani (Option A): This parasite has an indirect life cycle, requiring transmission by the bite of an infected sandfly.

Trypanosoma brucei (Option B): This parasite causes African sleeping sickness and has an indirect life cycle, requiring transmission by the bite of an infected tsetse fly.

Plasmodium vivax (Option D): This is one of the causative agents of malaria and has a complex, indirect life cycle requiring transmission by an Anopheles mosquito.

214.question_text: Based on the CDC figure of the Toxoplasma gondii life cycle, which stage is depicted in the image below as being shed by the definitive host and is necessary for the infection of intermediate hosts?
214.explanation:
• Sporulated oocysts: Correct; these are shed in the feces of definitive hosts (cats) and are the infective stage for intermediate hosts.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: Tachyzoites: Incorrect; these are the rapidly dividing form found in intermediate hosts and are not shed in feces. Tachyzoites are not shed; they multiply within the host, making them non-infective when excreted.
  • Option B: Bradyzoites: Incorrect; these are dormant forms found within tissue cysts in intermediate hosts and are not excreted.Bradyzoites exist within tissue cysts and are not shed into the environment by definitive hosts.
  • Option D: Tissue cysts are present in intermediate hosts and are not involved in fecal shedding by cats.

Key Takeaway: Sporulated oocysts are shed by cats and are essential for infecting intermediate hosts in the life cycle of Toxoplasma gondii.

Tags: fmge 2023

Reference: CDC guidelines on Toxoplasma gondii life cycle.

214.question_text: Which of the following statement regarding Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is INCORRECT -
214.option_a: Occurs in 2-10 % of patients of kala-azar
214.option_b: Skin lesion caused by Leishmania tropica
214.option_c: Complication of systemic infection due to L.donovani
214.option_d: Develops 1-2 years after recovery from systemic infection
214.explanation:
Option B - PKDL is a condition which develops 1-2 years after recovery from kala-azar. It is seen mainly in Indian and African form. About 2-10 % cases of patients of Visceral leishmaniasis in an endemic area develop lesions on skin which start as macules progress to nodules, which do not ulcerate. This is a feature by which it differs from L.tropica which produces oriental sore in which nodules formed at site of bite, ulcerate.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -57

214.question_text: Which of the following pair for rapid antigen detection test for parasites is inappropriate?
214.explanation:
Option C - RAT (Rapid antigen detection test) is a common procedure for diagnosis of parasitic infection employing species-specific antigen in which monoclonal antibodies against the specific antigen are bound to the membrane. Lateral flow of the sample will result in binding of antigen to specific monoclonal antibodies resulting in color band formation.pLDH is an antigen present in all species of Plasmodia. It is not a species-specific antigen. Species specific antigen in P.falciparum is pHRP-2.

Option A,B & D - are examples of diagnosis of parasitic infection using their species-specific antigen.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -7

214.question_text: In order to diagnose one of parasitic infections, a laboratory reared and starved vector is fed to a patient suspected of having a disease. This type of diagnostic technique is used for diagnosis of
214.explanation:
Option A -Xenodiagnosis is a diagnostic method used to document the presence of pathogen by exposing possibly infected tissue to a vector and then examining the vector for the presence of the pathogen, it may have ingested.Not only parasites, it is also useful to diagnose many bacterial infections like Rickettsial infections and Lyme disease caused by Borrelia. Chagas disease is a parasitic infection caused by T.cruzi transmitted by reduviid bug. Traditionally used to diagnose Chagas disease, it was also used previously for diagnosis of Babesia and filariasis. However, with development of newer diagnostic techniques like molecular tests, it is now rarely used for other infections.

Option - B - Amoebiasis trophozoite and cyst are excreted in feces and not present in the blood of infected patients.

Option - C & D - though transmitted by vectors and presence of parasites in blood, there are many other comparatively easier techniques available for diagnosis of malaria and leishmania than cumbersome Xenodiagnosis.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -8

214.question_text: Which of the following is NOT the  infective form ?
214.explanation:
Option C - Amastigote is intracellular multiplying and diagnostic forms of L.donovani. Promastigote is an infective form of L. donovani which gets converted to amastigote inside the body.

Option A, B & D - Sporozoite is an infective form of Plasmodium species in mosquitos. Oocyst is an infective form of Toxoplasma gondii excreted in cat's feces. Metacyclic trypomastigotes are infective forms of T. brucei.

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -54

214.question_text: Modified acid-fast stain is used to demonstrate all of the following parasites EXCEPT :
214.explanation:
Option D - B.hominis is best demonstrated in stool smear by giemsa or iron hematoxylin or trichrome stain. Option A, B & C are examples of coccidian parasites which are acid fast in nature stained by Modified Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun's stain. All the three mentioned parasites are causing severe protracted diarrhea in immunocompromised persons like AIDS patients.

Reference : Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -236

214.question_text: The vector responsible for transmitting Leishmania donovani is -
214.explanation:
Option C - Sand fly transmits L.donovani. Many parasitic infections require vectors for transmission. Sometimes, these vectors can also act as a host, when parasites multiply in them or they undergo development as part of their life cycle.

Reduviid bug - T.cruzi - Intermediate host

Tsetse fly - T.brucei - intermediate host

Anopheles mosquito - Plasmodium spp - Definitive host

Culex mosquito - Wuchereria bancrofti - intermediate host

Reference: Paniker's textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -54

214.question_text: Malignant form of muco-cutaneous leishmaniasis associated with invasion of oro-nasal  mucosa
214.explanation:
Option C - Leishmania infections is classified as visceral leishmaniasis, cutaneous leishmaniasis and muco-cutaneous leishmaniasis. 214.question_text: A person who has taken bath dips in the holy water of a river with his nose and mouth closed by fingers, now afraid of acquiring one of parasitic infections. He should screen himself for which parasitic infection if symptoms develop.

214.question_text: A 62-year-old woman in Finland suffers from macrocytic anemia. Her history is significant for frequent consumption of pickled fish. A stool sample reveals parasitic ova like the one shown in the figure. What is the likely diagnosis ?

Patient Presentation:

  • A 62-year-old woman in Finland.
  • Suffers from macrocytic anemia.

Relevant History:

Stool Sample Findings:

  • Stool sample reveals parasitic ova.

Likely Diagnosis:

  • C) Diphyllobothrium latum is the likely diagnosis.

Rationale for the Diagnosis:

  • Diphyllobothrium latum is a fish tapeworm known to cause diphyllobothriasis.
  • Diphyllobothriasis can lead to macrocytic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
  • The patient's history of consuming raw or undercooked fish, especially pickled fish, is significant, as this is a common route of infection for Diphyllobothrium latum.
  • Diphyllobothrium latum is prevalent in regions like Finland, where the practice of eating raw pickled fish is prevalent.

In summary, the likely diagnosis for this patient's condition is Diphyllobothrium latum (Choice C). The patient's history and stool sample findings are consistent with this diagnosis.

214.question_text: What is the primary method of prevention for hookworm infections?
214.option_b: Wearing shoes to prevent skin contact with contaminated soil
214.explanation:
• Hookworm larvae penetrate the skin upon contact with contaminated soil, making it essential to protect the feet to prevent infection.
  • Wearing shoes in areas known to have hookworm infections, especially in warm, tropical, or subtropical regions, significantly reduces the risk of skin contact with the larvae.
  • Proper hygiene, such as washing feet and maintaining clean living environments, can further help reduce the risk of infection.

Why Not Other Options:

  • C) Insect repellent is ineffective against hookworm larvae, which do not spread through insect bites.
  • D) Drinking purified water does not play a role in preventing hookworm infection since the transmission route is primarily through soil contact rather than water Incorrect.

Key Takeaway: Preventing hookworm infections primarily involves wearing shoes to avoid skin contact with contaminated soil, effectively reducing the risk of larvae penetration.

214.question_text: What is the role of diethylcarbamazine (DEC) in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis?
214.option_c: It reduces the transmission of the parasite by killing both adult worms and microfilariae
214.option_d: It is used primarily for vector control
214.explanation:
• DEC is an effective drug used in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis, acting on multiple life stages of the parasite.
  • It not only kills microfilariae, which are the larval forms present in the bloodstream, but also targets adult worms residing in the lymphatic system.
  • By eliminating both stages, DEC helps to reduce the overall parasite burden in infected individuals, which is crucial for decreasing the transmission risk to others.
  • DEC treatment can lead to significant improvements in clinical symptoms and reduce the likelihood of chronic manifestations associated with the disease, such as lymphedema and hydrocele.
  • The drug's use also aids in the prevention of disease transmission, as fewer microfilariae in the bloodstream mean reduced chances of transmission to mosquito vectors during bites.
  • It is typically administered as part of a mass drug administration strategy in endemic areas to achieve community-wide benefits and tackle the public health issue of lymphatic filariasis.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A) Incorrect. DEC targets both life stages, not just adult worms.
  • B) Incorrect. DEC has an effect on adult worms as well, so it does not target microfilariae exclusively.
  • D) Incorrect. DEC is a treatment option, not a method for controlling the mosquito vector.

Key Takeaway: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) plays a crucial role in reducing the transmission of lymphatic filariasis by effectively targeting and killing both adult worms and microfilariae, thereby helping to manage and control the disease.

Tags: inicet 2023

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter-20: Filarial worms , pp - 208

214.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of hookworm infections?
214.option_a: Hookworms typically cause severe abdominal pain and diarrhea immediately after infection
214.option_b: Hookworms penetrate the skin and migrate through the bloodstream to the lungs before reaching the intestines
214.option_c: The eggs of hookworms are usually found in contaminated water sources
214.option_d: The primary host for hookworms is livestock, such as cows and pigs
214.explanation:
• Hookworms are parasitic nematodes that enter the body through the skin, often from contaminated soil, such as walking barefoot on infected ground.
  • After penetrating the skin, larvae travel through the bloodstream to the lungs, where they are coughed up and swallowed, ultimately reaching the intestines.
  • In the intestines, they mature and attach to the intestinal wall, causing iron deficiency anemia, fatigue, and gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A) Incorrect. Initial hookworm infections may be asymptomatic or cause mild symptoms, not severe abdominal pain immediately.
  • C) Incorrect. Hookworm eggs are found in contaminated soil, not water sources.
  • D) Incorrect. The primary host for hookworms is humans, not livestock.

Key Takeaway:

  • Hookworms enter through the skin, travel via the bloodstream to the lungs, and ultimately migrate to the intestines, where they can cause anemia and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter-197 Hookworm , pp - 187

215.question_text: A patient presents with painful subcutaneous nodules on the face and edema of eyelid as shown in the photo. Which of the following acts as a vector in transmission of this disease?
215.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is of Chagas disease. The photo shows Romana's sign (U/L edema of eyelid and conjunctiva) and the nodules on face are suggestive of chagoma.

Trypanosoma cruzi is the causative agent of South American trypanosomiasis or Chaga's disease.

T. cruzi is transmitted to man by rubbing its vector reduviid bug's feces on abraded skin.

Human cycle:

  • The trypomastigotes from the bite wound are carried to various tissues where they transform into amastigote forms.
  • Amastigotes multiply actively. They are the intracellular form found in tissues such as reticuloendothelial cells (spleen, liver, lymph node, bone marrow), muscles (cardiac, skeletal and GIT) and nervous tissue.
  • Trypomastigotes: Amastigotes transform back to trypomastigote forms, which are motile C-shaped non-multiplying, extracellular forms found in peripheral blood (as long slender or invasive forms and short stubby forms). Invasive forms migrate to many organs and short stubby forms are ingested by reduviid bugs during a blood meal.

Vector cycle: In the gut of reduviid bugs, the trypomastigotes transform into epimastigotes, which further develop into metacyclic trypomastigotes in the hindgut, and are excreted in the bug's feces.

  • Trypanosoma brucei complex. They are transmitted by the vector tsetse fly. They cause African sleeping sickness.
  • Sandfly is a vector of leishmaniasis.
  • Simulium fly is a vector for onchocerciasis.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 366

215.question_text: Xenodiagnosis is done for
215.explanation:
Xenodiagnosis is a diagnostic method where a lab-raised, disease-free vector (insect) is allowed to feed on a suspected infected individual, and later, the vector is examined for the presence of the pathogen.

  • This method is commonly used for detecting Trypanosoma cruzi, the causative agent of Chagas disease.
  • The vector used is usually the reduviid bug (kissing bug).
  • After feeding on the patient, the bug's gut is examined for the presence of T. cruzi.

Incorrect Options Explanation:

Choice B (Trypanosoma brucei):

  • Causes African Sleeping Sickness, transmitted by the tsetse fly.
  • Diagnosis is usually done by blood smear, CSF examination, or serology, not xenodiagnosis.

Choice C (Plasmodia - Malaria parasites):

  • Diagnosis of malaria is done via peripheral blood smear, rapid antigen tests, or PCR.
  • Xenodiagnosis is not used for malaria.

Choice D (None of the above):

  • Incorrect, as T. cruzi is diagnosed by xenodiagnosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Xenodiagnosis is mainly used for Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease).
  • Involves allowing a lab-raised vector (reduviid bug) to feed on the patient, then examining the bug for the parasite.
  • Not used for T. brucei or Plasmodium species.

215.question_text: What is the primary method of locomotion for amebae?
215.explanation:
• Pseudopodia are temporary extensions of the cytoplasm used for both movement and feeding in amebae.
  • Amebae move by extending pseudopodia, a process called amoeboid movement, allowing cytoplasm to flow into the pseudopodium, pulling the cell forward.
  • Pseudopodia are also crucial for phagocytosis, where amebae engulf food particles like bacteria and other microorganisms.
  • Amebae have a flexible cell membrane, enabling them to form pseudopodia in multiple directions, allowing efficient adaptation to their environment.
  • Pseudopodia play a key role in survival by facilitating movement, feeding, and escape from harmful conditions.

Why not others:

  • a) Flagella:
    • Flagella are long, whip-like structures used for locomotion by flagellates (e.g., Giardia). Amebae lack flagella, so they do not use this method for movement.
  • b) Cilia:
    • Cilia are short, hair-like structures used for movement in ciliates (e.g., Paramecium). Amebae do not possess cilia and do not use them for locomotion.
  • d) Axopodia:
    • Axopodia are rigid, thin pseudopodia found in radiolarians, primarily used for prey capture. Amebae do not have axopodia.

Key Takeaway: Amebae use pseudopodia for locomotion and feeding, enabling amoeboid movement and phagocytosis. This differentiates them from other protozoa like flagellates and ciliates.

Tags: neet 2019

Reference: Paniker, CK Jayaram. Paniker's textbook of medical parasitology. JP Medical Ltd, 2017.Chapter 3: Amebae pp.-15

215.question_text: A 27-year-old woman presented with complaints of pain in the right hypochondrium. Ultrasonography revealed a single space occupying a cystic lesion in the right lobe of the liver. The cyst was removed surgically and subjected to histopathological examination, which revealed three layered cyst walls with attached brood capsules. Identify the disease and the causative agent.
215.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Hydatid cyst disease caused by E.granulosus.

Clinical Features:

  • Infection usually occurs in childhood but gets manifested in adult life.
  • Site: Most common site of the cyst is liver (60-70%, right lobe) or lung (20%), followed by kidney, muscle, spleen, soft tissue, brain, bone and others.
  • Asymptomatic: The cysts grow up to 5-10 cm in size within the first year and can survive for years or even decades, without any symptoms.
  • Symptoms: Few patients develop symptoms which may be due to: Pressure effect of the enlarging cyst: Leads to palpable abdominal mass, hepatomegaly, abdominal tenderness, portal hypertension and ascites.
  • Obstruction: Daughter cysts may erode into the biliary tree or a bronchus and enter into the lumen to cause cholestasis, cholangitis, and dyspnea Secondary bacterial infection, causing pyogenic abscess in liver.
  • Anaphylactic reactions: Cyst leakage or rupture may be associated with a severe allergic reaction to hydatid fluid antigens, leading to hypotension, syncope and fever.
  • In amoebic liver abscess: Anchovy sauce pus: Liver abscess pus is thick chocolate brown in color. The fluid is acidic and pH 5.2-6.7 and is composed of necrotic hepatocytes without any pus cells and occasionally amoebic trophozoites (mainly found in the last few drops of pus) as amoebae multiply in the wall of abscess.
  • In Fascioliasis: Liver: Migration of metacercaria larva into liver causes fever, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly and eosinophilia. Liver parenchyma is inflamed with formation of multiple subcapsular abscesses (called liver rot).
  • In pyogenic liver abscess: Fever and right upper quadrant tenderness are the most consistent clinical manifestations.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 495

215.question_text: Which of the following bacteria confirms recent fecal contamination of water:
215.explanation:
Hospital water and water-containing devices may serve as a reservoir of healthcare associated waterborne pathogens. Microbial contamination of water in healthcare settings is broadly of two types.

  • Category 1 (Enteric Pathogens): This results from fecal contamination of drinking water supplies. This group of waterborne pathogens are more common in community settings than in hospitals. These agents are transmitted by ingestion of contaminated water. Most of them cause diarrheal outbreaks, while few agents cause extraintestinal illness. Examples include:
    • Bacteria: Gram-negative bacilli such as diarrheagenic E.coli such as O157:H7, Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae, Campylobacter.
    • Viruses: Rotavirus, Norovirus, hepatitis A and E viruses, polioviruses Parasites: Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora, and Schistosoma spp.
    • Category 2 (Common Hospital Pathogens): These include multidrug resistant Gram-negative bacilli (MDR-GNB), nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), legionella, etc. This group of waterborne pathogens are more important in hospital-setting, than community. They are commonly present in hospital environments and can contaminate various hospital water reservoirs such as potable water, sinks, dialysis water, ice and ice machines, etc. They are transmitted by various routes such as ingestion, contact, aspiration, etc.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no: 279

215.question_text: A 28 year old male patient presents with complaints of abdominal pain and 10 episodes of passing foul smelling dark stool mixed with blood and mucus. There is no history of fever and tenesmus. There is localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa on examination. What is the infective form of the causative organism?
215.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of amoebic dysentery caused by Entamoeba histolytica.

Entamoeba histolytica:

  • Majority of infections (90%) result in asymptomatic cyst passers.
  • The remaining (10%), develop intestinal amoebiasis; characterized by: Amoebic dysentery: Symptoms include bloody diarrhea (up to 10 times per day) with mucus and pus cells, colicky abdominal pain, fever, prostration, and weight loss. Amoebic dysentery should be differentiated from bacillary dysentery. Amoebic appendicitis: Presented with acute right lower abdominal pain Ameboma: It presents as palpable abdominal mass. Fulminant colitis: Presents as intense colicky pain, rectal tenesmus, more than 20 motions/day, fever, nausea, anorexia and hypotension.

Differential diagnosis:

  • Giardia is often asymptomatic, but in some cases can lead to fat malabsorption, dull epigastric pain, and flatulence.
  • Campylobacter presents with fever, pain, and watery diarrhea. The stool contains leukocytes and blood.
  • Shigella causes bacillary dysentery which is characterized by fever and generalized abdominal tenderness.

Reference: Essentials of Medical Microbiology, by Apurba Sastry and Sandhya Bhat, 3rd edition, page no. 430

215.question_text: A 32-year-old emigrant from West Bengal, complains of fever and weight loss for the past 3 weeks. Laboratory tests revealed anemia and leukopenia . Multiple blood cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative. p24 antigen test for HIV was negative. A bone marrow biopsy was performed and a Giemsa stained smear revealed the following intracellular parasite in the picture shown. What is the likely diagnosis ?
215.explanation:
Option A - These are intracellular amastigotes of L.donovani. They are also called as L-D bodies and are important histological findings for diagnosis of Kala-azar. Residing in an endemic area (West Bengal), fever and weight loss are clues for diagnosis, which however can also occur in HIV. However, a highly sensitive p24 antigen test which is usually performed early in infection (window period) before development of antibodies, is negative here excluding diagnosis. Symptomatology along with anemia, leukopenia and a positive bone marrow smear are clues to diagnosis. P.falciparum usually does not cause weight loss, T.brucei causes sleeping sickness and T.cruzi causes acute and chronic chagas disease.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -59

215.question_text: Characteristic which is NOT observed in infection by T.brucei infection is -
215.explanation:
Option B - Romana’s sign, a chagoma found over the eyelid, is a marker of acute Chagas disease, an infection caused by T.cruzi. Also known as the periorbital swelling syndrome, it refers to periorbital swelling, palpebral edema and conjunctivitis seen 1-2 weeks following infection with Trypanosoma cruzi.

Reference : Paniker’s textbook of Parasitology - 8th Edition, Pg. No. -44-46

215.question_text: Which form of Giardia lamblia is typically found in the environment and is infectious?
215.explanation:
• The cyst form of Giardia lamblia is the environmentally resistant stage that remains dormant outside the host and is capable of surviving in various conditions.
  • Trophozoites are the active, motile form found in the intestines; they are not infectious as they cannot survive outside the host.

The above images a and b are cyst and trophozoites of giardia respectively.

Giardia shows falling leaf like motility.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: Trophozoites are the active form but cannot cause infection when outside the host.
  • Option C: Oocysts are specific to different parasites and do not apply to Giardia lamblia.
  • Option D: Sporocysts are linked to other protozoa and are irrelevant in the context of Giardia lamblia.

Key Takeaway: The cyst form of Giardia lamblia is the infectious stage that is typically found in the environment, highlighting the importance of proper sanitation and hygiene to prevent infection.

Tags: fmge 2023 | fmge 2021

Reference: CDC - Giardia, CDC Giardia

215.question_text: Human infection occurs through the ingestion of quadrinucleate cysts found in contaminated food or water. Which of the following organisms is the most probable cause of this infection?
215.explanation:
Explanation:

Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite responsible for amoebiasis (also called amoebic dysentery). Infection occurs through ingestion of quadrinucleate cysts present in contaminated food or water. Once ingested, these cysts transform into trophozoites in the intestines, causing symptoms that range from mild diarrhea to severe dysentery and, in some cases, liver abscesses.

E. histolytica leads to amoebic dysentery and other invasive diseases, such as amoebic liver abscesses.

Morphology includes three stages:

  • Trophozoite
  • Precyst
  • Cyst

Life Cycle:

  • Host: Humans (single host)
  • Infective form: Mature quadrinucleate cyst
  • Transmission: Primarily fecal-oral route, but also sexual (anogenital or orogenital contact) and very rarely mechanical vector transmission from feces

Development in the Human Intestine:

  • Small intestine: Excystation occurs
  • Large intestine: Multiplication and colonization take place

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Asymptomatic cyst carriers
  • Amoebic dysentery
  • Invasive amoebiasis

Encystation happens as lesions heal and the patient recovers; trophozoites convert back into cysts in the large intestine, which are then excreted in the feces and remain infective.

Explanation for other options:

Giardia lamblia (Option A): Giardia lamblia's life cycle begins with the ingestion of cysts through contaminated food or water. These cysts then transform into trophozoites in the small intestine, where they multiply and later form new cysts. These cysts are passed in the feces, enabling transmission to new hosts. This process causes the infection known as giardiasis.

Cryptosporidium parvum (Option C): This protozoan causes cryptosporidiosis and is usually transmitted through contaminated water, but it does not produce quadrinucleate cysts.

Cyclospora cayetanensis (Option D): This parasite causes cyclosporiasis, also spread via contaminated food or water; however, its cysts are not quadrinucleate.

215.question_text: Identify the parasite shown in the image
215.explanation:
Explanation:

The image represents the trophozoite stage of Giardia lamblia.

Life Cycle & Features:

  • It exists in two stages:
    • Trophozoite (vegetative form)
    • Cyst (cystic form)
  • Infective form: Mature cyst

Mode of transmission: Feco-oral route
Habitat: Duodenal and upper ileal mucosa

  • Infection can occur after ingesting as few as 10 cysts. Within about 30 minutes of ingestion, a cyst releases two trophozoites, which multiply by binary fission and colonize the duodenum. Under unfavorable conditions, encystment takes place, and the cysts are excreted in stool, remaining viable in soil and water for several weeks.

Life cycle: Human host → ingestion of contaminated food/water → cysts ingested → excystation → trophozoite formation.

Diagnosis:

  • Sample: Stool
  • Microscopy: Demonstrates cysts and trophozoites
    • Trophozoite: pear- or tennis racket–shaped, with 2 nuclei and 4 pairs of flagella
    • Cyst: oval, with 1–4 nuclei and no flagella
  • String test: Capsule containing a string is swallowed; after reaching the duodenum, the capsule dissolves. When the string is withdrawn, microscopic examination detects organisms.
  • Duodenal biopsy: Shows Giardia in the lumen, appearing sickle-shaped, with falling-leaf motility.

Treatment:

  • Metronidazole
  • Tinidazole (single 2 g dose)

Explanation of other options:

Trichomonas vaginalis (Option B): Trophozoite is pyriform or oval with 4 anterior flagella; a 5th flagellum forms an undulating membrane. A prominent axostyle runs along the body.

Trypanosoma (Option C): A hemoflagellate exhibiting four morphological stages (amastigote, promastigote, epimastigote, trypomastigote), all containing a single nucleus and kinetoplast.

Cyclospora (Option D): A coccidian protozoan identified by its oocysts. Sporulated oocysts are round, acid-fast, and contain two sporocysts, each with two sporozoites.

Key Takeaways:

  • Giardia trophozoite → "tennis racket shape" + "falling leaf motility."
  • Causes malabsorption and chronic diarrhea.

215.question_text: Which of the following statements accurately describes Trichomonas vaginalis?
215.option_b: Twitching motility is seen on a wet saline mount
215.option_c: Cysts are seen on a wet saline mount of vaginal secretions
215.option_d: The infective form is a cyst
215.explanation:
Explanation:

The statement accurately describes that Trichomonas vaginalis has twitching motility when seen on a wet saline mount.

Trichomoniasis

  • Trichomonas vaginitis is the most common cause of vaginitis in women of reproductive age.
  • The characteristic appearance seen is 'Strawberry cervix,' an erythematous and edematous cervical mucosa with characteristic punctate red papules. It is caused by microscopic punctate haemorrhages of the cervix.
  • Symptoms include :
    • Sudden, profuse, yellowish-green, frothy, foul-smelling discharge
    • Irritation and itching in and around the vaginal opening
    • Painful urination
    • Pain during intercourse
    • Recurrent infections
    • Inflamed vulva
    • Inflamed vaginal walls with small, punctate haemorrhages ("strawberry cervix")
  • The standard treatment is Metronidazole 2g PO single dose.

Explanation for other options:

Trophozoite has 2 nuclei (Option A): Trichomonas vaginalis exists only as a trophozoite, which has a single nucleus and four anterior flagella, not two nuclei.

Cysts are seen on wet saline mount of vaginal secretions (Option C): Trichomonas vaginalis does not form cysts; it exists only as a trophozoite.

Infective form is cyst (Option D): The infective form of T. vaginalis is the trophozoite, not a cyst. It is transmitted through sexual contact, and the absence of a cyst form contributes to its reliance on direct human-to-human transmission.

Key Takeaways:

215.question_text:
Which of the following are advantages of a saline mount compared to an iodine mount in stool microscopy?
1.Demonstration of trophozoite motility
2.Visualisation of cyst internal structures
3.Differentiation between bile-stained and non-bile-stained ova
215.explanation:
Explanation:

Saline Mount (Normal Saline Wet Mount)

  • Preserves motility of trophozoites (Statement 1) → Useful for observing Giardia lamblia ("falling leaf" motility) and Entamoeba histolytica (directional motility).
  • Assesses bile staining (Statement 3) → Saline mount allows clear visualisation of colour differences in ova:
    • Bile-stained eggs (e.g., fertilised Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura) appear golden brown.
    • Non-bile-stained ova remain colourless.
  • Limitation: Does not enhance the internal details of cysts.

Iodine Mount

  • Best for internal cyst structures (Statement 2)
    • Iodine stains glycogen vacuoles and nuclei, improving visualisation of protozoan cysts (Entamoeba, Giardia).
  • Drawbacks:
    • Kills trophozoites → motility cannot be assessed.
    • Cannot differentiate between bile-stained and non-bile-stained eggs.

Other Methods in Stool Microscopy

  • Direct Wet Mounts:
  • Saline → detects trophozoites, helminth ova, larvae, and differentiates bile staining.
  • Iodine → highlights cyst nuclei and internal structures.
  • Permanent Stains (e.g., Trichrome, Iron-hematoxylin, Modified Acid-Fast):
    • Provide detailed morphology of cysts and trophozoites.
  • Concentration Techniques:
    • Sedimentation (e.g., formalin-ether): increases the yield of eggs/cysts.
    • Flotation (e.g., saturated salt solution): recovers light ova but misses heavy or unfertilized eggs.

Key takeaway:

  • Saline mount → motility + bile staining.
  • Iodine mount → cyst nuclei and glycogen vacuoles.

215.question_text: The cervix shown in the photo is seen in?
215.explanation:
The photo shows a strawberry cervix which is seen in infection with trichomonas vaginalis.

215.question_text: What is the infective stage of Entamoeba histolytica to man?
215.explanation:
E.histolytica exists in three forms

a)Trophozoite

b)Precyst

c)Cyst

Mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form. It is passed in the feces of convalescents and carriers. The cysts remain viable under moist conditions for about 10 days.
